Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 18:38:46 GMT

If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

And can anything be done about it?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, 15% of England's adult population - those aged 16 and over - in 1993 was obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.

Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.

This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.

Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.

Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight".

"With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."

Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.

Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.

Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.

Reports estimate obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately £126bn per year, including £12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.

Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.

Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.

Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.

The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.

During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.

Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.

In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.

Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.

Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.

People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.

Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.

A new daily pill is already available in the US and could soon launch in the UK.

The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.

It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.

Earlier this year, England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.

He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.

Now the question is what do we want to learn?

'Like a bus seat back in the day' - new Wales kit leaves fans divided

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 18:35:31 GMT

Wales football fans have been left divided over the country's new home kit, with some comparing the pattern on the red shirt to that seen on bus seats.

The new shirt was revealed on Thursday by the Football Association of Wales (FAW), which said it was "inspired by the rich tradition of Welsh double cloth weaving".

It is the first Wales shirt produced by sportswear brand Sudu, after the FAW parted ways with Adidas after 13 years.

FAW said the reaction to football kits was "subjective", adding it remained "incredibly proud of the creative process behind the new Cymru home kit".

The association said the kit rejected "reused designs", and that Sudu had worked with the association and fans "to understand the DNA of the nation".

A "pro" version of the adult shirt costs £90, with a matching pair of shorts and socks costing a total of £136.

A replica adult shirt costs £70, while a full kit for a child including shorts and socks costs £89.

Home nations rivals England have their most expensive adult home shirt on sale for £134.99, while Scotland's is £75.

But people who were not pleased with the kit slammed it online, with one describing it as the "worst Welsh shirt in history".

Speaking to a BBC Wales reporter at the Eisteddfod on Thursday, one fan said the new kit reminded her of "a bus seat back in the day".

But not everyone thought the kit was bad, with some arguing the reaction would be different had Adidas released the same design.

Before the shirt was revealed, BBC Wales Sport spoke to Noel Mooney, CEO of the FAW, on 9 June about the kit.

He said: "We've had a brilliant, more than decade-long relationship with Adidas.

"At the same time we have to keep thinking about what is the best for the FAW in terms of design, in terms of the amount of kit that we get."

He added: "We've got to fund the grassroots game here and we'll always look at opportunities for getting more resources for the grassroots game as well.

"We need to grow Welsh football and we will always look for the option that's best for Welsh football."

The FAW said the shirt was designed "with incredible passion and care" and the "bespoke pattern draws on elements of traditional Welsh tapestry".

A spokesperson said: "We understand that change is difficult but we are incredibly excited to start this new journey. It has been heartening to see the views of supporters who connect with the meaning behind the shirt and the sense of Welsh pride that it evokes.

"The shirt has also been on display at the National Eisteddfod this morning, with feedback from supporters in person being overwhelmingly positive."

Flintoff leaves England Lions head coach role

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 18:06:59 GMT

Andrew Flintoff played 227 matches for England between 1998 and 2009

Former England all-rounder Andrew Flintoff has stepped down as head coach of England Lions.

The 48-year-old, who has been in charge of the Lions since September 2024, thanked England managing director Rob Key in his leaving statement for "trusting me with one of the most important roles in English cricket."

Flintoff was named head coach of Australian Big Bash franchise Sydney Thunder in June, taking up his first overseas T20 coaching role.

He was initially set to continue in his Lions role, leaving a planned tour of South Africa early to join-up with Thunder, but now departs the national set-up.

"Unfortunately I've made the decision to step away from my role with the Lions," said Flintoff.

"Not only have I enjoyed my time having the opportunity to work with the best young cricketers in the country, but have taken great pride in seeing them develop.

"I'd like to thank the coaches and staff for all their passion, tireless work and support they give everyday.

"I can't wait to get started with the Thunder later in the year and see where coaching takes me."

Flintoff also spent two seasons as Northern Superchargers men's coach in The Hundred, leading the Leeds-based side to fourth and third-placed finishes.

He was not retained for 2026 after the franchise was taken over by the owners of the Sunrisers group.

Prior to his appointment with the Lions, Flintoff helped coach England's white-ball sides on an informal basis, having left his position as a presenter on television driving programme Top Gear.

His last assignment in the Lions role was South Africa A's tour of England in May and June, where his side lost both four-day matches and two of three 50-over games.

"Fred has helped to transform the Lions environment into a programme that has had a major impact on young players," said England and Wales Cricket Board men's performance director Ed Barney.

"Coaches have also flourished alongside him, whether early in their coaching journey or with decades of experience, and he has consistently maximised the expertise around the group.

"We wish him the best in the next stage of his coaching career and look forward to a time he returns to the English game."

Mike Yardy will step in as head coach for the four-day Professional County Club Select XI match that serves as Pakistan's warm-up before their three-Test series against England later this month.

The fixture begins at Beckenham on Wednesday, 12 August, while the Lions will also be the opposition for Sri Lanka's two T20 warm-ups at the start of their limited-overs tour of England in September.

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:45:06 GMT

Gianni Infantino, pictured with Colombian FA president Ramon Jesurun, is attending the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella

Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol, who praised both his record and the "enormously successful" 2026 World Cup, saying "we stand with Gianni".

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

It may not be that easy.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

This video can not be played

Infantino questioned in Colombia

Gianni Infantino apologised for the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, but now it seems to be business as usual for the Fifa president

A cavalcade of blacked out Mercedes, flanked by police cars, rolled into the Fifa headquarters in Rabat, Morocco, earlier this week.

Infantino had summoned a select few members of the Fifa management board to discuss his plan to sell off 21% of the commercial and ticketing business to a private equity firm.

This is how the Swiss-Italian travels - in between flights on the Qatar Airways Executive jet which has been made available to him. The plane enabled him to take up to three flights a day, watching two games, throughout the 2026 World Cup.

That type of arrival does look presidential - only more like a president of a country than a sports body.

It enables him to travel the globe, visiting Fifa's official offices like Rabat, where he was based over the past week as the Fifa Forward Enterprise controversy developed.

In his role Infantino is expected to visit the 211 member nations, to see the grassroots projects Fifa has funded.

Part of his remit is to unify football, which cannot be achieved from within the Fifa headquarters in Zurich.

It requires international travel to attend confederation meetings, and the global tournaments Fifa organises. Infantino needs to build relationships with officials and politicians.

In April, before the Fifa Congress in Vancouver, local authorities rejected a request for a level-four motorcade, usually reserved for heads of state or the Pope.

New Zealand police said they had declined a similar request during the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Alongside the cavalcade of cars and the private charter flights comes a large salary, too, three times what he first earned when elected in 2016.

Infantino, who was paid about £1.3m 10 years ago, now takes home about £4m - a base salary of £2.2m plus a confirmed variable bonus payment of £1.8m.

His predecessor Sepp Blatter was paid a £2.6m package for his final year as Fifa president.

Infantino gets a 'per diem' too to cover expenses and living costs, worth £20,500 a year on top of his salary.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

There was also the Fifa Peace Prize, awarded to Trump weeks before the US invaded Venezuela to depose president Nicolas Maduro and launched air attacks on Iran.

Despite criticism, the Fifa ethics committee did not respond to complaints about Infantino's political neutrality over the prize.

At the start of the year, Infantino made a surprise appearance at the inaugural meeting of Trump's Board of Peace, set up to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza.

The International Olympic Committee, of which Infantino is an invited member, said its rules on political neutrality had not been breached.

However, many felt he had positioned himself too close to the US president.

This was heightened when USA striker Folarin Balogun escaped a ban after being sent off at the World Cup.

It was an unprecedented move by Fifa's disciplinary committee, with Trump saying he had personally called Infantino asking for the red card to be reviewed.

Infantino insisted it was a decision taken by an independent body over which no-one could have an influence.

On the final weekend of the World Cup, Trump and Infantino appeared together at Trump Tower in New York. The US president said he had called the Fifa president who "made another great decision".

Then, perhaps the culmination of Infantino's close association with Trump, came Fifa Forward Enterprise.

The private investor was to be a company linked to the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Infantino has held open news conferences, taking questions from the media, just twice in the past four years

Independent questions of Infantino's methods and decisions are rare because he does not often speak to the media.

In the past four years he has given just two news conferences, both lasting an hour and held before the start of the World Cup.

Other than that, Infantino generally appears in Fifa-produced interviews issued through their official channels.

Before the 2026 World Cup, Infantino tried to head off at the pass any queries about high ticket prices and supporters' visas.

But, at the news conference before the World Cup, his reply of "just, you know, chill, relax" about Somali referee Omar Artan, who had been denied entry to the USA at Miami Airport, sparked concern.

By issuing statements through Fifa channels, Infantino can seek to shape the narrative.

The Fifa statement issued on Wednesday offered some contrition. But there was a rebuke, too.

It gave Infantino the chance to bite back, saying Fifa would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The allure of the role is great, underscored by the fact there have been just four permanent Fifa presidents since Stanley Rous was elected in 1961.

Outside of Europe, the record revenues achieved by Infantino have funded the football operations of many countries. That has created loyalty, and it is a vote winner.

Yet for Uefa, and a few other national associations, the rap sheet is now too long.

Fifa cannot be run as an autocratic project any longer, claim his critics - many of them within European football.

Expanding the World Cup was in Infantino's election manifesto, and an increase to 64 teams for 2030 seems highly likely if he gets a fourth term.

There was also the expanded summer Club World Cup. The trophy is engraved with a personal tribute - "Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino".

The unique allocation of the next two men's World Cups helped ensure Saudi Arabia, another close ally of Infantino, would get the 2034 event.

The draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair. Trump was front and centre, as was Infantino.

Many supporters felt the price of tickets was too high, while some who were prepared to pay for them were denied visas.

Fifa opted to use a secondary market place with uncapped prices and a 30% share on each ticket sold.

Critics said profit had become more important than the supporter experience, with the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey subpoenaing Fifa to answer questions about its ticketing practices.

Even with all these controversies, Infantino was expected to be re-elected, such was his support around the world in many member associations.

Indeed, before the World Cup 111 had already declared for him - enough to guarantee re-election.

Now that picture is uncertain amid the fallout from Fifa's failed private investment plan.

Uefa sees this moment as its chance to force him to step down.

But, as his attendance at the Colombia president's inauguration shows, that may be incredibly difficult to achieve.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

Uefa accused Infantino of prioritising "private political interests" and staged a walk-out.

There was also the Fifa Peace Prize, awarded to Trump weeks before the US invaded Venezuela to depose president Nicolas Maduro and launched air attacks on Iran.

Despite criticism, the Fifa ethics committee did not respond to complaints about Infantino's political neutrality over the prize.

At the start of the year, Infantino made a surprise appearance at the inaugural meeting of Trump's Board of Peace, set up to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza.

The International Olympic Committee, of which Infantino is an invited member, said its rules on political neutrality had not been breached.

However, many felt he had positioned himself too close to the US president.

This was heightened when USA striker Folarin Balogun escaped a ban after being sent off at the World Cup.

It was an unprecedented move by Fifa's disciplinary committee, with Trump saying he had personally called Infantino asking for the red card to be reviewed.

Infantino insisted it was a decision taken by an independent body over which no-one could have an influence.

On the final weekend of the World Cup, Trump and Infantino appeared together at Trump Tower in New York. The US president said he had called the Fifa president who "made another great decision".

Then, perhaps the culmination of Infantino's close association with Trump, came Fifa Forward Enterprise.

The private investor was to be a company linked to the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

Uefa boycott right thing for future of game - Bronze

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Infantino has held open news conferences, taking questions from the media, just twice in the past four years

Independent questions of Infantino's methods and decisions are rare because he does not often speak to the media.

In the past four years he has given just two news conferences, both lasting an hour and held before the start of the World Cup.

Other than that, Infantino generally appears in Fifa-produced interviews issued through their official channels.

Before the 2026 World Cup, Infantino tried to head off at the pass any queries about high ticket prices and supporters' visas.

But, at the news conference before the World Cup, his reply of "just, you know, chill, relax" about Somali referee Omar Artan, who had been denied entry to the USA at Miami Airport, sparked concern.

By issuing statements through Fifa channels, Infantino can seek to shape the narrative.

The Fifa statement issued on Wednesday offered some contrition. But there was a rebuke, too.

It gave Infantino the chance to bite back, saying Fifa would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The allure of the role is great, underscored by the fact there have been just four permanent Fifa presidents since Stanley Rous was elected in 1961.

Outside of Europe, the record revenues achieved by Infantino have funded the football operations of many countries. That has created loyalty, and it is a vote winner.

Yet for Uefa, and a few other national associations, the rap sheet is now too long.

Fifa cannot be run as an autocratic project any longer, claim his critics - many of them within European football.

Expanding the World Cup was in Infantino's election manifesto, and an increase to 64 teams for 2030 seems highly likely if he gets a fourth term.

There was also the expanded summer Club World Cup. The trophy is engraved with a personal tribute - "Inspired by the Fifa president Gianni Infantino".

The unique allocation of the next two men's World Cups helped ensure Saudi Arabia, another close ally of Infantino, would get the 2034 event.

The draw for this summer's World Cup was a long, lavish and outlandish affair. Trump was front and centre, as was Infantino.

Many supporters felt the price of tickets was too high, while some who were prepared to pay for them were denied visas.

Fifa opted to use a secondary market place with uncapped prices and a 30% share on each ticket sold.

Critics said profit had become more important than the supporter experience, with the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey subpoenaing Fifa to answer questions about its ticketing practices.

Even with all these controversies, Infantino was expected to be re-elected, such was his support around the world in many member associations.

Indeed, before the World Cup 111 had already declared for him - enough to guarantee re-election.

Now that picture is uncertain amid the fallout from Fifa's failed private investment plan.

Uefa sees this moment as its chance to force him to step down.

But, as his attendance at the Colombia president's inauguration shows, that may be incredibly difficult to achieve.

US appeals court halts Trump ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:41:30 GMT

The Trump administration has been ordered to stop construction on President Donald Trump's $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House.

A federal appeals court dealt the latest setback to the controversial project on Friday, testing Trump's presidential authority. He has vowed to appeal to the Supreme Court.

"Whether or not a ⁠massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the panel's ​majority said.

The order upholds a preliminary ​injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued after the administration tore down the ​East Wing last year to begin the project without congressional approval.

"Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's ​House — to fit a particular President's desires," the panel said.

The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, said: "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence."

"The President has no - and claims no - constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people," the opinion said.

The administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction on the ballroom, while still allowing underground work to proceed.

The ruling on Friday upholds the order blocking above-ground construction without congressional approval. The appeals court delayed implementation of its ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Justice for comment.

Trump railed against the "horrendous" and "politically motivated" decision on social media, highlighting the dissenting judge's opinion that the order is "a blatant abuse of discretion".

He said the military and Secret Service viewed the ruling as a national security threat.

"This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," he wrote.

He also repeated that the ballroom was being built ahead of schedule and under budget, as a gift to the American people funded by a coalition of private donors.

However, Republicans have sought to use a portion of $1bn (£740m) in taxpayer funds for Secret Service security upgrades - a plan that was brushed aside by a budget watchdog in May.

President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".

The ballroom building would consist of the large entertaining space above ground and also a security complex below ground. Trump doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the ruling on Friday, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action.

"The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust.

"The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."

Trump has touted the ballroom project repeatedly since he unveiled plans for it in July 2025. It would have been the most substantial structural change to the presidential residence in more than 70 years.

But the project has been mired in legal issues since October, when the Trump administration demolished the East Wing, which was built in 1902, to begin construction. Trump initially said the project would be "near" the East Wing, not that it would be demolished.

Government lawyers have argued the additional security complex and features included in the ballroom project are needed to protect the White House complex from drones, ballistic missiles, biohazards and other threats - changes essential to protecting the president, his family, and staff. Trump said on Friday that construction includes bomb shelters, hospital and medical facilities and top secret military facilities.

But the Trust said there was no basis to "disturb" the White House and argued that having a ballroom isn't a national security emergency.

The three-judge appeals court panel said on Friday that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom.

"What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:09:32 GMT

The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

Among the claims by Arday that have been viewed as outlandish is one, made in an interview with the Guardian, that he was paid "1.4 million" for his memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, due to be released next week. He did not specify the currency.

While not inconceivable, publishing insiders cast doubt on a figure such as Arday being able to attract such a large advance payment.

Publisher Simon & Schuster has said it plans to press ahead with the publication despite the controversy surrounding Arday.

But the Atlantic reported on Thursday that there were discrepancies between an advance copy of the memoir and the proposal for the book from 2024 it had obtained.

Among the differences, the magazine said the proposal gave his suicide attempt as happening before the Covid pandemic, whereas in the memoir it occurred during, and that the proposal detailed Arday being hit by a car as a teenager before "miraculously" reawakening, an episode omitted from the finished book.

It comes after the Telegraph reported that Arday had claimed to have already published a book entitled Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse.

Palgrave Macmillan, which was attributed to its publication, told the newspaper it had accepted a proposal for the book but did not publish it.

The BBC has contacted Simon & Schuster and the Good Law Project, which has publicly represented Arday during the plagiarism row, for comment.

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:53:25 GMT

Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assault

Wes Streeting has said he is "absolutely sickened" by reports of rape and sexual abuse of young female recruits at the Army Foundation College (AFC) in Harrogate.

Four women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed while attending the North Yorkshire college, and described a culture of misogyny and sexual violence.

The defence secretary said he would be "looking in detail specifically at what's gone wrong at Harrogate, but also looking more broadly at how we lead a programme of culture change across our armed forces and across defence."

The Army said "unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our armed forces" and urged victims and witnesses to come forward.

AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:45:04 GMT

Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

Spice Girl Mel C paid tribute, posting that it had been "such an honour to have worked with this great man" on her 1999 debut solo album Northern Star

"Sending all my love," she added.

Nicole Appleton of girl group All Saints wrote: "We were fortunate enough to work with him on many occasions and on many songs. In the studio, he made me feel so confident, comfortable and always brought the best out in me.

"He was a treasure in the music industry and we had the most amazing times in the studio and socially. We will forever celebrate him as a music icon. Sending love to all his friends and family."

Skunk Anansie frontwoman Skin noted: "Been dancing to his music for literally decades, thank you for all the great music we shall have forever."

Sister Bliss from fellow London dance act Faithless wrote: "Genius and pioneer... wouldn't have a life in music without him."

Modern electro-pop artist Georgia added: "It was an honour to work with William, I will cherish it forever, long may he live with the electronic acid sounds in the sky."

Speaking to the Official Chart company in 2015 about the process of making Ray of Light, Orbit said: "We got in studio, broke all the rules and didn't really think about the consequences.

"I'm very proud of my work on that record - I think it still holds up today," added the musician and composer.

Madonna and Orbit combined again to great effect in 1999 on her number two UK chart hit Beautiful Stranger, which he co-wrote and played on.

The track, which earned them another Grammy, also featured on the soundtrack to the second Austin Powers movie, The Spy Who Shagged Me.

In 2000, Orbit worked on Madonna's album Music, as well as releasing his own Grammy-nominated solo LP, Pieces In A Modern Style - a critically acclaimed electronic-classical crossover record.

He and Madonna reunited in 2012 when he produced six tracks on her MDNA album.

With Blur, Orbit produced the 1999 album 13, which saw the Britpop band take a darker and rawer lyrical turn, providing hit singles such as Tender, Coffee & TV and No Distance Left To Run.

He later worked on their track Sweet Song from 2003's Think Tank album.

Orbit's collaboration with pop star Pink, Feel Good Time, from the soundtrack of 2003 film Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle, brought more success, reaching number three in the UK and bagging another Grammy nomination.

His signature soundscape gave many of his recordings a dreamy, blissful aura - whether on upbeat hits by Madonna or Pink, or slower songs like Pure Shores and Black Coffee by All Saints.

Group member Shaznay Lewis and Orbit wrote Pure Shores for the 2000 film The Beach, starring Leonardo DiCaprio, and the track went to number one in the UK.

Lewis posted a broken heart emoji in response to the news of his death.

His other collaborators included Beth Orton, including co-writing her 1996 single She Cries Your Name; and U2, producing the Irish band's 2002 single Electrical Storm.

Orbit released 12 studio albums as a solo artist, the best-received being 1999's Pieces in a Modern Style, which featured his interpretations of various classical pieces.

The album reached number four, and a dance remix of his version of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings was a club smash and went to number two in the singles chart.

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:37:49 GMT

An Irish fast food chain locked in a long running dispute with McDonald's has been told it can register its name and logo in the UK.

The UK's Intellectual Property Office ruled the average consumer would not make a link between Galway-based Supermac's logo and name and McDonald's existing trademarks including Big Mac and McCafé.

Supermac's was founded by Galway businessman Pat McDonagh in 1978 and is now the largest Irish-owned fast food restaurant firm in the Republic of Ireland.

The two chains have been embroiled in a long running legal battle over the right to use brand terms including "Mac".

The UKIPO said there were significant visual, aural and conceptual differences between the Supermac's and McDonalds marks, which were "sufficient for a consumer not to directly confuse the marks".

According to Irish broadcaster RTÉ News, it further said that "no link will be made by the consumer" in relation the Mc/Mac elements of the branding.

Speaking to RTÉ McDonagh said: "We've never had their scale or resources, but we've always believed every business deserves the same protection under the law, regardless of its size."

The UK ruling comes just weeks after the European Union Intellectual Property Office upheld a decision that means Supermac's cannot register its name as a trademark in the European Union.

In June, EUIPO's board of appeal said Supermac's logo and signage was too close to its US rivals Big Mac trademark.

EUIPO said there was a likelihood of confusion between Supermac's and the Big Mac trademark for English and German speaking consumers.

That ruling does not impact on Supermac's trading in Ireland.

The Irish fast food chain had been seeking to appeal a ruling made last year that found allowing Supermac's to register its name as a trademark within the EU would lead to the likelihood of confusion.

Supermac's first applied for a trademark in the EU in May 2016.

McDonald's opposed that move, saying Big Mac has been registered as a trademark for meat sandwiches since December 1998.

In 2024, following a legal challenge from Supermac's, the European Court of Justice ruled McDonald's no longer has the exclusive right to use the label "Big Mac" in reference to chicken burgers sold in the EU.

Why there's a row about standing up while drinking in central London

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:22:08 GMT

It has been claimed so-called vertical drinking is under threat in the heart of London's West End.

But is it true?

In short: standing up to have a drink, often outside.

The borough of Westminster has more licensed venues than anywhere else in the UK with about 500 pubs, bars and wine bars, and roughly 1,750 cafes and restaurants.

It follows a report on page three of Thursday's Guardian newspaper, headlined "Time at the bar? Council accused of trying to stop pubs being pubs with 'no standing' plan". The headline in its online version of the story has since been tweaked.

By 1 October, Westminster City Council (WCC) needs to update its current licensing policy - drawn up in 2021.

It has therefore published draft proposals as part of a consultation which closes on Sunday, which the Guardian report was based on.

In the draft plans, WCC said it wanted to "discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking".

One policy is to refuse pub, bar, fast food or music venue licences in an area known as the "West End cumulative impact zone": an area roughly between Oxford Street and Trafalgar Square, taking in Leicester Square and Soho.

"The introduction of measures to reduce the extent of, or to remove opportunities for, vertical drinking could address the underlying reasons for the policy," the document reads.

The guidance suggests applicants for new licences should aim for "a predominantly seated operation with fixed seating", alongside waiter service replacing vertical drinking and restrictions on customers consuming alcohol while standing.

WCC insists there is no plan to ban pub-goers in Soho from drinking while standing up, branding reporting of anything of that nature "utterly ludicrous", and on Friday afternoon it published a "myth-busting" response to the proposals.

Tim Barnes, WCC deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning, said: "There is no plan, and never has been, to ban drinking while standing up in a Westminster pub.

"Suggesting otherwise is a wilful misreading of the policy proposals with clauses taken out of context.

"We want people to go out in the West End and have a good time. Our guidance is simply about encouraging venues to manage their customers so people don't pack on to pavements or excessive drinking doesn't disturb others passing by."

Responding to the Conservative council's consultation, a spokesperson for the government said: "Busy pubs full of people talking to each other is not a public nuisance, it is British life and it is thousands of jobs.

"Soho did not become world famous by taking last orders early, switching the lights off at 10 o'clock."

While the Labour mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, said that you "can't run a world-famous nightlife district with a village-hall mindset".

A Conservative Party spokesperson called for WCC to strike a balance between the needs of the night-time economy and residents' concerns.

A spokesperson for Soho Business Alliance, which represents businesses in the area, said WCC "don't want the late-night economy" and accused it of "trying to reduce the capacities in these venues".

They added: "It's been like that for years where people are standing and drinking, it's not causing crime, it's not causing issues.

"It's them trying to change the nature of Soho and it's quite sad that they've gone to such lengths to sanitise the area."

Local community organisation, the Soho Society, has previously stated that "alcohol-related harm, including risks to women and vulnerable people at night, must be considered" in decisions on licensing.

The group has previously expressed concern about "the unmanaged cumulative impact of a high concentration of licensed premises in a small area on Soho's whole ecosystem", including crime, anti-social behaviour, public safety concerns, public nuisance and disruption to the area's day-to-day functioning.

How a 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:11:32 GMT

The power failure which hit a Network Rail operations centre in Manchester was a rare incident.

But after commuters were left facing chaos, it has raised questions about how a short outage at one operating centre could have a widespread impact.

Network Rail will face scrutiny for how its systems coped and responded to the outage.

That's the publicly-owned body whose job it is to operate and maintain Britain's railway infrastructure. That means the tracks, signals, embankments and major stations.

It was at Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester that the problem started. Its operating centres are where crucial controls are housed that let trains run safely across the country, with Manchester's centre responsible for large parts of the North West.

It was hit by a power cut in the area, which was resolved within 90 seconds. Given the centre's importance, backups are in place. But questions have been raised about how they responded.

Chris Wright, north-west route director at Network Rail, told the BBC "we didn't experience a 90-second interruption," insisting its systems were back online sooner.

But he said some of Network Rail's communications systems "did not respond how we would have expected, and then needed reconfiguring and replacing".

"We've got to work really hard very quickly now to understand why that's the case," he added.

Because signalling was affected - think of that essentially as the traffic lights of the railway - trains had to stop.

Systems had to be rebooted. But there was some damage to those that control signalling, which took time to fix because of the need to replace certain parts.

Thinking about how busy parts of the rail network are, and how many trains and crews were left out of position across the North West of England and beyond, helps explain why the impact was so big.

Network Rail has apologised to customers and opened an investigation.

Bosses say engineers have been working hard to "build additional resilience into our signalling systems to ensure that this doesn't happen again".

Network Rail has moved towards having 12 so-called Rail Operating Centres across Great Britain, replacing a previous structure of hundreds of older signal boxes. They are meant to be high tech hubs which centralise control of the network.

Manchester's Rail Operating Centre was opened in 2014.

Experts have warned consolidating in this way means that if one centre is badly affected, the impact is much broader.

Rail writer Christian Wolmar said the problem they have created is that "if one thing goes wrong, it can wipe out, as we saw, quite a lot of the network".

"So really they've got to start thinking about both resilience, but also whether the centralisation of all the signalling and communications into a very small number of places is the right thing to do," he added.

There's nothing to specifically link this particular incident to other recent problems experienced by rail users; for example the impact of speed restrictions and infrastructure failures during the recent extreme heat.

But it is unlikely to inspire confidence among passengers who have in the past few years suffered from issues such as poor performance among operators, strikes and rising ticket prices. Regulated fares have been frozen in England this year.

Rail engineer and writer Gareth Dennis also drew a link between the incident and the funding pressures and job cuts Network Rail has faced. He said it raised questions including: "Are their staff suitably resourced? Are there enough staff to be ensuring that things like those checks of that supply are happening?"

Network Rail gets five-year funding settlements, signed off by the government. The latest one started in 2024.

The government committed £44.1bn for the 2024-29 period of the strategic business plan, a £3bn increase from the previous five years.

Factors including rising costs due to inflation and a rise in extreme weather events have left its funding under severe pressure.

Introducing Network Rail's new business plan, former chief executive Andrew Haines said that, given the constrained budget, funding would "need to go further than ever before".

The government's current rail policy centres around nationalising the passenger rail operators who weren't already in public control (a number of operators had already been nationalised under past Conservative governments) - then bringing the running of train services and the infrastructure under a new organisation called Great British Railways.

Network Rail is expected to be abolished as a separate entity. Ahead of that, some joint management teams have been formed, for example in the South West.

The question of how much taxpayer money to spend supporting both passenger rail services, and investing in infrastructure, is a significant one - and government budgets remain squeezed.

France set to take part in U20 Women's World Cup

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:35:22 GMT

Paris FC's Maeline Mendy has captained the France Under-19 side that reached the European Under-19 Championship final in 2025.

France say they are still planning to compete in the Under-20 Women's World Cup next month despite a threat from Uefa to boycott Fifa competitions.

It is not known whether England will play or not, with the Football Association unable to provide a comment when asked by BBC Sport if the team will take part in the tournament in Poland, which is due to start in 29 days.

After Fifa president Gianni Infantino announced a plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors, European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the proposals were dropped.

The plans have since been aborted - with Infantino apologising for his "errors".

In a statement on Thursday, Uefa said the boycott could still go ahead, but when contacted by BBC Sport the French Football Federation (FFF) said its plans for the tournament had not changed.

"For now, France will be participating to the Fifa U20 Women World Cup," it said.

Six European teams - England, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and hosts Poland - are scheduled to play in the tournament.

Women's football would be the first to be significantly impacted if Uefa's stance is upheld:

5 September: Women's Under-20 World Cup due to start

October: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all have qualifiers for next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil

October: The Under-17 Women's World Cup is scheduled to take place in Morocco

June 2027: Should they not feature in the play-offs because of Uefa's boycott, European teams - including defending champions Spain - would not be able to participate in the Women's World Cup

Mexico break ranks to join Argentina in backing Infantino

Infantino sorry for errors but stays Fifa president

This video can not be played

How Uefa's boycott could impact women's football

England defender Lucy Bronze says a Uefa boycott of Fifa competitions would be the "right thing" for the future of the game, despite the impact it could have on women's football.

"I think the players who play in those competitions, the European players, we stand by our beliefs and what the right thing is for our game," said Bronze, who was speaking in New Zealand on Chelsea's pre-season tour.

"And if that means boycotting competitions, then that has to happen.

"It's for the future of the game and not just for me today and tomorrow.

"It's for all the little girls or little boys who come after us to make sure that they're in a good place when the game's moving forward in decades to come, not just tomorrow."

Lucy Bronze is a two-time European champion with England

Speaking to BBC Sport last week, former England defender Anita Asante said: "The first casualties will be women's football tournaments.

"If this isn't resolved by the time of England's qualifiers, then the impact could be huge and it is already a busy schedule."

Baroness Campbell, former Football Association director of women's football, said it was "tragic" that women's football could be first to be affected.

The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino, while Wales, Albania and Croatia are among other individual associations to have turned their back on the 56-year-old.

Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:29:23 GMT

The senior investigating officer in the PC Andrew Harper case has told BBC Breakfast he is "appalled" that two of the killers will become eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died from catastrophic injuries in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

Two of his killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – will be eligible for early release next year under revised government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

Stuart Blaik, who investigated the killing, said it was "particularly hard to understand" their case for early release and said police officers were shocked at the prospect.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release from prison.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Friday that early release is "not okay" - adding that no government should have been put in the position of having to deal with limited prison capacity.

Contains flashing images.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

PC Harper and Lissie had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.

On Thursday, the police officer's widow said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.

She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets.

"Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."

Thames Valley Police Federation chair Aileen O'Connor began the petition this week.

"My ask is that the prime minister, the home secretary and everybody else in government gets on the right side of this and does the right thing and makes the changes that keep the two killers behind bars," she said.

"We have been working closely with Chief Constable Jason Hogg and Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber from the outset on this.

"We are all united in our frustration and dismay at the government's ridiculous plans when it comes to releasing from prison early the killers of police officers."

The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.

The justice secretary Alex Norris previously said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme.

"If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," said Norris.

Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.

Prisoner release row proving to be Burnham's first big test as PM

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:18:00 GMT

Three weeks into his premiership, Andy Burnham has "hit bumps in the road" in the estimation of one long-serving Labour MP with the row over the early release of some prisoners from jail.

His political opponents are already sharpening their attacks, believing they have found an issue with which to discomfit a new prime minister early in his time in office who had, until now, displayed a pretty deft political touch.

Conservative Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "This the most important decision Andy Burnham has made since he became prime minister and he's got it wrong."

For Labour MPs, however, this week has shown Burnham is prepared to confront difficult choices and take decisions which, as he said in his first speech in Downing Street, are "more about problem solving than point scoring".

Burnham's first two weeks in the job were pretty problem free, with a succession of announcements, from a cap on bus fares to a determination to overhaul of social care, along with a blitz of social media videos, all designed to portray a more relaxed PM with a focus on everyday issues.

The overcrowding crisis in our prisons has presented him with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices.

Crucially too, they are some of the first difficult choices Burnham has had to make in office.

The issue long predates his arrival in Downing Street. In 2023, with space in jails on the verge of running out, the last Conservative government started releasing prisoners 18 days early. That was only a temporary fix.

Just days after becoming prime minister in July 2024, Sir Keir Starmer had to contemplate a more far-reaching prisoner release scheme, saying "it is shocking for our country to have got into a state where we have too many prisoners and not enough prison places".

In January this year, Sir Keir's government passed the Sentencing Act under which several thousand prisoners will be released early starting this autumn, including some convicted of very serious crimes.

Andy Burnham, aware of how sensitive this would be, immediately ordered a review.

His frustration was evident when he announced he was removing some categories of prisoner from early release, rapists and child sex offenders among them, but not others.

"The truth is I wanted to go even further," he said, "I have pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

The Conservatives seized on the fact that his decisions mean that among those still being let out early will be some who committed grooming-related crimes as well as some killers, including those of PC Andrew Harper.

"The Labour government has made mistake after mistake on this early release scheme," said Chris Philp.

"Despite our warnings in Parliament, they initially planned to release rapists and dangerous criminals.

"But, even after Andy Burnham's review, it turns out they still plan to release cop-killers and men involved in the grooming gang scandal early. It's an insult to PC Harper's family and many other victims."

Up against Sir Keir, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch managed to find issues she could use to force him on to the back foot and into what turned out to be a damaging series of policy shifts. She has seized on the early releases to do try to do the same with his successor.

A first sign of that came when Burnham had to "personally intervene" this week, his spokesperson said, to order officials to find out how many people convicted of grooming-related offences might still be getting early release.

That came after Badenoch highlighted the issue in an open letter to him.

The Conservatives are now considering how they can keep the pressure up when parliament returns in September.

They will aim to place Labour MPs in an uncomfortable position if the issue can be debated in the Commons.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy has called on the government to introduce "emergency primary legislation as soon as Parliament returns in September," as he says that is the only way to permanently exclude "killers - like the killers of PC Harper - child abusers and grooming gang members from early release".

For now, Labour MPs are off on their summer breaks.

"There is no point in bemoaning what is going on" one says phlegmatically, "Andy Burnham's inherited this vexed issue that our jails are full, it's in the nature of being PM.".

"I have every confidence in him. Over all the years Andy Burnham has never been fearful of speaking to victims directly," adds the MP who has served on the justice select committee.

But they added: "We need to have an honest conversation about who we are sending to jail as we don't have the spaces to accommodate everyone we are sending."

Another MP, from the left of the party, said Labour members still felt overwhelmingly positive about their new leader despite the row over prisoner releases.

"They don't believe he has a magic wand. I don't blame him for the overcrowding crisis and I don't think voters do".

And the MP added "at least we have a recognisably Labour government. It feels like we are in play again, with a second chance to make a difference, maybe even to win a second term".

Campaigners call for Jared Leto's concerts to be cancelled after criminal sexual conduct claims

BBC News Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:28:50 GMT

Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong language

Women's safety campaigners are calling for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts in the UK to be cancelled after frontman Jared Leto was accused of criminal sexual conduct.

A BBC investigation published last week heard from four women who have accused the US musician and actor of behaviour which includes sexual assault and grooming.

The alleged offences took place in the 2000s and 2010s when the women were teenagers and Leto was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.

The musician - who strongly denies the claims - is currently scheduled to perform with his band at two of the UK's biggest arenas next April.

The End Violence Against Women coalition and domestic abuse charity Women's Aid have told BBC Newsbeat they have concerns about the upcoming events in London and Manchester - urging organisers not to go ahead with them.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted the promoters, venues and the band for comment, but has not received any responses.

A spokesperson for Women's Aid told Newsbeat it is "troubling to hear that UK concerts are still planned to go ahead that will put an alleged abuser in the spotlight".

"In light of the very serious allegations of criminal sexual conduct, we would urge organisers to put safety over profit and avoid platforming figures like this."

Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said she backed the charity's call.

"I think it really is about putting people over profit in this instance, and particularly women and girls' safety," she said.

Walker said tickets still being sold for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts at London's The O2 and Manchester Co-Op Live was "really worrying".

"Particularly for victims and survivors of violence against women and girls, they'll be seeing these reports and then seeing that things are moving forward seemingly without any consequence," she said.

"I think that will cause a huge amount of alarm and frustration and anger."

Walker said the coalition wants the industry to consider whether platforming groups and individuals "sends a message" about whether they "condone particular forms of behaviour".

"And that's the choice that I think is in front of them."

US rock band Thirty Seconds to Mars, known for hit songs including The Kill, This is War and Kings And Queens, was formed by Leto and his brother Shannon in the late 1990s.

They began touring in the 2000s and progressed to headlining major arenas around the world.

As part of the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret, two men who worked with Leto's band for many years recall how uncomfortable staff felt about the way Leto would interact with teenage girls.

One alleges that crew members were instructed to invite young girls backstage after they would join Leto on stage at gigs.

Another says at one point there would typically be about two girls a day stopping by to see Leto at a house where the band was working.

Among those who have accused Leto is ex-model Alex, who says her agency was invited to a Thirty Seconds to Mars' concert at London's O2 arena in 2013.

She says she was later invited to an after-party by Leto's female assistant and, although she was 19 at the time, she says to protect herself she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger when she met Leto.

She says she told him she was 17, and that Leto, then 41, replied: "Age is just a number, and anyway, we're in Europe."

Alex says one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to go to another party at a nearby hotel later, but only Leto was in the room when she arrived.

When she asked Leto if she could sleep on the chaise longue in the room, Alex says the star responded by saying that, if she did, she would wake up "with a dick in her ass".

Alex says she tried to dismiss what happened, but she now believes the hotel encounter had been "all planned out".

In total, 10 women have spoken to the BBC documentary, with nine of them sharing their stories publicly for the first time.

Despite repeated attempts to contact Jared Leto before publication of the original story, he did not respond to the allegations put to him by the BBC.

After the story was published, Leto said in a statement released by his representatives to the BBC: "I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false".
