The Tenancy Tribunal has released new guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence after concerns that the use of the technology was clogging up the system with “AI slop”.

The principal tenancy adjudicator published the guidelines this week to “explain how AI may be used in Tenancy Tribunal proceedings” and highlight “the potential benefits and the risks of relying on AI-generated material”.

Property Brokers general manager of property management David Faulkner told the Herald the guidelines are “certainly a very positive step”.

“Everything that they say is actually in the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), but it’s good referring to the fact that if people are going to make frivolous and vexatious cases with what we call AI slop, then there’s a small threat that they may end up paying court costs.”

Faulkner said his organisation has seen an increasing amount of claims believed to be created using AI with “very lengthy” submissions asking for compensation of as much as $70,000.

“They all have the same pattern,” he said. “We’re providing a lot of training to our property managers on how to deal with this and not to panic, because when you get a claim with, say, 200 pages against you, it can be quite intimidating.

“A lot of what the AI spits out, is actually also incorrect.”

Contact the Herald newsroom

In a case last year against Property Brokers, a tenant reportedly submitted a 101-page report, along with 215 pages of evidence, asking for $40,000 in compensation – all seemingly created by AI. The tenant ended up being awarded just $80.

Faulkner said these kinds of claims not only require more time and resources, but also cause delays in the Tenancy Tribunal.

However, the use of AI is not only being used by tenants, but by landlords and property managers, says Tenancy Advisory director Sarina Gibbon.

Her organisation provides education and advice around residential tenancy law, and Gibbon was less sympathetic about the bloated and complex claims caused by AI.

She said it’s “part of their job” for property managers and adjudicators to find solutions “in the face of an emerging technology”.

Gibbon believes the drawbacks of AI ultimately disadvantage tenants the most.

“Unfortunately, AI hallucination, AI bloat, the mis-setting of expectations tend to really disadvantage tenants because fundamentally, just as a rule of average, tenants are just generally a little less knowledgeable about the RTA.

“So they’re not able to even be able to figure out when AI is hallucinating and when they’re not.”

Gibbon said she’s seen AI deployed “so beautifully” in a way that “really lifts” applications, but it’s “very rare right now”.

The “biggest letdown” of how tenants use AI is the unrealistic expectation it gives about compensation.

“I see AI emboldening applicants to expect that they would have a huge monetary payout,” Gibbon said.

“And then these applicants come to my business, or they go to the Tenancy Tribunal, and they’re incredibly let down when they find out what they will get is nowhere near that.”

Gibbon said she was a big fan of the AI guidelines because it “reminds you of your core duties as an applicant”.

“If you just let AI hallucinate fact patterns that never happened or make fanciful and outlandish arguments to sort of stretch your rights, you’re going to be disappointed.

“You’re going to be under scrutiny, and [they’re] going to ask you questions, and you’re not going to be able to answer them.

“Fundamentally, AI does not reduce or enhance your rights and obligations under the RTA.”

Faulkner advised tenants who aren’t happy with how they’re looked after is to, first and foremost, speak to their landlord or property manager.

A Tenancy Services and Tenancy Tribunal spokesperson told the Herald they have seen “an increase in the apparent use of AI in the materials that we receive”.

“In some instances, the apparent AI-generated material has added significantly to the length and complexity of the claims. In other cases, it has been concise and relevant and assisted the tribunal in identifying and understanding the relevant issues.

“The tribunal received nearly 30,000 applications last year, most of which had no obvious AI component, so it is difficult to determine the overall impact of this increased AI use on the tribunal as a whole.”

Helen Clark’s ‘restraint’ lesson for Christopher Luxon - Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald August 07, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

One word from the Right Honourable Helen Clark has stayed with me for almost two decades: “Restraint”.

She offered that advice after I wrote a particularly excoriating column about Right Honourable Winston Peters in 2008.

At the time Peters was serving as Foreign Minister outside Cabinet while New Zealand First supported Labour through a confidence-and-supply agreement.

Clark neither disputed my analysis nor defended Peters’ conduct. She simply said: “Restraint”.

It was a deceptively simple observation that revealed a great deal about how she exercised power.

Clark understood that coalition leadership was never about eliminating disagreement. It was about containing it.

Ministers could argue fiercely behind closed doors. Coalition partners could push the limits of patience. But once decisions were made, the Government spoke with one voice.

That discipline was tested repeatedly during Labour’s third term. New Zealand First opposed the China free trade agreement, although as a confidence-and-supply partner rather than a formal coalition member, its dissent was easier to accommodate.

The real test came in August 2008 when allegations surrounding political donations to New Zealand First prompted a Serious Fraud Office investigation.

Peters offered to stand aside as Foreign Minister while the inquiry proceeded. Clark accepted. She neither sacked him nor pretended nothing had happened.

It was a textbook exercise in political judgment.

Peters had not been charged with any offence and was entitled to due process. Yet Clark also recognised that New Zealand’s chief diplomat could not credibly represent the country abroad while under official investigation.

She temporarily assumed his ministerial responsibilities herself. When the SFO later cleared Peters of personal wrongdoing, she nevertheless declined to restore his portfolios before the general election.

There was respect between them. But there was never any doubt who was in charge.

That is the distinction that increasingly invites comparison with Christopher Luxon.

Nearly three years into office, his coalition increasingly resembles a Government where authority is negotiated in public rather than exercised in private. Nowhere is that more apparent than in foreign affairs.

Instead of projecting a coherent New Zealand position, the Government has repeatedly presented competing voices to allies, trading partners and adversaries alike.

China provides perhaps the clearest example.

Peters’ extraordinary instruction that Chinese-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan should “go back to your own country”, coupled with his assertion that China is “where they lie like a flatfish”, prompted a formal diplomatic protest from Beijing and generated international attention.

A Prime Minister has two choices in moments like these.

He either stands unequivocally behind his Foreign Minister and accepts the consequences. Or he makes it unmistakably clear that such conduct falls below the standard expected of a senior minister and imposes discipline.

Luxon chose neither.

He described the remarks as “attention-seeking”, acknowledged they were racist, distanced himself from his Foreign Minister, yet imposed no discernible consequence.

The result was the worst of both worlds. The Government appeared divided while the authority of the Prime Minister appeared diminished.

The same pattern has repeated itself.

Official Information Act documents released after the Iran crisis exposed differences over New Zealand’s diplomatic response to the United States-Israeli strikes.

Rather than those disagreements being resolved internally, they spilled into public view after material emerged from Peters’ office, raising legitimate questions about whether New Zealand’s foreign policy was being directed from the PM’s office or two floors down.

India exposed an even deeper fracture.

Luxon understandably hailed the long-awaited free trade agreement as one of his Government’s defining international achievements.

Under the coalition’s “agree to disagree” clause, Peters criticised aspects of the FTA, including its associated immigration settings, yet went on to cite confidential Cabinet briefing material in Parliament to support claims officials had concealed policies capable of damaging New Zealand’s relationship with India.

The extraordinary spectacle that followed saw the Prime Minister, Trade Minister Todd McClay and Immigration Minister Erica Stanford publicly contradicting their own Foreign Minister. McClay accused Peters of spreading misinformation. Stanford defended Cabinet confidentiality while refusing to publicly release the relevant documents to journalists.

Luxon rejected Peters’ interpretation. Yet Peters remained Foreign Minister.

Even Luxon’s own diplomacy has not escaped public correction.

When the Prime Minister proposed closer co-operation between CPTPP members and the European Union, in response to rising protectionism (an initiative which is now underway), Peters publicly dismissed the idea as “all very premature” before adding the withering observation: “I hope he’ll call me next time”.

Each incident can be explained away. China was one diplomatic controversy. Iran reflected differences over international strategy. India exposed coalition tensions over immigration. The CPTPP disagreement was another policy dispute.

But politics is rarely judged incident by incident.

The pattern that Luxon’s Government increasingly projects is one of competing centres of authority, particularly on foreign affairs.

The Prime Minister announces policy. The Foreign Minister qualifies it. Other ministers contradict the Foreign Minister. The Prime Minister then explains the disagreement rather than resolving it.

This is coalition management conducted in public.

Against that backdrop came this week’s reports that Luxon referred to coalition partners as “numpties” and “yahoos” while canvassing the possibility of a referendum on MMP.

Whether the remarks were made in frustration, humour or campaign banter is almost beside the point.

The more revealing question is why a Prime Minister who publicly insists coalition relationships remain strong would publicly make comments which Ministers from NZ First and Act who currently serve in his Cabinet took as disparaging them, even though Luxon later declared they were not meant personally.

Either he genuinely believes such Ministers are liabilities – in which case voters are entitled to wonder why he has been unable to impose greater discipline. Or he does not – in which case he appears prepared to diminish his own Government for short-term political advantage.

Politics is ultimately about power. Clark understood that instinctively.

Her advice about “restraint” was never an argument for timidity. It was a lesson in how authority is exercised. It was the discipline to ensure disagreements remained behind closed doors and that, when Government spoke, it spoke with one voice.

Luxon has chosen a markedly different model. Too often he appears content to accommodate public indiscipline rather than extinguish it. Too often he has explained coalition conflict rather than contained it.

Every Prime Minister must compromise. But there is a line between compromise and the gradual erosion of prime ministerial authority, which Peters has made an art form of testing.

As New Zealand moves towards the election, voters are no longer simply deciding whether National, Act and New Zealand First deserve another term.

They are deciding whether Luxon has demonstrated that he – not Peters, not David Seymour, not an uneasy balance between them – is unmistakably in charge.

Helen Clark understood the difference nearly 20 years ago.

“Restraint.”

Rotorua cold snap exposes hidden homelessness health risks

New Zealand Herald August 07, 2026

Sub-zero mornings in Rotorua and Whakatāne have put extra pressure on rough sleepers. Main photo / Peter McIntosh

Freezing Bay of Plenty temperatures have left unhoused people facing a night-long battle against hypothermia and illness.

Support organisations say the bitter conditions are placing vulnerable people at greater risk, adding hardship.

The region awoke to another chilly morning on Friday, with Rotorua’s -5.6C its lowest temperature since records began 55 years ago.

It beat -5.2C in 2011 and 1996, while Whakatāne dropped to -3C and Tauranga Airport reached 1.2C.

Rotorua Salvation Army community ministries manager Darnielle Hoods said the cold snap posed a serious health risk for homeless people.

“Winter in Rotorua isn’t just uncomfortable or cold; it is also a real health risk.”

She said spending nights in shop doorways, parks or vehicles exposed people to prolonged cold, increasing the risk of illness and hypothermia.

It made it hard to get adequate sleep.

Hoods said homelessness extended beyond those sleeping on the streets.

“Many are sleeping in cars, moving between friends and whānau, or living in overcrowded homes that simply aren’t safe or warm enough.”

She said the Salvation Army was seeing more people forced to make impossible choices.

“We have also seen people who don’t fit the stereotype of homelessness, like working families, kuia and kaumātua, and tamariki who are quietly struggling.”

She said people would be surprised by how much homelessness in Rotorua remained hidden.

“It is not just someone sleeping in the doorways of our businesses in town. Whānau are sleeping in cars; many are couch-surfing; grandparents are taking in extra whānau because they have nowhere else to go; and whare are with far too many people trying to keep warm together.”

Hoods said winter always increased demand for support. The cold snap and ongoing cost-of-living pressures saw more people seeking help.

“We are seeing more people asking for kai assistance, warm clothing, blankets, financial mentoring, and support to navigate housing options.”

Love Soup Rotorua co-founder Elmer Peiffer said homeless people were “very vulnerable”.

“I’ve seen some with piles of blankets on them, just trying to keep their body heat trapped inside.”

Peiffer questioned whether Rotorua had sufficient support services.

“When you’re dealing with the homeless and accessing all aspects of their life and their circumstances, I don’t know if there’s enough to be able to take care of all of their needs.”

He said the cold snap highlighted the need for additional support during winter, including more overnight shelter options.

Peiffer said if freezing temperatures continued, he was concerned about the health of rough sleepers.

“If I’m looking at the ones that are exposing themselves throughout the night, I can see cases of hypothermia.”

Wayne Shadbolt, who runs the Tūmanako Project at Tauranga’s Oak Lane Community Church, said many people arrived at the church’s weekly breakfast struggling to stay warm.

“Some of them have only got jandals because they haven’t got shoes. They’re just absolutely cold.”

He said people arrived wrapped in blankets and sleeping bags, trying to protect themselves from freezing temperatures.

“Once you’re chilled to the bone, like they say, once you’re cold to that degree, it’s very hard, no matter what you wrap yourself in, to stay warm.”

Shadbolt said showers, fresh clothing and medical support were available at the weekly breakfasts.

“They really look forward to it because it does bring the warmth back from the inside.”

He said fresh clothing was particularly important, especially warm socks for people exposed to wet and cold conditions.

“One thing they look forward to is being able to get a fresh pair of woollen socks. If their feet are warm, their head’s warm with a beanie, that does help them internally to keep that body temperature right.”

The service runs every Thursday at 7am and usually draws up to 55 people. Numbers increased as temperatures dropped.

He said some people were too cold to leave their sleeping spots, so the church delivered hot food and supplies.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

New Zealand Herald August 07, 2026

Rafaella Melo examines the role technology is playing in transforming the lives of Hawke’s Bay seniors in her The Years Ahead series.

Margaret Thomas wakes up about 8am each day, and before her feet even touch the floor, she starts talking to one of her closest daily companions.

“Alexa, turn the radio on.”

In her Havelock North retirement village townhouse, the 79-year-old has turned artificial intelligence into part of her daily routine.

Alexa turns on the lights, boils the jug, starts the TV, plays music in the bedroom and adds items to her shopping list.

When she wants a cup of tea, she does not walk first to the kitchen.

“I just say, ‘Alexa, cup of tea’,” Margaret said.

The jug starts boiling.

For some people, artificial intelligence (AI) is still something distant, strange or even frightening.

For Margaret, who lives at the James Wattie Retirement Village, it is already threaded through the ordinary parts of her day.

“Everybody thinks I’m a geek,” she said.

Margaret has been using Alexa at home for about five years, after her family first gave her an Echo Dot and later an Alexa device with a screen.

She worked for about 30 years as a legal executive and says she has always been willing to learn new things.

Now, other village residents occasionally come to her for help with phones, computers or technology.

“If I don’t know what’s going wrong, I look it up online and try to learn how to fix it ... AI gives you the answers,” she said.

Her home is not exactly The Jetsons, but it is close enough to it to make visitors look twice.

If the power goes out for too long, Margaret laughs – she would be “lost”.

The next thing on her list to upgrade is her vacuum cleaner, to a robot.

“A good thing about AI and technology in general is that as you’re getting older and things are harder to do, you can get AI to help you do it,” she said.

Margaret said using AI also made her life “fun”.

Recently, she used an AI music app called Suno to create a song for her granddaughter’s 21st birthday.

She fed the app details and words she wanted included, chose a genre and voice and let the programme turn it into verses and a chorus.

The song was a surprise gift.

“There were a lot of tears,” Margaret said.

She also uses AI for quizzes, to settle family arguments over facts and to explore new ideas.

On a trip to Japan last year, she used a travel app called Find Penguins, which let her family follow where she was each day and later turned her travel diary and photos into a printed book.

“You tap your diary in each night, put photos in and at the end of your trip, a book is produced without too much effort,” she said.

The travel app and AI music app were some of the digital tricks Margaret shared with this 36-year-old reporter, who surprised her 65-year-old mother in Brazil with a custom-made birthday song.

The lesson here? Never assume who’s teaching who.

And Margaret is far from the only older Hawke’s Bay resident embracing new technology.

She was among 43 people, aged 60 to 92, who attended Love Heart Social Learning’s first Hawke’s Bay AI workshop in June, led by educator and Love Heart Social Learning co-founder Frances Valintine, who said learning it helped give seniors the confidence to feel connected to the world.

She said older people were often underestimated.

“I think other people make them feel left behind,” Frances said.

“Too many people put them in a box, saying they are of a certain age. My experience is that a lot of them are all over AI.”

Frances said AI could help older people research holidays, create personalised cards, understand basic health information before seeing a doctor, or stay mentally engaged.

But she also warned about the risks, saying AI “doesn’t have a scamming ability as it’s just generating a probability response”.

But “people are using AI to do a deepfake, to pretend to be someone and all that ... every interaction we have online with someone we don’t know should be assumed is a scammer”.

Love Heart co-founder and managing director Fee Webby said the programme was designed for people aged over 60 who were still curious and wanted both learning and connection.

“We need to make sure that we keep people cognitively engaged and we know the importance of ongoing learning for the brain to keep them stimulated,” she said.

“But also, more importantly, is that face-to-face connection.”

For Margaret, technology does not replace people.

“I still think there needs to be human interaction,” she said.

She is not interested in a future where robots replace nurses or carers entirely, although she can see the benefit of technology helping with physical tasks as people age.

For now, AI is simply a companion in her day.

And when she is ready to sleep, Margaret doesn’t reach for a switch.

She simply calls out and the system turns off the TV and lights.

“Alexa, good night.”

Rafaella Melo has more than 10 years of experience as a journalist in Brazil. She has worn many hats, from radio and TV presenter and producer to magazine editor before joining the Hawke’s Bay Today team as a multimedia journalist.

Time for a reset in Parliament and Aotearoa NZ – Letters

New Zealand Herald August 07, 2026

The focus is on Parliament and the behaviour of politicians as the election approaches. Photo / Mark Mitchell Parliament Buildings, the Beehive and Parliament House, photographed at dawn, Wellington. 02 September, 2025. Photo / Mark Mitchell

The disgraceful behaviour of particularly minor-party politicians during the past three years does not mean we need an MMP referendum, Christopher Luxon.

I believe the majority of eligible New Zealand voters are over the destructive distractions of minor-party politicians, their whacky policies, their waste of money and waste of everyone’s time.

What we want is a reduction of 50 politicians to a total Parliament of 70 members; a reduction of the unproductive Public Service to a maximum of 35,000 people, whole departments amalgamated or closed; a Government that can focus on strict financial management and an ability to prioritise spending within our income.

Consolidate local councils, eliminate unproductive tribunals and start listening to voters rather than the costly consultants and legal leaches bleeding this country to bankruptcy.

New Zealand is in dire need of a reset. Campaign on that, Christopher Luxon.

Gary Carter, Gulf Harbour.

Is anyone surprised that unemployment figures are rising? It was inevitable.

AI and self-service checkouts have taken jobs previously done by humans. It is sad that there are few jobs available for students who now have to rely for a living on parents, possibly on stretched incomes themselves.

I refuse to use self-service checkouts on principle.

Anne Martin, Helensville.

I have a young grandson who is now in his third year of unemployment. Being so-called work ready, money is put into his bank account on a regular basis. This is just programming him into becoming a beneficiary long term.

When I look at the state of rubbish on our streets and roadsides and other jobs that could be done in the community, I believe it is way past time the PEP schemes run under the Muldoon Government were brought back, and young people like my grandson were picked up and given jobs to do.

This would give them a reason to get out of bed in the morning, get off their phones and iPads, boost their self-confidence meeting others in a similar position, plus teach them that nothing is free. It would also have the added bonus of making them aware one shouldn’t throw rubbish out of a car window.

David Little, Whangārei.

What’s the received wisdom about the state of the New Zealand economy?

It’s on its beam ends, right?

Then how come, according to Xero, in the June quarter small business had its best quarter in nearly four years with sales rising 8.6% year on year?

Unsurprisingly, agriculture was the standout, with sales up 16.3%, helping drive the national result.

Construction rose 11.0%, and manufacturing increased 8.6%. Retail trade grew 6.4%. Even hospitality, supposedly in a death spiral, was up 2.9%. All this suggests that the New Zealand economy has at last turned the corner.

David Morris, Hillsborough.

NZ has a documented history of poor decisions regarding major national projects. Poor decisions, cost blowouts and billions of dollars wasted.

We’re about to do it again with the Southland AI data centre, now given consent. Hundreds of groups across the US and internationally are protesting such centres because they use immense amounts of power and vast quantities of water. New York State has imposed a moratorium to give itself time to finalise standards.

Surely it seems only common sense for us to exercise a similar degree of caution before going ahead with this. Nobody wants higher power prices and contaminated water.

The Green Party recommends a one-year period to think about it before a decision is made. Think now, instead of “Think Big”?

Susan Grimsdell, Auckland Central.

In the 80s, when the US and the Soviet Union were armed to the teeth with thousands of nukes, we used to remind people on August 6 every year about the nuclear devastation that one small nuclear bomb equivalent to 15 kilotons of TNT did to the people of Hiroshima in 1945.

Of course, three days later the bombing of Nagasaki was commemorated in much the same way. At the same time, we were discovering the horrific damage done to Pacific Islanders from nuclear testing in the Pacific.

Nowadays, the world has moved on. We seem to think that MAD (mutually assured destruction) is keeping us safe from nuclear annihilation by the so-called super-powers. But since 1945, many smaller states have acquired them, so that in the minds of many there are safe nukes (USA, Israel) and unsafe nukes (Iran, China, Russia).

Conveniently forgetting that Osama Bin Laden was a Saudi, President Trump was recently happily giving Saudi Arabia nuclear technology. The Saudis backed out when, after pressure from Israel, he tried to include the normalisation of ties with Israel in the deal.

This whole Iran war is about nuclear weapons, although we were told by Trump himself last year that their whole nuclear capability was destroyed.

It’s time again to revisit the devastation of Hiroshima and reflect that there are no good nukes. As we used to say, “All children need smiles, not nuclear missiles”.

Sue Rawson, Tauranga.

I am very surprised that Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown is able to put a positive spin on the CRL.

Many of the neighbouring businesses that he is so sure will enjoy a surge have gone bankrupt. The CRL is a dreadful waste of public money, and the only business that will enjoy increased patronage is the casino.

Auckland downtown is a disaster zone, and why people would like to visit is beyond me. The cost blowout is a result of fiscally incontinent people wasting public money on gold-plated underground cathedrals.

Better is the enemy of good enough, and good enough was all we needed and could afford; we are not a rich country.

Neville Cameron, Coromandel.

We were chatting with friends this week about power bills – living in Papamoa, Te Puke, and the Hutt Valley. All pay just over $500 for the month – how is this even possible?

Extra fees, fixed charges, and whatever other tricks up their sleeve they have, it is just rampant.

It is a battle of wits with these greedy corporations, as they sure have no problem in giving us the middle finger.

Glenn Forsyth, Taupō.

If Winston Peters lands in hospital, will he tell the nurse caring for him to “go back to his/her own country”? That would be a disaster because our hospitals rely on overseas-trained health care professionals. And I hope he doesn’t end up in a rest home; if we send all the aged-care workers “back to their own country” the sector will collapse. Will Winston instruct NZ First supporters with British accents to go back to their own country? Oh, that’s right, they’re not immigrants, they’re expats.

I came to Aotearoa New Zealand 40 years ago and I’m still shocked when people around me grumble about “immigrants” while clarifying that they don’t mean me. I came from Canada, and for reasons too easily identified, I’m not considered by them to be an immigrant.

Although I’m not sure what I am, beyond sad. Because racist behaviour like that from our Minister for Foreign Affairs is a sad indictment indeed.

Leanne Pooley ONZM, Ponsonby.

Your correspondent Jim Arrowsmith criticises Luxon’s business ability because he has never started a business. Fair enough, but maybe he could enlighten us with how many of the other current leaders have started a small business or even worked in a leadership role in a private enterprise.

Patrick Grant, Stanmore Bay.

Good to see some clear career pathways with the new school subjects promoting further study and supporting our industry needs. I would’ve thought that with the chaotic transition into adulthood, students would also benefit from learning about financial literacy, flatting, legal rights, job-seeker skills, mental resilience and navigating change.

Alison Redfern-Daly, Titirangi.

AI will fail simply because it was designed by humans, who are intrinsically flawed. Unless of course the perfect human being can be found. The only one who would come even close was Jesus of Nazareth and he passed away some 21 centuries ago.

Gary Hollis, Mellons Bay.

Prime Minister Luxon is not happy with our MMP system of voting, and the situation he is in with two “rogue” coalition partners. There is another option that he did not consider in 2023, but he might like to consider after the 2026 election; he could negotiate a grand coalition with the Labour Party and form a centrist coalition Government.

Peter D. Graham, Helensville.

Fifty years of friendship: How I saw the world beside a poetry great

Sydney Morning Herald August 08, 2026

Artist Tom Carment reflects on five decades of bushwalks, brutal art reviews, and stylish typewriters with the late poet Robert Gray.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Driving along the expressway up to the Blue Mountains under heavy grey clouds, the end of one of Robert’s poems came to me: “This blustery wind/brings rain – just/short hairs/ on a barber’s sheet,/marking the windscreen”. I thought too that barber’s sheets in the 1970s, when I first met Robert, were usually white, but now it’s reversed, the sheets are black and my hairs are all white.

Palings Record Store 1975. Robert and I were flicking through album covers, rows of them arranged in boxes alphabetically. I looked right towards D and noticed a young woman pull out Bob Dylan’s Blonde on Blonde and frown in concentration at the album notes. “She looks like a nice girl,” I said to Robert. “Wait a sec,” he replied. I looked across and soon he was standing next to her with one hand in the pocket of his tapered John and Merivale jacket, the other elegantly gesticulating. He was smiling, relaxed, and a couple of times she looked shyly in my direction. Robert walked with her back to where I’d been standing. “Marguerite would be happy to go on a date with you.” I shook her hand, blushing.

The next weekend I drove 20 kilometres to her family home in Elanora Heights, where she introduced me to her father, the minister at a local church. We had an early dinner in Chinatown, and I drove her home by the 10pm curfew. A few days later I received a neatly written two-page letter saying how much she’d enjoyed our date. It was signed, “Yours in Dylan, Marguerite”. From time to time I remember that letter, and it pains me to recall that I never wrote back.

In the mid-1970s Robert met his life partner Dee, who had a daughter, Harriet, two years old. Dee was working as a hairdresser then and saved up her money to buy Robert a teal grey Olivetti Lettera portable typewriter, the epitome of elegant Italian design. He loved this small machine and sometimes took it out with him on the ferry to Manly to work on his poems. He sat there for hours, he told me, traversing the harbour back and forth, on a single fare. Forty years later Robert finally started writing on a computer, but soon the tremor from his Parkinson’s disease made it too hard to manage the sensitive keyboard. His old Olivetti had been given away by then, so I lent him my Hermes Portable typewriter. He was confident it would provide a solution – he could pound its keyboard with his shaking hands. Last week I took it back home again. I don’t think he ever used it.

Robert never drove and he loved to be a passenger on a car journey or on a train heading north, watching the landscape pass by out the window. He had a white scar on his nose which he sometimes hid with one hand, the result of a bad car accident he told me, from when he travelled up to Queensland in the 1960s with landscape painter Lance Solomon. Another time he said the accident was in Sydney and that he’d woken up in hospital and refused a blood transfusion, in unconscious deference to his Jehovah’s Witness family. A few times in the 1970s I drove Robert up along the Pacific Highway to Coffs Harbour, where he’d grown up, and where I’d first met him, in my cousin Diana Wood Conroy’s house on a bush block north of Bellingen.

One summer afternoon, as we looped through the tall eucalypts outside Bulahdelah, the windows of my EJ Holden down (no air-conditioning), Robert pulled out a notebook, screwed up his face and started writing. The cicadas outside were extremely loud – it was one of those bumper years. He shouted across to me, above the din, “The cicadas sound like someone pouring shells onto a huge pile of shells.” He was always jotting down similes and thoughts in that book, and I’d read some of them, printed, later, worked into a poem. His first few books had many poems about journeys, homecomings, almost baroque in their excess of descriptive detail. I loved them.

As a child Robert had heart disease and wasn’t expected to live into his 20s but, against his doctors’ predictions, he survived, the hole in his heart grew over. I feel that the outpouring of poems written following this recovery represented his joy at being alive. Sometimes he was criticised for just being a descriptive writer but in my view, his level of observation and looking was, in itself, an unwritten philosophy. In later years Robert grew to dislike the use of similes in these early works and changed most of them into metaphors. He reworked other things too, made numerous refinements, he thought. Robert’s old friend, the poet Jamie Grant, and I doubted this was an improvement. “You’re a different man now,” I told him, “with a different voice. I don’t go around repainting all my pictures from the 1970s and 80s.” He disagreed and defended his editing eloquently, citing Walt Whitman’s constant revision of his opus Leaves of Grass. Once, as I sat next to Robert at a friend’s funeral, he whispered to me that he was itching to edit the words of Abide with Me.

When I first met Robert he’d already had a book of poems published, Introspect, Retrospect (Lyre-Bird Writers 1970), which he told me he no longer liked and would steal from libraries, to destroy. After he died Dee and I found a copy of this slim, blue, saddle-stitched paperback in his desk drawer, every page of type covered in a spiderweb of pencilled corrections.

On weekends we often went walking and drawing together, carrying our A3 cartridge paper pads into the bush. Dee and Harriet would usually come too and we’d catch the train or cram across the bench seat of my Holden ute and head up to the Blue Mountains, Cowan or along West Head Road for a bushwalk. Afterwards we’d stop at a milk bar and drink cool vanilla malted milkshakes out of battered aluminium containers. At Bundanoon we rented old back-pedal brake bikes near the station and hid them in the bush before walking down to the edge of the cliff face. One day we made a pilgrimage to D. H. Lawrence’s house in Thirroul, Wyewurk, where he lived in 1922 and wrote the novel Kangaroo. We went down steps to the rocks below the house, where Lawrence and his wife Frieda would have gone swimming, and started drawing, looking south. An elderly man came up behind us to watch and after a while said: “Drawing are you? It’s a great sport!”

Fisher Library 1979: A book entitled Gout and Goutiness in the medical section, marked the place to turn left, down the corridor to the Fine Arts section towards the books you’d never see in a bookshop, in German, French and Italian about Caspar David Friedrich, Corot, Gericault, Paula Modersohn-Becker and many more. Robert had recently worked there and had a borrowing card which he rarely used, preferring usually to reshelve these wonderful books after we’d looked at them. Sydney University’s Fisher Library Stack, the section where books were kept for post-graduate use, was our Nirvana. We were both autodidacts, browsers, with no tertiary education. Robert was nine years ahead of me in his reading and life experience and I was trying to catch up.

He often lent me poetry books from his own shelves: Elizabeth Bishop, William Carlos Williams, Thomas Hardy, Edward Thomas, D. H. Lawrence, Philip Larkin, with a pencil tick on the contents page to mark the ones he liked best. I once said to him (perhaps ungratefully) that I’d rather not see these ticks, I wanted to discover what I liked by myself. He was offended. I guess in some ways I was his protégé in those days, a role from which I slowly withdrew. In the 1970s he liked coming over to view my latest paintings and drawings and was always confident in his opinions, telling me what he thought was an advance and what was a backward step. “This one’s a real breakthrough!” he’d say with excitement.

I recently re-read some letters he wrote to me then, in which he expounded his theories: “To be an expressionist is essentially a linear talent. To try and be an expressionist with colour leads to terrible excesses…” I didn’t always agree, but he had a very good eye. Sorting the good from the bad, in writing, art or film was not a trivial matter for Robert – it was life or death, with no middle ground. He was always making lists of best artists, best films, and the reverse. After he died Dee and I found, written in one of his notebooks from the 1980s, a list: “Worst painters consistently given a lot of wall space: Renoir, Chagall, Georgia O’Keeffe.”

Royal National Park 1982. We stopped for a break at Wattamolla and sat on some rocks near the sea, pulling out our wrapped lunches, a Granny Smith apple in each one. We’d started our journey before dawn at Central Station – our goal was to walk from Bundeena to Otford in one day, 28 kilometres. Robert took a bite from his green apple and dipped it in the sea and then another, and dipped it again. On that hot day the salty tang was great. “My father used to do this,” he said. We walked on, refreshed, looping over headlands where the path was cut deep into the headland like a WWI trench and through the palm forest above Burning Palms. The sun was getting low and Robert checked his watch and saw that we’d have to speed up to get the next train from Otford, to avoid an hour of waiting in the dark on the platform for the next one. So we started jogging along the narrow track. “Keep your eyes about you,” he shouted back to me, and I knew his meaning was not to watch out for trip hazards but to keep observing things as much as we had when walking slowly – the shape of the angophoras, the lichened rocks and the arching eucalypts, all rushing past us.

Robert rang up and asked if he could help our oldest son Felix with his HSC English. He’d just finished editing (with Geoff Lehmann) a big anthology of Australian poetry and now had some free time. The allotted poet that year was Gwen Harwood. Felix and I cycled over to the Rose Bay flat and laid out seven poems by Harwood on the pine dining table, worn pale on one side by Robert’s writing arm. For nearly two hours he patiently analysed them with Felix, line by line, succinctly and in plain language. As we were leaving he confessed to me that he wasn’t previously much of a Gwen Harwood fan, but “now I like her a lot better.” A few years later Robert himself was selected as poet for the HSC English students and a slim paperback of his selected poems, entitled Coast Road, was printed in a large edition. Robert chose my painting Morning, Scotts Head for the cover – houses by the sunlit sea.

Robert was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 20 years ago and the illness increasingly clamped down on his body and his mind. He never complained about having got it but railed against its restrictions. I visited more regularly. I think he felt comfortable with me there. Old arguments were put aside and our friendship entered a new phase of honesty. After 50 years of shared experiences, there was no need for him to put on a good show, or impress me. By 2024 he often left a sentence hanging in the air, unfinished. I could sometimes guess where it was going, and, if not, I valued the fragment. Some days I slowly translated the text from his French art books.

If you live long enough it isn’t death you fearbut what life can still do.(from Robert’s poem about his mother, In Dying Light)

A few weeks before his death, Dee had caught the flu and so I went in to the Waverley nursing home, Illowra, to feed Robert his lunch, small spoonfuls of the soft, aged care food. He ate more dessert than mains. It was hard for him to move or speak by then, so I tried to amuse him with anecdotes from our mutual past: the greasy breakfasts we’d been served in 1974 at the People’s Palace in Brisbane (I ate both), the afternoon we’d been dive-bombed by swallows above the water reservoir near the Thames, the boat trip to Den Haag to see Vermeer’s View of Delft.

After a while Robert shook his head, said, “No more, thank you,” and pushed my hand away; “Tom… I’d like to ask you a favour”. I leaned in to listen as he gathered energy for the next sentence. “Could you hail me a taxi to Central Station? I need to take the train to Bellingen.” “The train doesn’t go through Bellingen,” I replied, “We’d have to get someone to pick us up from Coffs Harbour, or Urunga… and today’s North Coast train has already left the station.” I rolled the food tray away towards the window and, while my back was turned, he swung his thin legs away from the bed. Before I could catch him, he’d launched himself forward and crashed to the floor.

As a teenager Robert’s favourite piece of descriptive writing, he told me, came from Robert Louis Stevenson’s Treasure Island – the scene where Jim Hawkins shoots the murderous Israel Hand. The sailor falls dead into the shallow sea and sinks slowly until his body lies huddled on the bright sand. “Sometimes, by the quivering of the water, he appeared to move a little, as if he were trying to rise.”

On Robert’s last day I ran across the park from the bus stop not expecting to find him still alive. He’d not eaten or drunk anything for five days and his last words to Dee were a few days before. “I’ll see you, soon,” he’d said. As I ran I remembered his admonition, “Keep your eyes about you”, so I slowed down and noticed the art nouveau elegance of the tree trunk shadows as they spooled past me. The carers had given Dee a fold-out bed pushed next to Robert’s and for the past two days she’d been holding his thin, veined hand and reading to him, while he gasped for air – Chekhov stories, the Constance Garnett translations he preferred.

In a bookshop before Christmas I found a single copy of Coast Road in their poetry section. I placed it face-out, covering a stack of books by a popular author who I knew might have topped Robert’s list: “Worst writers consistently given a lot of shelf space”.

What else is happening in the book world?

In the grips of Sir Joh’s moral panic, Felicity made a life-changing call

Sydney Morning Herald August 08, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It was a time of fear and panic. A mysterious illness was spreading, and young, gay men were rapidly falling sick.

Felicity Young, aged 24 when the HIV epidemic emerged in Queensland in the 1980s, describes a state gripped by hysteria.

“It terrified the shit out of people,” recalls Young, now 66.

In the kitchen of her apartment in the Brisbane suburb of Newstead, Young traces the early years of HIV.

A stack of archival material – Condoman comics, AIDS campaigns from the ’80s, policy manuscripts she wrote while living overseas – sit within reach.

The sunlit morning retrospective has been prompted by Young’s recent decision to retire from HIV advocacy after 40 years.

“When I first started as a volunteer, I didn’t know that it would be this arc,” she says. “But it has been a privilege.”

Young was living in nearby New Farm when a New York native visiting Sydney became the first person in Australia to be officially diagnosed with AIDS, the condition caused by human immunodeficiency virus, in 1982.

In the NSW capital, the virus emerged on the coat-tails of the women’s and gay liberation movements. Queer communities and activists winning the fight for same-sex acceptance were primed to mobilise against HIV.

It surfaced in Queensland in a vastly different social climate.

“In those early days, it was really difficult because the Joh Bjelke-Petersen line was morality. Gay men are, I don’t want to say the word, but scum, basically,” Young says.

“[He felt] that they were deserving of the disease.”

Before it had a name, HIV was colloquially referred to as the “gay plague” or “gay syndrome”. Hospitals in New York diagnosed Wrath of God Syndrome (WOGS), and medical researchers coined Gay-Related Immune Deficiency (GRID) to pathologise the illness affecting mostly young, gay men.

When HIV reached Queensland, Bjelke-Petersen, the longstanding ultra-conservative premier, decried the virus as a moral failing rather than a public health issue.

“There were calls to remove gay men from society [and] put them on an island, like the whole leper approach,” Young says, referencing plans to resurrect Moreton Bay’s former leper colony on Peel Island.

“When Queensland was being forced by the federal government to do something about HIV, Joh didn’t want to do anything.

“He said: ‘Morality is what’s going to save us. Abstinence is going to save us. This is a punishment from God.’ ”

In 1984, Queensland’s then health minister, Brian Austin, announced three babies had died after receiving blood transfusions contaminated with HIV. The father of one urged the donor, a gay Brisbane man, to suicide.

Bjelke-Petersen seized on the tragedy to stoke moral panic.

In this fraught climate Young, a newly graduated social worker in her mid-20s, met two men infected with the virus while working at Wolston Park Hospital, instigating a decades-long career in HIV advocacy.

Young was assigned two locked wards at the hospital in 1986: Osler House, a maximum-security unit for women deemed “criminally insane”, and Pearce House, a high-security ward for violent men with mental illnesses.

“For some reason, someone thought it was a really good idea to put a 26-year-old inexperienced woman inside this locked ward,” Young says.

The HIV-positive men were admitted to the hospital in 1987. Driven by fear and misinformation, they were excluded by hospital staff and approached “like lepers”.

“I thought, it just doesn’t seem right that you would treat people like this, particularly in a healthcare setting, that you would further marginalise and discriminate against them,” Young says.

She rang the Queensland AIDS Council, a grassroots organisation formed despite bureaucratic indifference. With their support, she ran educational sessions on HIV for the hospital.

“Did it dampen down the hysteria? I’m not really sure, but we did our best.”

That same year, Young volunteered on the Grim Reaper campaign. While aimed at raising awareness, the commercial was later criticised for contributing to violence against the LGBTQIA+ community.

“The campaign terrified everybody,” Young says.

“They would run the ads and then there’d be a phone number you could ring up … [people would call asking] ‘Can I get it from a coffee cup?’ or ‘My neighbour is gay, should I move out of the building?’

“Just fear, fear, fear. I don’t think I ever took a call from anybody who was actually at risk.”

Bjelke-Petersen resisted calls for safe-sex education and the instalment of condom machines in public facilities, and prohibited funding to the Queensland AIDS Council. But pressure from the federal Labor government to act against the spread of HIV was mounting.

Young describes Mike Ahern, Bjelke-Petersen’s health minister, as a more progressive person whose hands were tied. His federal counterpart, Neal Blewett, found a solution by granting funds to the Mater Hospital, run by the Sisters of Mercy.

The hospital’s Sister Angela Mary Doyle helped to funnel the money to the Queensland AIDS Council, a move that led Blewett to later describe the Sisters of Mercy as “the most altruistic of money launderers”.

“The whole thing about Joh was morality and God, and yet you had the Catholic Church [doing this],” Young says.

“Angela Mary and her leadership were compassionate. They saw sick people who needed care … There’s always people on the margin, people inside, people outside, working.”

Young left Wolston Park after two years and began working for the state government as a health promotions officer.

Inside a repressive government, she got to work slowly. By the late 1980s, infections were growing among drug users and sex workers, and like Doyle, Young began moving money where it was needed.

Bjelke-Petersen resigned in 1987 and was replaced by Ahern, who allowed a clean needle pilot out of a methadone clinic in Fortitude Valley.

“We did a lot of work with the police department to lay off people who were getting needles and syringes, and likewise with condoms,” Young says.

“There are always practical people and people who appreciate the greater good is to do exactly that. As an advocate, you’ve got to learn to work all of those channels.”

The role brought Young to the frontline of fighting the virus, to people whose health was deteriorating rapidly.

“I remember young, gay men – beautiful, handsome men – wasting, getting very, very thin, very quickly, becoming very frail,” she says.

“Getting pneumonia was really common, so hacking coughs, moving into hospital or hospice care and then dying really quickly.”

Young married Graham Neilsen, the doctor tasked with writing the scripts for needles and syringes in the Fortitude Valley methadone clinic.

When the pair moved to Sydney in 1990 for Neilsen’s studies, Young, then aged 30, was appointed the executive director of the Australian Federation of AIDS Organisations, now Health Equity Matters.

“Sydney was more progressive … but there was still nothing to blunt the disease because there weren’t effective treatments,” she says.

“Prevention was condoms only, and clean needles and syringes.”

In 1995, Young and Neilsen moved to Indonesia to continue their work in HIV advocacy. There, the government saw HIV as a Western disease that did not pose a threat to Indonesian citizens.

“It was like banging your head against a brick wall,” Young says.

The pair moved between countries where prevention and health policy was falling behind the devastating pace of the virus for the next 30 years: South Africa during the Mbeki denialism years, Thailand, Cambodia, Papua New Guinea and Fiji.

“Gay men and drug users are always hard to find when it’s highly illegal … but there’s always that underground movement to tap into,” Young says of the cultural and political barriers she’s faced.

“What I’ve tried to do is divert power and therefore resources and move it to communities, because I actually believe that the people closest to the epidemic are in the best position to drive the response.

“[It’s] people moving money, moving power, bringing people in who are on the outside, having people on the inside.

“Advocacy is like a pincer movement. Everyone’s kind of working.”

The walls of Young’s apartment are lined with art collected from her international postings, vignettes of the worlds she tapped into while fighting the spread of HIV.

In 2024, Young was appointed an Officer of the Order of Australia (AO) for her work developing Health Equity Matters’ international programs and her distinguished service to public health.

This year, she made the difficult decision to retire from her longstanding position.

She finds a framed cover from a 2011 edition of The Economist, the headline daring to posit “The end of AIDS?”.

“I had the foresight to think, I’m going to frame that because this is my life’s work, and it’s saying it’s almost over,” Young says.

Fifteen years later, HIV is far from eradicated, with South Pacific nations Fiji and PNG in the grip of a fast-moving epidemic. Young says it proves how relentless the virus is, with HIV rising in communities on the back of the international drug trade.

Back home, Queensland, like other Australian states and territories, has committed to working towards the virtual elimination of new HIV transmissions by 2030, with a focus on prevention, testing and treatment. But even in progressive nations with robust healthcare systems, barriers mounted by political ideology and access continue to present challenges.

Last year, the Queensland government brushed aside calls to introduce a needle-exchange program in the state’s prisons, after reports up to 300 prisoners may have been exposed to HIV. The LNP’s calls for abstinence – “there should be no needles in prisons” – bore the familiar hallmarks of a former government’s refusal to engage in effective public health measures.

“This isn’t about ‘safety’ or condoning drug use, even though that is how it is often framed,” Young says.

“The fight against HIV is fundamentally about human rights … [and] prisons are where human rights arguments get tested the hardest.

“Health interventions cannot succeed without first addressing the social and political structures that deny people their dignity and equality.

“We make progress when we treat people as people – not problems to be solved, but individuals deserving of respect, support and opportunity.

“What I am proudest of, beneath all of the achievements and milestones, is having understood and advocated for this truth: that every gain in HIV prevention, treatment and care began with a fight for human rights.”

‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster

Sydney Morning Herald August 08, 2026

“Adaptation” has not been at the forefront of climate change discussions, but many experts argue it is time to learn to prepare for – not simply react to – the growing number of climate-linked disasters.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Scene one: Bayden Bedwell feels trapped. In the raging October 2022 flood that swept through Greater Shepparton, the worst in the Victorian regional city in more than a century, water rose 40 centimetres above the floor of his three-bedroom home. Insurance was enough to repair it to the way it was, but the house is as vulnerable as ever in a city named in one study as the most susceptible to flood in the country. Bedwell, 28, says “you can still hear the cracking of everything at night”. He and his wife Chloe would like to move their two young children somewhere safer, but they’re stuck – a house on the same street was for sale for nine months, he says, “then went really, really cheap, about $90,000.”

Scene two: Just after 9am at a Darwin cafe, 30 degrees already and heading for 33, Phil Blum and fellow members of the Darwin cycling club recover after a two-hour ride. It’s April, the brutal summer months almost behind him, but Blum, a doctor at Royal Darwin Hospital, isn’t sure how much longer he can deal with the heat. “It’s too hot, and it’s getting hotter,” says the 58-year-old of the capital city with the highest temperatures and humidity in the country. “In 50 years, it will be unliveable.” Blum’s family once opened the doors to let in the breeze; now, they close them. “We use air-conditioning six months of the year, all the time, night and day.” He plans to move south in the coming years. “You don’t want to be having to hide in the air-conditioning all day.”

Scene three: The Tweed Shire, in the far north of NSW, is used to floods. Mayor Chris Cherry rattles them off: 2017, 2022, 2024 and then ex-tropical cyclone Alfred last year. The visitor centre in Murwillumbah was destroyed in the floods of 2017 and, despite works to fortify it, was again “completely annihilated” in 2022. It’s been moved to higher ground. People are on the move, too, with 175 government “buybacks” approved so far of Tweed homes deemed impossible to defend. There’s pressure for more housing. Cherry says, “The community is crying out for reducing the standards and building in places that we normally wouldn’t allow, just because it’s easier, and it’s cheaper land … but we just can’t relax those standards because then we’re just making the same mistake all over again.”

There are thousands of such stories across the country, unique in their details but with a common thread: Australians are confronting the consequences of global warming now, and it will get worse in our lifetimes – or our children’s lifetimes. Whether you talk to climate scientists, insurance companies, and even some politicians, the message is the same: we are doing far too little, far too slowly, to adapt to a climate that has already changed and will be unrecognisable within a generation or two. Governments across the country make commitments and adopt plans, but routinely fail to fund or follow through.

Australians are “psychologically unprepared for the world we are moving into”, writes Professor Clive Hamilton in 2024’s Living Hot: Surviving and Thriving on a Heating Planet. “We urgently need a sustained national conversation … about where we live and how we live as the Earth takes us way outside our climatic comfort zones.”

In climate jargon, preparing to live in a hotter, more extreme world is “adaptation”. It’s different from reducing global-warming emissions through moving away from fossil fuels to renewable energy, for instance – that’s mitigation. The UK’s fourth climate change assessment, released in May – the hottest May on record in the UK – was called A Well-Adapted UK. Greenhouse gas emissions responsible for global warming had dropped in the UK (as they have in Australia) but “there has been little progress on preparing ourselves for the changing climate”, the report said. “Adaptation cannot wait. Keeping people secure is a fundamental duty of the state.” But it would cost – about £11 billion ($21 billion) a year from the public purse and industry.

Australia has been slow – the government published our first national adaptation plan late last year. It was cautious compared to the UK’s clarion call, containing no strategy or cost estimates, but it did warn that the number of resilience projects across the country is “not high in comparison to the current and projected risks, and the low numbers in high-risk regions, such as in the Northern Territory, suggest significant adaptation shortfall at present”. Dr Russ Wise is a senior principal research scientist at CSIRO and has been prodding governments for 15 years to prepare for a transformed climate. Australia’s adaptation plan was an “incremental first step”, he says. What we need is AUKUS-level focus and funding – up to $15 billion a year, including public and private investment. We need “big strategic thinking and planning in every single region around Australia”.
