Adaptation and Australia’s climate crisis

From floods to extreme heat: The human cost of Australia’s changing climate

It’s been a decade since 195 parties, including Australia, signed up to the Paris Agreement to work to keep global warming to “well below 2 degrees” – with the aspiration of holding it to 1.5 degrees – to avoid the worst impacts of global warming. (President Donald Trump has withdrawn the US, the second-highest emitter after China, from the agreement.) Temperatures vary year to year, but climate scientists say that nothing can stop the 1.5 degrees being breached now. Climate change is accelerating. The past three years have been the hottest on record, with 2024 hitting 1.55 degrees of warming. Climate scientists say that the catastrophic heatwave and fires in Europe this year would have been “virtually impossible” without global warming. The “super” El Niño now upon us almost certainly means next year will break another record, bringing devastating heatwaves, storms and bushfires.

Climate science is imprecise, but 2 degrees of warming will be far worse than 1.5, and credible estimates indicate the world will sail past that red line around mid-century, less than 25 years away, with close to 3 degrees predicted by the end of the century. Australia’s first climate-change risk assessment report, released late last year, clarified what we face. Australia “experiences compounding and cascading hazards, and this is going to increase”. One example: by mid-century, more than 1.5 million people will be living in areas of high-sea-level rise and coastal flooding.

The Paris Agreement aimed to treat adaptation with the same urgency as reducing fossil fuel emissions. But it’s a dull word – adaptation – not sexy enough for a culture war, and until recently the poor relation in climate change. It’s about nuts-and-bolts policy, delivered at scale, to prepare for, rather than react to, the impacts of global warming. It’s about individuals upgrading their homes, community sea walls, banning building on flood plains, government “buybacks” and “managed retreat” from areas impossible to defend, and “greening” cities to cool them down. It’s about where and how we live.

Scene four: Rania Omar dreads the upcoming summer. The 26-year-old lives in a granny flat in Blacktown in Sydney’s west, a suburb that can be five degrees hotter in summer than Sydney’s CBD, which is blessed by sea breezes. In a heatwave, it can be 8 to 10 degrees hotter. Omar suffers fibromyalgia, a chronic disorder that causes severe pain and fatigue, and heat makes her seriously unwell. “I’m honestly really nervous,” she says. “I have bad days and good days … but I feel like when that heat hits, I will be having no good days at all.” Western Sydney councils participate in Heat Smart and Cool Centres programs, designating local libraries, swimming pools, community hubs and shopping centres as air-conditioned refuges. Over summer, Omar spends most of the time at home, saving expensive air-conditioning for the hottest days, and getting by with a portable fan and a cooling towel. Even taking the bus is hard; most bus shelters around Blacktown and nearby Penrith council areas don’t have shade.

The insurance industry’s job is to assess and price risk, and it argues Australia is out of time to start protecting its citizens from the impact of climate change, especially the soaring cost of floods and other natural disasters, which are already eye-watering. Federal spending alone on disaster recovery has more than tripled compared to the early 2000s: in the 2024 federal budget, disaster response projections were $11.4 billion; in the May budget, it was up to $16 billion. States also spend billions each year, heavily skewed towards clean-up and recovery – historically, only about 3 per cent of government spending on disasters goes towards prevention, although that has improved recently.

There’s a hard truth to face, says the CEO of the Insurance Council of Australia, Andrew Hall. “We have spent a lot of money on our own emissions reduction but, in fact, the more urgent challenge we’ve got is resiliency because emissions reduction is not going to make any difference to the climate events we are experiencing … number one is you want people to live in a home that’s not going to get destroyed every five to 10 years.”

Hall’s view is contentious, but this debate is swirling across the Western world. Support for taking action on climate change remains strong in Europe and in Australia, but there is fatigue, with immediate cost-of-living pain and ebbing political will. Trump called global warming a “con job” at the UN General Assembly last September.

Living Hot, the book Clive Hamilton wrote with George Wilkenfeld, was provocative. The authors argue that while emissions reduction matters, we have not confronted the reality that nothing Australia does will stop the worsening impacts of climate change here – to pretend otherwise is “wishful thinking”. They also argue that if governments lead a discussion about what we can realistically save and what we can’t, Australians can flourish – but only to a point. The more temperatures rise, the harder it will be to adapt.

“I agree with this much,” says federal Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen. “Even if the world stopped emitting carbon today, there would still be implications from climate change, and those implications would be very real, and we have to deal with the adaptation to climate change … I would agree that adaptation will be and needs to be an increasing focus of governments around the world.” Where Bowen has a “quibble” is with any suggestion that we should rebalance our priorities towards adaptation over emissions reduction. “Yes, Australia is only 1 per cent of [global] emissions, but most countries are 1 per cent of emissions, and if every country took that approach, then you wouldn’t reduce emissions, and we must reduce emissions.”

Independent MP Zali Steggall argues adaptation is urgent and requires national leadership through an independent adaptation commission – based on the UK model – to set priorities, oversee funding, manage insurance gaps and report back on how we’re going. (Australia’s first adaptation report was done in-house in the Environment Department and included no funding estimates.) Steggall proposes a quarter of one per cent of GDP be set aside to fund resilience, because research indicates that every dollar spent preparing saves as much as $10 in cleaning up and rebuilding from disasters down the track.

“This is a matter of national safety and security,” Steggall says. “We’re miles behind. If I did a defence analogy, we’ve got the army amassing on our border, and we don’t actually have any capability. We’re hoping for local communities to take up pitchforks to deal with it.”

The Albanese government is not embracing Steggall’s approach, although after years of Coalition inaction, it gets credit for pushing ahead with a detailed risk report, so at least we know what we face. “We are a federation; that’s not going to change,” says Bowen, whose view is that the federal government can provide a framework for levels of government to work together, but not lead adaptation efforts. That’s up to the states. “The adaptation approach for Cairns does not necessarily need to be decided from Canberra.”

The result is a patchwork, with states doing their own thing – Queensland and NSW have “buyback” programs for homes deemed too unsafe in some areas; Victoria does not, despite pleas from some councils including Shepparton in Victoria, where 80 homes were destroyed in the 2022 floods. The response from the state government was “clearly nothing”, says Greater Shepparton mayor Shane Sali.

Queensland gets credit for initiative. The state’s Reconstruction Authority was established after massive floods in 2011, and is charged with both recovery after disasters and resilience. Its job is to rebuild damaged infrastructure such as roads and bridges to a higher standard than the conventional “like for like” repairs. It’s worth the money. A review of $244 million spent on projects in Queensland between 2013 and 2024 found about $988 million was saved in avoided reconstruction costs – roughly a four-to-one return.

Andrew Hall from the Insurance Council says Brisbane is way ahead, too, in giving residents information. “The council has gotten really good at it; they’ve had to because Brisbane has been, for a very long time, a river with a city problem.” The Brisbane City Council’s Flood Awareness Map provides free details including local history of flooding and aerial maps of your property. NSW’s flood data is available only by region, not by property, although some local councils offer more detail. It’s similar in Victoria, where statewide flood maps are being updated.

“There is no central source of truth about the peril data in this country,” says Hall. You should be able to search on the web for a property and “click on a button and say, ‘Overlay the bushfire or the flood risk of this property,’ and you just get it straight away. ‘What’s the heat risk? What’s the high-tide risk?’ There needs to be a way.”

If there is no one-stop-shop for consumer risk, soaring bills tell their own story. A new study prepared for Good Weekend by insurance consultancy Finity found that since 2021, the average home insurance premium has risen 63 per cent to $4680 in NSW, 43 per cent to $4335 in Queensland and 66 per cent to $2646 in Victoria. Not all of it is due to climate change, but Finity principal Stephen Lau says flood risk is the biggest reason for the increases, particularly in northern NSW and in Shepparton in Victoria.

Scene five: Rob Page, 71, the owner of East Bundaberg Engineering in regional Queensland, says flood damage has cost his business close to $1 million. The latest deluge was in March, but the record Burnett River flood of 2013 was “the real killer, my whole complex was underwater up to the roof … I’ve never seen so many grown men cry.” Page says he can no longer get flood insurance for his business, but it wasn’t meant to be this way. In 2023, the federal and Queensland governments approved funding for a 1.7-kilometre concrete levee to protect Bundaberg’s CBD and eastern suburbs. It was ready to go, until Mayor Helen Blackburn withdrew her support, saying it would be too costly for ratepayers to maintain. “It was a no-brainer,” says Page. “If the levee was in place, I wouldn’t have a drop of water.” If it floods again, he’ll walk away. “I’m just getting old and tired of losing money.”

Among the most exposed places in the country is the Northern Territory. In June, the NT government released its first climate change policy, a three-page resilience plan with not a single mention of “heat”. A few weeks before this, residents of Papunya, a small community north-west of Alice Springs, sued the NT government in the Federal Court for failing to protect tenants from extreme heat exacerbated by climate change. Residents were fainting due to dehydration, said their lawyer, while old people struggled to sleep at night. The risk assessment points out that northern Australia is especially vulnerable to climate change.

Heat is relative – 30 degrees in Hobart is a normal day in Darwin. By local standards, Darwin now has between six and eight heatwave days a year, defined as when both daytime and nighttime temperatures are unusually high for at least three days. If we reach 3 degrees of global warming, more than a third of the year – up to 120 days – could be a heatwave. It’s not just heat, either – the NT has just been through five natural disasters in a single wet season.

The outgoing executive director of Environment Centre NT, Dr Kirsty Howey, is unusual in that she argues the environment movement needs to evolve from its single-minded focus on lobbying governments to phase out fossil fuels and increasing renewable energy projects. Those issues are important, but “we are going to be shifting. It’s a dualism with the climate movement, where we’ll say, ‘fossil fuels out, clean energy in and the problem is solved.’ [yet] it’s not solved here because no matter what Australia does with its emissions and its renewable-energy buildout, we’re looking at being unliveable. I don’t even call it ‘adaptation’ any more. It’s just like, how are we going to live here?”

It’s a question those living in flood-prone areas are also asking. The Insurance Council identifies 24 river catchments across the East Coast needing urgent investment. It is lobbying for a flood defence fund of $30 billion over 10 years, to be paid for by the federal government and the states most impacted: Queensland, NSW and Victoria. So far, there is little interest. The insurance industry is preoccupied by floods because that’s where it is most exposed. It estimates that there are 242,000 residential dwellings facing the highest flood risk across Australia, with more than 186,000 – three-quarters of them – uninsured for flood, in some cases due to prohibitive cost.

The industry is reluctant to reveal exactly where those communities are for commercial reasons, but Climate Valuation has taken up that challenge. It’s a company that provides climate risk analysis to property owners and, working with the Climate Council, last year named Australia’s 86 most vulnerable towns and suburbs. It says that these areas are in “critical climate risk zones” and without large investment will become hard to insure, a disaster for those wanting to buy or sell, and economically crippling for these towns and suburbs. The list was topped by Shepparton in Victoria, whose mayor, Shane Sali, says, rightly, that the analysis did not take into account the work his council has done to strengthen resilience – including new infrastructure, flood overlays in the planning scheme and a mapping project that measures the flood risk of every property. The next riskiest towns, according to the modelling, are Ballina and Tweed Heads in NSW, and Belair in South Australia.

Climate Valuation founder and director Dr Karl Mallon concedes the study’s limitations, but says it’s based on the best data available, similar to that held by insurance companies that don’t release it. It’s an early warning sign. “What we said is, ‘Take a very good look at Lismore [a NSW regional city devastated by floods in 2022]. And if you’re in one of these 86 places, you’re just waiting for a flood to hit.’ And that was controversial.” He applauds Shepparton’s efforts and says insurance companies should be required to consider prevention efforts when setting premiums.

Mallon says the insurance crunch has been coming for decades, and it shouldn’t be up to individuals, often on lower incomes, to pay to upgrade their houses; fossil fuel companies should pay their share. “We’ve got a bunch of people in Australia who are suffering, and we’ve got a bunch of fossil fuel producers in Australia and, if you do the numbers, they are responsible … Making polluters help pay for the damage isn’t a pipe dream but right now, it’s a ‘buyer beware’ market.”

In December 2022, the national cabinet agreed that “the days of developing on floodplains needs to end”. That has not quite happened – although more restrictions do apply – in part because the housing crisis means there is intense pressure to build 1.2 million new homes by 2029.

In NSW, the biggest climate risks are floods and coastal hazard – about 85 per cent of the NSW population lives within 50 kilometres of the coastline. NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully says there are “200-odd years of decision-making in NSW, where if we had our time again ... we wouldn’t have let homes be built in particular areas”. The task is huge. Committee for Sydney chief executive Eamon says natural disasters have cost the NSW government an average of $1.6 billion a year since the 2019-2020 bushfires. This is 1000 per cent higher than the $154 million a year in the six years before that. Governments need to “shift their mindsets” to deal with the two great intergenerational challenges – housing and climate change, he says: “We should be treating them with the same level of existentialism.”

The state has made progress. It now embeds climate resilience into the planning laws, funds councils to plant street trees, and this year adopted a Build Back Better policy. The Reconstruction Authority, established by the former government in 2022, has produced a disaster mitigation plan and is working on regional versions for the high-priority flood-prone Hawkesbury-Nepean Basin in western Sydney and the Northern Rivers in the state’s north.

“The government’s taken a very deliberate position after the 2022 independent inquiry into floods that we wouldn’t be building homes on dangerous floodplains any more,” Scully says. But opinions differ about what constitutes a “dangerous” floodplain, and the pressure to release land for development to solve the housing crisis is real. After initially ruling out rezonings planned for thousands of homes in Marsden Park North and West Schofields in western Sydney, the government later decided to allow a reduced number of new homes with “strict conditions”.

In the Northern Rivers, the NSW government tried a buyback program for homes deemed impossible to defend – by the end of June, 826 buybacks had been completed. A related $100 million Resilient Lands program was meant to fast-track flood-safe land for homes, providing 4382 lots. So far, it is yet to deliver any land for housing. A report by the NSW Auditor-General in May this year was scathing, branding both programs as “not effectively planned before implementation”. Scully concedes the problems, but insists things have improved. NSW is given credit for solid plans, but so far, the funding is not there. “Because of the sheer volume of disasters that have occurred in the last half-decade, there is a growing anxiety among local councils in regional areas that it’s getting out of control,” said Darcy Byrne, president of Local Government NSW and mayor of Inner West Council. “We don’t have enough funding to mitigate risk before disasters occur.”

In Victoria, the government has recently taken over responsibility for flood mapping the whole state and to become the decision-maker when imposing future planning restrictions. Until now, this has been the responsibility of individual councils, one that many were not meeting. Updating flood maps is often controversial among locals who see their home decline in value. In 2022, the shire of Baw Baw completed the mapping but, in the face of a backlash from residents, dropped its planning amendments.

Some floodplains are still being developed for housing. In Echuca, one development was approved on a piece of land that was underwater as recently as the 2022 floods. Planner Jane Keddie, the vice-president of the Planning Institute of Australia, said climate adaptation policies in Victoria were taking a back seat to building 800,000 affordable new homes by 2034, “even when an application (to build) will result in more people being exposed to that hazard”.

Victoria’s policies on bushfire resilience in new buildings led Australia, and it allocated $264 million towards adaptation in the 2025-26 budget – though close to one-third of that is going to rebuilding after the summer bushfires in the state’s west. Victoria has eight high-level Adaptation Action Plans, but a recent upper house parliamentary committee report found that “actions identified by the [government’s adaptation] strategy were underfunded and under-resourced”.

The pressure largely falls on local governments – those managing planning schemes and most sensitive to local needs. Melbourne’s Lord Mayor Nick Reece explains the dysfunction: “The federal government has all the money, the state government has all the laws, and the local government has all the problems.” Councils can pass amendments to insist on higher environmental standards than the legislated minimums, but they must be approved by the state government. Six years ago, Reece’s council proposed then-leading environmental rules for new commercial buildings, including mandates for solar energy, and options for cooling, such as green roofs and the retention of mature trees. It had the support of the Property Council, the peak body for the development industry and, says Reece, while upfront costs would be higher, the “payback is extremely quick” because the buildings would be cheaper to run. The amendments went to an independent panel of experts, which approved them in October 2024. Since then – nothing. Until she lost her job in a reshuffle, it sat unapproved on the desk of the state planning minister Sonya Kilkenny. “It’s extremely frustrating,” says Reece. Kilkenny declined an interview.

The wet season is nearly over and Darwin, Australia’s northern capital, is lush. Large trees emerge from the centres of roundabouts, the sea beyond the northern suburb of Nightcliff sparkles and around the CBD, white high-rise apartments nod to the relaxed air of the tropics.

Look deeper, and Darwin is in trouble. Heat is known as a “silent” killer: major heatwaves have caused more deaths since 1890 than bushfires, cyclones, floods and severe storms combined. It’s not just heat. Northern Australia faces what are called “cascading” risks. In the tired office of Environment Centre NT – the territory government cut its $100,000 funding last year – Kirsty Howey checks her phone. It’s March and she and everyone in greater Darwin has received a “boil water alert” after torrential rain pushed Darwin’s dam to overcapacity and the pump station shut down. Water authorities called it an “unprecedented situation” to avoid contamination. Howey, a lawyer who joined the centre as its head in 2020, ticks off the past few months. First, Cyclone Fina in November, the most intense cyclone system since Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Eve 1974, and “a remarkable early-season tropical cyclone” as reported by the Bureau of Meteorology. Winds were so strong that a section of the Royal Darwin Hospital ceiling collapsed.

Then another “unprecedented” event, according to NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro. On March 7, after what was already weeks of massive rainfall, the Katherine River peaked at 19.2 metres. Residents huddled in schools and patients were evacuated from the local hospital. Hardly a breath was taken before severe Cyclone Narelle made landfall in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia, an extremely rare event.

“Everything’s falling apart,” says Howey, soon to become the CEO of the Wilderness Society. She knows that sounds hyperbolic but insists, “it really is. I’ve been here [in Darwin] for 21 years. I’ve never seen anything on this scale, and there’s no money.” The NT Environment and Planning Minister, Josh Burgoyne, declined an interview. In a statement, he said that recent floods and cyclones “have demonstrated the importance of ensuring our communities, infrastructure and economy are prepared for extreme weather events”. The government had made announcements including a $100 million Flood Recovery Fund to include early-warning systems, flood mitigation and resilience projects.

Scene six: Under a tree at Batchelor, James Parry relives the “rivers roaring” and a crocodile turning up in his backyard before he was evacuated from his home in Daly River, known as Nauiyu, south of Darwin. In March, almost 400 people were evacuated, many by helicopter. They were moved to Darwin before shifting again to temporary accommodation in Batchelor. The damage and mud in Daly River was so severe it would be three months before the last resident went home. That flood was the second in just over a month – Parry, 53, was evacuated twice in a single wet season. It’s time, he says, for the Aboriginal community to move to higher ground, and “get out of the water zone; otherwise we’re going through this every time we get rain, the river comes up.” That idea has been voiced many times, but so far, has not happened. It’s not clear who makes that decision, and who pays for it.

Greater Darwin is home to 159,000 people who love it for its casual lifestyle, the fishing, the spectacular sunsets, the long walks along the beach. It’s hot year-round, but it’s the “build-up” in October and November that is most oppressive, with crippling humidity unrelieved by rain. November is the hottest month, with an average nighttime minimum of 25 degrees and, during the day, an average maximum of 34 degrees which, because of the humidity, feels more like 42 degrees. That is dangerous, and it’s not just about temperature. It was once believed that humans could adapt endlessly to heat – Territorians are proud of their toughness. But a 2010 study co-authored by Professor Steven Sherwood, the deputy director of the Climate Change Research Centre at the University of NSW, put a hard limit on heat stress. A “wet bulb” temperature of 35 degrees – a combination of both temperature and humidity – was the upper limit for human survival because the air becomes so moist, sweat cannot evaporate to cool down the body’s core temperature.

That landmark work has since been refined, especially in real-world “heat chambers” that have found lower limits to heat stress, a 31- or 32-degree wet bulb temperature for even younger people under high humidity, and as low as 23 to 28 degrees for those older than 65. That is deadly, and northern Australia is bumping up against those limits. On oft-quoted study in 2023 found that if global warming reaches 2.7 degrees – highly likely – much of northern Australia faces “near unliveable conditions”.

Sherwood says that at 2.7 degrees of global warming, few people could handle living in Darwin and the health of those who did would suffer. Humans – as well as many native animals and livestock – have not lived under those conditions before. “It tells you that there would start to be heatwaves that people would find very, very difficult to cope with.” Grandiose plans proposed by governments over the years to “populate the north” to 4 or 5 million people make Sherwood “shake my head”. “That might have made sense without global warming, but I think that’s not going to work. I don’t think we move people up there; we’re going to end up moving back.”

If there is a farcical symbol of the Territory’s failure to protect people from heat, it is the 55-metre shade structure over a section of Darwin’s Cavenagh Street, where surface temperatures can reach 70 degrees. In 2017, then chief minister Michael Gunner led a delegation to Singapore, a “green oasis” that could teach Darwin a thing or two about how to flourish in a tropical climate. With him was award-winning NT architect Lawrence Nield, who developed a vision to cool Darwin by 2.7 degrees by mass-planting the right kind of trees, coating black bitumen to cool it down, and creating a Cool Darwin Authority to oversee urban planning. Cavenagh Street was a trial — tropical vines would grow over the structure in about 18 months, a quicker solution than waiting for trees to mature.

What followed was a comedy of errors. The vines chosen weren’t suitable, they were pruned too savagely, and they never grew over the structure. The opposition at the time – now the government – mocked the idea of greening the CBD as a foolish priority compared to crime, health and education. A few months ago, the government announced the vines would be removed.

Nield, the architect of Cavenagh Street and now retired to Sydney, looks on in despair. Yes, the vines didn’t work but they should have been replaced by something better, he says – and the need to cool down Darwin remains urgent. “I feel my six years [as NT architect] were wasted,” he says. The local council is doing its best to boost the canopy cover over Darwin, but it only controls 13 per cent of the municipality. It has given away thousands of native trees for residents to plant in their own backyards.

Nield wrote an article back in 2018 headlined “Requiem or Renewal?” about Darwin’s cool-down experiment. He was hopeful then. So, which was it in the end? “I think it’s a requiem,” he says. “There’s very little renewal.”

Clive Hamilton says it doesn’t have to be this way. Preparing for climate change could be a positive story, he says, a national project. We can’t tell China or the US or India what to do on emissions, but we “can make a really big difference to how lives are lived in Australia”. If we get on with it, “it’s a hopeful message.”

Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 21:44:38 GMT

Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta

Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

Leeds extend lead at top of Super League after thrilling late win at Wakefield

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 21:12:26 GMT

Wakefield 22-24 Leeds

Hankinson’s try seals victory after 16-point deficit

Whisper it quietly but perhaps that was the performance of a champion side. All week the talk had been about Wakefield Trinity and whether this could be the night they declared themselves as a Super League force in front of a sell-out crowd against Leeds Rhinos.

In the end, they probably did that, despite the result. These two West Yorkshire rivals served up a classic under the Belle Vue lights but in the end, despite never leading until the 77th minute, it was Leeds who mustered up all their strength and championship credentials to complete a comeback which began when they trailed by 16 points with half an hour left.

At that stage it felt inevitable that Wakefield would be going joint-top of the table with Leeds. Trinity, a Championship side just two years ago, looked as though they were about to deliver their biggest statement yet that they could be about to end their 60-year wait for a major trophy. However, the Rhinos dug deep and found a way.

James McDonnell’s try gave them hope before three minutes later Cameron Smith, the game’s outstanding player who will play for Wakefield in 2027, scored to mean a 22-6 lead for Wakefield had suddenly been reduced to 22-18. As it entered the championship rounds, it was Trinity who blinked, as Chris Hankinson seized on a Jake Connor kick, with Connor converting to win it.

This was a result and a performance born out of Leeds and Brad Arthur’s darkest moment together. Last year they were beaten in the final seconds by St Helens in the playoffs and the Rhinos spent all pre-season warning there would be no repeat. This felt like living proof of that; Leeds showing they can go to the well in the toughest of times to secure a huge win.

“That’s the evidence of us learning from it,” Arthur said. “We’ve done the work. Under a bit of pressure we kept our composure, our key players kept composure. I challenged them at half-time to go right to the 80th minute ... boy, they did it.” Leeds were outplayed for large stretches here, with Wakefield good value for their 16-6 half-time lead.

Tries from Isaiah Vagana, Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Jayden Myers put Trinity in control, and had the majority of this sell-out crowd dreaming of going joint-top. Brodie Croft’s try just before the break gave Leeds hope but when Jack Sinfield scored against his former club to make it 22-6, it looked as though the momentum was back with Wakefield.

The Rhinos were on the ropes. But this group are built different in 2026, with McDonnell’s try starting the comeback and Hankinson’s finishing it – with Leeds surviving a frantic final few moments to go four points clear with five games left. With this win Leeds are now heavy favourites to finish top: their first piece of silverware in six years.

As for Wakefield, they will be bruised by this. Having lost by four to Wigan in the cup quarter-finals and now by two here to the league leaders, this was perhaps a subtle lesson again about the final step Trinity still have to take. They should, however, take great pride from this – and great heart from what they did for the most part if they meet Leeds again in the playoffs.

US police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at border

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 20:49:24 GMT

Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute

A Texas police officer has been arrested in Mexico after authorities there accused him of killing three people and critically injuring the mother of his child in what investigators say stemmed from a dispute over the custody of the minor.

The Coahuila attorney general’s office said 35-year-old Chad Eberle was arrested on Wednesday at the border on a warrant accusing him of femicide and qualified homicide, according to La Razon de Mexico, a newspaper based in Mexico City. Under Mexican law, femicide refers to the intentional killing of a woman or girl because of her gender.

According to La Razon, the deadly shooting happened in July in Saltillo, Mexico, after an argument over Eberle allegedly not having permission to take his three-year-old son. Two women and one man were killed in the attack.

The victims were identified by La Razon with the first names and ages of Ana Laura, 44; Laura Jaquelín, 22; and Emanuel, 44. The child’s 26-year-old mother was also shot in the head and remained in critical condition, officials said.

Investigators said Eberle was arrested while attempting to cross from Mexico into Texas through the international bridge at Piedras Negras, across from Eagle Pass, KTXS reported. Eberle had left the residence with his son in a gray Chevrolet Silverado, prompting investigators to launch a manhunt as they tracked the vehicle toward the Texas border, the US Sun reported.

He was then intercepted before he could re-enter the US with the child. The three-year-old was unharmed and was later placed in the care of Coahuila’s child welfare agency.

The San Antonio Express identified Eberle as a police officer in the central Texas town of Santa Anna. Before that, he worked as a deputy constable with Bexar county – which includes San Antonio – and also served as a police officer for the Northside independent school district.

The Express reported that Eberle also held law enforcement positions in the Texas communities of Somerset, Marble Falls, Gregory, near Corpus Christi, Lockney in the state’s panhandle, and Bangs in the west. According to the newspaper, a 2022 Facebook post from the Lockney police department described Eberle as an army veteran.

In a social media post on Thursday, Coahuila attorney general Federico Fernández said: “It is reported that at [9.59p] Chad ‘N’ has been admitted to the Saltillo men’s penitentiary in compliance with [an] arrest warrant, where he has been placed at the disposal of the competent judicial authority, in accordance with the corresponding procedure.”

He added: “Likewise, the minor is already in the city of Saltillo, under the custody and care of the prosecutor’s office for boys, girls and the family (Pronnif), in order to guarantee the comprehensive protection of his rights.”

Texas news outlet Coleman Today obtained a statement from Santa Anna city officials which described Eberle as “one of our reserve officers … [who] was on a personal leave of absence until December.

“The Santa Anna police department has been in contact with the US consulate in Mexico and [the Texas commission on law enforcement].”

That statement also said Eberle was “an unpaid reserve police officer hired in November 2025 and worked one weekend per month.

“Due to the ongoing investigation, no other public comment will be made.”

Sky Country: Indigenous fashion weaves culture and climate together

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 20:00:26 GMT

First Nations designers, models, artists and artisans from across Australia gathered on Larrakia Country in Darwin this week for the Country to Couture runway show and the National Indigenous Fashion awards. In between, Guardian Australia photographed several of the featured models and designers

Delvene Cockatoo-Collins wins National Indigenous Fashion award for textiles harvested on Country

First Nations fashion celebrates weaving, wattle and waterways at Country to Couture 2026 – in pictures

Keep scrolling

Models CJ Rankin, a Kiyak woman, and Nelson Baker Bardi, a Nyikina man, wear Nagula Jarndu Designs.

The art centre Nagula Jarndu (Saltwater Woman) began in Rubibi/Broome in 1987 as a place for Yawuru women to gather, preserve language, share knowledge and keep culture strong. Their hand-carved woodblock prints on cotton and silks, shown at Country to Couture, share stories of saltwater, plants, family and Country.

CJ Rankin wears Corella & Crow.

Shown at Country to Couture, the Madhan (Tree) collection by Corella & Crow uses upcycled materials including reclaimed curtains, alongside dyeing, printmaking, beading and embroidery, to celebrate the cultural and ecological significance of trees. Slow fashion processes are a way for the label to honour and care for materials, story and place.

Yvonne Rankin (left) and CJ Rankin wear designs by Yarrenyty Arltere Artists.

Yarrenyty Arltere Artists’ collection Thepa Ilpalha is the work of Rhonda Sharpe, Dulcie Sharpe, Marlene Rubuntja, Louise Robertson and Sheree Inkamala, who bring their love of painted and soft sculpture birds to life in bold structured pieces on cotton.

Model Jake Powers, a Yaruwu and Kija man, wears Lucas Schober.

Model turned designer Lucas Schober showcased at Country to Couture for the first time. This ensemble, modelled by Jake Powers, is inspired by the gakinga (magpie goose), a migratory bird whose arrival to the Northern Territory symbolises the beginning of balnba (wet season). Here, Schober has taken feathers from the bird and hand-stitched them over a linen cape, which he has also printed with emblems of the bird.

Powers was named this year’s Cecilia Cubillo Young Achiever at the National Indigenous Fashion awards. The 21-year-old Bardi, Yawuru and Kija man, who grew up watching international couture shows on YouTube from his home in Broome, also served as a stylist and production assistant at the ceremony.

Powers told Guardian Australia he is working toward launching his own collection. “We’ve found a different ways to tell stories through garments, which is a whole other level of creativity and innovation that this industry needs,” he said.

Photograph: (A)manda Parkinson/The Guardian

Photograph: (A)manda Parkinson/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

From left: Jake Powers, Yvonne Rankin and Nelson Baker Bardi, all wearing Lucas Schober.

Yvonne Rankin wears Bobbi Lockyer x Skye Lockyer x Mali Isabel.

A three-way artist collaboration shown at Country to Couture, Bobbi and Skye Lockyer and Mali Isabel’s collection the Mermaid Collective is inspired by saltwater Country, mermaid mythology, cultural storytelling and activism. It blends streetwear with handcrafted details such as beadwork, weaving and embroidery. The “Save Lee Point” T-shirt refers to the ongoing campaign against defence housing expansion at Lee Point.

Keep scrolling

CJ Rankin wears Bábbarra Women’s Centre (left) and Jaymee-Lee Chaquebor.

The National Indigenous Fashion award’s Community Collaboration prize celebrated a cross-cultural printing partnership between Bábbarra Women’s Centre, based in the remote community of Maningrida, and Bengaluru’s Tharangini Studio. Bábbarra artists travelled to India to translate their ancestral lino-cut designs and cultural stories into woodblocks used for printing, while sharing techniques.

Bardi artist Jaymee-Lee Chaquebor’s Jarrabinmy collection was shown at this year’s Country to Couture. The garments’ prints are deeply rooted in Bardi culture, storytelling and the relationship between land and sea.

Keep scrolling

CJ Rankin wears MumRed.

National Indigenous Fashion award finalist Samala Cronin is best known for her one-of-a-kind pieces. This year, she showcased her first ready-to-wear collection under her label MumRed at Country to Couture. The Flow State collection is designed to honour and celebrate every stage of the menstrual cycle.

CJ Rankin wears Noongar Arts Fashion.

Noongar Arts Fashion made their debut at this year’s Country to Couture with a collection titled Kambarang, a series of dresses celebrating the Noongar season of transformation and birth, when Wardandi Country comes alive with wildflowers – golden wattle blossoms, vibrant kangaroo paws, delicate orchids and everlastings.

At least one person has died in a wildfire burning in the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range that officials believed was sparked by a man using a chainsaw.

Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has destroyed seven buildings, scorched more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county and killed a well-known dog breeder in the town of Angels Camp.

In an interview with KCRA, Smith told reporters he did not mean to spark the fire. Monday was his birthday, he said, and he had been using machinery to cut scraps in order collect money for a celebratory meal with his wife.

“I’m so sorry for everything that’s happened,” Smith told the news station. “This is going to destroy my life, one way or another.”

Officials allege that Smith is responsible for “recklessly causing” the blaze on Monday while “operating equipment capable of producing sparks” without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California department of forestry and fire protection. Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges.

In 2018, Smith was charged with igniting another fire, KCRA reported, and was accused of “willfully and unlawfully [setting] fire to any forest, brush, or other flammable material which is on any land that is not his own, or under his legal control, without the permission of the owner, lessee, or agent of the owner or lessee of the land”. He pleaded no contest and received a sentence of 36 months’ probation.

As of Friday morning, the Gann fire had burned more than 10,000 acres and was about 40% contained.

Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home near the town of Angels Camp, the Calaveras county sheriff’s office said. Friends have identified the victim as Susan Solari and a neighbor told CBS Sacramento that she refused to leave her dogs.

“I told them she was there, that her dogs were there and she couldn’t get her dogs out,” Joan Wilson told the outlet. “She wasn’t going to leave them.”

The Gann fire comes amid a grueling fire season in the American west. Three major fires have continued to burn around the city of Spokane in north-eastern Washington and have destroyed at least 800 buildings. A 37-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly sparking one of the fires, and court documents accuse him of studying how to maximize the blaze’s destruction.

No deaths have been reported in Washington. Officials reported on Thursday that cooler temperatures and calmer winds have allowed firefighters to make progress.

Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 19:04:48 GMT

People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area

A smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford.

On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in the Norfolk market town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers.

“The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town.

“Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers.

For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said.

However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions.

“I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.”

Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday.

Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited.

“I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices.

The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere.

If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger.

Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by the Home Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.

“The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy.

“I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.”

Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office.

Social media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others.

In answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand.

The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023.

Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs.

Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”.

He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford, and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers.

Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said on GB News on Friday that people had a right to protest but that the disorder in Thetford had been “horrendous”.

“What we’ve seen is spilling over into violence, which is just not acceptable,” she said. “Nobody should feel harassed, intimidated or threatened in their home, and certainly we shouldn’t see our emergency workers and our police attacked in the way that we have seen.”

Infantino’s World Cup sell-off debacle has rocked football but Fifa’s crisis has deep and rotten roots

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 19:00:25 GMT

It has been a remarkable few days for an institution that may be irredeemable but this is a story that stretches back to a decision in 2010

There are decades in which nothing happens, and weeks in which decades happen, and those weeks tend to result in leaders being toppled. Not even a fortnight ago, Gianni Infantino was taking his victory lap on Instagram, attacking “those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours” who had dared to question elements of his World Cup, which had generated a record $15bn in revenues. But the next day came the revelation of his plan to sell the World Cup to outside investors and a backlash that has him scrabbling to save his presidency.

It has been a remarkable few days, but this is a story whose roots stretch way back, to the decision in Zurich in 2010 to award the 2022 World Cup not to the US but to Qatar, to a furious Bill Clinton hurling an ashtray across the room and demanding action, to an FBI inquiry into corruption, and to the flipping of the larger-than-life Concacaf general secretary Chuck Blazer, who had two apartments in Trump Tower, one for himself and one for his cats.

Blazer now appears as the cheery, bearded, acceptable face of Fifa corruption. He drove about on a mobility scooter with his parrot, Max, on his shoulder and once high-fived Vladimir Putin after the Russian president suggested he looked like Karl Marx. But it was Blazer’s evidence that led to the arrests at Zurich’s Baur au Lac hotel in 2015 and the resignation of Sepp Blatter six days later.

The overwhelming favourite to replace Blatter was the president of Uefa, Michel Platini. He, though, was unacceptable to the US, because it was his decision to switch his vote to Qatar, following – although he maintains not as a result of – a meeting at the Élysée Palace with the then French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the crown prince and prime minister of Qatar.

Conveniently, evidence was found of a payment he had received from Fifa in 2011 leading to his suspension. The Berne federal prosecutor, Michael Lauber, broke protocol to name Platini as something “between a witness and a suspect”. It was enough: Platini stepped aside and Infantino stepped in as Uefa’s candidate. Lauber subsequently became attorney general of Switzerland only to resign after secretly meeting Infantino while investigating Fifa. Platini was subsequently cleared and is suing both Fifa and Infantino.

At the time, Infantino was the secretary general of Uefa, notable largely for his comical earnestness while conducting Champions League draws. He was elected Fifa president in February 2016, defeating the Bahraini Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the president of the Asian Football Confederation, an avid hunter of wild boar who denied allegations of complicity in the torture of pro-democracy campaigners. Key had been a late change of mind by the Caribbean bloc: Sunil Gulati, the president of the US Soccer Federation, took credit for his persuasiveness.

With an ally elected, the US, Mexico and Canada won the right to host the 2026 World Cup. “You wanted to have it there and I wanted to have it there, and we really did it before we came to office,” Donald Trump, performing his classic trick of supervillain exposition, told Infantino at a dinner in Davos in 2020. The order of events is worth reiterating: Infantino was elected in February 2016, Trump was inaugurated in January 2017, the World Cup hosting decision was taken in May 2018.

The US has been a constant in Infantino’s presidency. He took power at a time when the US attorney general, Loretta Lynch, was promising to swill corruption out of Fifa but in terms of decisive action that has amounted to little more than a handful of cases involving dodgy South American broadcast rights deals. In May 2019 Fifa appointed as legal representatives the US law firm Paul Weiss. A few weeks earlier Paul Weiss had named a new senior partner: the former US attorney general Lynch. The following year, she praised Fifa’s newfound “transparency and ethical behaviour”.

Few would agree with her. Infantino arrived promising reform, yet within a year he was removing two leaders of Fifa’s ethics commission. The same weekend that Trump sacked James Comey as head of the FBI, in part for investigating Russian interference in US politics, Infantino fired Miguel Maduro, the chair of the governance and review committee, for blocking the re-election as a Fifa vice-president of the head of the Russian Football Union Vitaly Mutko on the grounds that as Russia’s sports minister he breached guidelines on political involvement.

Infantino repeatedly bypassed the Fifa council, ducked the scrutiny of press conferences and came increasingly to rule by fiat. The plan to sell off a chunk of the World Cup is just the most egregious example. Why would he keep a plan of such revolutionary significance from his senior staff? Why would he give his members 53 days to consider such a plan, offering them a cash bonus to acquiesce? Why would he undermine his own tournament with hydration breaks and a half-time show in the final? Why override disciplinary protocols so the right players will be on the field, seemingly to highlight the tournament’s commercial appeal to potential investors?

The people who were in on the deal were connected to the Trump family, specifically Joshua Kushner, the brother of the president’s son-in-law. Again, questions immediately arise. Why would you sell off 21% of all future revenues for only 28% of what this World Cup made? Infantino’s relationship with Trump – awarding him the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize, appearing with him at world events, giving him a Club World Cup trophy, renting an office for Fifa in Trump Tower that is seemingly barely used – had already brought criticism.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Uefa’s robust and united response, the threat to boycott Fifa tournaments, was evidently not anticipated. The plan is dead, at least for now. Infantino, damaged, clings on, having rallied at least some senior Fifa staff at an emergency meeting in Rabat this week. The chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, one of the two members of the five-man inner council who voted against the plan when informed about it the day before the World Cup final, was, notably, not there. Plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams, rallying Infantino’s base, have been accelerated.

Letters of support that had looked as if they would ensure Infantino a further term unopposed are being withdrawn. On Friday, perhaps impressed by the promise of the 2030 World Cup final being in Casablanca, the Confederation of African Football pledged its support, joining Mexico, Argentina, Qatar, the UAE, Lebanon, Kuwait, Bhutan and Sri Lanka in backing Infantino.

Perhaps there will be an election, as scheduled, next March. Perhaps Infantino can muster a majority among Fifa’s 211 members. But Uefa has vowed to “paralyse” Fifa until he is gone. The first tournament that might be boycotted is the Under- 20 Women’s World Cup, which begins in Poland on 5 September. Poland has made significant investment in infrastructure and is keen for the tournament to go ahead as scheduled but its football federation would be unlikely to step outside the Uefa bloc.

The politicking goes on although already the discussion seems more about who might challenge or defeat Infantino than about how to change Fifa, where clientelism has reigned since João Havelange won the 1974 presidential election. The institution itself is rotten; it may be that it is irredeemable.

It’s very hard to know how genuine Infantino’s attempt to reform Fifa was, but it quickly foundered. And so Fifa’s attempt to move on from the crisis caused by the executive who rented an apartment for his cats in Trump Tower has wound up back in Trump Tower, with a president who rents an office there.

In the end there was a clear winner. And Jay-Z’s latest victory came only 24 hours after the first record featuring him actually rapping for four years had been released by his wife, Beyoncé, on an extended remix pack of Morning Dew (Donk).

These days, the man who remains one of the most influential artists in hip-hop has his fingers in many pies, from the streaming service Tidal and his own streetwear brand, to champagne and cognac. But it is Roc Nation Sports – an offshoot of his entertainment company of the same name founded in 2008 – making headlines in the summer transfer window.

Established five years later in partnership with Creative Artists Agency, it began mainly representing players from the NBA, NFL and MLB, including Kevin Durant. Bayern Munich’s Jérôme Boateng was the first football client, in 2015, before Roc Nation Sports International (RNSI) was established four years later with a focus on stars at big European clubs.

Based in London, it now has more than 100 players on its books, including Vinícius Júnior – the Brazil forward who signed a lucrative new contract with Real Madrid this week believed to be worth around €25m. That came after Arsenal had been linked with a blockbuster move for the 26-year-old. In July 2023 RNSI took over the successful Brazilian agents TFM – who already represented Vinícius, Gabriel Martinelli, and Endrick – and renamed it Roc Nation Sports Brazil.

In negotiations that have lasted two years, it had hoped to persuade Real to increase their star asset’s salary to €30m a year to match Kylian Mbappé, and allowed his contract to enter its final 12 months in an effort to drum up interest elsewhere. While Arsenal – now exploring other attacking options including Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye – are believed to have been willing to pay a big fee for Vinícius, it is understood that they thought signing him on a free transfer next season was more likely.

Nonetheless, Real upped their offer and Vinícius stayed. It is a decision that looks likely to cost them the chance to sign Rodri from Manchester City after Barcelona stole a march on their great rivals.

On the same day as the new six-year contract for Vinícius was announced, Yan Diomande flew to the Spanish capital to complete his record £115m transfer from RB Leipzig. The 19-year-old – who has made only 46 appearances at senior level for the German club and for Leganés in the Spanish second division but is already the most expensive African player in history – was pictured with his agents, Nathan Campbell and Kareem Gbaja on a private jet. RNSI has been reported to have been paid up to £17m in commission and fees.

A long-running saga that began when Liverpool had a £70m bid rejected by Leipzig in June ended with Diomande signing a seven-year deal at the Bernabéu on Thursday. It has provided a telling insight into the mechanisms of a modern transfer, with every week bringing a fresh twist. Having been told they must pay in excess of £100m to sign Diomande, Paris Saint-Germain withdrew from the race at the end of July after releasing a statement that said the European champions “will not engage in the inflationary and manipulative games of certain player agents”.

RNSI has also had to fend off two legal challenges, including one from the former Bournemouth winger Max Gradel who claims that his agency, Maxidel Management, had an existing agreement with Diomande. Gradel has filed a complaint with Fifa, although world football’s governing body did not block the player’s move to Real. Dez Bamba – who is president of Diomande’s first club, AFI Sud Comoé in Côte d’Ivoire – has said that the winger was persuaded to join RNSI after receiving a call from Vinícius. RNSI has not commented on the case.

Meanwhile, the Rainbow World Group instigated proceedings at the high court in London and the British Virgin Islands against Diomande in mid-June “to enforce binding image rights and intellectual property agreements tied to his early career development”. It is claimed Rainbow invested significant resources in the winger, including taking him for trials at Chelsea, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Newcastle before he was signed by Leganés. RNSI has not commented on the case. Given Diomande’s meteoric rise, perhaps it is no surprise that clubs are flocking to invest in African academies.

Jeff Luhnow – the former general manager of the Astros and St Louis Cardinals who won three World Series baseball titles and owns Leganés as part of his Blue Crow network of clubs – told the Guardian last year Diomande was expected to be the first of many after they set up recruitment and development programmes in several African countries, including Ghana and Zambia, in the past several years. “We’ve got more players like that in our pipeline,” said Luhnow.

RNSI announced in November that it has signed eight young African stars, including the Ghana Under-17 midfielder Joseph Narbi and Francis Gomez, a Gambian winger currently at AC Horsens in Denmark. “We believe Africa is a hotbed of untapped footballing potential, and our expansion here is a natural progression of our global vision,” said Campbell.

In the dog-eat-dog world of football agents Jay Z’s new kids on the block are certainly making their presence felt.

Argentina’s government posts ICE-style video of immigration operation

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 18:40:03 GMT

Social media video shows 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs, but she was released minutes later

The Argentinian government posted a video on social media showing a 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs by two federal police officers during an immigration operation in Buenos Aires.

The woman’s face is shown unblurred in the video, which has nearly 1m views and depicts one of hundreds of such operations carried out by the administration of the far-right president, Javier Milei, directly inspired by Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown in the US.

Visibly distressed, appearing to be in pain and with one hand bandaged, the woman is shown against a heavy metal soundtrack as the words “Illegal foreigner or criminal record? Out!” flash across the screen.

In another video, she is described as “a Peruvian national subject to an arrest warrant for fraud and robbery”.

But there was no arrest warrant for her.

The woman, who asked to be identified only by her initials, PLS, said she was released just minutes after being paraded in handcuffs before photographers and television crews covering the operation, which took place last February.

“They just drove me around the block and said: ‘Get out. You’re free.’ I asked: ‘Why did you put me through all this?’” she said.

“My face was everywhere on social media. I started getting calls from relatives living abroad – back in Peru, in Spain, the US and Germany – asking me: ‘What happened? What did you do?’” she added.

According to her lawyer, PLS is a legal permanent resident and was subject only to a “whereabouts inquiry” – requiring her to be notified about a separate case – which, under Argentinian law, does not entail arrest or any other form of coercion.

“Her detention was unlawful, and the authorities used it as propaganda for their operations against immigrants,” said Lucía Galoppo, a lawyer at the NGO Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), which is representing PLS.

CELS sees her case as a striking example of how Milei is reshaping the country’s immigration laws to bring them closer to those of Trump – whom the Argentinian president openly admires – including by creating an Argentinian version of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Checks on people’s immigration status existed before, but they have become far more frequent, large-scale operations involving not only immigration agents but federal police.

Much like Trump, Milei has turned raids in poorer, traditionally immigrant neighbourhoods into a “public spectacle”, said Galoppo.

Since taking office in December 2023, the self-styled libertarian has introduced a series of changes to immigration law by decree, bypassing congress.

The latest came in late July, when Milei invoked his claim that there had been an “anti-Argentina” wave since the World Cup to justify a decree allowing the deportation of foreigners who promote “messages of hate” against the country or any Argentinian citizen.

Critics pointed to the irony that, had countries Milei recently visited adopted the same rule, the president himself could have been expelled after insulting Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez.

Other decrees include ending the automatic right to permanent residency for foreigners who have a child born in the country or marry an Argentinian citizen, and requiring immigrants to prove they have sufficient financial means to support themselves – in a country where more than 40% of workers are informally employed.

While making it harder to obtain documentation, Milei has also restricted free access to public hospitals, previously available to everyone but now limited to permanent residents, except in emergencies.

“The state is manufacturing a problem to manufacture a security-based response,” said Galoppo. “Argentina doesn’t have an immigration problem,” she added. In the 2022 census, immigrants made up 4.2%, the lowest proportion since records began in 1869.

Galoppo believes Milei is targeting immigrants as part of a strategy to create an “internal enemy” that distracts from domestic problems – alongside corruption scandals, his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen.

Milei did not respond to requests for comment.

CELS filed freedom of information requests with the government about its immigration operations. There were 851 between 1 January and 26 June. The government provided further details on only 590 of them, in which just 2.2% of the foreigners stopped were found to have irregular immigration status.

“These operations are highly theatrical, deploying hundreds of police officers in an attempt to imitate raids in the US, but the tiny number of people found to have irregular status shows they are not justified,” said Galoppo.

In the lawsuit filed against the state on behalf of PLS, CELS alleges that she was subjected to unlawful deprivation of liberty, degrading treatment, public humiliation and abuse of authority. PLS has lived in Argentina since 2006.

The “whereabouts inquiry” involving her relates to a 2021 case. In it, a person whose phone was stolen alleged that money had been transferred from their account to one in PLS’s name and then to a third account. PLS denies any involvement, saying her own phone had been stolen months earlier and may have been used to create an account in her name.

Her lawyer said being sought for notification did not justify her detention.

The security ministry also did not respond to requests for comment.

PLS said she felt ashamed and afraid to leave home after the operation, costing her her livelihood as a street food vendor. “If I saw a police officer, I was frightened thinking they might arrest me,” she said.

But she added that she had no intention of leaving: “I’ve done nothing wrong. I’m not a criminal. I’m someone who works. I liked Argentina, and I want to stay here.”

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 18:00:23 GMT

Millions of adults and children in England face being forced to wait longer for mental health care, with more than two-thirds of NHS providers planning to cut services and half expected to axe jobs, the Guardian can reveal.

With mental health services already under extraordinary pressure amid soaring demand for support, experts warned the proposed cuts – drawn up by trusts to plug holes in their finances – would also have “significant” consequences for the wider NHS, the economy and public services.

Key services such as child and adolescent mental health care, talking therapies, addiction support, help for adults undergoing a mental health crisis and community programmes, including those for ethnic minorities and low-income groups, are among those that may be affected.

Seven in 10 (68%) NHS trusts providing mental health services are likely to reduce or shut some of their services in 2026-27, according to the results of a national survey conducted by the NHS Alliance and seen by the Guardian.

Of respondents, 59% said they expect to freeze vacancies, with more than half (57%) likely to cut the number of clinical staff they employ this year.

Earlier this week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029. Writing on LinkedIn, he said: “These services will make it much easier for people to get the right support, at the right time, in the right place.”

Mental health charities welcomed the ambition but said if funding for staff and services was being cut, meaningful improvements to care would be “impossible”.

One of the NHS mental health trusts affected, East London foundation trust, plans to cut a wide range of services and axe hundreds of jobs to close a £25m hole in its finances, the Guardian reported on Monday.

NHS mental health professionals at other trusts said similar plans were being drawn up where they work. They fear the cuts will strip back services so much that they will not be able to properly perform their duties or guarantee safe care in their areas.

An NHS consultant psychiatrist, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “This is not an isolated example in east London. Many mental health trusts are in a similar, if not worse, situation and are responding in similar ways through cutting jobs and compromising service delivery.”

A mental health service manager at a third NHS mental health trust said: “Many mental health trusts are in a similar position. They have faced declining funding for the last couple of years alongside cost reduction targets.”

Alex Stewart, assistant director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said: “Mental health services are coming under extraordinary pressure as a result of rapidly rising demand for care and very tough financial conditions.

“Despite this, we see many examples of innovation and great care which give real grounds for hope. But it’s increasingly evident that the trade-offs and difficult decisions over jobs and services which we warned about are making their mark.

“Mental health leaders face particular pressures when finances are tight because a higher proportion of their expenditure goes on staff.”

The French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday.

Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back to France.

The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’”

Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”.

In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true.

“I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.”

Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said.

On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings.

Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land.

Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year.

The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings.

UK officials believe that government initiatives to “stop the boats” by financing the French authorities with another £660m in April have disrupted the business model of people smugglers in northern France and reduced the number crossing to the UK.

Gangs are adapting their tactics. Boat launches have spread further along the coast, with some leaving from Belgium and others from as far south as Dieppe, a journey of 70 miles (113km) to the UK, compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles.

Officials are concerned the trend towards “mega-dinghies” – larger motorised boats – is putting more people at risk. More than 170 migrants were rescued on Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire.

The sustained drop in crossings was a welcome development for Burnham, allowing him to focus his early weeks in government on setting out his policy agenda.

Shabana Mahmood, who Burnham has kept in post as home secretary, has been reluctant to celebrate the recent drop because she is conscious the trend could change if there is an increase in arrivals in the late summer and autumn months.
