Kasia Niewiadoma took a spectacular solo victory on the legendary Mont Ventoux, securing a slim overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes after leaving behind her fellow race favourites Marlen Reusser and Demi Vollering.

“It’s hard to describe my feelings because I’m still blown away by what just happened,” Niewiadoma, who won the yellow jersey in 2024, said of the first Tour stage victory of her career.

In one of the most memorable climbing performances on the fearsome Giant of Provence, the 31-year-old Polish rider took back the best part of two minutes on Reusser, who had led the race since Tuesday’s individual time trial. With two stages remaining Niewiadoma leads overall by 15sec from Vollering, the 2023 champion. Reusser trails by 39sec in third after stage seven.

Vollering’s initial attack, which came on one of the climb’s few hairpins, the Virage du Bois, was promptly closed down by Reusser and Niewiadoma, who, just as they had at Mont Brouilly on stage five, stuck doggedly to the Dutch rider’s wheel. Their collective effort was enough to force the issue, and the trio rode ahead to contest the stage.

Niewiadoma’s decisive acceleration came just under 10km from the summit, after she, Reusser and Vollering had moved ahead of the front group. Vollering and Reusser seemed more focused on each other, hesitating as Niewiadoma went clear. That sealed their fate. Since its rebirth in 2022, Niewiadoma has always finished on the podium of the Tour, and her epic duel with Vollering on Alpe d’Huez in 2024 may yet be replayed in this weekend’s racing in the hills around Nice.

“It means the world to me to get the yellow jersey by winning on the Ventoux,” she said. “A lot of work went into it. Each year you have to come to the Tour even stronger than the year before because the level is going up so much.”

Niewiadoma’s pace took her clear on the approach to Chalet Reynard, while Reusser and Vollering appeared to be riding through treacle. In fact, it was more of a tactical stalemate that was finally broken when Vollering attacked Reusser in the final kilometre to finish second on the stage. Reusser crossed the line in a weary fourth place but there was plenty of suffering elsewhere on a stage in which a number of big names fell by the wayside.

Among those to leave even before the stage started was Anna van der Breggen of SD Worx-Protime, who dropped out on Friday morning. The 36-year-old Dutch rider, who finished second overall in the Vuelta and third in the Giro earlier this year, was described as “not feeling at her best”. “We kept hoping she would start to feel better as the race progressed, but unfortunately that improvement never came. We decided not to take any unnecessary risks and to give her the rest she needs,” said the sports director Danny Stam.

A US federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to halt construction of the US president’s $400m White House ballroom, in a fresh blow to the controversial project.

Donald Trump, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.

But in a major setback in a case testing ⁠his presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of ​appeals for the District of Columbia circuit upheld a preliminary injunction in a divided 2-1 order on Friday.

The appeals court put ⁠its ruling on hold for two weeks, allowing the administration to appeal to the ​US supreme court. Writing on social media, Trump described the ruling as “totally wrong” and said an appeal would be filed.

Explaining their majority decision, Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia wrote: “Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.”

The judges also said it was for US Congress to determine whether the ballroom could ultimately be built. “Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” they wrote.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” the judges added. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom.

“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the constitution and laws require.”

Trump criticized the decision, which he argued “severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working”, at the White House. “This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.”

A third judge on the panel, Neomi Rao, who was appointed by Trump, dissented and sided with the president’s assertion that the ballroom project was within his authority. Her position earned praised from the president in his social media statement on Friday.

The injunction was won by the National Trust for Historic ⁠Preservation, which sued last year after the Trump administration tore down the East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360 sq meter) ballroom without seeking authorization from Congress.

The latest decision supports an earlier ruling issued by a US federal judge in April, which limited the construction project only to the undergound part of the project deemed necessary on national security grounds while blocking the hospitality facility envisioned by Trump for entertaining guests.

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:00:14 GMT

Serious failings by one academic, and his bosses at the University of Cambridge, should not be allowed to undermine wider progressive goals

Jason Arday’s resignation from the University of Cambridge on Wednesday marked a full stop of sorts, but not an end to the furore surrounding his promotion to a professorship at the age of 37. Academic colleagues have demanded, with justification, that an investigation into his appointment to the faculty of education in 2023, and the subsequent fallout, should include people from outside the university. Allegations of plagiarism and claims made by Mr Arday about his background, career and charity fundraising remain under scrutiny. The memoir for which he said he had received a huge advance, billed as a triumph over adversity including an early autism diagnosis, is scheduled to appear later this month. His publisher, Simon & Schuster, ought to pause while inquiries run their course.

But several things are already clear. By failing to do due diligence on Mr Arday before launching him, with fanfare, as Cambridge’s youngest-ever black professor, and through its inadequate response to later challenges, the university has done a serious disservice to black and neurodivergent scholars more widely. It has also set back the efforts of all the people and groups who have worked in good faith, over many years, to boost the presence of underrepresented groups in influential positions.

Such imbalances, which remain pronounced in many areas of public life, including academia, are the consequence of prejudices and discrimination, as well as unequal access to resources and opportunities. The glee with which some rightwingers have pounced on Mr Arday’s fall from grace is not solely due to relish in his exposure – or the angst among liberals that this provokes. It is because they want to stoke a sense of grievance among white supporters, and to pour scorn on diversity initiatives across the board.

Such efforts to discredit policies aimed at supporting autistic people, and those from ethnic minorities, to achieve their full potential must be strenuously resisted. With hindsight, it seems extraordinary that details of Mr Arday’s remarkable life story were not examined sooner. He was wrong to report a Times Higher Education journalist, Jack Grove, to the police, on the basis of a series of emailed queries. But Mr Arday is an individual. While there are lessons to be learned from his over-hasty ascent, the answer is not to give up on equity as a goal.

The scandal comes at a bad time in more ways than one. Rightwing parties continue to make hostility to migrants part of their core offer to voters, and will seek to capitalise on what will be presented as “Black Lives Matter gone mad”. But consequences within the academy must be taken seriously too. Universities are under massive strain owing to funding shortfalls, which have been worsened by new limits and levies on international students. Some are at risk of going bust, and the reputational blow to the sector inflicted by this scandal can only make the situation worse.

The discipline of sociology, already a target of intellectual conservatives who dislike its radical roots, may also see adverse effects, as its standards are questioned. Needless to say, Cambridge colleges will be relatively insulated from such collateral damage, which is likely to be most severe at less wealthy universities with less privileged intakes. This is a grim irony, and one that should prompt serious self-reflection by an elite institution that should have known better than to be so careless.

The Guardian view on Gianni Infantino: in the interests of the game he professes to love, he should go

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:57:07 GMT

The Fifa president’s attempt to brazen out the storm, after attempting to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity, adds insult to injury

“How did you go bankrupt?” a character is asked in Ernest Hemingway’s novel The Sun Also Rises. “Gradually, then suddenly” comes the reply. Right now, Fifa’s justly besieged president, Gianni Infantino, is experiencing something similar in relation to the loss of his own authority.

Since taking over the running of world football’s governing body in 2016, Mr Infantino has survived regular criticism of a monetising approach which has often come at a sporting cost. But since egregious plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law were leaked to the media, his credibility has been draining away at speed.

After crisis talks this week at Fifa’s lavish new African headquarters in Rabat, Mr Infantino authorised a half-hearted and incomplete apology, acknowledging that the now aborted project “could have been handled differently”. But it is very hard to imagine how a sell-off to private equity that would have imperilled the governance of the world’s most popular sport (and possibly led to Mr Infantino’s personal enrichment) could have been handled well. This was, simply, a betrayal of the game’s interests by the president of an organisation that already sits on billions of pounds worth of reserves.

Mr Infantino should resign. But despite crushing condemnation of his actions from senior Fifa figures, and football greats such as Arsène Wenger and Luís Figo, he appears determined to brazen out the storm. As a result, what happens now looks like becoming increasingly messy. Over the course of 10 years, Fifa’s president has carefully cultivated allies in the global south. Breaking ranks with their regional federation, Mexico and Argentina on Friday joined African nations in expressing support for his continued leadership.

Much will therefore depend on European football’s governing body, Uefa. On Thursday it responded witheringly to Mr Infantino’s attempt to draw a line, and restated a loss of confidence in his presidency. On Friday, Norway became the first federation to call directly for Fifa’s president to stand down. The next step will be to follow through on a threat to boycott Fifa-run competitions, starting with the Under-20 Women’s World Cup due to be held in Poland next month.

That, clearly, would be a very serious move. But it was a serious abuse of power to negotiate a deal mortgaging the World Cup’s future to speculators seeking to extract even more wealth from it. From the dubious award of the 2022 World Cup to Qatar, to Fifa’s suspension of inconvenient red cards, Mr Infantino is used to provoking and ignoring controversies. This one must come with consequences.

With haughty presumption, the statement from Mr Infantino’s Rabat bunker said the organisation “will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process”. The chutzpah is almost impressive. But really, dream on. Unless Fifa’s president resigns, is forced out, or is ousted via an election next March, the global game is in danger of descending into an ugly civil war – all because of one man’s attempt to sell off the family silver in unprecedented fashion. Mr Infantino was much mocked for his “Today I feel gay … today I feel [like] a migrant worker” response to critics prior to the Qatar World Cup. It would be greatly to the benefit of the sport he professes to love if he could show some self-awareness now.

The Jason Arday affair has much to say about the current state of academia

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:57:02 GMT

Guardian readers reflect on the university system’s approach to Black academics and how it deals with job applications and promotions

Yes, the recent Jason Arday scandal should be a wake-up call to the left, as Jason Okundaye suggests (The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left, 6 August), but it should also be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about university systems and protocols around appointment and promotion.

What I have seen at UK universities suggests that Arday was not simply an individual who slipped through the net, but that university systems often fail to detect or challenge exaggerated claims. If anything, those with greater institutional privilege are more likely to get away with exaggerations, embellishments and even falsehoods on their CVs and promotion applications.

I have witnessed and reported on what appeared to be falsehoods in promotion applications with no repercussions; in fact, in both cases the applicants were promoted (and both were white). In one case, an applicant claimed to have given several keynote addresses, while conference websites indicated that he had been only an ordinary conference speaker. In another, an applicant claimed to be a co-author of a book when she was listed as a “data collection contributor”.

Why, after I highlighted inaccurate claims, were these people still promoted? I cannot say. But from speaking with colleagues at other universities, this is far from unusual. Those willing to stretch the truth can rely on overworked colleagues with little time to factcheck and a system depending heavily on applicants’ honesty.

This lack of accountability is grossly unfair on the many academics who report honestly on their accomplishments and do excellent work without resorting to such tactics. Perhaps the pressure to meet increasingly demanding and sometimes unattainable standards is driving this behaviour.

The number of permanent academic jobs has not kept pace with the number of PhD graduates, and competition for academic posts has intensified. Nevertheless, we need more checks and verifiable criteria to help prevent future scandals and to restore confidence in academic integrity. Name and address supplied

The case of Prof Jason Arday is an important insight into the academic world. Public expectation of academia and its most prestigious institutions is that these are purely meritocratic. In my experience this is not the case. One of the questions we should be asking is why an academic would be moved to fabricate a CV? Academic pressures can be intense, as evidenced by the needless suicide of Prof Stefan Grimm in 2014.

Furthermore, low-level racism is common in the university setting, in which there is a “chumocratic” culture that promotes similar or like-minded individuals. Ethnic minorities, or those who question the establishment, may be excluded from reaping the full benefits of their academic endeavours in an environment in which career-defining decisions such as promotion, publication and grant success are subjective.

At present, pending full investigation, it may be unclear if Jason Arday is perpetrator or victim, but the academic environment in which he has operated is unlikely to be completely blameless. Salim KhakooProfessor of hepatology, University of Southampton

Jason Arday’s story has divided opinion among my friends and associates, and Okundaye’s piece articulates why. Whether the accusations of plagiarism or lying hold up, only time will tell. But in the meantime, a man and his family are in an intolerable position.

What troubles me equally is the frame surrounding Arday before any of this surfaced: the youngest Black professor in Cambridge’s history, a story of triumph over adversity. That framing is seductive – it’s the stuff that films are made of – but it sets a trap. It suggests Black excellence is only coherent when it becomes a redemption story. But that isn’t equal opportunity; equality doesn’t require anyone to be a miracle.

I don’t know if Arday lied. I’m not signing petitions declaring the allegations “entirely false”. But I will still buy his book, because I think he has been let down by more than himself. Memuna FornaLondon

Here’s what I think Jason Arday represents: an obsession among liberal Britain with Black people’s “inspiring stories”; a man for whom making things up became a sad habit, and what happens when you become trapped in it; a reminder that, depressingly, the path to flourishing while Black is to be better than perfect, and some people will never believe you’re there by merit; and how a victim of a coordinated campaign can be taken down. All these points are true. It’s a sad story. Colton RichardsLondon

I really appreciated the down-to-earth sanity of Jason Okundaye’s piece on the case of Jason Arday. So much hype, so much spiteful sniping, seldom thoughtful or without an agenda. Underneath it all, I can’t help feeling that Cambridge University did little to cover themselves in glory.

However, I suspect that few have thought about Jason Arday, the person, and what he might be going through. I feel a sense of admiration for him, without being in a position to judge any of the allegations made against him. Some compassion would go a long way. Linda RheadHampton, London

It is a deeply concerning to hear of the resignation of Prof Jason Arday, a huge loss. Your report (5 August) refers to the Guardian’s own investigation, with revelations that this professor may have inflated his running achievements and overstated threats to his personal safety. On the former, instances of much more egregious displays of ego in academia are far from rare, without any apparent damage to the standing or careers of many professors.

On the latter, one has to ask what it takes for an institution to act to protect Black staff and students. Experiences of racism are far from unusual, and the psychological toll they take is well documented. Rather than undermine those who seek help in the face of abuse, the Guardian might wonder: what does it take to make us listen and understand?Dr Isabel ShutesLondon School of Economics and Political Science

Within higher education, Jason Arday is well known for the kindness he promotes; many thousands of the students and staff he has encountered over the years will attest to this. In today’s world – particularly within the context of recent coverage surrounding Arday – the significance of this should not be underestimated.

The accusations against Arday raise many polarising and contentious issues, and debates will no doubt continue for some time. In all of this, I urge commentators and commenters to remember the principles of respect and humanity, not to mention kindness. Name and address supplied

Let’s all get on board with travel etiquette

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:56:49 GMT

Readers add to a guide for handling tricky situations on public transport

Re your article on travel etiquette (The ultimate guide to travel etiquette: how to handle 36 tricky situations, from manspreaders to smelly armpits, 4 August), it’s totally wrong to advise people not to give up seats for a woman any more. Women could be menstruating, in the first trimester of pregnancy (the most exhausting time, and not one you advertise with badges saying “Baby on board”), perimenopausal, menopausal or have endometriosis (excruciating pain). Women live with a level of pain and discomfort as routine, for much of their lives. Yes, of course men can be suffering with specific ailments at specific times, but it is not part and parcel of being a man. Gentlemen, please just do it. Helen Walker London

To your list of dubious travel behaviours, I’d like to add constant sniffing and its more guttural and nauseating relation, snorting. It seems that handkerchiefs, tissues and even the concept of blowing your nose have gone out of fashion. I am frequently nauseated by this on planes and trains, and if I don’t have headphones with me I have to resort to blocking my ears. I have not yet had the courage to speak to a culprit (although I have often been tempted to pass them a tissue). Judith MilburnHartlepool, County Durham

I enjoyed your guide to travel etiquette. It was very sensible and reflective of our modern society. I had to smile at the guidance for offering your seat to elderly people – as a man in my mid-50s who is (happily) fit and healthy, I always have to remind myself that people offering me a seat aren’t commenting on my physical state, they are just being kind to a stranger.

Given the increasing incidence of harassment on public transport, particularly of women, it might be helpful to give some guidance as to what to do if you see someone being harassed – that’s a tricky balance of ensuring the safety of yourself and those around you, but it is (sadly) a reflection of the times.

However, you didn’t go into enough detail about one of my biggest bugbears – people who insist on keeping their backpacks on on crowded buses and tubes where standing space is at a premium. It’s frustrating, and occasionally very problematic, when people aren’t aware that the space they’re taking up by keeping the backpack on is much larger than their unencumbered body. As they move or turn they bump into whatever you’re holding, and it reduces the opportunity for others to join the service.

It’s a simple rule: take the backpack off and have it at your feet – always – to avoid encroaching on other people’s personal space and to free up space for others. Or maybe my middle-aged grumpiness is just getting the better of me on this one. Peter AntolikLondon

Recently, after a three day-visit to London, I returned home to Devon and jokingly complained that Londoners constantly made me feel old. Every journey I made on public transport, someone offered me a seat. On two occasions a woman offered me a helping hand as I descended the stairs on a bus. I am a six-foot, healthy 80-year-old and can easily manage to stand for a short journey but, as my wife pointed out, it is much nicer to smile and accept the offers. On another bus, a woman offered to move so that my wife and I could sit together. In conclusion, I felt I should point out that Londoners, in my experience, do not really need much of your advice. They already have an embarrassment of politeness riches and made me feel much happier about the human race. Paul WesleyTotnes, Devon

I love football, so I support lots of clubs

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:56:45 GMT

Millwall remain my main club, but others have turned my head, writes Michael Opitz. Also letters from Neil Bage and Ariel J Friedlander

I read Luke McLaughlin’s article with a great deal of empathy, yet still with some uneasiness about the taboo of having more than one club (Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone, 1 August). A world I inhabit.

I too was at the Millwall v Forest game marred by crowd trouble. It was my first! My family are mostly Millwall, who remain my club, but having seen them drop down the divisions and play in the third tier, my head was turned by better technique and Tottenham- and Arsenal-supporting friends. They will never understand my soft spot for both clubs.

Not to mention family in Germany giving me a Freiburg shirt, making them my German team. Then the gift of a Champions League ticket at Celtic Park put another team in the mix, so I’m checking a lot of scores. Now in the Borders, I am agitating to see Gala Fairydean Rovers this season. They will be yet another team for me to keep an eye on.

To this day, when people ask me which team I support, I pause sheepishly and say, “Millwall but…”. I suppose I just love football!Michael OpitzKelso, Roxburghshire

Over the course of his life, a man could well change his wife owing to personal choice or events outside his control. It is quite likely that his political views will sway depending on the ineptitude of governing parties or his own finances. His religious persuasion may be amended or completely turned off. But he must never, ever, change his football allegiance, particularly for the heinous crime of glory-hunting, else he shall always be known as a plastic fan. Neil BageBourne, Lincolnshire

If Luke McLaughlin wants to change teams, good for him. I often wish that I could. However, similar to the last words of Queen Mary I, when I am dead and opened you shall find my blue and white hooped heart. It’s not just that QPR was our local team. It’s not just that going to matches with my father was our time, unbreached by family or his congregation.

Despite its rather rocky record over the last 50 years, I’ve stuck with the club. Chairmen, managers and players come and go. There are promotions and relegations (we don’t do cups). The fans remain. And the longer we stay (and the longer we suffer), we begin to understand how our commitment to the cause is at the root of the club’s identity. We hold its memories, and create new ones. We give it life. And it gives us hope. I understand that Luke feels this is too much for him. I’ll give him a wave at the Millwall game next week. Ariel J Friedlander Modena, Italy

China’s AI ecosystem is not as open as it claims. Nor is any other country’s

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:56:34 GMT

Responding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK, Prof Paul H Cleverley advocates shared openness standards, while Dr Claire Jenkins says British AI can offer a distinctive path

Ambassador Zheng Zeguang rightly celebrates openly released AI models, and the Chinese labs behind Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi have led the way – competition that benefits everyone, especially where models can run on modest hardware in the developing world (The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together, 30 July).

But his claim that openness is a defining feature of China’s AI development deserves scrutiny. Take GeoGPT, the geoscience system from Zhejiang Lab showcased at last month’s World AI Conference as a model of jointly governed open science. It is promoted to countries as open, yet under the model openness framework – endorsed in a recent UN report – it would not qualify as open at all. It releases model weights (built mainly on Alibaba Qwen, whose licences are not Open Systems Interconnection-compliant), no training data or application source code is released, and its governance committee answers to Zhejiang Lab itself.

Domain rivals show what fuller openness looks like. The European Space Agency’s Earth Virtual Expert (EVE), also built for the Earth sciences, releases its training and evaluation tooling, while the US non-profit Ai2’s OLMo goes further still, publishing everything needed for reproducibility.

The distinction matters. A free hosted service is not an open one: GeoGPT’s users route their data through China’s legal jurisdiction, creating real dependency and sovereignty risks.

None of this is unique to China. The US private-enterprise model raises much the same concerns. That is really the ambassador’s own point extended: no country’s ecosystem is quite as open as its diplomacy suggests. If the UK is to gain from the cooperation he proposes, it should press for shared openness standards like the UN-recommended model openness framework as the basis for any joint work. Honest measurement, not just the language of openness, is where real partnership begins. Prof Paul H Cleverley Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen

Your article rightly argues that Britain cannot afford to be a passive consumer of AI while the US and China shape the technologies that will define the future. Yet the debate should not be reduced to a geopolitical race.

The real question is what kind of AI Britain wishes to build. Our greatest strength is not simply our research universities or life-sciences sector, but the NHS, our public institutions and a long tradition of ethical inquiry. These provide an opportunity to develop AI that is trustworthy, transparent and directed towards the public good rather than solely commercial advantage.

Healthcare illustrates both the promise and the risk. AI can reduce administrative burdens, improve diagnosis and widen access to care. However, public confidence depends on strong governance, meaningful human oversight and assurance that patient data serves citizens rather than corporate or geopolitical interests. Recent work by the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency’s national commission into the regulation of AI in healthcare has highlighted exactly these concerns.

Britain should resist the temptation to imitate either Silicon Valley’s market dominance or China’s state-led model. Instead, it could offer a distinctive path: AI that combines innovation with democratic accountability, scientific excellence and social justice. That would be a form of leadership worthy of Britain’s traditions – and one that others might choose to follow. Dr Claire JenkinsWollaton, Nottinghamshire

A ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one way

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:53:09 GMT

Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes

The Keminaissance will be delayed. For nearly a year, Conservative optimists and a clutch of supportive pundits have been forecasting an upturn in the fortunes of Kemi Badenoch, confident that her party will emerge from the crater it fell into in 2024, overtake Reform UK to become once again the main party of the right and, who knows, maybe, with a following wind, even push Labour aside and return to government. Every sign of strength from the Tory leader – a robust conference speech here, a viral clip on social media there – has been hailed as evidence of the coming Keminaissance. On the evidence of the past week or so, we will have to wait a little longer.

It’s quite true that Badenoch’s personal ratings are better than those of her party. True, too, that she ended a long losing streak when the Tories won a Westminster seat at the Aberdeen South byelection in June. But there is a more recent election result that should temper the boosters’ enthusiasm, along with a series of decisions that confirm that, when it comes to both strategy and judgment, Badenoch is badly lacking.

Start with that contest from a week ago. For many, the standout fact of the byelection to replace Andy Burnham as mayor of Greater Manchester was that Reform came a very poor second, taking just 21% of the vote to Labour’s 47%. It was indeed a crushing defeat for Nigel Farage’s party, which a matter of weeks earlier had talked up its chances of winning the mayoralty.

But run your finger further down the vote tally until it finally reaches the Conservative candidate on a mere 7.7%. In all the previous mayoral contests in Greater Manchester, the Tories were in second place. This time they were fifth, behind Restore Britain, a party of the hard right that has become home to all manner of racists and white supremacists.

A Tory result that bad among such a large electorate suggests not merely that Badenoch is making slow progress, but that she is moving her party backwards. When it comes to challenging Labour, other parties are either level with the Conservatives or ahead of them. In that context, it seems an undeserved compliment to call Kemi Badenoch the leader of the opposition.

Her strategic response to this competition on the right has been to move towards her rivals, hoping to blunt the appeal of the nationalist populist parties by matching their offer. The latest step came late on Thursday with, as the Telegraph billed it, a Tory “promise to end council housing for foreigners”. Badenoch’s pledge is to evict almost 230,000 non-EU foreign national households from their homes.

Never mind that many of those turfed out will include people who, while not UK citizens, have been living, working and paying taxes in Britain for years, while others will be refugees fleeing war and persecution. Never mind that, once evicted, those families, including their children, will be rendered homeless, leaving local councils with the choice of either abandoning them to the streets or providing (much costlier) emergency accommodation. Never mind that it’s unclear who exactly would identify and locate these families, unless Badenoch plans to create a British equivalent of ICE, mounting raids, snatching terrified people from their cars and throwing them into detention. Never mind all that; Badenoch doesn’t care.

So much for the policy; now consider the timing. The Tory leader decided the right moment to demand foreigners be kicked out of their homes was as the Norfolk town of Thetford entered its third night of violence and disorder, triggered by a mob surrounding the accommodation of suspected asylum seekers, some in the crowd trying to force their way in, as others threw rocks and chanted: “We want them out.” Into this tinderbox of a situation walked the Conservative party leader, clutching a petrol can.

Just a day or two earlier, she had been defending the selection as a Somerset council candidate of Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a man who has served long jail sentences for, among other things, a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment and abuse of the Jewish former MP Luciana Berger, a campaign that saw Berger branded an “evil money-grabber”, her face superimposed on the body of a rat and photographs of her doctored into multiple, sexualised images.

Badenoch argued that Bonehill-Paine had renounced his past as a self-described “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and now works to prevent others succumbing to what he calls the disease of antisemitism. In April, he published a lengthy account of how he had come to see Jews as the malign, all-powerful “force operating behind events”, a text that contains some useful insights. (Among them, as my colleague Rafael Behr has pointed out, is an arresting admission by Bonehill-Paine that, though then a full-strength neo-Nazi, he “welcomed Jeremy Corbyn’s election as Labour leader”, which should give pause to those who, at the time, so adamantly dismissed Jewish fears that Corbyn was a draw to those who hate Jews.)

Though candid, the essay is not wholly reassuring. For one thing, it contains no apology to Berger or any of Bonehill-Paine’s other victims. For another, he explains that what changed him was reading the Bible and coming to realise that Jews are “God’s chosen people”. I suspect few Jews will find comfort in that. Instead, they will worry that the would-be politician has traded antisemitism for philosemitism, which means he still singles out “the Jews” rather than seeing Jews as regular people, with the right to be as ordinary and flawed as anyone else.

Still, even if Bonehill-Paine’s disavowal of his past were wholly convincing and he should be regarded as fully rehabilitated, that doesn’t make it obvious that he is acceptable for public office. The bar for that is higher, a point Badenoch herself implicitly conceded when she hinted that Bonehill-Paine would not have cleared the threshold to become an MP. Serving as a councillor was different, she explained, as he would be responsible for nothing more than “parking and bins” – thereby, and at a stroke, insulting the many thousands of Conservatives who devote themselves to public service in their local communities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Bonehill-Paine eventually withdrew his candidacy, but that did not draw a line under the episode. In her stubbornness, the Tory leader said the former neo-Nazi would now serve the party as an adviser, thereby giving him a role on the very national level she had earlier said was off-limits. Worsening matters still further, the shadow cabinet member Claire Coutinho posted that, while, “Luciana and others are unable to forgive Joshua, I do,” attributing this vicarious generosity of hers to her Catholic faith, and so, doubtless unconsciously, reinforcing that age-old trope of the forgiving Christian and the vengeful Jew.

What a mess to have made in just a few days. If it were only tactical blunders and in-the-moment misjudgments, one might be more, er, forgiving. But the flaw is strategic. Badenoch has chosen to fight a race to the bottom against Reform, but it is a race she can never win. Farage will always be willing to go further. Take that latest proposal on housing. She would give foreign nationals six months to get out of their homes; Reform promises to boot them out in three. The penny has still not dropped that in a contest of Reform v Reform Lite, the real thing will always have the edge.

All the while, as Badenoch chases after Farage supporters, moderate Tory voters grow more disenchanted. There may be room for ex-fascists in Conservative ranks, but the leader will allow no place for Conservatives who support net zero targets and do not want the UK to leave the European convention on human rights. The result is that those “blue wall”, southern Tories who defected to the Lib Dems in 2024 have every reason not to come back.

So, yes, Kemi Badenoch may score a win now and then; she’s bound to land the odd blow on Burnham when normal hostilities resume in September. But a Keminaissance? For the Tories, it looks like the dark ages have a while to run yet.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Cambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason Arday

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:49:15 GMT

Group calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny

The University of Cambridge has announced a review into the way it vets and hires senior academic staff in an effort to fend off external and internal criticism of its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor.

But a group of Cambridge academics quickly rejected the university’s response, saying: “We strongly believe that a thorough and transparent investigation into the wider circumstances of this damaging episode is essential.”

Arday resigned earlier this week after mounting scepticism over his personal and professional claims, three-and-a-half years after he was acclaimed as Cambridge’s youngest black professor with a life story of educational disadvantage, including being unable to speak until the age of 11.

Cambridge sources said that university and college leaders had hoped Arday’s resignation would end the controversy. But internal anger has continued to grow over his appointment process and the threats to the university’s black staff from toxic media commentary.

In a statement issued on Friday, Cambridge said: “Jason Arday has resigned from his post at the university with immediate effect. Regardless of this, and for clarification, the university will continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday’s appointment and tenure.

“The findings will feed into a review of the process for the appointment of senior academic roles. In addition, and as previously stated, the university’s research policy committee will review the misconduct in research policy.”

The Guardian revealed on Thursday that Cambridge academics were demanding the university carry out a thorough investigation.

The letter sent on Friday to Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, highlights the “toxic and frequently racist commentary” that has accompanied much of the online and media coverage, adding: “These manifestly false claims have the potential to set back the modest progress Cambridge has made in addressing historical underrepresentation, and to deter any Black academic from applying for or accepting a position at the university in the future.”

Prentice became vice-chancellor of Cambridge in July 2023, after Arday’s appointment earlier that year.

The letter states: “We therefore ask that you appoint an independent body comprising senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge to address these issues, with a clear timeline for completing its work and a commitment to share its findings with the university and the public.”

The nearly 100 signatories are senior professors and Cambridge academics, including Suchitra Sebastian, a professor of physics, and Mónica Figueroa, a professor of sociology, as well as Timothy Gowers, a past winner of the Field medal for mathematics. Other prominent names include Nicholas Guyatt, a professor of North American history, Mary Laven, a professor of early modern history, Anuj Dawar, a professor of logic, and Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature.

The signatories want an independent investigation into the circumstances of Arday’s appointment, and any risk assessment made by the university’s management “when crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential”.

It also wants details of the university’s handling of allegations of academic misconduct against Arday, including whether the university was involved in efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations.

The university has denied supporting Arday’s efforts to stop publication of critical coverage in the Times Higher magazine last year, or funding his use of lawyers.

The signatories also call for an evaluation of the “enormous damage this episode has done to people of colour within and beyond the Cambridge academic community, and what can be done immediately to reassure them – and the wider public – that anti-racism and academic integrity at Cambridge are both essential and mutually reinforcing.”

However, Cambridge’s Jesus College – where Arday was a fellow – has said it will drop its previously announced plans to carry out a parallel “process” to the university’s investigation first revealed on Wednesday evening.

A message to staff from Sonita Alleyne, the college’s master, said: “Because Professor Arday’s college fellowship was contingent on his university appointment, his resignation brought his fellowship to an end. The college’s acceptance of his resignation concludes the process announced in last night’s statement.

“This is a very difficult time for Professor Arday and his family. As he requested in his resignation letter, we hope that they are now afforded peace and privacy.”

One Cambridge academic said the message showed that the university wanted to “draw a line” under the affair in the hope that it would subside.

Arday’s resignation on Wednesday followed intense media scrutiny, beginning with accusations of plagiarism and followed by questions over a string of his claims ranging from endurance running and charity fundraising to confrontations with masked assailants.

Cambridge initially defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” before announcing that it would conduct an internal investigation of “new information” regarding Arday, who then resigned shortly after.

On Friday night, the University of Glasgow said it would review its past appointment of Arday as a professor.

A university spokesperson said: “Jason Arday was employed as professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023.

“He left the university to take up his role as professorial chair at the University of Cambridge.

“The principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future.”

It must be tricky for Farage to remember what’s what. It’s so hideously complicated

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:45:16 GMT

I can’t pass up the moment the Reform leader celebrates his byelection victory against ‘the establishment’ – a man with a dustbin on his head

You would have thought that after 35 years of writing for the Guardian I would have mastered some of the basics of holiday protocol by now. Apparently not. While I had remembered to let the newsdesk know I wouldn’t be writing the political sketch for two weeks, it had completely slipped my mind to inform the Saturday editor. So rather than leave her with the headache of an empty page, you’re getting an extra dose of me this week. And, in truth, I don’t mind because, for what is a usually empty August, there’s an awful lot still going on. I’ve even told the newsdesk that I’d like to write next Friday as I can’t pass up the moment Nigel Farage celebrates his byelection victory against the “establishment”, AKA a comedian with a dustbin on his head. This summer has been quite the reckoning for Reform. First some excellent investigative reporting from the Guardian and the Sunday Times, followed by even some of the party’s most loyal followers in the Spectator and the Telegraph beginning to turn. We will know the game is up when GB News begins to have doubts about Nige. It can only be a matter of time.

This time last year, Reform was dominating the polls and setting the news agenda with weekly press conferences. Now it’s as if Nige has placed himself in a witness protection programme as he tries to avoid anyone asking about his financial arrangements. There again, it must be tricky for Nige to remember what’s what as it all seems so hideously complicated. There’s the £5m from Thai crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne that was first a gift to spend on Ferraris, then to pay for his security and now could be a downpayment on the £1m per year Nige said he would need to make it worth his while to return to full-time politics. Then there are funds travelling from various offshore bank accounts from George Cottrell – the boy who liked to call Nige “Daddy” – to his mum, Fiona, and then on to Dicky Tice. Some of which – no one is quite sure which – seemed to end up in Reform’s bank accounts. Nor can Nige even quite remember when he did decide he was politically active despite owning a majority share in Reform. Confusion doesn’t seem to begin to cover this. Nige still has a week to get his story straight for the Clacton voters.

What with one thing and another – first Jill’s cancer and then breaking her shoulder – it’s looking unlikely we will be making it to Minneapolis to see our daughter, Anna, and her husband, Robert, for a second year. . Instead they have come to visit us for a week, so we have been trying to plan fun things to do in London. Today, given Robert is American, we thought we should all go to see the exhibition to mark the 250th anniversary of American independence at the British Museum.

Truly, five minutes that none of us will get back. I’m trying to be generous to the museum here. Perhaps the trustees and curators have become so obsessed with not tearing the Bayeux Tapestry to shreds that they completely took their eye off the ball. Because this exhibition was an embarrassment. A darkened room with just four items on display. A peace medal made by Paul Revere. A tomahawk that doubled as a peace pipe and had been given to a British general. A wampum belt that had been made by Native Americans. All of which looked like they had been dug out of the museum’s storage department as an afterthought.

Then the piece de resistance: a facsimile of a declaration of independence, complete with a notice saying that the original, which is kept in Chichester, would be on display in September. Thanks for nothing.

What was the British Museum thinking? You’d have been disappointed if any of that had been on display at your local library. I guarantee that anyone coming to my house to see the ceramics I have collected over the years would have had a better time.

No one wants to kick a man when he’s down, but I can’t help thinking that Jason Arday – the professor of sociology who has just resigned from the University of Cambridge – has been badly let down by his former employer. Surely someone must have thought of putting his PhD thesis through a plagiarism detector before offering him a job? The most alarming thing about Arday is that he seems clearly unwell. A fantasist who makes it hard to take almost anything he says as the truth. The list is seemingly endless: his claim to be a world-class athlete who once ran 600 miles in six days, or saying he had been part of the epic TV documentary series Seven Up. A programme that has been watched by millions of people over the years.

Somehow, though, Cambridge managed to overlook all this and more. The greater the fable, the more the university defended him. And in the process it has done far more damage to him than if it had quietly and systematically gone through the evidence and declined to offer him a professorship. Thanks for applying, but no thanks.

Worse still, Cambridge has done a huge disservice to other academics of colour because it has opened the gateway to rightwing critics who will now claim that many other professors at other universities got their jobs on a nod and a wink. Jason has a book coming out later this month. If Simon & Schuster has any thought for its own credibility and Arday’s wellbeing it will quietly announce the book has been delayed “indefinitely”.

Maybe there’s something in theair, but Kemi Badenoch seems to be having a bit of a moment. Having appeared on the Political Currency podcast this week to accuse Reform of “woke” politics and to rubbish Andy Burnham for having done nothing of any value – er, it’s only been two weeks and he’s already promised to solve social care. I guess there’s no pleasing some people.

Badenoch has now nailed herself to the cross of defending the former neo-nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who was jailed for harassing the Jewish Labour MP Luciana Berger. In Badenoch’s view, Bonehill-Paine is a reformed man and deserved a second chance to serve as a Tory councillor because all he would be doing was sorting out the “bin collections”. Bonehill-Paine clearly had second thoughts when some of his CV turned out to be nearly as creative as Jason Arday’s and he withdrew as a Conservative candidate. Only for Kemi to appoint him as a Tory special adviser.

Now I’m all for second chances. But Badenoch didn’t seem to think the Labour cabinet minister Lou Haigh deserved rehabilitation to atone for her phone fraud: a conviction that predated Joshua’s by many years. As far as Badenoch was concerned, Haigh still had to repay her debt to society. It’s also curious to know what is and isn’t acceptable in today’s Tory party. A bit of previous for antisemitism and Hitler loving? Just fine. Believing in net zero and the European convention on human rights, not so much. Grant Shapps has been banned from standing as a Tory MP because he happens to believe in the climate crisis. There again, maybe Kemi understands her party better than most. The columnist Tim Stanley caused huge waves in the Telegraph by writing that maybe climate change was true after all, and got 9,000 comments of complaint. All for saying what 99.9% of the rest of us know to be true.

It’s been hard to keep up with the excesses and moral corruption of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino. As I write, various football bodies and national organisations have expressed their lack of confidence in him but for the time being he appears to be just about hanging on to his job. Maybe he will even ride this one out. But it has struck me that one person has remained silent throughout the scandal: David Beckham. For the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, Beckham was paid millions to be a Fifa ambassador. His one contribution was to say he hadn’t spotted any gay people being persecuted. Top detective work from DB. This time round in the US, David seemed content being an unofficial ambassador, there to be filmed sitting in the VIP seats wearing a suit and looking miserable most of the time as he notched up another £24m that he doesn’t need in advert endorsements. He seemed to be Infantino’s mute puppet. He said nothing when Gianni devalued Fifa by awarding Donald Trump a peace prize. He said nothing when Gianni introduced hydration breaks and extended the half-time interval during the final. He said nothing when Gianni bowed to Trump’s demand to overturn Folarin Balogun’s red card. And he has said nothing while Gianni has tried to sell off stakes and reinvent the competition as an even fatter cash cow. It all feels so sad. A mini tragedy. David used to be almost a national treasure. Someone who appeared to have both a sense of what is right and wrong and also a good sense of humour. Now he just appears to be obsessed with wealth and status. Over the last few months, he could have been a voice for the country, speaking up against the commercialisation and obvious corruption of Infantino’s regime. We would all have loved him for it. Instead he has trashed his brand by being complicit. The only obvious reason for his silence is that either he doesn’t think Infantino has done anything wrong, or he just isn’t bothered as long as the cash keeps coming. It would be nice to be proved wrong. We want our Becks back.

Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis finds

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:35:26 GMT

Counter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify message

Accounts with links to the Russian military promoting far-right messages reached more than 500,000 people in the days following the mass influx of people into Ceuta, according to an analysis by 411, a counter-disinformation group.

Russia-linked social media accounts frequently spread destabilising narratives in Europe, often promoting far-right talking points about immigration.

But 411 and other experts suggest the scale and coordination of the disinformation that followed the Ceuta crisis is significant. Groups spreading disinformation are more organised and powerful than they were several years ago.

“We keep seeing this across Europe and we find it very interesting. It seems like there is some type of machinery in place, or structure,” said Saman Nazari, the lead researcher at Alliance4Europe, a Brussels-based nonprofit.

“Quite regularly, we are seeing this escalation happening across Europe now, with these types of crises. It is too much of a coincidence to be a bandwagoning effect.”

The barrage began on 1 August, the day after tens of thousands of people reportedly attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco overnight. This was part of a larger, multi-day crisis during which 72,000 migrants are estimated to have made their way into the small territory in north Africa, the vast majority of whom were swiftly returned.

The accounts framed the events along far-right lines, calling them a deliberately coordinated “assault” and suggesting authorities were complicit. Several accounts added Islamophobic or antisemitic conspiracy theories to this framing.

These narratives were rapidly reproduced in seven languages and reached more than 720,000 views over the course of six hours on 1 August, according to 411’s examination of roughly 4.5m social media posts.

Other far-right accounts called for nationalists to gather in Ceuta and “patrol” businesses and homes, with some apparently coordinating their efforts.

Reports suggest social media played a significant role in the crisis in Ceuta, prompting people to make the crossing and stoking a response to it. Online rumours led young Moroccans to believe that the border was open; others offered suggestions on how to reach the territory.

The analysis by 411 confirmed reports that there was substantive “peer-to-peer logistics chatter” between potential migrants on social media over how to make the crossing. Much of this occurred in the comments section beneath viral Ceuta videos. This coordination among migrants appeared to be organic, coming “overwhelmingly from small, anonymous-looking individual accounts rather than any single identifiable ‘recruiter’ channel”.

A separate, rightwing backlash began on social media as the crossings continued. One origin of the propaganda barrage was Rybar, a Telegram channel with links to Russian intelligence. Rybar’s parent company has faced sanctions in Europe.

A network of “repeater” accounts then amplified and spread Rybar’s posts. These included accounts linked to the Pravda network, an operation spreading Kremlin propaganda worldwide.

Nazari suggested that disinformation efforts appeared coordinated and that investigations should be made to determine if there were closed forums or similar structures in which far-right influencers discuss how to spread talking points.

Ned Mendez, the lead researcher at 411, said disinformation about the Ceuta crisis spread far more quickly than it did in May 2021, during a similar incident in which 8,000 migrants crossed the same border from Morocco into Spain.

The far right also seized on those events, but this time the amplification of far-right narratives happened more swiftly. The far-right mobilisation calls brought nationalist groups to the main square of Ceuta within days, 411 noted. In 2021, similar calls went out but it took much longer for nationalists to mobilise.

“You could compare the process to a highly specific and organised information superhighway,” said Mendez. “If a piece of content or disinformation is placed on to that privileged superhighway, then it will receive a degree of amplification and boost that other types of content just don’t have access to. Events like this across Europe suggest that some pieces of content are being selected for the onramp, and those content pieces share similar characteristics.”

The 411 analysis said: “That machinery is the real thing to worry about, more than this particular crisis. The next time there’s a border incident anywhere on the Mediterranean, those same relay networks are already in place, ready to pick it up and run with it again.”

Additional reporting by Majida Chowdhury

Monsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatment

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:00:21 GMT

Director Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworld

Through the fear and general miasma of the Covid pandemic, TV brought people together like never before. Among the most-watched series of 2020 was of course Tiger King, Netflix’s hit about an improbably twisty feud between a gay, polyamorous big-cat breeder and convicted felon, and the conservationist rival whom he accused of murder (more specifically, of feeding her missing husband to the tigers in her sanctuary – which she denies). It was the perfect hit for quarantine: bold and ridiculous enough to get everyone talking, and with precisely no bearing on the grief and awfulness that was all around. Producer and co-director Eric Goode has made a smattering of Tiger King follow-ups since then, as well as another series, Chimp Crazy, about the self-described Dolly Parton of the primate world. His latest project – a co-production between his own outfit, Goode Films, HBO, and A24 – continues the theme, focusing this time on the reptile trade and taking its lead from the 2008 book The Lizard King by journalist Bryan Christy. It’s stuffed full of wild stories and even wilder characters: there are canny smugglers, underworld crime gangs, and even legitimate zoos that are said to have turned a blind eye to the provenance of their big, scaly friends. The series is centred on the US – although clearly the supply chain is global – and the two men who kickstarted the illegal trade: Hank Molt and copycat trader Tommy Crutchfield. Like Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin before them, there is no love lost between Crutchfield and Molt, and no odd biographical detail too trivial to skip over. Hank, says Tommy, “will turn anything good into bad”, while Hank reckons that Tommy is “one of the angriest and most bitter people I’ve ever met”. Along the way we learn that Hank used to be a mayonnaise salesman, and that Tommy worked at an extremely on-the-nose Florida establishment named Snake-a-Torium as a teenager, where he would later have his wedding reception.

What follows is the story not only of their enduring beef and betrayals, but of other adjacent vendettas in the illicit reptilian market. Despite environmental concerns becoming increasingly en vogue in the late 60s, a “don’t ask, don’t tell” attitude still pervaded the world of wildlife trading, with many zoos happy to acquire what they needed from whoever happened to have it. There were, however, serious consequences for some of the creatures involved. With the police on his back, Molt once buried a stash of animals alive in New Jersey’s Pine Barrens, a location which would later become infamous via The Sopranos. When he was eventually arrested, Crutchfield would become the go-to guy. He supplied cobras to the makers of a Hollywood blockbuster, he says, and sold tortoises to Michael Jackson. He even bred distinctive white albino alligators, which he sold for £175,000 a pop. The gruesome, revenge-fuelled culmination of the men’s feud at the end of the first episode is the high point of Monsters of God, which then limps through four more instalments. The illegal animal trade gets entangled with the (less interesting) drug trade in the 80s, and – somewhere along the way – the story becomes less punchy and more of an attempt to shoehorn in every strange character and weird/shocking/grim (delete as appropriate) anecdote that the producers had access to. A tangent about a federal agent who wore a gorilla costume in a sting operation is rather funny but, er, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? It does feel like Monsters of God could have been a two-parter, but then maybe it’s simply too hard to kill your darlings when you have so many of them. The story of a German man who collaborated with Crutchfield (and who attempted to escape the feds by running across eight lanes of traffic, in handcuffs, and wearing Birkenstocks) is hardly essential. But it is clearly entertaining. Monsters of God may lack that tight narrative thread that makes you want to recreate lockdown and spend five hours parked in front of the TV. But Goode is a conservationist as well as a film-maker, and it’s clear that he is interested in what became of the species whose existence was endangered by men like these. Much of the final episode is dedicated to notorious dealer Anson Wong from Malaysia, and the smuggling that meant that the ploughshare tortoise became all-but extinct in the wild. There is one final bit of good news, though, and a sense that nature – perhaps – is healing. It might not be a conclusion ripped from the bizarre world of Joe Exotic, but it’s the perfect ending to a wildlife documentary.

Monsters of God is on HBO Max

Police and prosecution errors left proven sex offender free to murder two women in London

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:41:48 GMT

Delays to sexual assault charges and failures to report past convictions in court hearings gave Simon Levy chance to attack more women

Violence against women: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?

Catastrophic errors left a persistent and proven sex offender free before he murdered two women in London, it can be revealed.

On Friday, an Old Bailey jury found Simon Levy, 40, guilty of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later.

Levy was on bail as a suspect for the first murder when he committed the second, after police said they lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.

Months before the first killing, police arrested Levy for sexual assaults of women on trains but made errors that delayed charging him. While on bail, he carried out further attacks, taking the total to 10 across London. Although charged with most of the offences, Levy remained free and went on to commit his second murder.

Prosecutors also admitted to bungling efforts to have Levy remanded in custody, by failing to provide three court hearings with key information demonstrating the full extent of the danger he posed to women.

Yet even before the attacks on women travelling by train, police and prosecutors knew Levy posed a serious risk.

He was first jailed for a sexual offence in 2021. While in prison, he sexually assaulted a female prison officer.

After his release, he carried out a series of sexual assaults on trains across London between 2023 and 2025. He was also the prime suspect in a rape investigation.

In January, March and August 2025, Levy, from Tottenham in north London, savagely attacked three women who provided sexual services, killing two and leaving one seriously injured.

The jury convicted him by an 11-1 majority of the murder of Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in a partly disused tower block on 17 March 2025. The scene was close to where Levy had lived after his release from prison following his first convictions for sexual offences.

The jury was unanimous on all other verdicts and found him guilty of the murder of Wilkins, 39, in a Tottenham car park on 24 August 2025.

He was convicted of raping and attacking a third woman, 35, in January 2025, who survived. She was attacked in the same Tottenham car park, eight minutes’ walk from the home Levy shared with his mother and sister.

Levy was impassive, wearing dark glasses because of an eye injury, as the jury delivered its verdicts, which condemned him to the mandatory life sentence for murder. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.

The Crown Prosecution Service, the Metropolitan police and British Transport Police have admitted making errors.

Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, which investigated the killings, described Levy as a “predatory monster”. He said Wilkins, the second woman murdered by Levy, would probably have been alive were it not for what he described as “collective system failures”.

The litany of failings can only be reported now that Levy’s murder trial has ended, leading to the lifting of reporting restrictions on that and a trial earlier this year.

A jury in February convicted him of 10 sexual assaults on trains, including one on a daughter travelling with her mother, as well as the attack on a female prison officer while he was in jail.

Police arrested Levy for a number of attacks on trains in November 2024, with CCTV tying him to the scene of the assaults. Six more occurred in the first five months of 2025. By May 2025, police wanted Levy remanded, fearing he posed a “high risk of reoffending” with his crimes “escalating”.

The CPS admitted errors at three court hearings in May, June and August 2025, which ended in Levy remaining free. It would not specify publicly what those were, but a source authorised to speak for the organisation said they included failing to mention he had been arrested for Valencia-Trujillo’s murder, and that it could find no record or mention of Levy’s past sexual assault convictions, nor that he was a suspect in a 2024 rape.

The CPS said: “We accept there was relevant information regarding bail that was not provided to the court when bail applications were being considered. Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect … We could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail.”

Other errors and questionable decisions included:

Levy failed to attend three crown court hearings for the train attacks, and the CPS accepts there is no evidence of a warrant being sought for his detention. For two he claimed illness, for the other that he had not been informed. His final non-appearance in crown court was on 11 August 2025. A fortnight later he murdered Wilkins. A CPS source said individuals involved in the Levy case had been disciplined.

The assaults on the London tube network and trains were investigated by BTP. Officers arrested Levy, who was travelling on a stolen Oyster travel card, but handed it back to him, unaware it was stolen. With it he travelled to south London to commit his first murder, and carried out further sexual assaults on trains.

BTP admitted the charging of Levy for his sexual assaults on trains in November 2024 was held up because of a delay in holding an identification parade after his arrest. His bail was extended, and during this delay he attacked and raped another woman and murdered Valencia-Trujillo. BTP said it had not referred its errors to the police watchdog. Instead it has moved one officer, who it says delayed the holding of the ID parade, out of investigations, and given a supervisor words of advice.

BTP identified Levy as a suspect and charged him but never searched his home. Peter Fulton, BTP’s head of crime, said: “There’s a fine line between going fishing and breaching someone’s human rights.” He said that every woman who had reported Levy for attacking them on a train had seen him charged and convicted. When the Met, which investigated the murders, searched Levy’s home, evidence was found about his attack on the prison officer.

The police watchdog has placed two Met officers under investigation over whether Levy was supervised correctly as a person on the sex offender register. A constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, meaning he could be dismissed. The other officer, under investigation for misconduct, is a detective sergeant.

The Met downgraded his risk as a sex offender from high to medium in August 2024, in part because Levy was blind in one eye. The attack that damaged his eye occurred days after Levy is alleged to have raped a woman in May 2024 in north London, and detectives believe it was a reprisal for that.

The failings come despite decades of promises from police chiefs, senior prosecutors, courts and government that the criminal justice system will better protect women from male violence after a series of scandals.

Harriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said an independent inquiry was needed, while Andrea Simon, London’s victims’ commissioner, said: “There are striking parallels with other cases where escalating risk was not acted upon, with devastating and preventable consequences.

“Critical opportunities to intervene were missed, despite him being a known violent offender.”

The crime and policing minister, Sarah Jones, described Levy as a monster and said the failings that had allowed him to remain free were “deeply concerning”.

Jones signalled the government would allow the relevant institutions and police watchdog to establish what went wrong. “The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning,” she said. “It raises serious questions that require urgent answers.”
