Kemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory direction

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:36:43 GMT

Some in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversy

There was a moment in the middle of this week when a news alert raised eyebrows among the politically committed. It read: “Kemi Badenoch: Former neo-Nazi candidate would just be sorting out bins.” It was a collection of words that might prompt palpitations in the most sanguine of communications professionals, followed by panicked advice that retreat was necessary. But as a deeply weird week for the Conservative party came to a close on Friday, its leader appeared adamant she would hold the line.

With Badenoch accused of aping Reform UK on policy and purging centrists from her party in recent weeks, her decision to stand by a man who was jailed after creating sexualised images of a Jewish MP and calling her a “rodent” has prompted concerns about the leader of the opposition’s political antennae and the Tories’ wider strategy.

On Monday it emerged that Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist convicted of the sexist and antisemitic harassment of the Labour peer Luciana Berger, had been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.

A little over 48 hours later, Bonehill-Paine – creator of pro-right viral AI clips that often depict politicians on the left in an ugly light – withdrew his candidacy, saying Badenoch had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, focusing on how young men become radicalised.

As pressure mounted, Badenoch said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”, chastising those who had called her judgment into question.

“Piling on [people who have changed] and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties,” she wrote on social media. “But this is a different Conservative party.”

Her stance has left some in her party delighted by her persistent pugilism but others scratching their heads and looking to the door. For opponents, it has been a moment to savour, with Reform saying her support “beggars belief”, while locally focused Liberal Democrats delighted in criticising Badenoch’s insistence that as a councillor Bonehill-Paine would only have been “looking at parking, sorting out bins”.

The embrace of Bonehill-Paine has come at a critical moment in Badenoch’s leadership. Last month she embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party, writing in the Telegraph that it was “not a retirement home for failed politicians” and warning that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights (ECHR) would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election.

The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party. Sources said multiple Reform members had been blocked from joining the party. “To do that while welcoming this chap has definitely raised a few eyebrows,” one source said.

The purge had left many young Tories and centrists politically homeless, said the former Tory activist Cody Butler, who resigned last weekend as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left the party. He said centrists, members worried about the climate crisis and conservation, and remainers – those who Margaret Thatcher may have referred to as “Wets” – were “running out of road”.

“We keep hearing the parliamentary party has never been more united,” Butler said. “But I think the real truth is the arsonists have taken control, and they’re trying to set the great oak tree of Toryism alight.”

Badenoch also announced this week that a Conservative government would evict foreign nationals with leave to remain from social housing, prompting Reform’s Zia Yusuf to accuse her of trying to copy his party’s policy, and the homelessness charity Shelter to warn the policy would “drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils”.

Despite the private worries of some in the Tory party, delight in Badenoch’s unabashed tack rightwards is not difficult to find among the rank and file. “It’s going down really well,” said one MP. “The party thinks Kemi is doing brilliantly.”

A senior Conservative adviser said the party was being clear on what it believed and why. “At the last election, voters would tell us they didn’t know what the party stood for. Kemi is changing that,” they said.

But rightwingers are not the only ones enjoying the ride. Labour sources said they had been looking on and reaching for the popcorn this week. “Just as you think Kemi might finally be sorting out their tent, she spends a week focused on totally irrelevant nonsense,” said one. “Nothing trumps a person’s instincts and hers are just wrong.”

In the yellow corner, gleeful Lib Dems point out that under Badenoch the Tories seem to be showing little interest in taking back any of the 60 seats they lost directly to their party in 2024 as part of a drubbing in which the Conservatives shed a record 251 seats.

Once the near unchallenged flagbearer of middle England, the Conservatives now have zero MPs in Oxfordshire, for the first time since 1777. A committed leftwing hiker could walk from Land’s End to London without passing through a Tory constituency. Despite Badenoch’s insistence that the May local elections showed “the Conservatives are coming back”, the party lost about 500 councillors in England and ceded control of three local authorities. Even now, the Tories are skittering along at 19% of the vote, compared with Reform on 24 and Labour on 23, according to Politico’s poll of polls.

A senior Lib Dem source said: “It was widely expected that the Conservatives were at their lowest ebb in 2024 and would quickly start making progress. In fact, it’s us that have taken loads off them rather than the other way round.

“Whether it is [on] fighting for more action on the climate or defending human rights, the Conservatives sound more like Nigel Farage than former leaders who were popular with middle England. It is genuinely giving us the biggest opportunity against them we have ever had.”

Given current polling – and the results of the 2024 election in which the Conservatives lost about a third of their votes to Reform – attempting to woo those who voted for Farage was logical, said the pollster John Curtice. “The Tories are in a pretty dire state but not quite as dire as they were a few months ago,” he said. “By my calculation, they are now losing around 17% of those votes to Farage.”

Polling indicates Badenoch’s personal approval rating is on the up: a YouGov poll last month put her net favourability at -11, the highest of any Conservative leader in more than five years.

Curtice said the Tories were facing a dilemma: whether to try to build a more centrist coalition with the voters who had stuck with the party, or try to win back Reform voters. “But in [Reform] voters’ minds they are the party who failed to deliver Brexit properly and who created the Boris wave,” he said. “And the more fundamental problem is not to do with ideology, it’s to do with competence. Partygate trashed their ethical reputation, and [Liz] Truss trashed their reputation on the economy.”

Robert Hayward, a Conservative peer and polling analyst, played down the theory that Badenoch was increasingly moving the Conservatives to the right but said she would have to adapt against a Labour party under Andy Burnham.

Asked where it currently looked as if the Conservatives would gain seats on their current trajectory, Hayward was candid. “I don’t think that is very clear as yet, and that’s a major challenge to the party,” he said.

“But it’s a problem for everyone. People’s allegiance to any political party is weaker now than at any moment during my lifetime. Who knows where we’ll be in December 2026, never mind on the eve of a general election.”

Prince to Madonna, Blur to Beth Orton: William Orbit’s 12 greatest recordings

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:28:45 GMT

The late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever before

William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69

William Orbit’s first band were a curious business. Torch Song had one foot in the pop mainstream – their biggest success came about when one of their tracks was featured on the soundtrack of the Tom Hanks-starring sex comedy Bachelor Party – and one in the left field: they recorded at London’s anarchist hub Centro Iberico, famed for staging gigs by Crass and Throbbing Gristle; they covered the Velvet Underground’s Venus in Furs. Mothdoom Ecstasy is very much of its time – stuttering samples, booming drums – but in its hazy synth textures and ethereal female vocals, you can definitely hear intimations of Orbit’s future approach.

In the late 80s, Orbit did a series of mainstream pop remixes – for Belinda Carlisle, among others – and released the first in his series of solo Strange Cargo albums: its beatless synth-drifts and instrumental dance tracks sounded like the work of a man subconsciously waiting for acid house to happen. When it did, Orbit plunged in head first: a so-so track from Prince’s Batman soundtrack, The Future already had a distinct hint of house music about it, but Orbit’s remix – made in partnership with Mark Moore of S’Express – dragged it firmly into the centre of a sweaty rave.

Augmented by vocalist Sharon Musgrave and rapper MC Inna Onestep, Orbit’s new dance project had some odd ideas, a house version of Pink Floyd’s Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun among them, but their big hit – Top 10 in the autumn of 1990 – was a breakbeat-fuelled, dub-tinged dance-pop anthem. Again, it sounds very much of its era 36 years on, but that’s part of its charm: Fascinating Rhythm exudes the bright-hued, saucer-eyed optimism that dance music brought to the British charts in the years immediately after the Second Summer of Love.

In a sense, it’s a little cheeky including the Clubfield mix of Intoxication in a list of Orbit’s best tracks. His involvement with the music seems a little tangential – he’s credited with “vocal samples” – and besides, this version is all about Leftfield’s remix. But no survey of Orbit’s career would be complete without mention of Guerilla Records, the progressive house label he co-founded in 1990, which released Intoxication, alongside classics by Spooky, DOP and the Drum Club. And besides, it’s a total classic: any excuse to revisit its absolute beast of a rhythm track.

Orbit’s first Strange Cargo album seemed like a curio: an outlier in the pop landscape of 1987. By 1993, the project made a lot more sense. In addition, the music had developed a fresh sense of focus, as evidenced by the opening track of Strange Cargo III. With vocals by Orbit’s then-girlfriend Beth Orton, Water from a Vine Leaf was the perfect demonstration both of his ability to create a warm, cosseting, slowly drifting soundscape and of his melodic skill: it became a minor UK hit before enjoying a lengthy afterlife as a mainstay of chill-out compilations. And the Underworld remix is the perfect example of the then-emerging trio’s unique approach to dance music.

One Dove’s Morning Dove White was the post-club soundtrack of 1993 – a beautiful, Andrew Weatherall-produced blur of dub, dreamy electronics and girl-group influenced heartbreak – before becoming the great lost dance album of the early 90s: all-back-to-mine ubiquity ultimately didn’t translate into chart success. It was the kind of music for which Orbit had an innate affinity: his remix of Breakdown decorated the song with strings, harp and off-beam electronics, stretching it out for nine minutes, as if he – quite understandably – didn’t want it to end.

The most famous of Orbit’s solo albums, Pieces in a Modern Style, saw him reworking classical music at the suggestion of label boss Rob Dickins: a pretty ghastly idea on paper, but one that Orbit made work. A trance remix of Barber’s Adagio for Strings by Ferry Corsten propelled the track into the UK Top 5: ageing Gatecrasher kids would doubtless disagree, but the original, which gently warps Barber’s 1936 piece into nine minutes of soft-focus but sorrowful ambience – a distant relative of Brian Eno’s approach to Pachelbel’s Canon on Discreet Music – is better.

Orbit and Orton had a lengthy and fruitful musical partnership that outlasted their romantic relationship – they released a version of John Martyn’s Don’t Want to Know About Evil as Spill in 1992 and were still collaborating on Orbit’s final album, The Painter, 30 years later. Orbit recorded his own version of their co-authored song She Cries Your Name on his 1995 Strange Cargo album Hinterland, but it’s Orton’s take – the opening track on her fabulous Weatherall-produced breakthrough album Trailer Park – that’s the definitive version: careworn, misty, its sound strangely timeless.

Madonna employed Orbit as a producer and co-songwriter on 1998’s Ray of Light after being impressed by remixes he’d done of Justify My Love and Erotica. Orbit later said the singer’s demanding approach nearly “killed” him – “I was done in physically” – but the resulting album sold 16m copies, catapulted him into the premier league of pop producers, and may well be the best album to bear Madonna’s name. The five-minute opening track perfectly demonstrates how simpatico the pair were: Madonna’s voice – sounding far more intimate than usual – fits perfectly as Orbit’s musical backing continually changes shape – icy ambient, a beat with a whisper of drum’n’bass about it, guitars and a surprisingly intense climax.

Like Madonna, Blur employed Orbit’s services after taking note of the remixes he’d done for their Bustin’ + Dronin’ mini-album. As with the making of Ray of Light, the sessions for 13 were an intense and occasionally punishing experience: as the band were falling apart, Albarn likened Orbit’s role to that of a “psychiatrist”. And like Ray of Light, the end result was fantastic. Tender in particular seems to alchemise the frayed, exhausted mood into something remarkable. A depiction of Albarn’s relationship with Justine Frischmann collapsing, it’s alternately shaky, despondent and powerfully robust. Whatever Orbit did in the producer/psychiatrist’s chair pulled an extraordinary song out of the band.

Danny Boyle would only include All Saints on the soundtrack of his film adaptation of Alex Garland’s The Beach if Orbit agreed to produce their track: the pressure to come up with something caused the producer to expend so much effort – he spent two months working on it – that he “totally lost sight of its potential” and became convinced the song was “a turd”. In reality, it was a triumph: a brilliant distillation of Orbit’s skill as a producer of what would then have been called “chillout” music into a perfect pop format, infinitely hipper and more sophisticated than your average British girl group track of the time. It still sounds fantastic.

There’s a distinct note of what-if about the two tracks Orbit produced for inclusion on U2’s greatest hits album, The Best of 1990-2000. It’s hard not to listen to Electrical Storm in particular and wonder why they didn’t extend their partnership and make a whole album together: perhaps because of the track’s relative failure when released as a single in the US. That notwithstanding, it feels like a perfect melding of their respective styles: the guitar is immediately recognisable as the work of the Edge, the blanket of soft electronics over which Bono sings the intro is equally obviously pure Orbit.

Orbit’s mainstream success in the late 90s and early 2000s had unfortunate consequences. He became a blue-chip songwriter/producer for hire in LA, working with No Doubt, Britney Spears and Chris Brown among others, an experience he didn’t much enjoy; reuniting with Madonna on 2012’s MDNA noticeably failed to recapture the magic of Ray of Light. Returning to England, he vanished from public view, suffering a drug-induced nervous breakdown that led to him being sectioned. When he re-emerged in 2021, it was as a solo artist: a Guardian profile depicted him “fizzing with enthusiasm” about his new music, excitement borne out by his final album The Painter. Far closer to Strange Cargo than his pop smashes, Bank of Wildflowers drenches guest singer Georgia’s faintly Kate Bush-esque vocal in effects and sets it against beautiful piano arpeggios, shivering electronics and an intermittent mid-tempo house pulse, to hugely impressive effect.

It’s not just Homer: the new generation of poets enjoying epic success

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:04:36 GMT

Christopher Nolan’s film has made the Odyssey a bestselling book again, but a slew of new poets are breaking sales records, and have more in common with the ancient Greek than you might expect

The death of poetry – much anticipated, much prematurely mourned – has been put off again, this time by the Odyssey. Thanks to Christopher Nolan’s film, sales of Homer’s epic rose 1,400% in the weeks around release – and it’s not alone. Poetry collections are once again sailing up the charts: Lucas Jones, Donna Ashworth and Nikita Gill, among others, have all burst forth on to the bestseller lists.

The word bestseller, it must be said, conjures up certain images: a TV tie-in cookbook; a sexy thriller. It does not, generally speaking, imply poetry. Poetry is a genre more often relegated to the adolescent, the academic, or the words inside sentimental birthday cards: either over-emotional or elitist, depending on which poet and which perspective. What it certainly is not is a money-spinner: nobody gets into poetry to make the big bucks. Nobody gets into poetry – not these days, anyway, not since Byron’s day – for the fame or the fortune.

Poetry is the underdog of publishing and yet this year, according to a recent Guardian article, it is “expected to exceed £15m in annual sales for the first time since records began”; it might even, if the Greek epics continue to pull in readers (as they have for almost 3,000 years), climb to an astounding £17m. Even without the bolstering influence of Homer, poetry has been steadily climbing for the last three years, each one the best on record.

In fact, reports of poetry’s surprising rise have been kicking around for more than a decade: Rupi Kaur’s million-dollar debut, Milk and Honey, set new records in 2014, and continues to sell. US magazine The New Republic named Kaur the “writer of the decade”. And yet she came to stand not so much for great art, as for a kind of synecdoche for what was wrong with art: Kaur became the mockable face of “the new poetry”, Instagrammable and Instagrammed, and accessed primarily – of course – by the young.

A new audience is finding poetry, particularly (though not exclusively) through social media: a new generation of poets, particularly but not exclusively performance poets, have come to prominence through Instagram, TikTok, and other short-form video formats. These writers, while we can quote them on the page, lose something by being written down.

“At my funeral I’d like there to be sunflowers, a truly inconvenient amount / For I too will have spent a lifetime searching for the light,” runs a couplet from Harry Baker’s Sunflowers, but the poet’s charismatic presence somehow conveys something more of the full power of his meaning.

Many of these poems, beginning on social media and ending in huge sold-out tours, rely on a connection between speaker and listener: a pause, a stillness, a sustained thread in the chaos of the internet, of singular attention to one poem through to the end.

This is poetry for the social media age, for sure. But then, what is the Odyssey except social media? The Odyssey is meant to be read out loud; to be told; to be spread; to be shared. What we know as a single written text is, in fact, only the most static, frozen form of the original viral myth.

It is tempting to think of these bestsellers as a new kind of poetry, but it is in fact a very old one. It is unafraid of emotion, of sentimentality, of faith and love; it is concerned less with the establishment of a brand new voice than with the need to give voice to a collective thought. It is not about originality. (Hence, perhaps, the accusations of self-help; banality; and even plagiarism that have been flung at some of these newly popular poets.) These are poems designed to resonate rather than to disturb. In times of division, these poems are made to connect.

All writing is about connection, even when it’s not. But the immediacy of the connection between author and reader is somehow easiest in poetry: when it works, there’s a direct shot to the heart, a human-to-human hot-wiring together that compresses time and space to get to the point.

What social media offers these poets is a new way to gather people round the fire – and, for some, a way to get to be the one speaking at last. If poets can reach their audiences directly, then different poets may be, perhaps, given a chance not just to speak but to be heard: working-class poets, queer poets, poets who don’t fit the “male, pale and stale” classical canon.

This is how poetry thrives. Poetry needs the new so that it can keep on telling the oldest stories we have: love, despair, grief, hope, joy, community, companionship. Long may it live – as thrilling as every other bestseller on the charts.

Lucas Jones: actor, TikTok star, bestselling poet

Writes about: masculinity, faith, life, death and love

From I Saw God on the Train, from the new collection I Still Believe In Miracles:

You want white clouds and endless skies? Err, yeah. Look around. You don’t have to die […] I know it probably brings you some pain to think of the dead as just dust in a grave […] Life is the cloud, and death is the rain.

Hollie McNish: winner of the Ted Hughes prize, author of Slug, Lobster, Virgin, Plum and Nobody Told Me

Writes about: sex, motherhood, longing, politics, power and love

From call me:

call me even if you’re in the wrong place at the wrong time with a full moon and a lone wolf whimpering bloody-pawed from your insides [...] i do not care what you have done … i am no god i am no judge i am your mother – call me and i will come

Nikita Gill: permanently on the bestseller chart, 850,000 Instagram followers

Writes about: feminist-flavoured myths, magic, legends and love

93% Stardust:

We have calcium in our bones, iron in our veins, carbon in our souls, and nitrogen in our brains.

93 percent stardust, with souls made of flames, we are all just stars that have people names.

Lemn Sissay: Sunday Times bestseller, OBE, books include Let the Light Pour In

Writes about: family, adoption, the fabric of society, race, home, hope, and love

From Let the Light Pour In:

If the phone won’t ring make the call If the mountain won’t move shift it If the birds won’t sing, sing to them all, And if the sun won’t rise, lift it

Len Pennie: British book award winner, Scots language poet also writing in English

Writes about: language, linguistics, shame, stigma, suffering, surviving, the patriarchy, overthrowing the patriarchy and love

From The Vow, from Poyums Annaw:

To be loved through each compromise, question or qualm To be sheltered from storm and enshrined in the calm To be held, not like glass, but the end of a deal …

When it comes to marriage and divorce, is gen Z the sensible generation?

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 15:00:21 GMT

This happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for them

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported last month that the marriage rate is declining. As someone who champions marriage, is married and thinks a wedding is lovely, I think it’s great news.

According to the data, the crude rate of registered marriages per 1,000 residents aged 16 and over fell from 5.5 in 2024 to 5.3 in 2025, with the largest falls occurring among the 25-29s and 30-34s.

Why do I celebrate? Because these figures remind us that Australia is a sensible, progressive nation whose liberal social institutions have given individuals the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for our own lives.

This includes exercising our right to divorce, an event also represented in the ABS statistics. Divorces granted rose by 4.1%, the crude divorce rate up from 2.1 to 2.2.

The process of relationship breakdown is always painful, the circumstances causing marriages to fail are often sad, and legal separation is usually a practical nightmare. Yet it was within my own lifetime that Australian law once compelled people in relationships that were unbalanced, dysfunctional, mistrustful, unhappy or loveless to stay married if they couldn’t meet narrow legal criteria to make a case for their divorce before the courts.

As populist right political movements all over the globe push nostalgia politics and regressive social policies along with them, it’s worth remembering that the “good ol’ days” of divorce law in Australia once meant that even couples seeking amicable divorces could be obliged into deceit to obtain them. Before the present “no-fault” divorce framework arrived in 1975, practices like “staged adultery” involved recruiting hotel rooms, photographers and private detectives to meet evidence thresholds for divorce proceedings.

But even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place – which is why I’m excited about the decrease in the marriage rate, especially as it pertains to age cohorts.

Reporting on the ABS data, The Australian quoted a demographer claiming that “the expensive property market keeps the divorce rate unnaturally low, because it’s just too expensive to split up”. While that may be true, we should resist the temptation to interpret trends in Australia’s divorce and marriage rates within an exclusively material frame. Yes, Deloitte’s global survey of gen Z and millennials found these cohorts are delaying “life decisions” due to financial concerns, but Nick Tebbey from Relationships Australia made a pertinent observation: “people are more aware going into long-term relationships these days of who they are and what they expect out of it, so they are only making a commitment to marriage when they feel genuinely ready.”

Gen Z are a favourite target of chastising concern from elder generations, claiming the kids are lazy, entitled, undisciplined and unemployable; “snowflakes” who are too fragile to cope with adult life; blank, vapid and addicted to phones; lonely and anxious with poor mental health; and sexless.

Yet looking at the ABS data, I wonder if we may have stumbled on to the reality of the “sensible generation”, given gen Z’s habit of delaying marriage exists alongside their lower teen birthrates and lower rates of alcohol use.

As for their recorded anxiety, loneliness and existential tensions, just maybe these are problems you can admit and address when your mid-to-late 20s aren’t otherwise dominated by jobs that exploit you, kids you’re not equipped to parent, relationships you don’t know how to get out of and the consequences of staggeringly stupid decisions made while drunk.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

I am gen X; covered in the scar tissue of a far less sensible youth. I’ve been a longtime, pub-ranting advocate of banning marriage for everyone on the less-wrinkled side of 30. To make an emotional commitment to another person so serious and so total it bears the imprimatur of the state is a tough ask for a rookie player. The complex interchange of shared responsibility threatens to overwhelm me almost daily and I (a) didn’t get married until the age of 47 and (b) genuinely like the guy.

The gen X prophet Hal Hartley suggested in his 1990 film Trust: “A family’s like a gun – you point it in the wrong direction, you’re gonna kill somebody.” I suspect he witnessed the dysfunction of married-too-young family setups just as the rest of my generation did. By the mid-70s, the median age for a first marriage was just 23-24 for men and 21-22 for women, which are the ages of kids I’d still expect to stand up for me on the bus. Note: marriage ages began their climb to present medians of 31 and 30 after 1976, when Australia’s “no fault divorce” legislation came into effect. That year, divorce rates peaked – more than double the number of today’s. It was a backlog effect for a generation of couples finally able to do-over some youthful mistakes.

Of course, very young adults can and do make serious relationships work, but liberalisation of the marriage institution and the attitudes around it mean they can do so through marriage or unmarried cohabitation or living apart together, or they can enjoy a situationship, hooking-up, or any lifestyle variation from no partners to every available partner within walking distance – not from social expectation or cultural pressure but because they know themselves.

Gen Z should celebrate their good judgment and marriage advocates our progress. Marriage has not been rejected. It has been chosen.

Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnist

Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:16:01 GMT

Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were wounded

A Thai teenager killed his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence.

The 14-year-old wounded more than 30 people in the ⁠shooting at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school northwest of Bangkok. Nine people were in a critical condition, the Thai health department said.

For Prompong Namwong, an English teacher at the school, it was a normal morning until a panicked student from another class flung open the door, trying to find somewhere to hide. In the corridor, Prompong heard other teachers shouting that there had been a mass shooting downstairs.

When Prompong recounted the ordeal to the Guardian, he hesitated between calling the 14-year-old, whom he saw run in front of his classroom, “killer” or “student”.

At that moment, “I thought I was going to die, for sure,” he said.

The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds.

The suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV.

A lockdown at the school was declared over in about half an hour. Prompong said that when he heard a knock, he thought it was the end of his life, but instead it was the police coming to their rescue.

Images from the scene showed students running with only socks on their feet as they were evacuated from the school.

The children, as is customary across Asia, had taken their shoes off outside their classrooms, but in the panic to escape the grounds, the shoes were left strewn around lunch tables and the stairs outside classrooms.

By the afternoon, the sports area where the students would usually have been playing was filled with officials and the media, as the country’s leader vowed to implement new gun laws.

The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters the new law would allow only government officials on duty to carry guns, but did not provide any ⁠specifics, including whether the legislation would tighten gun ownership requirements.

Thailand has the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, and in 2017 the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey placed the country 13th worldwide for small-gun possession.

A number of mass shootings have occurred in recent years in Thailand, including incidents at schools and a large Bangkok mall, and a 2022 attack in the country’s north-east that ‌killed 37 people including 22 children.

The country’s licensing regime still lacks mental health screening for people applying to have a ⁠gun and does not require periodic reassessments ​for licence holders, according to Piyaporn Tunneekul, an ​associate professor at Nakhon Pathom Rajabhat University in Thailand.

Pichanan Thiengtham was in the teachers’ lounge when she heard the shots at about 10am. But she said she could not believe at first that it was a gun: “There were so many shots and they lasted for a long time without stopping.”

It was only when the art teacher saw one of the injured students that she realised what was happening. “I took the injured student to get first aid and then transferred them to the hospital [in the school] building.”

Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, an emergency worker, described arriving as the shooting was taking place. He said his team had treated students with injuries to the back, chest and arms.

They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds to her chest and arm, Kiatikhun said.

The school is part of the Debsirin network, founded by the Thai royal family. Its alumni include prime ministers, scholars and writers.

Prompong found out in the school’s group chat that some of his friends had not survived. “They’re all good teachers. I don’t know what to say.”

He said: “My life has to go on, but right now … it’s a very great shock. I never thought to myself that it would happen – really happen – in my school.”

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:07:53 GMT

Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities

Simon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bail

About 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, up a slip road for deliveries to a B&M homewares store, is a stretch of concrete paving behind a 2-metre wall topped with spikes.

This is the patch of ground that Simon Levy tried to turn into his personal killing field.

Twice he went with women, both of whom were sex workers, to the spot just eight minutes’ walk from the north London home he shared with his mother and sister. The spot is out of sight of CCTV cameras dotted around the area, and in the shadow of the Tottenham Hotspur football stadium.

One victim only just survived the sustained attack, including rape and strangulation, he inflicted on her in January 2025. Another, Sheryl Wilkins, paid with her life in August 2025.

Between those attacks Levy had travelled to south London and, in March 2025, he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.

His double murder trial, which ended in convictions on Friday heard from the survivor. Her testimony, the prosecutor Tom Little KC said during the trial, probably revealed what the other victims suffered.

Little said the victims were vulnerable, and Levy believed that by targeting sex workers he was more likely to get away with his crimes.

The survivor, who is 35 and has her anonymity protected by law, had been trafficked to Britain from eastern Europe.

After they went behind the wall for sex, she asked Levy to pay. He jumped on her with such force he broke her clavicle. While raping her, he also started to strangle her.

She told the Old Bailey jury he said: “Shut up. Be quiet. I have got you.”

She added: “He was sticking his fingers in my throat so I could not make noise. I believe I’m going to die. I could not breathe … I was unconscious completely.”

She awoke feeling “burning and pain”, and was bleeding from her genitals.

Days after the attack, the woman was arrested on another matter. She told officers of her ordeal and said she knew Levy by sight; she knew where he lived but did not know his name. She would later correctly pick Levy out of a police lineup.

The Metropolitan police say she was unable to make a full statement for a further six months, despite their efforts to obtain one. The court heard that she was withdrawing from drug use.

Levy, 40, was linked to the murders by DNA samples from the victims, travel card and phone data, and CCTV footage.

After his arrest, he told police his eye injury, sustained during an assault in 2024, meant he rarely went out. He needed an appropriate adult present when detectives interviewed him and had dyslexia, autism and learning difficulties. He is believed to have been long-term unemployed.

Neighbours knew little about him, and searches of his electronic devices showed some viewing of material about crime, violence and sex.

The attacks on the women in 2025 were not Levy’s first.

Levy is suspected of a sexual assault as far back as 2017, which is still under investigation.

His first convictions came in 2021: one for assaulting a woman at a party in Camden in 2018, putting his hands into her underwear and touching her vagina; another for sexual assault by penetration of a woman on her way to the Notting Hill carnival, having penetrated her with his fingers.

He was in prison first from 2021-23 during which time he sexually assaulted a female prison officer at HMP Brixton.. Searches of his electronic devices showed him writing about his attraction to her.

After his release, he carried out his first attack on a train in October 2023, for which he was only identified later.

In 2024 he allegedly raped a woman in Tottenham. He was recalled to prison to complete the sentence he received in 2021, but not charged over the rape allegation, which is under renewed investigation.

Released from prison later in 2024, he then intensified his attacks on London’s transport network, groping and sexually assaulting women on trains, often by trying to force his fingers into their vagina.

In other offences, the court heard, Levy used “the hustle and bustle of busy, rush-hour trains as his cover”. He would get close to women and conceal his hand with a jumper or coat before attacking them.

Peter Fulton, the head of crime for British Transport Police (BTP), said Levy’s victims, who were mostly in their 20s, were attacked at random and on impulse.

Levy crisscrossed London, armed with a stolen travel card, in one case boarding a train just minutes from his home, at White Hart Lane train station, to attack a woman.

After women reported the offences to BTP, Levy was arrested, charged and bailed.

There were so many signs Levy was a danger, but how clear was it that his offending could turn murderous?

After the first killing, in March 2025, Levy was arrested within days. The cause of death was inconclusive and he was bailed.

Police feel aggrieved that attempts to have Levy remanded in jail in May and June 2025, after he had been charged with several train attacks and was a murder suspect, failed.

The deputy assistant commissioner Kevin Southworth, head of public protection for the Metropolitan police, which investigated the killings, said: “I think on the basis that we put, and BTP put, this man before a court on two occasions and requested remand, I think the obvious conclusion is, had he been remanded at that time … he would have been in prison for sufficient period that he couldn’t have then gone on to commit a murder ….”

Experts in tackling male sexual violence see similarities between Levy’s case and that of Wayne Couzens, the Met officer who kidnapped, raped and murdered Sarah Everard in 2021. Previous, lower-level offending by Couzens, such as exposing himself to women, had been inadequately investigated by police.

Harriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the Levy case “shows a very clear pattern of escalating offending, from sexual assaults of women on public transport to rape and murder … perpetrators can become emboldened and move on to even more dangerous offending.”

Wistrich added: “The failure of the criminal justice system to tackle his offending must have given him the message that it was easy to get away with it.”

Southworth said he accepted crucial questions needed answering. “What did our officers know? And what should they have done, if they didn’t do it? I think one of the points of reflection … for the senior leadership of the Met is how do we, as a collective system, reflect on what went wrong here?”

The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the handling of the case.

The revelations follow scandal after scandal over decades about how the criminal justice system fails women.

Wistrich said: “The scale and variety of failings is shocking – in particular because had they been dealt with appropriately, two women need not have lost their lives.

“It is particularly concerning that this has happened within five years of the horrendous revelations around Met police officers Wayne Couzens and David Carrick, the Baroness Casey report into the Met [which found police to be institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic] …

“This type of scandal tells us little, if anything, has improved in practice.”

Swedish gummies, Parisian linens and Moroccan mint tea: what travel experts always bring home from their trips

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:00:19 GMT

Finding treasures is part of the fun of travel. Here, experts share their top tips on what to buy where

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Speciality tea

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

I love discovering local teas wherever I travel, whether it’s Moroccan mint, Japanese green or herbal blends I’ve never come across at home. I gave up coffee last year, and since then, tea – particularly matcha from Kyoto, which is really strong – has become my daily ritual. Adrienne Adhami, wellbeing coach and podcast host

Spanish olives

When in Spain, I always come home with Aceitunas gazpachas – these split manzanilla or hojiblanca olives are marinated with pickles and spices, and they’re completely addictive. I stock up in local organic food shops, which tend to have the best selection. Phillippa Fern Kenyon Shutes, private chef

Armagnac prunes

I grew up in the Gers region of south-west France, which is famous for preserving prunes in armagnac, so I always try to bring a jar of them back from the local Château de Cassaigne. They come in these lovely tall glass jars and make the most delicious after-supper treat. Patrick Williams, interior designer and founder of Berdoulat

Coffee beans

I always start my day with a pour-over coffee, so I make sure to stock up on beans whenever I travel. I like ones from Ethiopia or Kenya, especially when they’ve been naturally fermented, as they tend to have a lovely fruitiness and acidity, with notes of strawberry, candied orange peel or pineapple. Once I get home, I freeze the beans to preserve their freshness. Patricia Zhou, choreographer

Makrut lime leaves

Visiting Bangkok’s many markets (there’s one for everything) is always a highlight of a trip to Thailand. Phra Khanong is where local people buy their groceries. There are no tourists, it’s very affordable and the vendors are friendly. I always pick up my annual supply of makrut lime leaves for 50 baht (about £1) there. Kash Bhattacharya, travel blogger @budgettraveller

Local spirits

I buy alcohol from pretty much every country I visit. Looking at my collection, I have gin from Eritrea and Botswana, local spirits from Tanzania, and even a bottle from Laos with some sort of worm in it. I don’t actually open a lot of them – I just love having them there as memories of different places. If I’m travelling to a big wine-producing country, such as South Africa or Italy, I always bring a special wine suitcase with me, which holds 12 bottles. Jessica Nabongo, travel writer

Swedish gummies

Whenever I’m in Stockholm, I stock up on soft, chewy pick-and-mix sweets from any grocery store, such as Hemköp – they have big bins of them. Not just a packet or two – but a whole carry-on case full of them. Kate Berry

Extra virgin olive oil

I always come home with something edible. In Greece, Italy or Portugal, that’s usually a bottle of exceptional olive oil – often locally pressed – or a few bottles of the local wine we discovered over dinner and want to enjoy again once we’re home. Natasha Shafi

Macarons

Controversial opinion: Ladurée macarons, with their charming pistachio-green boxes, are not, in fact, the finest macarons in Paris. For those, head to Carette. The flavours are a little punchier (my favourite is salted caramel), the filling is more generous, and at about €3 (£2.55) apiece, they make the perfect sweet treat for the journey home. Jess Cartner-Morley

Chic but cheap childrenswear

Nowhere in the world gives you as much chic for your money as the childrenswear department at French store Monoprix. Think Bonpoint vibes at H&M prices. When my kids were little, I’d stock up every Paris fashion week, but there are branches all over France. They also do the most beautiful paper napkins which – being inexpensive, small and lightweight – make the perfect gifts to bring home. Jess Cartner-Morley, Guardian fashion editor

Evil-eye bracelets

Have you even been to Greece and not come home with at least one evil eye hanging from your wrist or ankle? I know it’s officially summer when mine is back on my arm. Lucy Williams, stylist and content creator

Luxury scarves and shirts

I always buy a scarf from Hermès and a Charvet shirt in France – plus socks from Mes Chaussettes Rouges and Tabio, because they personalise with embroidery. Kate Berry, US editor at Cabana magazine

Vintage jackets

Whenever I’m in Paris, I always make time for Skat Vintage and, if it’s the weekend, a wander around Saint-Ouen flea market. I can rarely resist a vintage silk scarf or jacket, although they’re often claimed by my daughter before they make it into my wardrobe. Natasha Shafi, CEO at Mr & Mrs Smith

White flower oil

I always pick up this oil from Hong Kong. With menthol, eucalyptus and wintergreen, it provides instant relief from headaches and insect bites, and even helps clear the sinuses. Just dot a few drops on your wrists, temples and behind the ears. Divia Thani, global editorial director at Condé Nast Traveller

Pudin Hara

In India, Pudin Hara is a traditional ayurvedic formulation. It’s a bright green blend of mint extract and peppermint oil that works quickly to ease all kinds of tummy-related issues, from cramps and acidity to bloating and indigestion. Divia Thani

Continental colognes

The first time I went to Spain, I remember catching a distinctive waft of cologne whenever I passed a suit on their way into their office in Barcelona. It was different from the muscular scents of home at the time; light, summery and somewhat continental. I finally plucked up the courage to ask someone what they were wearing, and it turned out to be Nenuco Agua de Colonia. Now I buy it whenever I go to Spain and literally bathe in it because it only costs a few euros. A Spanish friend recently told me, however, that it’s mostly used for babies. In France, I always buy Le Petit Marseillais Lait shower gel for the same olfactory associations with summer beaches. Andy Pietrasik, Guardian travel editor

Artisan candles

If you’re passing through Athens, you have to pick up something from The Naxos Apothecary. They make the most beautiful artisan candles, body products and fragrances from Greek flora. Lucy Williams

Melatonin

I stock up at a CVS pharmacy whenever I travel to the US. I’m a good sleeper, but for those rare nights when I’m not, their over-the-counter melatonin is a lifesaver. CVS is also the best place to find brilliant little beauty buys you can’t get at home – such as Pacha Soap Co’s natural deodorant. Teresa Tarmey, facialist

Handmade razors

In Italy, I always seek out the traditional men’s toiletries shops and usually come home with a handmade razor, brush or pair of scissors. Italians do things like this so well: practical, timeless and made to last. Kate Berry

Natural deodorant

I recently discovered the fragrance store Zielinski & Rozen in Amsterdam and fell in love with their natural antiperspirant. I’m drawn to the scent of essential oils, so now I always hunt one down when I come across their boutiques. Phillippa Fern

French pharmacy moisturiser

French pharmacies are a treasure trove. I always stock up on Ducray Ictyane emollient cream. It’s cheap as chips, and the one product that doesn’t leave my husband’s skin feeling tight. Teresa Tarmey

Colgate Wisps

These little on-the-go toothbrushes are one of my must-buys whenever I’m in the US. They’re perfect for travel. Natasha Sullivan, cabin crew

Luxurious sheets

As soon as I set foot in Paris, I head straight to Merci. The store was the first to make washed bed linen and napkins feel truly beautiful. Over the years, I’ve slowly added to my collection, so now I’ve got almost every shade. Lucinda Chambers, co-founder of fashion curation site Collagerie

Vintage digestif glasses

I rarely come home from a trip without a tiny glass and a bottle of whatever the country is best known for. The glass usually comes from a market or dusty antique shop, and the bottle is always something local that’s hard to find at home. I last picked up a Manuel Vermouth while in Biarritz. Kirthanaa Naidu, stylist, cook and creative producer

Vases and other ceramics

You have to hunt around Marrakech’s souks, but that’s part of the fun. I’ve brought back beautifully coloured vases – which I use as carafes – and mugs. I love LRNCE studio, which brings together textiles, art and ceramics, with a use of colour that feels subtle and distinctive. Lucinda Chambers

Jugs and bowls

Sifnos is known as Greece’s ceramics island, thanks to its abundant clay supply, and it is home to some incredible potteries that have been producing pieces for generations. Up in Cheronissos Bay, you’ll find Kostas Depastas, who still uses a foot-operated wheel. He brings his love of engineering to his work, cleverly designing jugs and bowls alongside simple, spiral-decorated pieces. Lucy Williams

Silicone baking mats

E Dehillerin in Paris has every kitchen tool you could possibly imagine, especially for desserts and pastry. Their own-brand silpats (silicone baking mats) are my favourite – chic green and white. I have about 10 in different sizes. Imogen Kwok, chef

Antique buttons and baskets

I always make a point of visiting the local flea market wherever I go – I can’t resist picking up exquisitely made antique buttons to sew on to clothes, as well as old picture frames. I’ll also always find a way to bring home a couple of baskets – the safest way is in a large plastic striped market bag with a good shoulder strap. I love that almost every culture around the world has its own tradition of weaving with natural materials. Hikari Yokoyama, founder of design studio Naum House

Rugs

We’re often in Istanbul visiting my wife’s family, and I always make time for Şişli’s Feriköy flea market. You can find all sorts of treasures there, including beautiful rugs at incredibly affordable prices. Patrick Williams

Art materials

In Milan, I came across Pellegrini Brera art shop after visiting the Pinacoteca di Brera, and now I go back every time I’m there. They have these brilliant architecture drafting stencils, which I use when putting together proposals for food installations – perfect for when I need a break from the computer. Imogen Kwok

Secondhand cameras

A highlight of any Tokyo trip has to be a visit to the Akihabara district – you feel like you’ve stepped into the future. There’s an abundance of used camera shops, and at Camera Kitamura I’ve picked up a mint condition, secondhand Fujifilm X10 at half the usual price. Lemon Camera and Imtiaz’s Camera Market are also great places to hunt for a bargain. Kash Bhattacharya

‘A pretty easy fix’: how I rid my kitchen of plastic – and seven of the best swaps

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 14:00:18 GMT

Worried about microplastics? Whether it’s titanium pans or loose-leaf tea, here are the changes you can make right now

The best sustainable subscriptions for greener, easier living

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

It all started with a black plastic spatula. When an article went viral in 2024 for suggesting we may be unwittingly infusing our food with harmful chemicals by using one, I, along with many I know, lobbed ours into the bin (without a backup in place, to the annoyance of my partner).

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

It later transpired that the study the article was based on had miscalculated the dosage by a factor of 10. UK regulations also limit certain hazardous substances in plastics, meaning that risks should be lower in this country. But alas, it was too late for our poor spatula.

Nevertheless, studies show that the amount of microplastics found inside human bodies is increasing rapidly, and the plastic in our kitchen is known to be a contributing factor, so I set out to minimise its presence.

According to Dr Stephanie Wright, who leads the microplastics team at Imperial College London’s Environmental Research Group, I am not alone in my desire to be rid of the stuff. “Plastic is useful, but it was never designed to be in our bodies,” she says.

Her belief is that any reduction in exposure is good. “We know from lots of other well-studied particles in our environment, like air pollution, that exposure to too much of any particle can be a bad thing, so reducing that burden is always going to be positive – I think the same is true for plastics.”

Yet it is only once you start trying to reduce plastic use that you realise how ubiquitous it is. Wright’s advice is to focus on one of the highest priority areas – the heating of food and drink, because heat accelerates the degradation of plastic, and eating and drinking are effective ways to transport chemicals into our bodies.

However, ditching plastics also poses an environmental threat, creating a conundrum for anyone wanting to reduce their plastics exposure. Rather than simply throwing away everything plastic in your kitchen, a good rule of thumb is to wait until it no longer has a use and then gradually replace items with non-plastic alternatives.

With all this in mind, here are my top seven plastic kitchen swaps.

Joseph Joseph metal utensils

Wooden spatula

Silicone spatula set

Joseph Joseph’s metal utensils are a good blend of style and function, and I use them for frying. However, they won’t work if your pans have a non-stick coating. Silicone utensils are broadly accepted as a better option than hard plastic ones because silicone has much higher heat resistance, is derived primarily from quartz rather than crude oil and has higher durability (meaning it’s not likely to leach chemicals into food). I use silicone spatulas for baking because batters don’t stick to them, but I prefer wood for other cooking because it’s a natural material.

Wooden chopping board

Bamboo chopping board set

Another place where food often comes into contact with plastic is the chopping board. This is a pretty easy fix: we got this set of bamboo chopping boards (any form of wood will work). The only downside is no longer being able to whack them in the dishwasher.

Pyrex zero plastic storage containers, three

I’ve accumulated a huge amount of plastic Tupperware over the years. I’ve replaced it with Pyrex cooking dishes with lids (and silicone seals that make them spillproof), and these tall glass jars, which we use for storing sauces, soups and curries. For any glass storage, check it’s freezer-safe (tempered or borosilicate glass) and ensure you leave space between the containers so the glass doesn’t freeze together.

Ascot glass kettle

Aarke steel kettle

My plastic reduction mission gave me a good excuse to buy this lovely glass kettle from Ascot. The only downside is that the glass is very unforgiving on limescale (a big problem where we live), which means I have to stay on top of the deep cleaning. If I had a bigger budget, I’d probably go for this stainless steel Aarke one.

For more, read the best kettles to save energy and speed up your cuppa, tested

Tea strainer

Bird & Blend loose-leaf tea, 50g

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Hampstead Organic English Breakfast teabags

Switching to loose-leaf tea seemed like a lot of effort, but I resolved to do it when I learned that many teabags contain plastic fibres in the bag or seal, which release microplastics when brewed. Even options marketed as plastic-free often use PLA, a plant-based bioplastic that has still been associated with microplastic release and effects on marine life. Truly plastic-free options include Hampstead Organic, considered a pioneer in this area. But switching to loose-leaf has been the one change I am borderline evangelical about because the tea is so much better. We bought several in-mug metal infusers and buy loose leaf from our local Bird & Blend (it is put directly into a metal tin, no plastic wrapping).

Bamboo baby elephant suction plate

Elk and Friends stainless steel bowls and lids, four pack

Elk and Friends stainless steel plates and lids, two pack

Munchkin Cool Cat straw cup

Mam Feel Good glass bottles

Moon Moon steel lunch box

My children’s plates and cups were mostly plastic and often lobbed in the microwave. We already had a couple of lovely bamboo plates from Bamboo Bamboo (they fight over who gets the elephant), but they can’t go in the dishwasher. To counter this, I bought a few stainless steel plates and bowls from Elk and Friends. Eating off a metal plate does have a bit of a scout-camp vibe, but the kids adjusted quickly. They come with detachable silicone suction pads in case you have a child who likes to throw food and the occasional utensil – I do, which is also why I didn’t trust the ceramic versions some of my friends have.

With sippy cups and water bottles, we scaled down massively, and, after a lot of research, landed on Munchkin bottles. We removed the plastic straws, which just means they need to be tipped a bit higher, and also means we don’t spend our lives searching for transparent plastic bottle pieces after washing them. The spout is made from food-grade silicone. We don’t put hot liquid in them, but the stainless steel does keep everything very cool.

Both of my children drank from plastic bottles before I gave much thought to the issue, but we recently got a couple of glass ones with silicone lids from Mam for our toddler, who is stubbornly clinging to them before bed.

We also switched to stainless steel lunch boxes that double as food storage containers. Our sturdy Moon Moon ones have a removable silicone seal – though be warned that they’re no longer leakproof if you take this out.

Our Place Titanium Pro pans, set of two

ProCook Elite Tri-Ply frying pan

Many non-stick frying pans are coated in PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, a plastic), which can flake into food if there’s any damage to the surface. We were due an upgrade so went for these titanium Our Place pans. Instead of a traditional coating, these have a non-stick technology, NoCo, which uses a micro-textured titanium surface to stop food from sticking. We were sceptical at first but have been impressed by how effective it is, and are now able to use metal cooking utensils without worry – a bonus.

Alternatively, you can choose a pan with a ceramic coating like the ProCook one, which has the same benefits and was rated the best ceramic-coated pan in the Filter’s test of the best frying pans.

For more, read how to make your bathroom more sustainable and readers’ favourite eco-friendly swaps

Rose Stokes is a journalist based in Bath who balances writing about women’s health and parenting two small humans

Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 13:49:18 GMT

Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank

Prosecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank.

Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleen filmed the settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him.

Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair.

Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder.

“This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.”

The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according to rights group B’tselem. Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths.

Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving.

Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios.

Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said.

Hathaleen had worked on No Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills.

“It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation.

“I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.”

Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but police released him after three days under house arrest.

He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem.

“The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.”

The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence.

Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair.

Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade.

Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians.

The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019 pleaded guilty to the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named.

Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli court ruled that a settler had thrown the stone that killed her.

Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public.

Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.”

Sufian Taha contributed reporting

‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 13:35:35 GMT

Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate

The Edinburgh festival fringe has said it is “not afraid of controversy” after it faced calls to cancel a sold-out show by Amanda Knox, who was wrongfully convicted for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy.

Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. A petition calling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 9,000 people.

Knox, from Seattle in the US, and her then Italian boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, were convicted in 2009 for the murder and sexual assault of Kercher, a British foreign exchange student living in Perugia. They maintained their innocence and, after years of legal battles, were acquitted by Italy’s highest court in 2015.

In a statement posted on Instagram, Knox, 39, said of the petition: “Cartwheel is a show about motherhood, raising a daughter in a world that is unfair and dangerous for women, and what it costs to be the kind of mother who tells her the truth about that. Neither the author of this petition nor anyone who signed it has seen Cartwheel.”

Knox, now a married mother of two, said the petition contained “many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show”. She added: “Cartwheel honours Meredith Kercher’s memory and calls out the violence that was done to her and to me.”

Knox has previously said the show did not “joke about Meredith’s death”.

Cartwheel is a reference to a story that alleged Knox did cartwheels in the police station after Kercher’s death.

Tony Lankester, the director of the Fringe Society, told BBC Radio Scotland: “We’re not afraid of controversy. The decision as to whether or not [the show] goes ahead lies with herself and it lies with the venue.”

He added: “As sympathetic as we are to individual cases that crop up, and absolutely as a parent I can relate to the pain that they describe, but that can’t be a criteria, it can’t be one of the lenses that we look through.”

Gilded Balloon Teviot, the show’s venue, said in a statement: “The Edinburgh festival fringe is an open-access festival. As a fringe venue, we provide a platform for a wide range of voices, in line with the fringe’s longstanding commitment to freedom of expression (within the confines of the law) and ensure our audiences can make informed choices.

“Artists and companies choose to participate at our venue and take on the financial and creative responsibility for their work. Amanda’s show is a one-woman piece exploring themes of motherhood, presented independently by her.”

Stephanie Kercher told BBC Breakfast that Knox was “naturally free to continue with her life as she wishes, but I think the problem with this particular project is that it is comedy”.

“And whilst I appreciate comedy is there to push the boundaries … it very much normalises and trivialises violence against women and Meredith in particular.”

Rudy Hermann Guede was convicted of Kercher’s murder in 2008. He was released from prison in 2021 after serving 13 years of a 16-year term.

Claire Cochrane, a professor emeritus of theatre studies at the University of Worcester, said: “What happened to both Meredith Kercher and Amanda Knox was dreadful and of course I understand the Kercher family’s continuing grief.

“However, vociferous campaigns mounted against artistic product based on unexamined assumptions about content and motivation undermines genuine attempts to deal with the personal legacies of violence and tragedy.

“Comedy thoughtfully deployed can be both cathartic and therapeutic. I’m not going to be able to see Knox’s performance in Edinburgh. But I think it should go ahead and be properly and thoughtfully scrutinised.”

Georgia Hunter Bell: ‘Getting the tube to work I was like … oh my God, I’ve kind of messed up my life’

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 13:25:35 GMT

The favourite for 1500m gold at the European Championships on her second chance after quitting at 23, learning from Keely Hodgkinson and eyeing an LA 2028 double

‘I grew up and was always just good at running,” says Georgia Hunter Bell, as she remembers the moment she felt her career was over at 23. “I always thought that I would be a professional athlete, go to the Olympics, all of that. So it was quite brutal when I had to make peace with the fact that it was not going to happen.”

At that stage Hunter Bell’s body was broken. Her teenage promise – she was the UK’s top 15-year-old having run a 2min 8sec 800m – worn away by injuries aggravated by overtraining in the US collegiate system. She retired; found a job in tech; didn’t run on the track for five years. And then came a comeback straight out of a Hollywood feel-good movie.

Over the past two years, the 32-year-old has won six major medals – including an Olympic 1500m bronze, world 800m silver and world 800m indoor and Commonwealth golds. And this week she arrives at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as Britain’s hottest favourite for gold in the 1500m.

But to understand Hunter Bell’s immense drive and fortitude – and what has made her the athlete she is today – you have to go back to the dark days, when her youthful dreams were struck down by life’s harsh realities.

“Actually the first year that I quit, I was like: ‘Thank God, I’m done,’” she says. “Because it had got quite sour towards the end. I was resenting it. I was racing badly. I was injured. I was completely falling out of love with it.

“But a year or two later, when I was back in London and getting the tube to work, I was just kind of being like: ‘Oh my God, I am an adult now. This is it. And I have kind of messed up my life’.

“I knew that the potential was there and it was never fulfilled, and I really struggled to deal with that,” she adds. “And there were a few bad years where I wasn’t very excited for life.”

She admits that the 23-year-old Georgia was a little lost. “When I look back, I feel really bad for her,” she says. “But that is now part of my strength. Because I’ve been through all of that, I have that perspective, and it makes me a way better athlete.”

The second-chance journey of a lifetime began with a March 2022 parkrun for fun in a not-too-shabby 5km time of 16min 14sec. Then, in November 2022, she reunited with her old coach Trevor Painter and his wife, Jenny Meadows, who guided Keely Hodgkinson to Olympic gold in Paris.

The world duathlon title followed in 2023 along with a 1500m in 4:06, just four seconds off the Olympic qualifying time. That winter she also went on her first altitude camp, when Painter and Meadows realised they had an unpolished diamond on their hands.

“They really made me believe,” Hunter Bell says. “They were looking at me keeping up with everyone. After one hill session, Jen pulled me in and was like: ‘You can run the Olympic qualifying time’ and that’s when I was like, ‘OK, I am going do this’. Then it went from ‘You can run the time’ to ‘You can make the team’ to ‘You can actually get a medal.’”

Meadows’s prophecy turned into reality. Days before her 30th birthday, Hunter Bell was able to quit her job to become a professional athlete. “Obviously they were a bit sad to see me go,” she says. “But they were like: ‘You’re living your dream. And to get another shot is so exciting’.”

And even at 32, Hunter Bell is still getting better.

This year, she is the second- fastest woman in the world over 1500m and the fifth-fastest over 800m. “It’s difficult deciding which to do because I feel like I’m actually pretty equal in both,” she says.

Her coaches can’t decide either. “Jen thinks there’s a lot more potential in the 800m, and then Trev thinks I have a better aerobic base, which is maybe suited for the 1500m a bit more,” she says, smiling.

What is clear is that she can beat anyone at either distance – as she proved by thrashing the 800m world champion Lilian Odira at the Commonwealth Games in a tactical masterclass.

For the first part of the race she went to the front and kept it steady. But with Odira out of position on the back straight of the second lap she struck for home, blitzing the last 200m in 27 seconds. “Jen and I watched the rounds,” Hunter Bell explains. “And we anticipated what we thought she might do.”

Beating Odira proved something else too: she could handle the pressure of expectancy. “I used to relish being the underdog in 2024,” she says. “But I found it quite a hard adjustment to be favourite. Last year I was like: ‘Oh, I don’t love this: people are asking me to do press conferences, people are asking me how I’m going to win.’ And I made some mistakes in 2025, which were really important to learn from.”

Gold medals over 1500m at the world indoors in Torun and the 800m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow showed Hunter Bell is a fast learner. And, unsurprisingly, she goes into the Europeans as a hot favourite to win the 1500m, with only the French athlete Agathe Guillemot, the sixth fastest in the world this year, looking a danger.

So what has allowed her to keep improving? Hunter Bell is full of praise for Painter and Meadows, whose coaching focuses on high-speed efforts on the track – with little time for slow running. On weekends, for instance, she rides her bike for hours rather than doing a long run.

She also emphasises the importance of recovery. “You have to be quite disciplined with what you do in your spare time,” she says. “You’re almost trying to be horizontal for as much as you can during the day. When you’re not training or racing, you’re chilling out and letting your body recover.”

Training with Hodgkinson certainly doesn’t hurt either. So what has she learned most from the 800m Olympic champion?

“We’re at different phases in our life, but we get on really well,” she says. “She’s very chilled, which I’ve really learned from.

“At college, I would be very regimented. If something went wrong, I felt that everything had gone wrong. Whereas she’s very like: ‘Oh, I forgot my spikes. I’ll get some others.’ She goes with the flow and is very composed when she gets on the start line. She also really relaxes me, and she’s quite playful and fun.”

And what has she learned from you? “I would be interested to hear what she would say,” Hunter Bell laughs. “Maybe because I have achieved something that on paper you wouldn’t think is possible, that’s helped her see that you can actually do anything. And maybe I’ve helped her be on time more. I’m always like: you need to go!”

For now, Birmingham is foremost on her mind. But Hunter Bell admits that she wants to emulate Kelly Holmes by going for an 800m/1500m double at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

She even talked with Holmes about attempting it last year at the world championships in Tokyo, before deciding against it. However, she believes it is a harder feat to achieve in the modern era – because there are so few slow races in the heats.

“The idea of me winning a gold in the 800 and 1500 in LA is kind of unthinkable because the races are so quick, and what they demand from your body is so much,” she says. “They are almost flat out sprints always, whereas they used to be a bit more tactical.

“That’s why I really enjoyed running a tactical 800m at the Commonwealth Games. Because, last year in Tokyo, it was balls to the wall from the gun.”

But given what she has achieved so far, would you dare bet against Hunter Bell defying sporting gravity again? Especially as she believes there is plenty left in her tank.

“I think my training age is a lot younger than 32, just because I didn’t have all those years of racing and being on the circuit,” she says. “Remember Kelly did her double Olympic gold at 34. Look at Messi at 39. What’s previously been seen as old has pushed way back.

“So everything is leading towards LA – that’s the north star.” And, like Hunter Bell, it is shining brighter than ever.
