William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 12:01:58 GMT

Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee

William Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive style invigorated work by Madonna, Blur, All Saints, U2 and more, has died aged 69.

A statement on his social media, attributed to family and friends, said he died at home on 23 July. “He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness,” the statement read. No cause of death was given.

Orbit was most famous for his collaboration with Madonna on her 1998 album Ray of Light: his strikingly original backings, rooted in trip-hop, jungle and techno, marked a new chapter for one of pop’s greatest stars, resulting in hits such as Frozen, The Power of Goodbye and the giddy title track. It had multi-platinum sales across the world, won Madonna three of the five Grammy awards she was nominated for in 1999, and has become seen by many as Madonna’s single greatest studio album.

But his work stretched far beyond one client, spanning Blur’s exploratory, emotionally scarred album 13, All Saints’ UK No 1 Pure Shores, Pink’s UK No 3 new wave hit Feel Good Time and more. He was credited as a guest artist on the latter, and released a raft of albums and singles under his own name: his electronic twist on Samuel Barber’s Adagio for Strings, aided by a trance remix by Ferry Corsten, reached the UK Top 5 in 1999.

Success came relatively late for Orbit – at least in pop music terms. He was born William Wainwright in 1956 and raised in north London, the son of two teachers he described as “decidedly working class and poor … they’d struggled to become middle class”. He left school at 16 and became what he described as a “post-hippie”, living in a squat, doing occasional low-paid labour and, by his recollection, consuming “a Mars bar and an acid tab a day”.

In 1980 he formed the electronic/ambient trio Torch Song with Laurie Mayer and Grant Gilbert, and were signed to the label IRS, releasing three albums between 1984 and 1987. Well versed in electronic music production after gradually assembling a studio full of digital and analogue gear, he was hired to create the soundtrack to the Rob Lowe and Patrick Swayze film Youngblood, and remixes for pop artists – including Madonna. Wielding hip-house breakbeats and puckish instrumentation, he gave a chirpier cast to her prowling, sexually infatuated early 90s singles Justify My Love and Erotica.

He was now on Madonna’s radar, but it would be later in the decade they would work together on original tracks. In the interim, Torch Song released another album in 1995 and he had another successful project, Bassomatic, whose psychedelic baggy epic Fascinating Rhythm hit the UK Top 10. He’d released his solo debut album in 1987, and found acclaim in the 90s with a series of albums with the title Strange Cargo. 1993’s Strange Cargo III featured a young Beth Orton on a track; Orbit produced her debut album Superpinkymandy the same year, and went on to remix her single Central Reservation.

Meanwhile, Madonna was struggling to make a new album and redefine herself: she had scrapped sessions with R&B producer Babyface in favour of a search for a new collaborator, and only had a small handful of songs for a new album. Orbit’s pedigree meant he was invited by her manager to submit tracks and was hired: “Just hang in there, work on your stuff, get your chops together and eventually you get a stroke of luck,” he later reflected. He and Madonna worked up much of the album together in studios in New York and Los Angeles.

“William is a complete madman genius,” Madonna said of the Ray of Light sessions. “I’d come to him with an idea of where I wanted to go musically, hum melodies or read lyrics, and then leave him alone in the laboratory. Sometimes he’d go in the direction I wanted and sometimes he’d swerve off somewhere else entirely. We’d end up with trance tracks that were eight minutes long and then keep adding and subtracting until we had real verses and choruses. We really put our noses to the grindstone.”

Orbit’s astonishing range of sound – heavy breakbeats, acoustic guitars, trance synths and more – was put to use on everything from sweeping ballads to the pell-mell acid house of the title track, re-establishing Madonna’s credentials as a vanguard pop star and earning her first non-video Grammy award wins.

Eager not to repeat herself, she switched her core producer up again for her next album Music, to Mirwais, though Orbit was retained for three of its tracks. He also produced two successful standalone Madonna singles which appeared on soundtracks: 1999’s Beautiful Stranger, from Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, and her 2000 cover of Don McLean’s American Pie, from The Next Best Thing (which she also starred in). Orbit returned for her 2012 album MDNA, co-producing six of its songs. Earlier this year, Orbit said: “I will always love that woman. For real. She made my career.”

The late 1990s were a hugely industrious period for Orbit. In 1999, he released Pieces in a Modern Style, an album of classical reworkings including his successful take on Samuel Barber (an earlier 1995 version had been deleted from sale after an objection from composer Arvo Pärt).

1999 also saw the release of Blur’s album 13: similarly to Madonna, Blur wanted to reinvent themselves after five albums with producer Stephen Street, and had been impressed by Orbit’s earlier remixes of their work (collected on the album Bustin’ and Dronin’). 13 charted Damon Albarn’s breakup from musician Justine Frischmann, and the frontman later described Orbit’s role on the album as “a psychiatrist”. Like Ray of Light, 13 is regarded as one of the most singular and brilliantly realised albums in Blur’s catalogue, with Orbit crafting experimental yet commercial material with the group, including hit singles Tender and Coffee and TV.

Ray of Light’s success meant that he was also courted by a range of pop artists in the years that followed, including Britney Spears, Melanie C, Robbie Williams, Chris Brown, Pink, No Doubt and ex-Girls Aloud singer Nadine Coyle. He collaborated with co-writer Beck on Pink’s Feel Good Time – another film soundtrack hit, for 2003’s Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle.

He brought the psychedelic Ray of Light palette of guitars, bleeps and breakbeats to two superb singles by British girl group All Saints: Black Coffee and Pure Shores, both UK chart-toppers. Regarded by pop fans as some of Orbit’s masterpieces, he told the Guardian in 2021 he initially thought the latter song was “pure shite” because it had taken so long to make: “When you really slave over something, it takes years until you can really listen to it with pleasure.” He worked with All Saints again on two tracks from 2018 album Testament.

Orbit produced two new songs for U2 which appeared on their compilation The Best of 1990-2000: Electrical Storm, which reached No 5 in the UK, and The Hands That Built America, which was used as the theme for Martin Scorsese’s 2002 film Gangs of New York.

Orbit’s only other full-album project for a pop artist was Katie Melua’s fourth album The House, released in 2010. His work rate slowed thereafter, though he did bring a long-lost pop curio to fruition: There Must Be More to Life Than This, a Freddie Mercury and Michael Jackson duet, originally recorded in the early 1980s but eventually produced by Orbit and released in 2014.

Orbit also continued to release solo albums, adding six more after Pieces in a Modern Style, including a 2010 sequel to that release. His most recent album is 2022’s The Painter.

In March this year, he scotched rumours of a possible new project with Madonna. “Let’s put this Madonna ROL [Ray of Light] 2.0 thing to rest here and now folks. Can get exhausting. Is not going to happen … I have an album ready that imho is indeed the successor to ROL. Everything about how it was made and how it sounds yells that from the first few bars. And I reached out. And there has been heard. Nil response.”

He told the Guardian in 2021 that he struggled with substance use four years before. As well as heavy marijuana use, he was taking “LSD, mushrooms, MDMA, coke, some hormones that everybody was experimenting with. Codeine. I wasn’t aware of what I was doing and I ended up having a psychotic episode.” He was sectioned. “Fortunately, once the drugs were out of my system, I finally got back to being normal – and out I was,” he said.

Melanie C was one of those paying tribute, writing: “Such an honour to have worked with this great man.”

Music industry mogul Merck Mercuriadis called him “a genius … arguably the most important producer of the 90s and noughties and his influence will forever be felt”.

‘It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written!’: kids’ TV composers tell all

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 12:00:17 GMT

Big cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secrets

How do you write TV theme music for children? Does it make you mega-rich? And does the tune itself eventually drive you (and parents everywhere) nuts?

We tracked down the creators of half-a-dozen of TV’s greatest children’s show themes in order to find out. As Bluey’s Joff Bush told us: “The key lesson is that if you’re going to write a theme tune, make sure you really like it because you’re going to hear it a helluva lot!”

From nostalgic cult classics to current hits, from cartoon animals to live-action school soaps, six composers confess the secrets of kids’ TV music …

Composer Julian Nott scores Peppa Pig, as well as Wallace & Gromit, Bing and Ben & Holly’s Little Kingdom.

It all started at the National Film and Television School’s animation department. Two fellow students became friends: Nick Park, who did Wallace & Gromit, and Mark Baker, who did Peppa Pig. They’ve been collaborators ever since.

Peppa was just another job that came along. I worked on the pilot episode for free as a favour. It wasn’t just the same theme tune as today, it was the same recording. We finally updated it last year but for two decades they used the demo version. It’s only 10 seconds long which is shorter than most title sequences. It was a challenge to write a short, sharp, catchy tune. It had to be fast and fun with a memorable melody. The gaps in it were exploited by Mark, who inserted oinking sound effects.

We classical musicians tend to laugh at pop writers for only knowing three chords but Peppa has two, which is probably a musical outrage. There was zero budget, so it’s all played on synthesisers and samplers. The instrumentation which became associated with Peppa – marimbas, timpani, glockenspiel, vibraphone – were only chosen because they were the most convincing samples you could get back then.

Peppa took over the world, so I hear my music all the time. I’m often in a cafe or airport and a child will be playing it on their iPad. I’m tempted to lean over and say: ‘I wrote that!’ but never have. There was a time when I couldn’t get on a train without hearing it. It’s a strange feeling. Kids watch their favourite shows on repeat, so it can drive parents mad. Toddlers work out how to switch on Peppa Pig and their parents get woken up at 6am by the theme music. It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written! But I’m very lucky that it’s given me financial security. Peppa Pig was like winning the lottery. It’s enabled me to sustain a career. It’s all upside and it’s marvellous.

Scott Gale wrote the theme song for NBC’s 1990s teen sitcom Saved By the Bell.

I was music coordinator on The Golden Girls. One Friday, the producer of this new teen comedy called and asked me to try out for the theme tune. My wife had left me that morning but I put down the phone, picked up my guitar and, bingo, it just poured out of me. It was the luckiest two minutes of my life. We recorded it over the weekend at my partner Rich Eames’s home studio.

On Monday morning, we handed in our cassette. Little did I know that executive producer Peter Engel had told all the other prospective composers not to include “saved by the bell” in the lyrics because he wasn’t sure the name would stick. But I never got that message, so the title appeared five times in mine. Peter later admitted he was glad I didn’t get his instructions.

Saved By the Bell was the first live-action Saturday morning kids’ show. Everything else was cartoons. I thought it’d be lucky to last seven episodes but it ran for four seasons. And the show, thank goodness, was heavy on music. We wrote it all. If there was a jukebox playing, we’d write the songs. The characters formed a rock group. We wrote what they played. There was something new every week.

Saved By the Bell was very good to me. I still get royalties from Spain, South Africa, everywhere. Those gigs are hard to get but it’s the gift that keeps on giving. I never tire of hearing it. I’ll chance across it while channel surfing and it whisks me back to those wild times. Nearly four decades later, I still get to talk about it. It’s nothing but wonderful.

Martin Brammer is the frontman of pop trio the Kane Gang, whose track became the basis of the theme tune to Byker Grove.

We’d already reworked our song Small Town Creed to be the jingle for Radio 1 DJ Gary Davies’s show. The makers of this local teen drama – a sort of Geordie version of Grange Hill – asked if the Kane Gang fancied doing the theme tune. Either out of expedience or laziness, we thought: “Hang on! Maybe we can get a third version out of it.”

It’s a challenge to create something impactful in 45 seconds. It became this tongue-in-cheek funk workout, a bit edgier than the average kids’ TV tune. A dozen of the cast came down to do the “Ooh, Byker Grove!” chants. That little laugh at the end was from Lyndyann Barrass, who played Spuggie. We liked it and left it in. People tend to remember that laugh. A few years ago, I got a request from another artist – Professor Green or someone – to sample it.

The show ran for 18 series, so royalties make a handy annual bonus. It’s not a life-changing amount of money but it’s hard making a living in music nowadays, so sidelines that tick over are invaluable. Midway through the run, we redid it slightly. Put a funky drummer sample on it to make it more contemporary. Byker Grove led to all sorts of connections. I did some work with Donna Air’s pop duo Crush and songwriting sessions with Ant and Dec as they were moving away from being PJ & Duncan. Lovely lads.

I’ve written hundreds of proper songs but the Byker Grove tune always gets a reaction. I write with Olly Murs now and he flipped when he found out. Now there’s a reboot in development. It would be madness to change the theme tune, right? Fingers crossed we get the call from Ant and Dec.

Joff Bush wrote the theme music and composes most of the soundtrack for globally loved animation Bluey.

I met Daley Pearson [Bluey’s executive producer] when we were students. In 2017, he said: “Would you be interested in coming up to Brisbane for this side project we’ve got? It’s called Bluey, for four to six-year-olds.” I was like: “I doubt I’m the right fit but I’ll check it out.” I’ll be forever grateful that I did. I met [Bluey’s creator] Joe Brumm and we clicked. I watched the rough pilot episodes and just fell in love. I had do it.

I knew exactly what the show’s sound should be. A bit hand-made with an almost chamber ensemble sound. It’s hard to describe but I could hear the chord progression in my head. When the writing’s that good, it’s relatively easy to score. Joe Brumm makes my music look better. I suggested building a library of music which we could reuse but Joe wanted something new for every episode. I was like: “That’s a lot of work!” But it became one of the beauties of Bluey.

They were going to license a track for the theme tune but I said: “Can I have a go at it?” And then I had 10 goes at it! Version eight unlocked it. Now it’s hard to imagine without the theme song. It probably sounds simpler than it is. There are little details in it that only I notice. Parents tend to be more impressed than children. If I tell a kid that I write the music for the show, they’ll ask: “Are you Bluey?” “No.” “Oh, OK.” They’re disappointed that I’m a 41-year-old man, not a six-year-old girl. That keeps your ego in check.

I’m fortunate that my work’s more famous than me. Bluey’s been great for opening up career opportunities and pretty lucrative. The albums have topped the charts. It’s enabled me to work on strange projects that I want to do, rather than taking adverts to pay the rent. I’m just starting on a ballet.

I recently became a father and suddenly understood why dads find Bluey so emotional. I messaged Joe saying: “I get it now!” My daughter’s two and last week, she came back from daycare going: “Doo doo doo doo, Bluey and Bingo!” I was like: “Do you like that song?” She said: “It’s pretty good.” We rerecorded it last year and I got some cute photos of her conducting the orchestra. I’ll surprise her with them someday. Then again, I was singing Wagon Ride to her to help her go to sleep. She woke up, put her hand over my mouth and went: “Different music.” She’s my harshest critic.

Pop and musical theatre songwriter Mark Mueller composed the theme tune for late 80s Disney series DuckTales.

I’d just had my first top 10 single, having written Nothin’ at All by Heart. That’s how I got the meeting at Disney for DuckTales. The execs told me: “Write a radio song, not a cartoon song,” with lots of action in the lyrics they could animate to. That’s why I came up with “race cars, lasers, aeroplanes ... it’s a duck blur”. I jammed as many moving images as possible into 60 seconds.

After the meeting, I drove back to my tiny apartment and wrote the song in 45 minutes on a second-hand Roland synthesiser. I was in a groove and it spilled out of me. I took the demo back to Disney and played it to them in person. They sent it all the way up to the head of the studio, who loved it. My head was spinning. Seldom does anything happen that quickly in Hollywood.

There are so many hooks in DuckTales. Everything from the intro bass lick to the “d-d-dangers” were meant to worm into your brain. The “woo-hoos” fitted perfectly into three empty beats. Vanity Fair called it “history’s catchiest single minute of music”. To me, catchy isn’t a dirty word. It’s what I strive for. My initial fee was $1,250, which definitely wasn’t Scrooge McDuck money. It barely paid for a month’s rent but thankfully, the royalties were good and they keep coming in.

After the show aired, I received a letter from the mother of an autistic child. She told me that she and her husband had never been able to communicate with their young son until he heard the DuckTales song. They would sing it to each other and it was the first time they truly connected. That touched me.

Its global reach is heady stuff. I went to South Korea and my rather somber tour guide had it as his ringtone. A few months ago in Portugal, a strait-laced female banker launched into it. I heard it from tinny speakers on a rickshaw in London. The impact that this minute-long song had on my life is immeasurable. The experience has been a perfect whirlwind – or should I say “duck blur”?

Writer, comedian and musician Mike Harding composed the scores for Danger Mouse and its spin-off Count Duckula.

“Manchester studio Cosgrove Hall Films were fans of my standup, so they asked if I had any ideas for animations. We made a pilot about a busking frog called Far-Out Fred and I did the music for The Reluctant Dragon. Then they said they’d got this mouse super-agent but it wasn’t quite working. I took a look and said: “You’re trying to make him a James Bond character, too rooted in the real world. You realise this is a mouse living in a pillar box? He can do whatever we like.”

I went away and wrote some scripts. I based arch enemy Baron Greenback on this real-life nemesis of mine called Alan Greenbank and made him an evil toad. When it came to the theme music, I studied 60s spy films and wrote a pastiche. Sort of Bond meets Dick Tracy. We dragged in local session musicians and put it together.

Danger Mouse became a classic of its time. David Jason and Terry Scott were terrific at the voices. The animators were amazing. It was a joy to be part of. People felt real warmth towards it. I once stood in for Seamus Heaney at short notice, giving the opening speech at an Irish school arts festival. When I said I wrote the music for Danger Mouse, the kids went wild. I got what my grandad used to call a “standing ovation”.

We still get royalty cheques. The biggest was one year when we got £14,000 from Japan for ringtones. There was a CBBC remake a decade ago which went worldwide but the royalties from Kuala Lumpur are tuppence. I only get a standing ovation from old people nowadays. But I still have a T-shirt saying “The bloke who wrote the music for Danger Mouse”!

Black barrister was told ‘it’s not for defendants’ at London court car park

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 11:01:30 GMT

Stephen Akinsanya says being mistaken for defendant shows lack of progress on racism within legal system

A black barrister has said a security guard told him he could not park in a court’s car park in London because “it’s not for defendants”.

Stephen Akinsanya, who in June was awarded an OBE for raising awareness of youth knife crime and its prevention, said the incident, at an east London court about four weeks ago, illustrated the lack of progress on racism within the criminal justice system.

He said: “It was a sort of reflection of what happened when I first qualified back in 1993, going into the same court, being asked by a security guard which case I was on trial in. And as a junior lawyer thinking: well, why does it have to be that I’m the one on trial? Why can it not be that I’m the lawyer?

“And then 33 years later, pulling up in my car to park in the same court building, a security guard saying: ‘You can’t park here.’ And when I said why, he said: ‘Defendants can’t park in the car park.’”

The barrister, who first mentioned the incident in a Criminal Bar Association podcast published this week, titled “Being Black in Criminal Justice – Is the Profession Racist?”, said he could not believe that “people are still prejudging an individual”. He said that, apart from the gown, he was wearing his barrister’s attire, which the security guard should have been familiar with. When he challenged the guard, “he was completely embarrassed” and raised the barrier to allow him to park, said Akinsanya.

Keir Monteith KC told the podcast: “We’ve probably all experienced that situation early on and not so early on in our careers where we’ve been asked to go and sit in the dock.” He said others were still experiencing it but he personally was not, which he suggested was because he was a KC and known in a particular court.

In 2020, the courts service apologised to two black barristers after one was mistaken for a defendant three times in a day and the other twice in a day.

Akinsanya said: “I’m privy to seeing how the bar has changed with a lot more people from diverse backgrounds entering the profession but there is still a perception that, if you’re black, you’re more likely not to be the lawyer, you’re more likely to be a defendant who’s attending court because you’re on trial.

“I just think: why are we still in this position in the 21st century? Which makes one think about the wider conversation we were having [on the podcast] about the lack of black judges.”

Judicial diversity statistics published last month showed that over the past 10 years the proportion of judges who are black has barely moved, creeping up from 1.4% to 1.6%, compared with 4% of the population in England and Wales. There are 79 black judges (43 in courts and the remainder in tribunals) out of 5,337 and just one senior black court judge, Mrs Justice Margaret Obi.

Akinsanya said: “I could speak of colleagues of mine who are 40-plus years in [the profession] who are more than capable, more than able, [who] I know have applied and have been turned down.”

He believes there should be targets to increase representation and a body that is held accountable if they are missed.

Laurie Anne-Power KC told the podcast an oversight and scrutiny board was needed because “something’s going wrong”. She added: “The only way we can find out what is going wrong in that assessment phase of the process is to have a board that oversees every single aspect. Carry out comparisons. For example, look at the difference between applications for white applicants and black applicants – is there a difference? If there is not a difference, why is there a difference in outcome?”

Monteith, who co-authored a 2022 report that said the judiciary was institutionally racist, criticised the “secret soundings” used to appoint judges, by which serving judges submit confidential assessments of a candidate’s suitability. “If we’re going to have a proper application of merit, then do it on what the individual brings to the interview room, not what people have in terms of chats that are never brought into the interview so the person can deal with it,” he said.

How divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find out

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 11:00:16 GMT

Social media-fuelled riots and fractured politics make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart

Take part in the National Conversation

Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion

When my late wife Jo Cox was killed by a far-right extremist 10 years ago, the phrase “more in common”, taken from her maiden speech in parliament, became a rallying cry against extremism and division.

The phrase succinctly articulated that, no matter our differences, we have more in common than that which divides us.

In the decade since, that solidarity has faded. But it hasn’t just faded as time has elapsed: it has been replaced by a cynicism and a polarisation that it’s hard to overstate.

In an era of hostile states, algorithms designed to incite rage and collapsing community institutions, repeating the mantra that we have “more in common” is no longer enough. It’s time we mapped out that common ground.

Because what we have in common matters. It’s the strength of our connections that defines what we are willing to commit to each other. It determines the strength of our democracy and is the basis of social solidarity. It defines everything from our commitment to the welfare state to our ability to fight wars and defend ourselves.

So it’s pretty remarkable that we haven’t mapped the strength and nature of those connections. I guess we have taken them for granted in the past. Yet with a digital environment that now actively seeks to escalate, exacerbate and exaggerate our divisions, that complacency is no longer an option.

That’s where the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion comes in, a cross-party group co-chaired by former Conservative chancellor Sajid Javid and former Labour MP Jon Cruddas. Central to the commission’s work is the National Conversation, a project with Oxford University to build the best picture we have ever had of what we have in common, what connects us, what divides us, and the kind of country we want to build together.

In any other era, that kind of national research exercise would have been prohibitively expensive. You would have needed thousands of researchers interviewing members of the public, classifying and coding responses, before trying to summarise the millions of data points.

AI makes this kind of exercise possible at scale for the first time. It means as part of the survey you can leave a 60-second voice note on your vision for the country. It means you can identify places on a map that bring you together or write open text. Our ability to gather all this information means the national conversation will provide the richest ever snapshot of what future we want to build together.

Our hope is that the results will help provide us all with a common understanding of our connections, perhaps some reassurance and a chance to play back to our country what vision connects us still.

But its insights will only be a strong as its inputs. Which is why I’m asking you to take just a few minutes to share your vision of the country you want to see. We’ll be publishing the results in a few months. Thousands of others have already joined the conversation but every voice that takes part deepens the insights and adds richness to our understanding of the nature of our connections.

In future, we hope the National Conversation will become an institution like the census – not answering who we are and where we live, but the country talking about what unites us. We’d like you to be part of the start of this journey by adding your voice today. Because in a world that is trying to tear us apart, the least we can all do is speak up for the future we want to see.

Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion

With their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselves

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 10:00:14 GMT

The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress

The Trump administration is waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury?

Project 2025’s Russell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget, initiated the rule change that would make any federal grant subject to review by political appointees – including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.”

Then there is the strategy recently presented by Trump’s science adviser, a former employee of Peter Thiel, with the unique distinction of having no relevant experience in research whatsoever. Michael Kratsios wants to shift decision-making from experts in universities to private corporations, which, helped by AI, are supposedly better positioned to spot potential breakthroughs. This constitutes a major break with the enormously successful approach the US took after the second world war: pour taxpayer money into basic, open-ended science which no private company would risk sponsoring – but with both citizens and American capital eventually benefiting from the inventions that came out of fundamental research. Kratsios wishes the government to adopt “the intentionality of a serious investor” in order to usher in a new “golden age of science” (declaring something “golden” seems enough to succeed in Trump-world). De facto, as critics have rightly pointed out, this seems a strategy to take money from what Trumpists perceive as their political enemies – universities – and shovel it to their allies in tech.

Meanwhile, the more directly ideological assault on universities continues. Having failed to tempt select institutions of higher learning with a “compact” to receive preferential federal treatment last year, Linda McMahon, the fake-wrestling-executive-turned-anti-education secretary, is now asking university presidents to pledge allegiance to the administration through statements on their websites: among other things, they are supposed to explain how they will increase “intellectual pluralism” (read: affirmative action for conservatives); deal with campus protest (read: police student speech the Trump administration does not like); and make education more provincial (serving America first) and instrumental (only immediate employability and vocational credentialism count) – and less critical of “our civilizational inheritance”.

In the spirit of Stephen Miller-type nativism, international donors are targeted no less than international collaboration in general; visas for PhD students are now limited to four years (an unrealistic time frame for many academic subjects), with possible extensions if students spend time and money on appealing to the Department of Homeland security (instead of doing actual research). The fact that many researchers in the past have stayed in the US after obtaining their doctorates, contributing to national wealth (just like America Firsters would presumably want) or went back to their countries with good feelings to the US – all that counts for nothing.

What explains such self-harm? Rightwing hostility to higher education is nothing new: from intellectuals supposedly being communist eggheads in the 1950s, to moral panics about “political correctness” in the 1990s and “wokeness” in recent years, there is the basic stance made explicit by JD Vance in 2021: “Universities are the enemy.” But Trump’s rule has brought together a novel coalition, one divided by many issues but united in their desire to destroy universities as we know them. Among them: the Maga hardcore with its traditional anti-intellectualism and nativism; the Silicon Valley oligarchs who imagine their companies replacing (and monetizing) university functions; and conservatives in name, but radicals in practice who want to take over higher education, but, failing that, would like to burn the whole system down.

Also novel, in the wake of Covid, is the commitment of so many on the right to the idea that, somehow, science and freedom are opposites, that not having ever to listen to people who know something better than you do is the essence of personal liberation. If that emotional fuel for the new anti-intellectualism were not powerful enough, there is a highly flammable desire for revenge – amply on display in the endless attacks on Anthony Fauci.

To be sure, Congress has not gone along with some of the major funding cuts for science Trump keeps requesting; even Republican politicians quietly resist when monies would stop flowing to their districts. And the new OMB rule, it seems, is being blocked in a funding deal reached in the Senate this week. But one cannot rely on such occasional pushback by one Republican or another, because none of them has offered a principled defense of the postwar model (in fact, given the conduct of the likes of the senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn this week, it seems fair to say that “principled Republican” is fast becoming a contradiction in terms).

University leaders and prominent scientists have to hold the line in opposing possible “deals” with the Trump administration; everyone could have learned by now that Trumpists will not stick to their end of the bargain. More importantly, those seeing things wrong with peer review, for instance, or too much administrative busywork for researchers – and some of these problems are real – have to realize that Trumpists are the last who can be trusted to solve them.

Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

Could England and Wales ever run out of water?

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 09:00:12 GMT

Last month in England was the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago. How concerned should we be?

Half of England and all of Wales are officially in drought. But what does this mean and could taps eventually run dry?

There is no single definition of drought and every drought is different. But they are all characterised by a prolonged period of low rainfall creating a shortage of water.

Some droughts are short and intense, like the recent “flash drought” declared across half of England, which developed quickly because of unusually low rainfall and high temperatures. Others can take a long time to develop over multiple seasons due to prolonged low rainfall.

Helen Wakeham, the chair of the National Drought Group, said this year’s drought was “exceptionally serious” and would have long-lasting impacts on the environment and the economy. In July, England received 7% of the long-term average rainfall, making it the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago.

There was also a record-breaking drought in 2022, which affected large parts of the country and was the worst in some areas since the infamous drought of 1976.

Yes, the UK does have a global reputation for its wet weather and we did see particularly heavy rain in the first half of the year.

While winter rainfall can help to replenish reservoirs and groundwater, summers are becoming exceptionally hot and dry. Combined with climate-induced heatwaves, we are using water faster than nature can replenish it.

Drought is only over when river, groundwater and reservoir levels are back to normal, and this can take time.

A key issue is also storing water during times of plenty. There has not been a new reservoir built anywhere in the UK since 1992. The National Farmers’ Union is calling on the government to streamline the planning system to make it quicker and easier for farmers to build on-farm water storage systems.

Additionally, research by Greenpeace UK found that 2.87bn litres of water a day is wasted by water companies through leaky pipes in England and Wales – enough to fill 1,150 Olympic-sized swimming pools and amounting to a fifth of all water pumped through the network.

Most of the water comes from lakes, reservoirs, rivers and groundwater. This is then pumped to water treatment plants before being directed to homes. The amount of water that companies can take is controlled by environmental regulators.

During times of drought, water companies can use drought permits and drought orders to take more water. Last year Southern Water applied for a drought order that allowed it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat.

No, water companies are not the only ones taking water from the environment. Agriculture, power generation, manufacturing, fish farms and golf courses are all big users of water.

Analysis by the Ends Report revealed 47bn kilolitres (kl) of water was extracted from the environment in England in 2023. Electricity generation took 26bn kl, public water supply took 9.2bn kl and agriculture took 2bn kl.

The Environment Agency has estimated England’s public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.

Water demand is going up as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is going down as the effects of the climate crisis kick in, and we have greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs.

Yes, there is a serious problem with water pollution. Recent government data revealed that every single English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals, while just 14.3% of surface waters achieved good ecological status.

The Consumer Council for Water has estimated the average person in England and Wales uses 139 litres of water a day. In Europe, this figure tends to be lower, for example in Germany individuals use about 120 litres per day. In the US, the average American is estimated to use 310 litres per day.

Smart metering programmes can help households look at their water consumption. The Environment Agency has suggested opting for a low-flow shower head, which uses about half the amount of water per minute compared with a standard shower head. You can also request a cistern displacement device from your water company, which can reduce each toilet flush by at least one litre.

However, one of the biggest ways you can reduce your water consumption is through your diet. Some estimates suggest a vegetarian diet could reduce your water consumption by 27% to 41%.

There have been three droughts in the past five years so becoming more resilient is essential. While we can all take steps to reduce our water use, investment is key.

The Environment Agency expects 60% of the predicted 2050 water deficit to be addressed by water companies managing demand and dramatically reducing leaks. The remaining 40% would come from boosting supply, including the building of new reservoirs and water transfer schemes.

About 40% of the population of England is under a hosepipe ban – officially called a temporary use ban – which is a legal restriction imposed by water companies to conserve water during times of low supply and high demand. Breaching the ban is a criminal offence and can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.

Water companies are all required to have drought management plans setting out what they would do in an “emergency drought” scenario. This could see rota cuts introduced where water is limited to a few hours each day.

Water companies can apply to the government for a drought order, which allows them to change someone else’s licence to take water from the environment. They can also prohibit or limit non-domestic customer uses of water under non-essential use bans, and can manage the water pressure in drought-affected areas.

As well as investment in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs, nature-based solutions can play an important role to help mitigate the impacts of dry weather.

Yes, without investment and reductions in our water use, we are facing a serious problem.

In some areas, the impact is already being felt. For example Sussex, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Norfolk have all seen housing and business development delayed due to water supply availability and ageing or inadequate water infrastructure.

South East Water said this week supplies in its area were “critically low” and warned customers they may lose supply unless demand for water in the area dropped.

In a report written in the aftermath of the 2025 drought, which resulted in the driest spring in 132 years, MPs warned that without action to reduce water use and build new supply infrastructure, England’s taps could run dry.

In the infamous drought of 1976, several water companies closed off supplies, with the public having to use standpipes in the street.

Dr Anna Murgatroyd, a lecturer in hydrology at Newcastle University, said the current conditions were equivalent to, if not worse than, 1976 and so “we could end up seeing similar shortages”. But she said it was hard to say at this stage whether that was likely given the uncertainty of the weather. She added that water companies had more efficient systems today than they did in 1976.

Water companies are channelling record investment into fixing leaks and while it has been more than three decades since a major new reservoir was built in England and Wales, several are in the planning stage.

But as the climate crisis intensifies, the risk worsens, and even if England and Wales manage their domestic resources efficiently, it will still face the knock-on effects as countries across the globe grapple with their own water shortages.

The headline of this article was amended on 7 August 2026 to refer to England and Wales, rather than the UK. Also, the average usage of 139 litres of water a day is for people in England and Wales, not in the UK as stated in an earlier version; and the 47bn kilolitres of water extracted from the environment in 2023 was in England only. Groundwater was added to the list of main sources of water.

I stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all?

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 08:00:11 GMT

The time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose out

It is unbelievable: unconscionable. Westminster Council is moving against “vertical drinking” in pubs, starting with Soho. It claims drinking standing up is noisy and disruptive. It makes pubs, the council says, boisterous places where customers crowd round bars, get drunk and become pains in the neck in the street outside.

Westminster’s new draft licences would require pubs to be only for seating, to have “table service in place of open bar space”. Pub users should, presumably, sit down, shut up and wait to be served, like decent Westminster people who use wine bars.

The council balks at claims it seeks a ban, but here’s the thing: the reason the council apparently dislikes vertical drinking is the reason Britons have done it for ever. It is liquid sociability. It suits all sorts and ages. It encourages people to chat with strangers, pick arguments, spill beer down jackets and reduce traffic outside to a crawl. No one has to book tables or be turned them away when it is “full”. They can come and go, or stay all day.

British pubs are now closing fast. In the past 10 years roughly one has closed every day, to an all-time low of 39,000. Numbers have taken two big hits. The first was the loosening of planning laws that have allowed the change of use of licenced premises into housing.

The other hit was the Starmer government’s stinging increase in business rates and jobs taxes, with its stamping out of casual youth employment. Some pubs faced bankruptcy overnight.

I have a pub a few yards from my front door. Most evenings the place is “vertically” packed, as is the forecourt and the street outside. The noise is a nuisance to some but it ends at 10pm. More to the point, the pub is a beacon for the surrounding neighbourhood. Old and young, elegant and shabby, British and foreign, all sit chatting inside and out. Argument and laughter echo down the street. They bring it to life.

In the years I have lived in this street, shops, offices and cafes have opened and closed. The pub, a free house, has survived them all. It is a point of reference, a place to meet, a refuge for stray dogs and sometimes stray people. The forecourt offers a gallery to watch the world go by.

When I briefly studied town planning, I now realise we were never taught a breath of sociology. Planning was like architecture. It was about buildings unrelated to the people who might use them. Humans rarely appear in pictures in architecture magazines. It is as if they spoil the show. Hence today, seeing the pub as a community institution does not register in the planner’s rulebook.

If anything is vexing social intercourse at present, particularly among the young, it is the decline in human interaction. The villain of the piece is the mobile phone and social media. My statistic of the year is Atlantic magazine’s report that the number of words people speak every day, from 16,632 in 2005 to 11,900 in 2019. We have turned to silence. Online has replaced conversation.

Experts are rightly calling the alarm. Talk matters to our brains. And that means talk in company. Nor is it just conversation that is important. It is casual conversation with people we do not know that needs mental effort. When Jane Jacobs, the urban theorist and author of The Death and Life of Great American Cities, studied the American street, she noted its role in making people adjust their relations with each other. A chat with an old friend is easy, but with a stranger it is an exercise in community. That is the value of the pub exchange, of vertical drinking.

Some pubs are simply very crowded. Long may they be so. But some are where older people go daily just to be in company. They were well satirised in Wodehouse’s classic Mulliner Nights, where characters named after their favourite drinks swapped anecdotes at all hours, led by “hot scotch and lemon”. These places are in effect A&E departments for the relief of loneliness, the endemic disease of our age.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

As “village” institutions continue to decline, in town as well as country, the church, the old people’s club, the sports centre, the corner shop are all disappearing as places of daily resort. We are retreating into ourselves. That the pub should go too, at the very moment of become the community’s last defining institution, is a tragedy.

Westminster may have problems with what it calls its West End “cumulative impact zone” – what we call crowds – but it should not take it out on the public house. As one pub after another closes at the bidding of the property market, these places should be fostered. They are more than fun. They are the last whirlpools of social connection before we all vanish online.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 07:00:10 GMT

As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay

It is rare for people to drop dead holding the incriminating packaging, but there is no longer any serious doubt that consuming a diet of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) risks a catalogue of life-shortening illnesses from heart disease and stroke to diabetes and cancer. Because these diseases are degenerative over time, the food and drink industry has been able to argue for decades that its UPFs are fine in moderation. It would have us believe that there is no such thing as a “junk” individual food, only poor diets overall, and that its products therefore should not be subject to any restrictions.

Just as with climate breakdown and smoking, the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled, but the industry continues to deny and distract to delay action. Two weeks ago, a new report highlighted the lengths to which big food has gone to stop governments implementing policies that would tackle the global crisis of diet-related disease.

Since 2010, it and its lobby groups have brought 235 lawsuits against governments. More than a third of cases where the plaintiff was identifiable were filed by top global brands, led by Coca-Cola, PepsiCo and Mondelēz. The cases add up to 595 years of litigation, according to the investigative group Lighthouse Reports, which has been monitoring the trend around the globe alongside academics, the Guardian and other media outlets.

The litigation strategy is cynical but effective and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization, is damning. “Litigation has been used to oppose or weaken public health measures on obesity and unhealthy diets,” he said. “These delays cost countries billions in healthcare and legal expenses and create a regulatory chill that deters governments from adopting vital protections.”

Protections are much needed. Around the world more than 1 billion people live with obesity and a further 2 billion are overweight. In many countries, including the UK, US and Australia, UPFs have become staples, and make up half the average diet.

​Hence the industry manoevres. Faced with mounting ​worldwide concern, ​it can no longer hold back the tide of evidence any more than fossil fuel or tobacco companies can, but like those sectors, it hopes to tie governments up for a few years more while it protects its profits, even if that takes us to a tipping point at which state health services are overwhelmed.

As with fossil fuels and tobacco, the problem is existential for the food industry. Although manufacturers say they are making their food and drinks healthier, the bald truth is that the economic structure of the agrifood system means that is not possible in any real sense. Manufacturers of UPFs take cheap commodity crops, most often corn, soya and sugar cane and sugar beet, and break them down into their constituent parts. These crops are cheap because governments, especially in the US and EU, have long subsidised farmers, who are a powerful voting lobby, to produce surpluses of them. Farm subsidies and exports of food surplus have been a plank in US geopolitical strategy since the end of the second world war. Donald Trump in fact increased support to farmers in the US in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.

Separated into processed parts – bulk oils, proteins, sugars, and starches – these cheap commodity crops are stripped of the fibre and many of the vitamins, minerals and other micronutrients we need for health. But they can be reconstituted as “added value” processed foods, with the help of flavouring, colouring and texturising additives to replace what has been lost, or sold as high-value animal feed for the world’s ever-growing intensive livestock industry. Unlike minimally processed foods such as perishable fruits and vegetables, they don’t go off and have the advantage of a long shelf life.

My general rule of thumb however, is that added shareholder value is in inverse proportion to human nutritional value. The arrival of anti-obesity drugs has seen the industry tacitly admit it. As people taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs find their appetites shrinking, they are buying fewer UPFs. Retailers have developed “nutrient-dense” but calorie light meals in response, for a premium, as if meals should be anything but nutrient dense as a matter of course.

The fact is we need to stop eating UPFs in any significant amount, just as we need to leave oil in the ground and give up smoking. The more the public realises that, the greater the industry’s need to keep marketing to us and block any government attempts to help us make better choices. It is no coincidence that the majority of lawsuits brought or threatened by the top food and drink companies occur in countries that have been in the vanguard of identifying the harm from UPFs, such as Brazil, or in restricting them, such as Mexico with its sugary drink taxes.

In the UK it was Kellogg’s that sued the secretary of state for health in 2021 over plans to control promotions on foods high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS), including many of its breakfast cereals. Its UK marketing company argued in the high court that the health secretary was acting beyond his powers and that such controls breached its rights under the Human Rights Act (by assault on its right to freedom of commercial expression and on its companies’ “goodwill” monetary value). Tellingly, its lawyers cited case law involving British American Tobacco. They also pleaded that, although more than half of its breakfast cereals fell foul of the HFSS limits thanks to their ingredients, if you took into account the milk people ate with its products, they looked much healthier. Kellogg’s lost its case, with Mr Justice Linden, the trial judge, noting that mixing a high-sugar breakfast cereal with milk does not “alter the fact that it is high in sugar”. But in losing, Kellogg’s tied up considerable government time and resource.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It would be transformative if governments across the world switched distorting agricultural subsidies away from corn, soya and sugar, crops which are also associated with ecological destruction. They could support greater local production of healthy fruit and vegetables instead. Negotiating global agreement seems overwhelmingly daunting, with individual states having few levers to pull.

But there is also a lesson here and it is that, as with so much policy, small battles patiently won do make a difference. Curbs on promotion – clearer labelling, no two-for-one offers, no end-of-aisle positioning – may seem small fry, but the fact that the industry and its lobbying groups choose to fight costly delaying litigation shows these incremental changes do have an effect. Manufacturers are right to see government action as a threat. It needs to be.

Felicity Lawrence is a former Guardian special correspondent, and is author of Not on the Label: What Really Goes Into the Food on Your Plate

Le Corbusier’s social housing was meant to be the dream. In a summer of extreme heat, it is a nightmare

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 04:00:07 GMT

When temperatures get to 40C inside, and French building regulations won’t even allow shutters, these tenants’ listed homes are simply unlivable

The population of Firminy, south-east France, has been dwindling for decades. Its recent history is one of factory closures in a region built by steel, and locals tell me that many people leave for better opportunities in neighbouring Saint-Étienne, or to live in the Haute-Loire’s countryside.

On the top of a hill, however, stands Firminy’s pride: l’Unité d’Habitation, an imposing tower of concrete designed by Le Corbusier. The architect’s final project is an oddity – a building for people, where two-thirds of the apartments are dedicated to habitations à loyer modéré (or HLM – social housing); but also a piece of history, whose facade and roof were listed as monuments historiques in 1993.

It was also designed for a 1960s climate, not the sweltering temperatures we have experienced for much of the summer. For its residents, the tower feels increasingly like an unlivable furnace – and because of its protected status, that is unlikely to change soon.

We are on the brink of the fourth heatwave of the year when I meet a group of residents at the bottom of l’Unité d’Habitation. They have had enough. Inside their flats, during a heatwave, the temperatures regularly reach 35C, and can rise to 40C.

“I slept on the floor because it was the only place I could stay cool,” says Aurélie Mohamed, who has lived in l’Unité d’Habitation for five years.

“I slept on the balcony,” says Nathalie Rouchouse, who moved in 15 years ago.

“My godmother was one of the original residents of Le Corbusier, and I can remember coming here aged nine,” Chantal Hospital tells me. “We marvelled at the building; we were so proud of it in Firminy. It’s been 26 years since I moved in, and now I’m doing my best to move out. I never want to live in a historic monument again.”

L’Unité d’Habitation has no shutters, but adding them would not be a straightforward task. Any change to the facade of a historic monument is subject to a long list of rules, and can’t currently be done without the authorisation of the architectes des bâtiments de France (ABF). For now, residents resort to DIY methods, hanging blankets or panels made from tinfoil across the windows, but it’s no substitute.

When a person owns a part of a historic monument, as is the case with the third of apartments in private ownership in l’Unité d’Habitation in Firminy, there are certain benefits to its listed status. They are entitled to a grant of 40% of the cost of the work when they carry out renovations, and they are able to claim some tax reductions.

But social renters are caught in the middle of the rules imposed on all historic monuments in the country, and the actions and investment of Habitat et Métropole, the social landlord that manages the HLM part of the building. Habitat et Métropole didn’t answer any of my questions regarding the Firminy site.

The relentless heatwaves have highlighted a class divide in France. The residents of l’Unité d’Habitation are far from the only ones living in HLMs to complain of 40C inside their homes, and in some respects they are better off than those in poorly designed buildings elsewhere. Le Corbusier’s famous pilotis allow for better airflow underneath the tower.

This class element is even more apparent in Firminy, where the Le Corbusier site, including parts of l’Unité d’Habitation, is also a tourist attraction. About 20,000 visitors a year come to see l’Unité d’Habitation, its showroom apartment and the kindergarten, which is no longer used as a nursery. Aurélie Mohamed, Nathalie Rouchouse and Chantal Hospital’s home is a living museum, but although tourists pay to visit their building, none of the money from ticket sales is injected back into the site. It is run as a separate operation and Géraldine Dabrigeon, the chief curator of Site Le Corbusier, says that the revenue from ticket sales only covers guides, advertising and insurance. Even though the part open to tourists is run separately, it strikes me as rather zoo-like to have people paying to visit somewhere while the residents swelter behind blankets hung to compensate for the lack of shutters.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Le Corbusier’s vertical towns were built at a time when social initiatives were booming, and they were designed to support those on lower incomes. Now, the very people these buildings are designed for are being penalised for living in a keepsake of France’s social history.

Under a new proposal, brought forward by the French government on 7 July in response to the heatwaves, local councils could gain greater power to modify historic buildings. Rather than the ABF having the definitive say on any modifications, its opinion would be regarded as merely advisory. Critics in the conservative newspaper Le Figaro say that such a move would lead to a “concrete and soulless France”. But the residents of l’Unité d’Habitation already live in a concrete block – one without shutters.

“At some point, a choice will need to be made,” says Chantal Hospital. “Does the building stay residential, as Corbusier intended, or does it become a museum?”

The problem isn’t necessarily that l’Unité d’Habitation is a historic monument, but rather that HLMs across France leave the poorest and most vulnerable suffering the worst of the heatwaves. To be both a historic monument and an HLM, however, means to have all the disadvantages of an underfunded HLM while also being subject to the list of strict rules imposed on historic monuments. It makes the prestige of their “monument historique” plaque rather hollow for the renters – especially when their makeshift provisions for the heat can be gawked at by visiting tourists. At what point do we respect architecture and history over people’s living conditions?

Speaking under the tower, residents told me they had been raising these issues for years. But the Fondation Le Corbusier only discussed the increasing impact of heatwaves on the various Le Corbusier sites this year, one board member said. It plans to look through his old architectural plans to see if it would be possible to install shutters that fit with the listed facade. If the foundation fights sufficiently for its residents, particularly those in HLMs, perhaps the renters will finally reap the rewards of living in a listed building. The fact that this is only just being discussed, however, makes me feel this may be too little, too late.

There is also a significant risk that the HLM renters of l’Unité d’Habitation will fall foul of the famous complexities of French bureaucracy, in a case of too many cooks. In that instance, the whole complex affair could drag on for so long that these homes become uninhabitable.

The number of heatwaves is expected to increase fivefold in France by 2050. While the rich are largely responsible for the climate crisis, those living in social housing, without air conditioning or shutters, will be the first to suffer the consequences.

Anna Richards is a journalist and travel writer based in Lyon

‘One Night Only’ Review: A 12-Hour Sexual Reprieve

The New York Times August 05, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

This dystopian rom-com follows Allie (Monica Barbaro) and Owen (Callum Turner), on their parallel hunts for passion.

By Natalia Winkelman

When you purchase a ticket for an independently reviewed film through our site, we earn an affiliate commission.

As if born of a conversation between libidinous boys in the back row of a school bus, “One Night Only” takes the premise of “The Purge” and makes it about sex.

The movie imagines a puritanical dystopia in which premarital encounters are a criminal offense except for an annual 12-hour reprieve. To enforce the prohibition, the government implants everyone with a neurochemical sensor. Should an unmarried person experience particular spikes near someone else, the police are alerted.

Save to your watch list:

Directed by Will Gluck (“Anyone But You,” “Easy A”), evidently our modern bard of bawdy romantic comedy, “One Night Only” opens with a title card describing the status quo. The ban was instituted three years earlier, and “it’s been … a lot,” the text reads. Cue the laughs, although they’re soon swallowed by a pop-heavy soundtrack that, for the movie’s remainder, seems to demand a minimum of three needle drops per act.

Spanning the exemption night, the movie follows Allie (Monica Barbaro) and Owen (Callum Turner), two New York romantics, on their parallel hunts for passion. Allie, an aspiring singer, hopes to use the hours to find her forever mate. Owen, who runs a pizzeria, plans to propose to his girlfriend (Maya Hawke), but instead gets dumped for the hunk downstairs. That leaves our lovelorn pie slinger searching for a temporary palliative while Allie, prone to Prince Charming reveries, chases the real thing.

Despite the evening’s sexual amnesty, the movie is mostly just a tease. The running joke is that, as couples around them go at it, neither of our lovebirds can catch a break, their efforts continually foiled by a spate of blunders and predicaments. Yet the absence of erotic spectacle doesn’t stop the movie from reveling in overtones. Women are assigned plunging necklines and miniskirts, and Turner’s muscled torso is bared more than once. At the pizzeria, he works the dough like an erogenous zone.

If this all sounds implausible, with the movie’s science-fiction conception of the birds, the bees and the biomonitoring, it is. Faced with such folly, people would surely devise ways around the ordinance, namely, by getting married and then divorced in droves.

But “One Night Only” lays no claim to logic. It traffics instead in charisma, and the combined likability of the leads is the putative solution to a premise that’s all flashy surface and no deeper inquiry. With nothing to say about sex or society, the repression plot mostly gets in the way of a movie that would prefer to be a routine romance, complete with a lovers’ rendezvous at a Manhattan landmark at sunrise. It’s too bad for Allie and Owen that the moratorium resumes at 7 a. m., but the courthouse is only a subway ride away.

One Night OnlyRated R for lust let loose. Running time: 1 hour 42 minutes. In theaters.

New Jersey Opens Civil Rights Investigation Into Delaney Hall

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The state attorney general said that her office had issued subpoenas and would investigate whether employees at the migrant detention center had violated civil rights.

By Ana Ley

The New Jersey attorney general has opened a civil rights investigation into a 1,000-bed migrant detention center in Newark, ramping up the state’s fight against the Trump administration.

The attorney general, Jennifer Davenport, said on Friday that her office had issued subpoenas and would investigate whether employees at the center violated the civil rights of detainees.

The announcement was made days after a detainee died and his family denounced the center, known as Delaney Hall, for failing to tend to his medical needs.

The detainee, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, was 41 and from El Salvador. His family has expressed concern that he might not have been getting the medication he needed to treat his diabetes and epilepsy.

The Department of Homeland Security and the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Geo Group, the private company that operates the detention center, referred questions to ICE.

“ICE and the Geo Group have continued to block our efforts for a full health inspection and there are now reports that visitations have been stopped,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey said after the announcement by the attorney general. “I have long opposed private detention facilities, and my position is clear that Delaney Hall should be closed.”

The federal detention center has been a persistent target of criticism from protesters and Democratic lawmakers since it reopened last year as part of Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Detainees have long complained of inhumane living conditions there, and demonstrators have responded by gathering at the center’s front gates, where clashes with federal agents have at times turned violent.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Tracey Tully contributed reporting.

Ana Ley is a Times reporter covering immigration in New York City.

Schumer Forges Ahead in Fight for Senate, Despite Setbacks

The New York Times August 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a phone call, the Democratic leader told the new Michigan contender who has opposed him to just win.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

For the third time this election season, Senator Chuck Schumer this week had to approach a newly minted Democratic nominee for Senate who had openly opposed keeping him as party leader and try to make common cause for a tough race ahead.

During a phone conversation on Wednesday with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who had just triumphed in Michigan over Mr. Schumer’s preferred candidate after a campaign that cast the Democratic leader as part of the problem with Washington, Mr. Schumer was eager to look past their divide.

“I said to him, ‘I don’t need you to like me,’” Mr. Schumer said in an interview as he recounted the conversation. “‘I just need you to win.’”

It is a refrain that Mr. Schumer, of New York, has returned to repeatedly during a chaotic campaign season in which he is working to recapture the majority, solidify his role as the Senate Democratic leader and set himself up for re-election should he decide to seek a sixth term in 2028.

It can be an awkward task as Democratic voters choose candidates hostile to him at a time when the energy in the party is coming from a left flank that disdains the establishment. Recent polling has also shown that Mr. Schumer’s overall public standing is poor, with just 15 percent expressing a favorable opinion of him and 44 percent unfavorable in a CNN poll conducted last month. He had the highest disapproval level of any congressional leader in either party in a survey that showed all four are deeply unpopular.

Despite all of that, Mr. Schumer this week projected optimism about his party’s outlook as the Senate breaks for the summer and the election looms three months off.

President Trump’s approval numbers are low and public discontent about the war in Iran and the price of everyday life is running high. Mr. Schumer said Senate Democrats began the congressional term focused on driving down the president’s popularity by concentrating on rising costs, how Mr. Trump and his family are profiting from his presidency and now the war with Iran — and have succeeded.

“We have been relentless about that in place after place after place, and it has worked,” Mr. Schumer said. “The public believes it is not just going after Trump. It is showing them that we are on their side and showing the division between us and them,” he said of Republicans.

Long the chief architect of his party’s Senate election strategy, Mr. Schumer set out to recruit top-tier candidates to give Democrats a chance of netting the four seats needed to regain the majority.

He scored what looked like notable successes in the key states of Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio and, critically, Maine, long projected the party’s best chance for a pickup by defeating Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, in a state carried by Democrats in the last two presidential elections.

Mr. Schumer secured the candidacy of Janet Mills, a two-term governor who would traditionally be considered a sterling recruit. But Mr. Trump’s tenure was shifting the Democratic Party to the left, and Ms. Mills was pushed out of the race by an untested populist oysterman, Graham Platner, who criticized Mr. Schumer and urged him to step aside.

Mr. Platner’s rise gave momentum to criticism that Mr. Schumer was increasingly out of step with the new progressive tide. But in a phone call after the Maine Democrat’s primary victory, that was water under the bridge; both men stressed the importance of beating Ms. Collins.

Mr. Platner’s campaign soon collapsed amid a series of sexual misconduct accusations, touching off a frenzied replacement process that ended with a new candidate, Troy Jackson, who also said he would not support Mr. Schumer for leader. The two have since met in Washington and had a cordial conversation, according to people familiar with it.

This week’s Michigan primary, in which the Democratic leader had favored Representative Haley Stevens, reignited backlash to Mr. Schumer for failing to embrace the progressive surge. But he said he had quickly engaged with Dr. El-Sayed and found some common ground with him as the two turned their attention to beating the Republican nominee, former Representative Mike Rogers.

“We had a really good conversation,” Mr. Schumer said. “I told him I think we’d agree on things: Beat Rogers, win Michigan, take back the Senate. He said I agree on all three.”

Mr. Schumer added that his takeaway from the call with Dr. El-Sayed was that “we have more that unites us than divides us.” In an interview on Thursday with The New York Times, Dr. El-Sayed, 41, described Mr. Schumer, 75, as “pragmatic.”

His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Mr. Schumer’s account of their conversation.

The primary winners who expressed resistance to Mr. Schumer have good reason for reaching a truce with the Democratic leader. They will need the full financial support of the Senate Majority PAC, the high-dollar political action committee aligned with Mr. Schumer, to have any chance of countering the Republican money that will pour into those races. The organization has already gone up with a digital campaign backing the new Democratic nominee in Michigan.

Republicans see an opening in the Michigan race with the nomination of Dr. El-Sayed, whom they have attacked as extreme, giving them an opportunity in a seat now held by a Democrat after playing defense elsewhere. Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, this week noted the leftward shift of the competition and said Republicans expected to retain the majority.

“We have quality candidates in all the key competitive races around the country,” he said. “They are going to be well resourced, and my hope would be that when it’s all said and done, we’re going to preserve and protect our majority.”

Among other issues that Mr. Schumer predicted would benefit the Democratic candidates in Maine and Michigan, two almost must-win states for the Democrats, is Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, which he said has caused significant economic disruptions in both those states that could hurt Republicans.

With most of the key general election matchups settled, Mr. Schumer and other Democrats say outcomes around the country have reshaped the map. Mr. Schumer now sees Democrats with a chance in places they would not normally be competitive given the president’s standing and the quality of their candidates, including Texas and Iowa, with long shots in Kansas and Mississippi.

“The way you build a majority is to expand the map,” Mr. Schumer said.

Mr. Schumer’s stewardship of Senate Democrats has stirred some grumbling from more progressive senators who resented his jumping into the primaries even though some endorsed primary candidates themselves.

But he said such criticism “goes with the territory.” He retains significant support for staying in a job that many senators do not consider that attractive given its pressure and demands.

Most of his colleagues assume that if Democrats capture the majority or significantly erode the Republican hold on the chamber, Mr. Schumer will stay on — though they are less certain about his intentions for 2028.

Mr. Schumer is not saying either way, brushing off questions about his future as he focuses on midterm elections that could help shape it.

“I am focused on winning the Senate in 2026,” he said.

Tim Balk contributed reporting.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.
