Prosecutor Sues Justice Dept. Over Dismissal After Right-Wing Influencer’s Claim

The New York Times August 07, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Will Rosenzweig joins a growing list of former prosecutors and federal agents who have gone to court to contest the purge of law enforcement deemed disloyal.

By Alan Feuer

One day last September, a right-wing influencer named Natalie Winters posted what she billed as an “EXCLUSIVE” on social media: A federal prosecutor in Miami overseeing a fraud case against “MAGA patriots” had once written a blog with comments critical of President Trump.

Ms. Winters, who has hundreds of thousands of followers, addressed her message to the accounts of senior officials at the Justice Department. Her demands for the prosecutor, Will Rosenzweig, could not have been clearer: “Fire him,” her message said.

Less than three hours later, the department did exactly that. Mr. Rosenzweig, who during his career had consistently earned praise for his work, received an emailed letter signed by Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, dismissing him from his position at the U. S. attorney’s office in Miami, effective immediately. No reason was provided.

On Friday, Mr. Rosenzweig sued the Justice Department along with Todd Blanche, who now runs the department, and Jason A. Reding Quiñones, the U. S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, asking for financial damages and his job back. In doing so, he joined a growing list of former prosecutors and federal agents who have gone to court in an effort to fight back against the widespread purge of law enforcement officials deemed to be disloyal to the president.

During Mr. Trump’s second term, agents and prosecutors have been fired for any number of reasons. Some were seasoned veterans who lost their jobs while trying to protect subordinates from being dismissed. Others were accused, sometimes incorrectly, of having worked on criminal cases involving the president. Many worked on cases stemming from the attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

Mr. Rosenzweig’s firing was one of several that shared a different twist: right-wing commentators claimed to be behind them. On the morning after he was terminated, Ms. Winters reposted a message from another far-right influencer, Laura Loomer, announcing the news. Ms. Winters’s message, punctuated by a smiley-face emoji, declared: “Got this guy fired.”

Many of Ms. Winters’s posts have since been deleted, but lawyers for Mr. Rosenzweig included screenshots of them in their lawsuit. In the posts, she said that Mr. Rosenzweig had “smeared” Mr. Trump in his writings by calling him “mentally unfit” and a “white supremacist.”

The Justice Department declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation. Ms. Winters did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.

Ms. Loomer, in particular, has used social media to target several administration officials whom she has accused of disloyalty to Mr. Trump. By her own account, she played a central role in Maurene Comey, a daughter of James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director, losing her job as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan last summer. After Ms. Comey’s termination, Ms. Loomer celebrated online, taking credit for a “pressure campaign.”

Another seasoned prosecutor, Michael P. Ben’Ary, lost his job in October after an online influencer accused him of being “part of the internal resistance” in the U. S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of Virginia to charging Mr. Comey with the first indictment brought against him.

In a farewell letter to colleagues posted on the door of his office, Mr. Ben’Ary, who spent much of his career working on international terrorism cases, expressed concern that important personnel decisions were apparently being made in response to online posts.

“Justice for Americans killed and injured by our enemies should not be contingent on what someone in the Department of Justice sees in their social media feed that day,” he wrote.

It remains unclear why Ms. Winters referred to the defendants in the fraud case that Mr. Rosenzweig was overseeing as “MAGA patriots.” The three men — Marcelo Kochen, Michael Kochen and Sandro Herek — do not appear to have any obvious public connection to Mr. Trump. They were charged with cheating Medicare out of millions of dollars in false and fraudulent claims.

Michael Kochen and Mr. Herek were convicted and sentenced to prison last week. Marcelo Kochen had his case severed from the others and has not yet gone to trial.

In their lawsuit, filed in Federal District Court in Miami, lawyers for Mr. Rosenzweig raised questions about how Ms. Winters had known that their client was working on the fraud case to begin with and was able to connect him to blog posts critical of Mr. Trump that had been written years earlier.

At the time Ms. Winters demanded that Mr. Rosenzweig be fired, the lawyers wrote, the Justice Department had never issued a news release about the case and the proceedings had received almost no attention in the news media.

Moreover, the lawyers wrote, Mr. Rosenzweig’s blog had been dormant at that point for nearly seven years, with no recent posts. And they were written before he had even applied to join the Justice Department.

“The primary source from which a member of the public might have learned about the case would have been through one of the parties,” the lawyers added.

Mr. Rosenzweig’s sudden dismissal came on the eve of the fraud case going to trial and threw his office into a “tailspin,” according to the lawyers. As the office scrambled to find a replacement for him, the government asked the judge overseeing the case to delay the trial. The defendants, who only one week earlier had also asked for a delay, abruptly changed course and insisted that the trial begin on schedule, seeking a tactical advantage.

Mr. Rosenzweig was observing Rosh Hashana on the day he was fired and did not see the email ordering his dismissal until nearly 8 p. m. He ultimately spoke with one of his supervisors who told him that Mr. Reding Quiñones had discussed his firing with officials in the office of the deputy attorney general, then led by Mr. Blanche, according to the suit.

The supervisor said it was after that conversation that the news about the dismissal “spread to Twitter,” the suit maintained. Mr. Rosenzweig’s lawyers acknowledged that they do not know whether the Justice Department received information about their client’s blog posts before Ms. Winters did or what effect the purported conversation between Mr. Reding Quiñones and Mr. Blanche’s office had on Ms. Bondi’s decision to fire Mr. Rosenzweig.

Regardless, Mr. Rosenzweig’s online writings criticizing Mr. Trump were “textbook examples” of speech protected by the First Amendment, his lawyers wrote.

“Mr. Rosenzweig published the blog posts as a private citizen, before he joined D. O. J., and his commentary addressed matters of public concern,” they added. “He did not make them pursuant to any official duty. Defendants terminated him because of that protected speech, or because of the political affiliation and beliefs they perceived from it.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

As Pressure Mounts, U. S. Hunts for Cuba’s Next Leader

The New York Times August 07, 2026

Crisis in Cuba

Advertisement

Supported by

Some officials warn that a more hard-line leader could emerge if the Trump administration moves forward with its plans.

By Tyler PagerJulian E. Barnes and Frances Robles

The reporters have been covering the Trump administration’s pressure campaign against Cuba.

The Trump administration has been looking for a current or former Cuban official who could be persuaded to take over the government in Havana as the United States ratchets up its pressure campaign, according to current and former U. S. officials.

The plan is more regime alteration than regime change.

The Trump administration has pressed its spy agencies to identify someone in the mold of Delcy Rodríguez, who became Venezuela’s interim president after U. S. forces captured the previous leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January.

U. S. officials viewed Ms. Rodríguez as a pragmatist who could seamlessly assume power and would be willing to work closely with them.

Some administration officials believe that a similarly pragmatic leader can be found in Cuba.

But American spy agencies have assessed that Cuba is less like Venezuela and more like Iran, according to people briefed on the intelligence reports.

There are few pragmatic officials who would be poised to take power if U. S. forces captured Raúl Castro, the former president of Cuba who still wields enormous political influence, or somehow forced out the current leadership, according to multiple U. S. officials.

Instead, the officials waiting in the wings in Cuba, like their Iranian counterparts, represent more hard-line factions.

The Trump administration has oscillated between wanting to work with Cuba’s Communist government and developing plans to overthrow it.

U. S. officials presented a list of demands to Cuban leaders in recent weeks, offering incentives if Cuba made progress.

The Trump administration wants Cuba to liberalize its economy, open up to American businesses, buy oil from the United States and push out Russian and Chinese intelligence operatives.

Few details are known about the incentives the United States has offered, but some involve providing more humanitarian aid and loosening U. S. sanctions imposed on the Cuban economy.

The current Cuban government does not appear willing, at least for now, to make those kinds of concessions, giving an urgency to the efforts to identify alternative leaders.

Cuba has announced major economic changes, allowing in more private enterprise, but the measures appear to have fallen short of what the Trump administration has demanded.

Representatives of the Cuban government did not respond to a request for comment.

The White House declined to comment. But an administration official said that while the United States is ready to open a new chapter with Cuba, the government in Havana was standing in the way of a better future.

Given the dearth of pragmatists, it is not clear whom the White House might prefer as an alternative leader.

The Cuban government appears to be supporting Oscar Pérez-Oliva Fraga, a grand nephew of Fidel Castro, as a potential successor. He has recently been more visible on state television and in government pronouncements, and even gave a rare interview to international news media.

But Mr. Pérez-Oliva Fraga would almost certainly be unacceptable to the United States. The Trump administration might be open to another Castro relative, Raúl G. Rodríguez Castro, known as “Raulito” or “El Cangrejo” (the Crab), Raúl Castro’s grandson. He long served as the former president’s bodyguard but has never held public office.

The current interior minister, Lázaro Alberto Álvarez Casas, may also be acceptable to U. S. officials.

When John Ratcliffe, the C. I. A. director, visited Cuba this year he met with both Mr. Rodríguez Castro and Mr. Álvarez Casas.

The C. I. A. has secretly established a Cuba task force, a signal that the Trump administration has set plans in motion for a more concerted pressure campaign against the Cuban government to make the changes demanded by President Trump.

U. S. and Israeli officials mulled a regime change plan for Iran when they launched their joint war more than five months ago.

At that time, Mr. Trump was obsessed with replicating the Venezuelan model in Iran, believing his administration could find a leader willing to work with the United States who might be in position to assume power after a decapitation strike against the government.

Some of the Iranian officials whom U. S. officials identified as more pragmatic were inadvertently killed in the opening strikes of the war that were aimed at killing the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

An Israeli plan that had the support of some in the U. S. government would have sought to bring Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, a former president of Iran, to power. Mr. Ahmadinejad was no moderate — while in office he called for the destruction of Israel. But after leaving the presidency, he became more and more critical of Iran’s clerical leaders. Israel began cultivating him and considering him to lead a new Iranian government.

But that plan went awry quickly. Mr. Ahmadinejad became disenchanted with the Israeli plan and ultimately left a safe house where Israel’s intelligence operatives had taken him.

In hindsight, the U. S. and Israeli strategy for regime change in Iran seemed far less planned out than the operation to grab Mr. Maduro in Venezuela.

The precise U. S. plans for Cuba remain unclear.

The U. S. government has imposed a de facto blockade on Cuba, bringing the island into crisis as energy supplies have nearly run out.

It is also not clear how far the Trump administration might go to force a leadership change. The Justice Department has unveiled an indictment of Raúl Castro. The U. S. government used an indictment of Mr. Maduro to justify the Special Operations raid that resulted in his capture.

But Mr. Maduro was the sitting president of Venezuela and his removal brought Ms. Rodríguez, who was then the vice president. In contrast, Mr. Castro, 95, holds no official office, and capturing or arresting him would not in itself prompt a leadership change.

In the months since the Maduro raid, Cuba has taken defensive measures to make it more difficult for U. S. forces to mount a raid to capture or kill Mr. Castro or the current president, Miguel Díaz-Canel, according to some American officials.

Adam Entous contributed reporting.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Frances Robles is a Times reporter covering Latin America and the Caribbean. She has reported on the region for more than 25 years.

Cassidy Will Back Blanche, Salvaging His Confirmation

The New York Times August 07, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Louisiana senator said that, despite reservations, he would back President Trump’s pick for attorney general, giving Republicans enough votes for a majority.

By Michael Gold and Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, said on Friday that he would support Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general, effectively saving the confirmation of President Trump’s pick after two other Republican senators said they would oppose him.

Mr. Cassidy, who lost his re-election bid to a Trump-backed challenger, said in a speech on the Senate floor that he had deep concerns about “apparent lawfare,” the phrase he has used to refer to the Justice Department’s targeting of the president’s political enemies.

But Mr. Cassidy said that after much consideration, he had come to believe that Mr. Blanche, who has served as the president’s personal lawyer, would be better positioned to push back against Mr. Trump’s norm-busting demands than an alternative.

“Mr. Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this,” Mr. Cassidy said. “But the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche. It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general, who may not run the department effectively under President Trump.”

He announced his decision hours after Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska became the second Republican to oppose Mr. Blanche’s confirmation, joining Senator Susan Collins of Maine. That threw the nominee’s fate into doubt, given that he could not afford additional Republican defectors, and intensified attention on Mr. Cassidy.

Ms. Murkowski said in a statement that she, too, harbored concerns over the “politicization” of the Justice Department. But the conclusion she reached was the opposite of Mr. Cassidy’s: She said that she feared that Mr. Blanche would “fail to check the worst impulses of this administration.”

Ms. Murkowski cited the department’s handling of the release of the Epstein files, which Mr. Blanche oversaw, and the settlement agreement that Mr. Blanche negotiated in Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I. R. S., which included the creation of a $1.8 billion compensation fund that could have been used to pay people charged in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

“The country needs an attorney general who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” Ms. Murkowski said. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”

Ms. Collins, who is running for re-election in a state that Mr. Trump lost in 2024, said on Tuesday that she would vote against Mr. Blanche over similar concerns. Given the continued absence of Senator Mitch McConnell, the Kentucky Republican who has been gone for nearly eight weeks because of illness, Mr. Blanche could afford to lose no more than two Republican votes and still win a majority for confirmation over the opposition of Democrats.

Ms. Murkowski, Ms. Collins and Mr. Cassidy are the only three remaining Republican senators in office who voted to convict Mr. Trump on impeachment charges and remove him from office following the Jan. 6 attack.

Mr. Trump had urged Senate Republicans to swiftly confirm Mr. Blanche, and Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, is hoping to bring his nomination to a vote before lawmakers leave Washington this weekend for their August recess.

Mr. Blanche’s nomination has had a rough road. The Judiciary Committee delayed advancing it to the full Senate after two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, raised questions about the $1.8 billion fund, which Mr. Blanche had said would not move ahead, and the extraordinary immunity from tax audits given to Mr. Trump and his businesses in his resolution of the I. R. S. lawsuit.

After days of negotiation, Mr. Blanche on Sunday night provided written assurances that the fund was dead and that the immunity for the president would be narrowed, and Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis dropped their objections.

But while Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis focused their demands on the terms of the settlement, both Ms. Murkowski and Ms. Collins made a much broader case that Mr. Blanche’s participation in the plan’s creation was itself disqualifying.

In her statement, Ms. Murkowski said that she also worried that Mr. Blanche’s commitments could be easily undone and the fund could too easily be restored after his confirmation, a concern shared by many critics.

“I am also keenly aware that the department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund — which likely would have rewarded Jan. 6 protesters — is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage,” she said. “Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds.”

Like Ms. Collins, Ms. Murkowski is a supporter of abortion rights. In announcing their opposition, both referenced Mr. Blanche’s telling anti-abortion groups that he would take a hard line in enforcing the Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade.

In his speech on Friday, Mr. Cassidy also criticized Mr. Blanche’s involvement in negotiating the fund and the audit protections, calling it “poor judgment.”

But he said that discussions with Mr. Blanche led him to believe that the acting attorney general viewed those decisions as mistakes. Mr. Blanche met privately with both him and Ms. Murkowski on Wednesday at the Capitol.

Mr. Cassidy said that he had been influenced in part by Mr. Trump’s threat to keep Mr. Blanche as the acting attorney general indefinitely, effectively ignoring any resistance from Congress. The senator said he believed a Senate confirmation vote would give Mr. Blanche “greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for” than he would have if he continued in an acting capacity.

He also cited Mr. Blanche’s support from William P. Barr, who served as attorney general during Mr. Trump’s first term but resigned rather than promote or investigate the president’s lies about the 2020 election.

Mr. Barr, who has established himself as an informal adviser to Mr. Blanche, has argued in private meetings with senators that Mr. Blanche has the temperament, access and approach to quietly mitigate the president’s demands. Mr. Barr’s own efforts to counter Mr. Trump were intermittent and had mixed results.

Mr. Cassidy, who has become more openly critical of the president since his election defeat in May, said his views about Mr. Trump did not factor into his decision about Mr. Blanche.

“I have a history with Mr. Trump,” he said, “but that history does not matter one bit.”

The Louisiana Republican, a doctor who leads the health committee, faced significant outcry last year after backing Mr. Trump’s choice of a vaccine skeptic, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., to be the health secretary, after securing promises from Mr. Kennedy that were later broken. That decision may have cost him critical support with moderate voters in his failed primary campaign.

On Friday, he appeared to grow emotional as he announced his decision on Mr. Blanche.

“I’ll be criticized for this vote,” Mr. Cassidy said. “What’s new?”

Then he paused to collect himself, his voice growing shaky as he said his constituents could be “assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision.”

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

By Lynsey Chutel

Vast swaths of Central and Eastern Europe are in the middle of a heat wave, with high temperatures reaching record levels this week. The heat has also brought drought conditions, drying rivers and creating a fire a hazard.

The Danube River’s receding water levels nearly forced the shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant in Hungary, the prime minister said this week, and, in Serbia, it exposed ships from a Nazi fleet that sank at the end of World War II.

Here’s what to know.

On Thursday, Slovakia broke a provisional heat record set just the day before, reaching 42.2 degrees Celsius, or nearly 108 Fahrenheit.

It was the first time that the air temperature at the Dolné Plachtince weather station in the south of the country had reached 42 degrees, the Slovak Meteorological Institute said on social media.

The Czech Meteorological Institute said on social media that this could be the highest temperature on record for all of Central Europe.

Hungary recorded a new national record for the highest maximum temperature in a day, with temperatures reaching 41.8 degrees Celsius, or about 107 degrees Fahrenheit, in the southern city of Kiskunfelegyhaza. The previous record, set in 1905 at a different weather station, was 40.2 degrees, or 104.3 Fahrenheit, according to the Hungarian meteorological institute.

Eastern and Central Europe will continue to experience high temperatures this weekend and into next week, with Skopje, Macedonia, a particular hot spot. Temperatures are expected to rise to 38 degrees, or about 100 degrees Fahrenheit, this weekend, according to a regional forecast by the Bulgarian weather service.

While the degree to which a single heat event is influenced by climate change requires specific attribution studies, scientists are certain that heat waves around the world are generally becoming hotter, more frequent and longer-lasting, and Europe is warming faster than any other continent.

In 2025, almost the entire continent was hotter than normal. Researchers estimate that in recent years, Europe has seen tens of thousands of heat-related deaths annually.

Many homes, schools and businesses across Europe were built for an older, cooler climate. In Britain, many were even built to retain heat, making cooling off amid heat waves especially difficult. Air-conditioning is not a quick fix. In France, installing such systems has become a political flashpoint, while in Britain, high energy prices deter many.

Even in hotter Mediterranean cities, where old-fashioned courtyards, heavy shutters and white-stone facades can keep homes cool, many newer buildings have been constructed using techniques that trap heat.

Notes: Forecasts are for 8 p. m. Eastern on Aug. 6, 2026, to 8 p. m. on Aug. 7, 2026. Averages based on data from 1979 to 2000.

By Lazaro Gamio and Zach Levitt

Staying cool and hydrating often are the two most important things to do to avoid feeling sick and discomfort in extreme heat. Here are some other ways to keep cool:

Block out the windows in your home — especially those that get afternoon sun — with a blanket or a darker sheet during the day to keep the heat out. At night, keep windows open and run fans to circulate the air.

Spritz your skin with a mist of cool or room-temperature water or wipe your forehead with a cool cloth. Cold showers can also help you cool down.

If you need to be outdoors, put ice cubes in your water bottle and drink cool liquids. If you plan to exercise, douse your head in cold water. Swimming is also a great way to exercise and keep cool.

When exploring or sightseeing, seek out cooler attractions such as museums, cathedrals or even subterranean exhibitions. Some cities have created public spaces to cool down: Barcelona has climate shelters and Paris has drinking fountains, for example. London has a Cool Spaces map to find spots.

Watch out for signs of heat stroke. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists some of them as dizziness, a rapid pulse, nausea, headache and fainting. But symptoms can vary.

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

‘Green and Pleasant’ No More, England Turns a Parched Brown

The New York Times August 07, 2026

Extreme Heat

Beset by historically dry weather, much of the nation is losing its signature hue.

A parched park on the south bank of the River Thames in central London on Thursday, with Tower Bridge in the background. Credit... Henry Nicholls/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Supported by

By Kieran Corcoran

Reporting from London, where his garden is not looking great

When William Blake conjured an idealized England in the early 1800s, it was of a “green and pleasant land.”

The image, from his poem known as “Jerusalem,” burrowed deep into the nation’s psyche. People sing it as a hymn in churches, at sports stadiums, in concert halls and at political rallies.

It is, however, increasingly at odds with the England of 2026, scorched and wilting under an unforgiving sun.

Officials in July declared half of England to be in a drought after a run of weather that set records and a month in which 19 of its 48 counties saw effectively no rain at all. To conserve water, many utilities have banned the use of sprinklers and hose pipes, which might have kept parched lawns and fields greener.

Here is how that looks in some of the country’s more recognizable places:

Sussex, Aug. 4

On Beachy Head, an outcrop on England’s south coast known for the striking contrast between its white chalk cliffs, blue sea and the green grass, an element is missing.

Wiltshire, July 28

The Neolithic site in southwest England, a draw for millions of tourists, has been left scorched and arid.

Windsor, July 31

The tree-lined Long Walk to the castle, a residence favored by Queen Elizabeth II, was without much of its usual vibrancy after weeks of relentless heat.

Berkshire, July 25

In Bray, a village on the River Thames west of London, only the cricket pitch kept any of its luster.

Kent, August 6

A seaside scene at Reculver Beach in Kent, nicknamed the “Garden of England.”

Yorkshire, July 29

Northern England, which is not under drought restrictions, has lost its color. Here is Saltburn-by-the-Sea, a town near the city of Middlesbrough.

London, July 27

On Primrose Hill, a prime viewing spot overlooking London from the north, little is left of a usually verdant expanse.

Kieran Corcoran is an editor covering breaking news and other topics for The Times in London.

‘Shame!’: An ICE Facility Roils a Tiny Town, With a House Seat in Play

The New York Times August 07, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Tiny Hudson, Colo., was mostly known as a speed trap between plains and suburbs. Then ICE announced it was coming, setting off months of protests.

Tiny Hudson, Colo., was mostly known as a speed trap between plains and suburbs. Then ICE announced it was coming, setting off months of protests.

Credit...

Supported by

By Jack Healy

Reporting from Hudson, Colo.

After the Pledge of Allegiance and a discussion of food truck regulations, the town councilors in tiny Hudson, Colo., reached the hard part of their weekly meeting: getting yelled at by dozens of protesters furious about an immigration detention center set to open in an empty prison on the edge of town.

“You’re Nazis!” several members of the crowd shouted, waving anti-ICE posters. “Shame! Shame!”

The protesters had driven in from blue cities along Colorado’s Front Range to fill the town hall in Hudson, a town of 1,600 with one stop light and no grocery store that sits in a sea of farmland and oil-and-gas operations in Northern Colorado. It is just a 45-minute drive from Denver but in a different political universe, where residents voted overwhelmingly for President Trump.

Until recently, Hudson was mostly known as a speed trap, but the arrival of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility has now plunged the town into one of the country’s most divisive debates and jolted the re-election campaign of one of the most vulnerable Republicans in Congress.

The detention center will sit along the border of Colorado’s Eighth Congressional District, a heavily Latino district served by Representative Gabe Evans, a Trump stalwart who ousted a Democrat two years ago.

Now, Democrats are hoping they can capitalize on growing anger over the high cost of living and Mr. Trump’s deportation campaign to retake the district and reclaim control of Congress.

Mr. Evans has expressed support for immigration detention centers, while his Democratic challenger, Manny Rutinel, a progressive state lawmaker, is campaigning on a pledge to “stop ICE from terrorizing our communities.”

When it opens, as early as next month, the Big Horn detention center in Hudson could vastly expand immigration enforcement in a corner of Colorado where immigrants from across the world work in meatpacking plants and fields. It would nearly double Colorado’s immigrant detention capacity, and opponents say it would sow fear across the plains.

Diana and Ernesto Cruz, who live in nearby Fort Lupton, Colo., voted Republican in 2024 after being fed up with inflation and scenes of chaos along the southern border under former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. But they said Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown had gone too far, and they did not want an ICE detention center down the road. They are planning to vote for Mr. Rutinel in November.

“There are more important things,” Mr. Cruz said on Wednesday, as he parked his big-rig truck outside the couple’s American flag-draped home.

Late last year, protesters rallied outside Mr. Evans’s district office in Greeley, Colo., to urge him not to support the detention center. A spokeswoman for Mr. Evans declined a request to discuss the issue.

Conservatives in Mr. Evans’s district said they welcomed the prospect of more immigration enforcement in Colorado, a Democratic-led state that the Trump administration has attacked for its sanctuary policies. They’ve also argued that the detention center would create jobs and revive a prison that has sat empty for more than a decade.

“It’s just sitting there,” said Denise Geddes, a nurse’s aide in Fort Lupton who described herself as “big time MAGA.” Unauthorized immigrants, she said, are “taking over the system.”

“We’re going to scoop your butt up,” she continued.

The GEO Group, one of the country’s largest private prison companies, has a $529 million contract to run the facility and is already advertising for security officers, starting at $35 an hour, and other support staff. On Wednesday, a few pickup trucks came and went from the property, but there was no sign that any detainees had arrived. Neither the GEO Group nor ICE responded to requests for comment.

Hudson’s leaders insist they are powerless to stop the center. Bryce Lange, the town manager, said the prison had been approved by town voters years ago and that it still had a certificate of occupancy, even though it has sat empty for more than a decade.

“We’re very limited in our abilities to do anything,” Mr. Lange said. “It’s already built.”

The prison building is owned by Highlands REIT, a Chicago-based real-estate investment trust, which did not respond to requests for comment.

The town’s inaction has only fueled protesters’ frustration. Opponents of the prison sued Hudson last month, arguing the building site is not zoned for an immigration detention center. The suit says the facility could strain Hudson’s water systems, roads and emergency services by housing as many as 1,200 detainees in a remote facility 12 miles from the nearest hospital.

“The town has thrown up its hands and claimed it does not have the authority to act — that is a lie,” said David Seligman, executive director of the progressive legal nonprofit Towards Justice, which sued Hudson on behalf of a faith group and a neighbor near the facility.

Dozens of protesters regularly flock to Hudson to march through the streets and demonstrate in the dusty field outside town hall. Thousands of people have deluged the town with angry written comments.

“It’s against every fiber of my being,” said Barbara Mills-Bria, a retired engineer who drove from suburban Denver to Hudson with two friends to attend a raucous council meeting on Wednesday.

A brass band strutted through a quiet neighborhood as organizers handed out leaflets opposing the detention center, prompting pickup trucks stuck behind the procession to honk in frustration. Chesney Baldwin, a college student who lives in Hudson, was puzzled as he watched the marchers go by.

“Everyone here likes ICE,” he said. “This isn’t Denver.”

Some residents and town leaders are tired of the scrutiny and say their normally staid town meetings have been hijacked by outsiders. Five police officers were searching bags and providing security at a council meeting on Wednesday as dozens of demonstrators waited to make statements opposing the detention center.

“These people don’t pay taxes here,” Tracy Trevarton, a Hudson resident said, as she stood in the entryway to town hall. “We can’t even get in here and conduct our own business. It’s tearing our town apart.”

Protesters, in turn, have accused Hudson of trying to stifle open debate by limiting public comments. The meeting this week grew so heated that the mayor abruptly adjourned it, prompting even more outrage.

Kerry Shaklee, a longtime resident and member of Hudson’s planning commission, walked away shaking his head. He said he opposed the detention center, which he characterized as a “travesty.” But he also felt for the besieged town government.

“They’ve been through the wringer,” he said. “I ran for council. Thank God I lost. I didn’t need to sit through all of this.”

Jack Healy is based in Colorado and covers the west and southwest for The Times.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

In an interview with The New York Times, Dr. El-Sayed recalled some of his conversations with establishment figures who once opposed his candidacy.

Credit... Nick Hagen for The New York Times

Supported by

By Tim Balk

Reporting from Ann Arbor, Mich.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who won a divisive Democratic Senate primary this week in the crucial swing state of Michigan with an unabashedly progressive message, has been flooded with calls from leaders of the party establishment he challenged during his campaign.

He spoke with Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader who had privately opposed him in the primary, about “taking back the Senate and taking on Trump,” Dr. El-Sayed recalled. He had more than one conversation with Representative Haley Stevens after he narrowly defeated her in the primary.

He also compared notes about campaigning in Michigan with former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost the state in 2024. And he chatted with both Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, a billionaire, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, a democratic socialist.

In an interview at a coffee shop in Ann Arbor on Thursday, Dr. El-Sayed spoke about his victory, the way progressive candidates resonated with young voters and some of the regrets he had about the bruising primary.

Asked about the possibility of becoming the first Muslim senator if he beats the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed said, “I’m just interested in being the next U. S. senator from Michigan.”

He argued that Mr. Rogers was “corrupt” and had no “vision” for the country. (A spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers, Alyssa Brouillet, responded in a statement saying that Mr. Rogers had spent his life “serving Michigan” and “exposing frauds like Abdul El-Sayed.”)

And Dr. El-Sayed addressed Jewish Michigan residents who expressed strong concerns about his vocal criticism of Israel, saying he was eager to speak to Jewish communities across the state about how “they’re feeling right now.”

He declined to say whether he would continue to campaign with Hasan Piker, a provocative streamer and critic of Israel whose appearances with him on the campaign trail became a flashpoint. “Look, I’m just a lot more focused on who I’m campaigning to,” he said.

But he appeared eager to set his sights on President Trump, who is unpopular and whom Democrats across the country hope to make the focus of the general election three months away. Mr. Trump has falsely described him and other Democratic candidates as communists.

Dr. El-Sayed said that the president had inherited his wealth and shown that he knew “nothing” about capitalism. He added that he would relish a chance to debate Mr. Trump.

“My hair is real,” he said, adding, “And my hands are way bigger than his.”

Below are excerpts from the interview, which have been condensed and edited for clarity.

Who have you heard from since you won? Anyone that surprised you?

My mom.

I hope that didn’t surprise you.

Nope.

What was your conversation like when Congresswoman Stevens called you?

We had a good, warm conversation. Obviously we had a hard-fought campaign. And I think we were able to define our differences. But they’re far smaller than our similarities.

Was there anything that made your campaign unusual, tactically?

Coherence. I want to make sure that when somebody touches our campaign — in any way they touch us — that our message is clear, it’s concise and it’s consistent. Even if you’re volunteering and you’re knocking on our door, the message you’re hearing is about: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all” — and this is why it matters to me. And as much as people want to pretend or act like we had a personality-driven campaign, it wasn’t. It was driven by a message. I can walk into almost any room, and I can say: “Money out of?” and everybody’s like: “Politics.” “Money in your?” “Pocket.” “Medicare for?” “All.” People know what we’re about.

Can I ask you about young people? How have progressives from New York City to Ann Arbor succeeded in inspiring volunteerism —

I think, again, it goes back to integrity. Are you who you say you are?

What do you think is the key to getting them to come out? To live events? To volunteer?

I think they want to come out. I think they’re just not willing to come out for candidates and campaigns that don’t seem consistent or —

So it’s the message?

It’s about the message more than anything else. Everybody focuses on style. I don’t think style matters, man. Everyone’s like, “Oh you campaign like a young person.” No. I campaign like a millennial dad, because that’s what I am. Right? But I am consistent. I say the same thing to everybody regardless of where I go.

It was a bruising race, even down to the end. Do you have any regrets about how —

Anybody who lives any life and says, ‘I have no regrets,’ is lying to you. Obviously, there are things that in hindsight, you would have done differently. But hindsight’s 20/20.

Well, in hindsight, is there anything you can tell me: Oh, yeah, I wish I hadn’t said that?

At the end of the day, when you’re in the heat of a very intense primary, there are always going to be things that you wish you could take back. I wish there wasn’t $60 million of spending against us. I wish we could have just fully transacted the campaign on ideals and ideas. Obviously, I would have loved to just keep the focus on the contrast between what we were hoping to do and what our opponents were hoping to do. And if I could go back and do it again, I would have just kept it on those contrasts.

What’s your message to Black voters going into the midterms?

We have a clear opportunity to fight for the kind of America where all people, regardless of the color of their skin can thrive. That’s been the work that I’ve been committed to since I took the job as health director in 2015 in the City of Detroit. And I’m hoping to serve in the same way that I served in the City of Detroit and Wayne County to fight for communities that are too often neglected and forgotten. That is the work that I have been doing for a long time. So I’m looking forward to continuing to build that relationship. Just like I have for the better part of 10 years.

There are Jewish folks in Michigan who say they’re anxious about some of your comments. They’re anxious that they could make them less safe in Michigan. What’s your message to them?

My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge. And we need to address it in all its forms. And I’m looking forward to continuing to get around the state to listen to Jewish communities to understand how they’re feeling right now and to share what we hold in common, and what we have yet to fight for.

We’ve spoken about capitalism versus socialism.

Do you want to talk about capitalism? Let’s talk about capitalism. Are you recording? Capitalism is about leveraging the laws of supply and demand to efficiently allocate capital expenditure to maximize value. When capitalism works, it’s because you have free entry and exit into markets. So if you believe in capitalism, you have to believe in government regulation to protect markets. In fact, right now, we have exactly the opposite. You don’t have to be a socialist to believe that you should be taxing billionaires their wealth. In fact, if you are a capitalist, you should believe in that. So, I’m capitalist who just knows about capitalism. I have a bad habit of reading, I’m so sorry.

How do you think Democrats combat the president saying they are communists? That’s one of his core arguments —

The man is so clearly a joker, except for everybody’s afraid of him. I am not afraid of him. Right? I would be happy to debate him on anything, anywhere, anytime, on any issue, in any place.

If you beat Mike Rogers, you would be the first Muslim —

I’m just interested in being the next U. S. senator from Michigan.

Do you think it would be meaningful, though, for —

I think it’ll say something about who our country is. There are a lot of people like Mike Rogers and like Donald Trump and like JD Vance who want to define America as being far smaller than I know America is. Born and raised here, and yes, I have an uncommon name, which they’re going to point to a lot. And they want to make it seem like I am somehow less American because of my uncommon name. If anything, I know that America is big enough for people with names like mine. And I’ve seen it every single day. Americans are big-hearted and open-minded. They are asking less about how you pray than what you pray for.

What did Vice President Kamala Harris tell you?

She congratulated me on a race well run and compared notes about campaigning in Michigan. And I was grateful for her outreach. She shared a lot of perspectives on what she had learned, and we shared a good conversation about what it’ll take to win Michigan — keep Michigan in 2026 for Democrats for the Senate.

Zohran Mamdani was asked about you yesterday. He said you could probably bench a lot more than him —

He’s better at soccer than I am.

Can you give me one word to describe Mike Rogers?

Just one?

Just one. Maybe two if —

Corrupt. Self-serving.

How about Haley Stevens?

Team player.

Zohran Mandani.

New York.

Chuck Schumer.

One word?

Or two.

Pragmatic.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Inspiring.

A Pope From Chicago Was Elected. The White Sox Were Resurrected.

The New York Times August 07, 2026

The elevation of Pope Leo XIV, a Chicago native and lifelong supporter of the Sox, was a godsend for a team failing on the field and with fans.

A mural depicting Pope Leo XIV is displayed near the seat where he attended a Chicago White Sox playoff game at Rate Field in 2005. Credit... Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times

Supported by

By Tania Ganguli

Tania Ganguli attended a White Sox game at Rate Field In Chicago and briefly sat in the pope’s seat. The White Sox won, as they often do these days.

On May 8, 2025, Mike Downey, the senior director of promotions and marketing for the Chicago White Sox, took a break from work to swing by the office lunchroom on the third floor of the ballpark. A news channel playing on a television screen said the papal conclave at the Vatican had finally selected a pope. Mr. Downey, a lifelong Catholic, checked social media for more details.

The pope was American, for the first time in the church’s history. Interesting, he thought.

The pope was from Chicago. How cool.

Oh, he’s from a suburb just south of Chicago.

Do I know him? wondered Mr. Downey, incredulously.

Word was that the pope was a fan of the Chicago Cubs, the White Sox’ rivals on the North Side. The Cubs quickly announced the news on their marquee (“Hey, Chicago. He’s a Cubs Fan!”) and posted a photo on X.

Around the White Sox’ office, staffers and executives lamented their bad luck. A South Side Cubs fan? What a shame!

Then, just as suddenly, came a rebuttal from the pope’s brother: No, actually, Pope Leo XIV, formerly Robert Prevost, was a White Sox fan.

Mr. Downey — who had the forlorn job of enticing Chicagoans to spend money to see the lowly White Sox — immediately recognized the opportunity before him.

He distinctly remembers his first thought: Oh my god.

In 2024, the White Sox set a record for the most losses in modern Major League Baseball history, with 121. More than a month into the 2025 season, they remained firmly in control of last place in the American League Central. Their average home attendance in both seasons was the fourth-worst in Major League Baseball.

It was Mr. Downey’s job to find something to celebrate amid the gloom. He and his team had a long list of promotions planned for 2025, the team’s 125th anniversary season. A plush blanket. A 1907 replica jersey. A 1972 Dick Allen M. V. P. bobblehead. A working radio shaped like Comiskey Park, the team’s home for most of its history.

“That also was, honestly, trying to shield people,” Mr. Downey said. “Make people forget about what happened the year before.”

On the day the new pope was elected, the White Sox rewarded his enduring faith in them by losing to the Kansas City Royals, 10-0. Still, the pope’s fandom gave the team a new promotional angle, a way to respectfully capitalize on the joy sweeping over the city.

After confirming that Pope Leo was one of theirs, the White Sox made sure everyone knew it. Their social media team cheekily corrected the Cubs’ marquee, posting a photo of the White Sox’ scoreboard with the words, “Hey Chicago, He’s a Sox Fan!” Sales of their primary baseball cap increased by 33 percent in the next week. By the end of the year, three of the 10 White Sox social media posts that got the most engagement had something to do with the pope.

But those were one-offs; gaining an ally in the 266th successor to St. Peter called for grander ideas, so Mr. Downey and his colleagues set to work.

The team’s senior director of design services created a digital mural of the pope for a wall between Sections 140 and 141. In the top right corner is a smaller image — a screenshot from a television broadcast of Game 1 of the 2005 World Series when Pope Leo, then the leader of the Order of St. Augustine, was caught on camera during the final out. The team also added a commemorative plaque to the seat he occupied that day.

The obvious next step was to get the pope back in the stadium, at least in spirit.

Chicago has a large Catholic population, and the Archdiocese of Chicago is the third-largest diocese in the United States. According to the Pew Research Center, 59 percent of adults in the city identify as Christian and 29 percent say they are Catholic, the largest of any denomination. The White Sox have hosted a small Mass for stadium employees for 30 years, when the Bertucci family, which still runs the Patio, the field-level hospitality area where the Mass is held, organized it.

A month after the pope’s election, the White Sox helped the archdiocese schedule a public Mass at Rate Field, where the team plays. About 35,000 tickets were sold at $5 each, during a season when the White Sox averaged 17,849 fans a game. Some tickets wound up on the secondary market for more than $1,000, according to The Chicago Sun-Times.

For Brooks Boyer, an observant Catholic who is the team’s chief marketing officer, having any kind of association with the pope was heady stuff.

“We’ve had sitting mayors of Chicago, we’ve had governors of Illinois that have been avid White Sox fans, we had a president of the United States in Barack Obama,” he said. “I didn’t expect anything bigger than the mayor when I started this job, but we’ve kind of climbed the ladder. What’s next? I mean, I feel like we’re one step away from God.”

The pope sent an eight-minute recorded address, his first comments to an American audience. He directed much of his message toward young people, saying that he recognized the isolation they experienced during the Covid pandemic but that they could still be “beacons of hope.”

He thanked them for gathering at Rate Field, but he didn’t call it that. He called it White Sox Park.

The bobblehead is the essential promotional giveaway of sports teams everywhere, regardless of whether the head on the spring belongs to an actual player. When you consider that the Atlanta Braves twice gave away Outkast bobbleheads with Big Boi and André 3000 in a red convertible, and the New York Yankees are about to hand out their third version of a George Costanza bobblehead, a Pope Leo bobblehead was all but inevitable.

Mr. Downey called the team’s bobblehead producer the day the pope was elected. He ordered four samples with Pope Leo wearing his traditional robes while holding a White Sox hat over his chest. (He later ordered four more based on a photograph of Pope Leo wearing a White Sox hat.)

He shared the prototypes with Mr. Boyer, who gave two of them to Cardinal Blase Cupich of the Chicago archdiocese during the stadium Mass. He hoped that on the cardinal’s next visit to the Vatican he could present the bobbleheads to the right parties for approval.

“We don’t use his likeness without permission of the Vatican,” Mr. Boyer said.

Mr. Downey felt sure that the Vatican would greenlight the idea.

“And then we just heard nothing,” he said. “Each month went by and it was nothing, nothing, nothing.”

In November, he emailed the Rev. Tom Hurley, who had officiated his wedding to his wife, “to make a last-ditch attempt on bobblehead approval.” Father Hurley sent Mr. Downey to another priest, the Rev. Tom McCarthy, a South Side native of the Augustinian order, the same as Pope Leo.

Father McCarthy had strong fan credentials. His mother had worked at a steak stand in the White Sox’ old stadium, and he had been to games with his father. Father McCarthy has known Pope Leo for 35 years, he said in an interview, but no longer has a direct line to him. Instead, he emailed a Vatican communications office. “I did get a response, and they just said that they were not interested.”

He laughed.

“I think they may think a bobblehead is disrespectful,” Father McCarthy said. “But in the United States, I think people understand a bobblehead can be very complimentary.”

The team communicates with the Vatican through the Archdiocese of Chicago, Mr. Boyer said. But when contacted by The New York Times, a spokeswoman for the archdiocese said, “The White Sox do not seek, and the archdiocese does not offer, approval of individual promotions.”

So anyway, no White Sox pope bobblehead.

Mr. Downey’s other promotional idea was to give away “the full pope get-up,” as he put it — the miter, robe and chasuble. He ran it by Father Hurley, who suggested sticking just to the hat.

The team planned to give out 1,500 pope hats to fans who bought a special ticket for the White Sox game this Tuesday against the Cincinnati Reds. The tickets sold out so quickly that they added 500 more. And then another 500.

Finally, Mr. Downey and Gareth Breunlin, the team’s vice president for marketing and advertising, approached Mr. Boyer sheepishly about giving the hat away to everyone who comes to the game. Mr. Downey recalled telling him, “The pope hat is going bonkers.”

Mr. Boyer agreed, which means miters for about 40,000 people.

It would be easy, in an article like this, to resort to cutesy speculation about God’s rooting interests, given the pope’s proclivities. We are above that. Still, it must be said that the White Sox, who lost 102 games last year and finished in last place, are now in first place in their division.

Nobody is saying God is a White Sox fan, but they’re not not saying it either.

During a game against the Kansas City Royals on June 26, pitcher Mike Vasil wore a microphone for the team’s broadcast partner. Catcher Drew Romo, who is Catholic, approached him in the dugout.

“Pope Leo, if you’re watching this game right now, say a quick prayer for a Jacob Gonzalez homer right now,” Mr. Romo said so the mic could catch it.

Seconds later, Mr. Gonzalez hit his first home run at Rate Field. Mr. Vasil bellowed, “It’s working, Leo!”

The White Sox scored 22 runs in that game, the most they had scored in a single game since 1970.

“I was having fun with that but also kind of being real,” Mr. Romo said in an interview. “Like, Pope Leo, if you are watching this game, your prayers probably would help the team.”

If the pope wasn’t watching live, he almost certainly heard about it the next day. When A. J. Pierzynski, one of the stars of the White Sox’ 2005 championship team, got an audience with Pope Leo in late June, he told him the White Sox were in first place. The pope said he already knew that.

Mr. Pierzynski presented Leo with the game ball from the final out of the World Series game the pope had attended.

“He gets a million jerseys,” Mr. Pierzynski said. “I had the ball. That was the one thing he could never get. I’m sure it means more to him than it does hanging on my wall.”

A few weeks later the Athletics, who were on a six-game losing streak, visited the White Sox. Their manager, Mark Kotsay, who is also Catholic, sought out the mural of Pope Leo.

“I was asking just for peace,” Mr. Kotsay said. “And, yes, a change of luck, for sure.”

For him, it didn’t work. The A’s lost their next four games, including all three against the White Sox, whose fans are noticing their success. On average, the team has drawn 6,135 more attendees per game this year than they did in 2025 — the fourth-largest increase in Major League Baseball.

Recently, the pope had dinner with Brian Burch, the U. S. ambassador to the Holy See. Mr. Burch, also from Chicago but a Cubs fan, joked in an interview that the pope’s rooting interest was “the first heresy of this papacy.”

The pope’s fandom, he said, “is a reminder of his American roots.”

“Often people kind of imagine the pope as some sort of ethereal, otherworldly spiritual leader,” Mr. Burch continued. “And because he’s the first American pope and because he does what Americans do, which is root for their hometown baseball team, and he’s a very devoted fan at that, there’s a sense of connection to the papacy that has never been possible before.”

The connection will be evident at Tuesday’s pope hat giveaway game, which is almost sold out, Mr. Downey said.

Still, Mr. Downey is keeping the bobblehead prototypes on his desk at Rate Field. The White Sox would not allow photographs of them for fear of getting on the wrong side of the church. But if the Vatican ever changes its mind, Mr. Downey will be ready.

I chose a Sunday to visit the White Sox ballpark to see the mass hosted for stadium employees. There were ushers, concession workers, the team's chief marketing officer, Brooks Boyer, and two opposing players, alongside their manager and his 18-year-old son. White Sox outfielder Sam Antonacci attended and posed for pictures afterward. He hit a lead-off home run later that day. I ended every interview with my tongue-in-cheek question: Are the White Sox benefitting from divine intervention? Manager Will Venable said, "Honestly, there's things that specifically at home that have happened this year that yeah you feel like there is something special."

Tania Ganguli writes about money, power and influence in sports and how it impacts the broader culture.

The Rom-Com Gets Political

The New York Times August 07, 2026

What to Watch

In “One Night Only,” Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner play singles living in a world where the government has banned premarital sex. How far-fetched is that?

In “One Night Only,” Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner play singles living in a world where the government has banned premarital sex. How far-fetched is that?

Credit...

Supported by

By Ashley Spencer

Visuals by Maddy Rotman

Boy meets girl. They banter. They gallivant around New York City. They’re trying to find love … under the thumb of totalitarian oppression?

That’s the setup of the new romantic comedy “One Night Only” (in theaters Aug. 7).

Directed by Will Gluck (“Anyone but You,” “Easy A”), the film is set in a version of the city that looks nearly identical to reality with one twist: Premarital sex is illegal, except for the one night each year when unmarried people are allowed to copulate at will. In the movie’s elaborate world-building, the law is the result of a conservative United States government and it is enforced through biosensors, though there is active resistance.

Against this backdrop, the hopeless romantic Allie (Monica Barbaro) and the recently jilted Owen (Callum Turner) keep getting thrown together via a series of chaotic events.

To get a sense of the film he was hoping to make, Gluck asked Barbaro to watch “Uncut Gems,” “After Hours” and “Midnight Run” — films with tight timelines and escalating stakes.

“I was like, OK, there’s not a single rom-com, but I know you’re the rom-com guy,” said the actress, whose turn as Joan Baez in “A Complete Unknown” earned her an Oscar nomination. She continued, “It felt odd, but it felt exciting.”

For Turner, a British actor best known for his work in dramatic fare like “The Boys in the Boat” and “Masters of the Air,” the film allowed him to tap into his sillier side.

“I loved how absurd it was,” he said. “I’ve always wanted to do an out-and-out rom-com. I did ‘Eternity,’ but it was more of a grounded performance, and this character is a goofball.”

Offscreen, the actors, both 36, have their own romances: Turner married the singer Dua Lipa in June, and Barbaro has been linked to her “Artificial” co-star Andrew Garfield.

In a joint video interview in July, the stars discussed “One Night Only,” their New York memories and their views on love. These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

This is a rom-com that’s explicitly political. The whole premise of the movie hinges on that. How did you feel about that throughline?

MONICA BARBARO While it does have that political undertone, ultimately, I think the movie is really just an allegory for dating. You can be living with a government you don’t agree with, but at the end of the day you still just want to find love, and maybe it means having to exist alongside a lot of discomfort and hardship.

CALLUM TURNER You know, the movie is about love. Ultimately, it’s not about anything political. For me, I never paid attention to that. What I really liked, actually, was that it’s not a dystopian future. It’s a New York that we recognize just with a slight twist. It’s also an absurd idea that the government made people not have sex.

BARBARO Well, some people feel like it’s absurd, and some people are like, That could happen. That’s the interesting thing.

Do you think it’s absurd or something that could happen?

TURNER I think it’s an absurd idea. That’s the point, right? It’s actually so far from our reality that we can then, as an audience, put ourselves in that situation. You’re like, Well, what would I do if I had this one night? Would I marry early? Would I hold out?

BARBARO I think the biosensors would never fly, but I actually am at a point where I have no idea. I think we’re well past absurdity in a lot of ways right now. I’m constantly shocked by what I read in the news, so who knows?

Your characters take digs at each other’s physical traits. (Allie tells Owen, “Your ears are like car doors.” Owen tells Allie, “Your nose is way too small for your face.”) How did you come up with those?

TURNER Monica improvised those lines. I couldn’t believe it.

BARBARO I was like, “I’ve got more.”

TURNER Monica and Will have an obsession with my ears, which is where that joke came from. When I was younger, everyone used to take the mick out of my ears because I think I was born with the size that I have now, and then my head grew into them.

Will Gluck is known for musical moments in his rom-coms. Here, Allie is a singer who records pop covers for pharmaceutical ads. What were the conversations like around the songs?

BARBARO I got to work with the same vocal coach that I worked with on “A Complete Unknown,” but obviously for that, I was hellbent on honoring the artist I was playing. In this, I was still anxious about the quality of work, but when I was singing the psoriasis song, we just kept bursting out laughing. Este Haim [a composer on the film] was really helpful in getting me to embrace the emotional heights of these songs. Then it just becomes that much funnier.

Callum, were you familiar with the concept of pharmaceutical jingles? [Direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising is banned in most other countries.]

TURNER No, I didn’t really understand it at the beginning. I’m aware of the commercials but not the jingles.

BARBARO I do wonder if it’ll make sense to people abroad.

TURNER I mean, I still haven’t heard a pharmaceutical jingle in real life. Yours are the only ones I know. [Speak-singing] “Psoriasis, say what you wanna say, and let your clear skin out.” I’m not a singer.

BARBARO That’s what I used to say.

This is a very New York movie. The city is almost another character in the film. Do you remember the first time you visited?

BARBARO I was 12, and it was a class trip to New York and D. C. I remember being enamored with it. Then I went a year later with my mom and my brother, and we walked by N. Y. U., and I was like, I want to go there. I did end up going to N. Y. U., and it was a dream come true. I had no interest in being a kid on campus with a football team.

TURNER I was 10. I came with my mum and her friend in that period between Christmas and New Year’s Eve. It was snowing and cold, and we stayed north of Times Square. I just remember it was like the movies. It was magic. We went ice skating in Central Park. Everything’s bigger and louder and brighter. I was really just in awe of it.

BARBARO That’s how I felt about London, to be honest. I was like, This is nothing like America. This is so cool.

TURNER I also remember being in the hotel room and watching “America’s Most Wanted.” I was like, What the hell is this? In England, we had “Crimewatch.” “Crimewatch” would be like: “A badger was stolen from his den. We have to find the culprit.” “America’s Most Wanted” was like, “Six-time murderer …”

What classic rom-coms have you rewatched the most?

TURNER I know Monica’s: “10 Things I Hate About You,” “How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days,” and “My Best Friend’s Wedding.”

BARBARO Well done. Yours is “Notting Hill.”

TURNER Yeah. I have, in the past, been on the way out of the house and ended up sitting on the sofa and watching the whole thing instead.

Do you believe in the idea of soul mates?

TURNER I do, definitely. I believe there are so many different types of love. There’s the slow burn. There’s friendships. There’s parents. Soul mates doesn’t have to be a partnership, it could be anything. Some of my soul mates are my best friends.

BARBARO I agree with that. There are also so many ways into love and lasting relationships, but I do think there’s a special karmic something to certain relationships.

In the film, Allie is concerned with finding something “real” amid the chaos. Being in the public eye, how do you make sure you’re able to have a real relationship in spite of all the noise?

TURNER It’s like everyone else. It’s a very normal relationship. It’s the truth.

BARBARO It is ultimately a very normal relationship and protecting privacy as much as possible in order to not open up to — yeah, protecting privacy is a big part of it.

Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids

Wired August 06, 2026

On a rainy New York morning earlier this week, a WIRED reporter strapped to his wrist a lavender and pink plastic child’s smartwatch and headed to work. As he approached his nearby subway station to commute to WIRED’s office, he texted Vangelis Stykas, the Greek security researcher who had shipped him the watch via Amazon, to let him know that he was going into the station and might lose cell signal.

“I know,” Stykas wrote back.

In fact, Stykas had been monitoring the reporter’s location via the watch since the moment he left his apartment. The watch’s GPS feature, intended to let a parent track their child, was malfunctioning, but the wearable device was still picking up and transmitting to a faraway server identifiers from every nearby Wi-Fi network, which allowed Stykas to nonetheless pinpoint the reporter’s exact location as he walked down a particular Brooklyn block.

A WIRED reporter wearing the GPS-enabled smartwatch while holding an umbrella and walking to the subway earlier this week.

When the reporter arrived at WIRED’s Manhattan headquarters half an hour later, Stykas hijacked a feature in the watch that allowed him to silently take a photo from its camera, capturing the moment when the reporter stepped into an elevator. After a few minutes, he took another snap of the reporter at his desk, then used a different feature to pick up audio from the watch’s microphone, transmitting it to another researcher, Felipe Solferini, who listened as the reporter’s coworker described his weekend visit to an art exhibition. At no point did the watch show any sign that it was listening, taking photos, or otherwise being hacked.

As WIRED reporter Andy Greenberg entered the elevator at WIRED's New York office, the hackers used the smartwatch to surreptitiously take a photo…

…and then again as he sat at his desk.

The watch’s insecurity and the spying it enabled might be expected given the gadget’s pedigree: It’s sold by an obscure company called CJC, costs less than $30, and was made by an equally obscure manufacturer, YiQingTeng Electronics, in Shenzhen, China. More troubling, perhaps, is that the online platform it’s built on—and the one that allowed Stykas and Solferini to so thoroughly hack it—is used by dozens of other brands of smartwatch, many of which have likely been left vulnerable to the same forms of digital stalking.

At the Black Hat cybersecurity conference today, Stykas and Solferini plan to present their findings from analyzing the supply chain and security of more than 70 GPS-enabled watches and car accessories. They found that more than 30 of those geolocation devices use the technology and backend servers of YiQingTeng, also identified by the brand name Wonlex, the name of a partner firm Shenzhen 3G Electronics, or their associated app, SETracker. Another 30-plus brands of tracking devices for cars and kids are all run on another Shenzhen-based platform known as NewGPS2012.

Combined with another major GPS platform known as SinoTrack that sells car trackers and smartwatches, the two researchers found that tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets came from just three supply chains. All three, the researchers found in their analysis, had significant security flaws—in some cases as simple as a lack of authentication that allowed anyone to access any device—leaving children’s watches vulnerable to tracking by a hacker, location disabling and spoofing, interception and spoofing of text and audio messages sent to them, replacement of emergency contacts with ones a hacker chose, silent audio eavesdropping, as well as photo and video capture for camera-enabled devices. (Once the GPS started working on the smartwatch WIRED tested, the hackers showed that feature, too, could be hijacked to follow the wearer’s every move.)

For some GPS-enabled car accessories, the researchers found they could similarly track the devices’ locations or spoof messages to them that could potentially unlock or disable cars, though the researchers didn’t go so far as to test this out on actual vehicles. They also say they found server-side vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information, would have allowed them to execute their own code on the servers, or even in one case appeared to show that someone else had already gained unauthorized access to the system’s backend.

“Millions of kids are being exposed and vulnerable to exploitation. It's just catastrophic. It's really low-hanging fruit for a lot of bad actors,” Stykas says. “Your criminal mind is the only limitation in exploiting those devices.”

The researchers say they’ve been warning the companies behind all three Shenzhen-based GPS platforms about their vulnerabilities for months. When WIRED reached a representative of SETracker, the person initially claimed in an email that “the issues you mentioned have been resolved long before,” adding that “we attach great importance to the security of Setracker and keep strengthening its security continuously.” When WIRED pointed out that researchers had been able to hack a smartwatch running on SETracker just this week, the person repeated their claim that the issues had been fixed, then asked for evidence of the exploitation, which WIRED provided.

Only today, hours before the researchers’ talk at Black Hat, did the researchers find that their hacking techniques against SETracker’s platform have stopped working—though they’re still not sure if the flaws they found are fully fixed. After this article published, SETracker wrote in a statement that it had blocked certain ports on its servers used by a “legacy” version of its clients' systems, forcing “a small subset of clients” on that older system to upgrade to protect “a small number of devices” that were affected. “The vulnerability has now been thoroughly remediated,” the SETracker staffer wrote. “Thank you for your oversight and attention.”

Sinotrack and the NewGPS2012 platform didn’t respond to WIRED’s requests for comment, and the researchers say their hacking techniques against those systems still appear to work.

For more than a decade, cybersecurity experts and privacy advocates have warned that cheap, GPS-enabled children’s smartwatches and aftermarket vehicle accessories are riddled with security vulnerabilities that leave kids and drivers susceptible to hacking and tracking. But the sheer number of different brands and models of those devices has often made identifying the truly insecure gadgets feel nearly impossible for consumers.

More than any specific vulnerability, Solferini and Stykas say, they wanted to highlight that much of that daunting diversity among GPS devices—along with consumers’ sense of choice among them—is essentially an illusion.

“A parent in Sweden buying a ‘SafeKid’ watch and a parent in Spain buying a ‘SaveFamily’ watch are both sending their child's location data to the same vulnerable myaqsh. com backend on Alibaba Cloud in mainland China, without knowing it,” they write in a whitepaper shared with WIRED ahead of their Black Hat presentation, referring to the online services of YiQingTeng. “The white-label model means a vulnerability in one backend aﬀects dozens of consumer brands at the same time, and consumers have no way to tell which backend their product uses.”

The smartwatch WIRED tested was made by Shenzhen-based YiQingTeng Electronics and runs on the SETracker platform used by dozens of brands and millions of devices.

Solferini and Stykas aren’t revealing the full details of the vulnerabilities they discovered in the three major platforms, in part because not all of them have been fixed despite sharing their findings with the companies for months. In the case of YiQingTeng, the manufacturer of the watch WIRED tested, however, they say an authentication security flaw would have allowed anyone to send commands to any SETracker-based device. That would let hackers exploit and take over devices at random or to target specific watches if they can determine an identifier for them, such as the parent’s email address the device is registered to. (To hack the smartwatch worn by a WIRED reporter, for instance, the reporter gave Stykas his email address but no other information about the device. Stykas says he could have easily targeted devices in other ways, such as hacking numerous watches and searching through them to find the nearest vulnerable devices or one associated with a target’s identifying information.)

In the case of SinoTrack, the researchers say they found that an account intended for demonstration purposes could be used to send commands to any of the platform’s millions of devices. They also found a SQL injection vulnerability—a flaw that essentially allows anyone to send commands disguised as data that are then executed by the SinoTrack server—that gave them access to tens of thousands of devices’ locations, passwords, and vehicle records.

Finally, for NewGPS2012 devices, the researchers say they found similar SQL injection vulnerabilities and were able to run their own code on the company’s servers. They also say they found evidence of a previous compromise of the company’s systems, suggesting other unauthorized users or hackers may have had access to it for an unknown period of time.

Given the sheer number of different brands and resellers of those Shenzhen-manufactured gadgets, the researchers didn’t confirm the vulnerability of all of the individually branded devices they found to use YiQingTeng’s SETracker platform or the NewGPS2012 platform. WIRED couldn’t independently confirm each device’s vulnerability either. But the table below lists brands whose products were based at least in part on those platforms, as well as the company’s response when WIRED reached out for comment on the researchers’ findings.

Stykas and Solferini’s Black Hat talk is far from the first warning about the dangers of cheap GPS devices—even from these researchers themselves. Stykas and another researcher, Michael Gruhn, revealed a broad collection of vulnerabilities in GPS-enabled devices in 2018, which they called Trackmageddon. GPS-enabled automotive devices plugged into the OBDII port on cars’ dashboards have proven again and again to be vulnerable to hacking and tracking.

Children’s GPS-enabled watches have also been shown to be especially prone to critical privacy and security vulnerabilities: Pen Test Partners and the Norwegian government issued warnings about certain hackable children’s watches in 2017 and 2018, and another study by the Münster University of Applied Sciences in 2020 tested six children’s smartwatches and found serious vulnerabilities in five. “It was crazy," Sebastian Schinzel, one of the Münster researchers, told WIRED at the time. "Everything was basically broken."

Yet somehow, Stykas says, people keep putting cheap, GPS-enabled devices on their loved ones. And the companies that make them, too, have often completely ignored his warnings about the hackable bugs in their devices. Instead, as he tested his surveillance techniques against the newly purchased smartwatch on a WIRED reporter’s wrist a few days ago, they worked as well as ever, and some of the devices’ flaws remain unpatched even now.

“I really hoped we could tell a nice story that there were vulnerabilities and they fixed them. But in many cases, they didn’t,” Stykas says. “It's a position I really didn't want to be in.”
