Two Fossil Fuel Companies Are Driving the Data Center Boom

Wired August 06, 2026

It’s been a banner year for oil and gas companies. Some of the world’s biggest oil giants have announced billions of dollars in quarterly profits over the past two weeks, boosted largely by the soaring price of oil thanks to the conflict in the Middle East.

But the artificial intelligence boom is also giving fossil fuel companies a new industry to sell their gas, pipelines, and power plants to: data centers. Two American oil and gas companies, Williams and Chevron, are presenting that demand to investors as a huge win.

Data centers are becoming “a big driver for both power and gas demand in the US,” says Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities and energy at BloombergNEF. The group published a report last week that found that increased demand for natural gas by the mid-2030s, driven partly by data centers, means that the US would need to increase production by 36 percent.

The boom could have big climate implications—even when considering projects that aren’t connected to the larger grid. Just five of the seven data-center-connected gas-fired power plants highlighted in these two companies’ second quarter results could emit as much as 21 million tons of greenhouse gases per year, according to their permit applications. That’s an amount roughly on par with the annual emissions of Guatemala, though the actual emissions may be lower than what’s on the permits.

Executives from both Williams and Chevron said on earnings calls that they expect to expand on facilities they are building now for the data center industry for years to come.

“The frightening thing about the tech and oil alliance is that this is a lifeline to an industry that we need to be phasing out,” says Lukas Shankar-Ross, deputy director at Friends of the Earth, an environmental nonprofit.

While it may not be a household name like Chevron or Exxon, Williams is one of biggest oil and gas infrastructure companies in the US—and it has also created a highly profitable data-center services business. Last year, Williams announced that it would build a power plant and associated pipeline infrastructure in Ohio solely for use by a data center. Building islanded infrastructure like this, also referred to as “behind-the-meter” power, has become an increasingly popular option for tech companies that don’t want to deal with long wait times to connect to the electric grid or impact consumer electricity prices.

Williams is now building six behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers across the country, including four projects serving Meta data centers in Ohio. (Meta declined to comment.) In mid-July, Williams announced more than $5 billion in investments for its data center ventures, including money from private equity giant KKR.

Williams’ four power plants that have filed permit applications could, according to those applications, emit up to 9.6 million tons of greenhouse gases per year, which is equivalent to the emissions from more than 22 average natural gas plants, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Williams spokesperson Alex Schott tells WIRED in an email that the facilities are “designed to operate well below permitted limits” and comply with state air requirements. The company’s modeling, Schott says, puts actual emissions from these plants at “potentially” two-thirds less than what’s on the permits.

The company is also building a 9-mile natural gas pipeline across an Ohio suburb. Williams executives say they envision the pipeline being used not just to serve its power plants for Meta in the area, but also to supply natural gas to the growing number of data centers in that region. In an earnings call in May, Williams president Chad Zamarin said the company “overbuilt the capacity” of a pipeline serving one of its Meta-affiliated power plants to “be an energy artery along which other projects could be developed.”

The largest behind-the-meter gas power plant Williams is building for Meta in Ohio is just under 700 megawatts. But Williams isn’t the only company betting big on providing data centers with power, and that project pales in comparison to the size of the 2.67-gigawatt project Chevron is building for a Microsoft data center in Texas. The oil giant reported its best quarterly profits in six years on Friday, and highlighted the partnership in all of its investor materials.

In June, Chevron confirmed that it had signed an agreement with Microsoft. The companies signed a power purchase agreement—an arrangement to purchase electricity at an agreed-upon price for a set period of time—that lasts for 20 years. (Williams’ agreements with Meta for its data center power are between 10 and 12.5 years.) Chevron says the project is the only “multi-[gigawatt]” project with such a “long-term” contract in place. As WIRED reported in April, the power plant quietly applied for a school district tax break worth millions, which was finalized by the state late last month.

The Chevron and Microsoft plant, according to its permit, could produce more than 11.5 million tons of carbon-dioxide-equivalent emissions per year. Chevron spokesperson Paula Beasley says the power plant is designed to comply with federal and state environmental requirements.

“Kilby's approach focuses on natural gas generation for reliable capacity, with the possibility of adding renewable generation in the future,” she says.

Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment.

Jeff Gustavson, the president of Chevron’s New Energies division, said on the company’s earnings call Friday that the project “provides a repeatable model” and that Chevron is already talking to potential future data center customers.

“The grid cannot keep up with the demand from hyperscalers and others, and we see that persisting for years,” Gustavson said.

While Williams and Chevron are early movers, Sethia thinks that “multiple players” stand to benefit from building pipeline infrastructure for data centers. “One of the patterns we are seeing is a lot of the new data center announcements are starting to cluster around areas which have gas pipelines,” says Sethia.

Building islanded power plants at the scale and speed that the AI industry requires is a relatively new phenomenon. With utility bills rising and helping to fuel the national backlash against data centers, the Trump administration is actively encouraging tech companies to figure out ways to keep their projects from impacting the grid, which includes bringing their own power.

Whether these massive plants will stay serving data centers only, or if they will eventually be connected to the grid is “a massive question for the future of power prices in the country,” Sethia says. While Chevron’s investor materials indicate that it expects to connect the Microsoft power plant to the grid sometime after 2030, Texas’ grid is facing significant delays for interconnection. Beasley says that an interconnection application for the plant has already been submitted. “Future interconnection could enable export of surplus power and provide additional system redundancy, if achieved,” she says.

Schott, the Williams spokesperson, says that the company is looking into technologies to increase the efficiency of their gas plants. “Future interconnection opportunities could be evaluated once the long-term load profile and system needs are better understood,” she says.

Large gas plants are long-term investments that can outlast the shorter-term political whims of presidential administrations. Building more fossil fuel infrastructure to power data centers now, Shankar-Ross points out, could delay the renewable energy transition that may pick back up if political winds shift.

“If, 20 years from now, there’s a public grid dominated by renewables, and a private grid dominated by fossil gas, Microsoft will bear some of the responsibility here,” he says.

The Best Coffee Subscriptions to Keep You Wired in 2026

Wired August 06, 2026

Atlas (12 Oz)

Trade (11 Oz Bag)

Podium (Gold Subscription)

Bean Box (Subscription)

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

You never need a cup of coffee tomorrow. You need it now. An empty bag signals panic, tragedy, and a trip to the store in your pajamas. The WIRED guide to the best coffee subscriptions is designed, in part, to make sure this moment never happens.

The promise of the internet is that you can access the best coffee delivery services in the country, and therefore the best coffee, from anywhere you live. The WIRED Reviews team has been testing and recommending monthly coffee subscriptions since 2018, when online coffee ordering became the norm. I've been writing about coffee on both coasts for more than 15 years, and it's not unheard of for me to go through four bags a week while testing coffee machines.

Even though I live in the coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon, online subscriptions have been a source of constant discovery. My top coffee subscription for most people, Atlas Coffee Club, brings in flavors from all over the world in a round-robin—while Podium Coffee Club tailors itself tightly to wild flavors for drip coffee nerds. Trade Coffee appeals to the widest variety of palates for cold brew, espresso, or drip.

This list represents the best and most interesting coffee bean subscriptions of 2026. Be sure to check our other java-related buying guides, including the Best Drip Coffee Machines, Best Mushroom Coffee, Best Espresso Machines, Best Cold-Brew Coffee Makers, Best Latte and Cappuccino Machines, and Best Coffee Grinders.

Updated August 2026: I’ve added Fire Department Coffee as a recommendation, updated prices and descriptions, rearranged and retested some subscriptions, and added new information on commodity coffee prices and tariffs.

Table of Contents

Atlas Coffee Club

Atlas (12 Oz)

Atlas (2 bags)

Atlas (6-month Gift subscription)

Atlas Coffee Club offers a true world tour of coffee: high-quality, single-origin beans from a different far-flung part of the world each month. This includes lesser-known coffee-producing regions such as Thailand or Yunnan, China, or a truly rare, chocolaty-nutty bag from Uganda.

Because Atlas is also the sole importer and roaster of each bean variety, you also skip the middleman and save money. Each bag arrives at your doorstep at a price competitive with the premium (but far less fresh!) beans at your local supermarket. Bags are a full 12 ounces, not the diet bags that have become popular among many subscriptions and roasters.

Here's how Atlas works: Each month, the Austin, Texas-based roaster offers beans from a different country—whether an Indian variety that tastes gently of marzipan, or one from Peru that brims with toffee. Those countries and farms keep changing, as Atlas forms new relationships with growers all over the world. I find the monthly switch to be an excellent rhythm for espresso in particular, since I'm dialing in a new bean for a new flavor each month. And unlike a lot of coffee subscriptions I've tried, neither I nor fellow WIRED coffee subscription reviewer Scott Gilbertson have ever received a late shipment.

Atlas’ roasts are excellent, the bags look pretty, and the service is outstanding. Choose between light-to-medium or medium-to-dark roasts—or both. Atlas tends to stay in the fat part of the bell curve where aromas are most pronounced and easy to extract. This can mean deep-chocolate Central American dark roasts best for espresso, or fruit-forward light-to-medium African roasts made for drip or pour-over. But note that Atlas also offers a premium “bright and expressive” option for $3 more a bag.

Subscriptions can be monthly or bimonthly. There is no weekly option, though you can adjust order size from a half-bag to four bags. You can also choose whether you'd like to receive whole beans, your favorite grind for your favorite brewing method, or pods fit for Keurig or Nespresso. Atlas has a subscription option for functional mushroom blends, the latte version of which earned top billing in our guide to mushroom coffee.

Using the code WELCOMECOFFEE, you can get your first month's order at half off.

Roaster. Delivery: Every two or four weeks, anywhere from a half-bag to four bags per shipment. Coffee changes each month. Priced per 12-ounce bag.

Trade

Trade (11 Oz Bag)

Trade (6-month gift subscription)

Trade Coffee is like a helpful coffee curator. Rather than roasting the beans themselves, Trade acts as a middleman, ferrying beans to your door from small roasters all over the country. To determine your tastes, Trade will ask you a series of questions about what you want out of your daily dose of caffeine: how you brew and drink your beans (with milk, without, etc.), how dark you like your roast, and whether you like balanced flavors or bold and fruity.

At the end, you'll learn what bags are coming based on your responses—whether a roasty, smoky espresso blend from Feast Coffee in California, or a light-bodied Kenyan from Tennessee that tastes like citrus and berry.

Trade's selection is huge, with well over 400 bags to choose from, and Trade is constantly adding new roasters and beans to its stable. This means you never have to repeat a bag if you don't want to. But more importantly, this makes Trade's subscription a great way to discover new brews, new growers, and new roasters. Last year, Trade added a cold-brew subscription with at least 90 bags specifically selected for how good they taste when brewed cold; new subscriptions come with a cold-brew device.

Retailer. Delivery: Every two or four weeks, starting at one 11-ounce bag per delivery.

Podium Coffee Club

Podium (Gold Subscription)

Podium (Platinum Subscription)

Podium Coffee Club sent the best coffee beans I've tasted in the past year, and introduced me to excellent new roasters like Seattle's Cozy Monster and coastal Oregon's Kissing Rock that I would not otherwise have known existed.

It works a little differently, though. Podium selects just a couple bags each month from roasters all over the country. Each roaster has been awarded by a national or international competition as one of the best java roasters. To quote Men in Black: “The best of the best of the best, sir! With honors.”

Basically, you choose either the Gold or Platinum tier, which are priced accordingly, and then you receive one—and only one—ridiculously good bag of coffee each month, roasted within 24 hours of when it's shipped. Your bags arrive with a little card explaining why each single-origin varietal, and each roaster, is so gosh darn interesting.

After testing multiple months' worth of beans, I can say each coffee from Podium has been interesting, special, or downright unique in some way—especially a bag of beauteously floral and pine-forward beans from Colombia growing legend Elkin Guzman, roasted by Podium cofounder Sam LaRobardiere's excellent coffee brand Theory Coffee.

Expect light-roast beans, best for lovers of drip, pour-over, and Aeropress. The Gold subscription is generally excellent, balanced, and aromatic. The Platinum tends to be adventurous, surprising, or maybe just rare: It's coffee that tastes like other coffee doesn't. So far, I've had no misses, and a recent favorite is a fruity “Pinkies Out” co-fermentation from Golden Bean World Series 2025 winner Lamppost Coffee out of Texas. Consider Podium a source of discovery, and an indulgent gift to yourself (or someone you like) each month, to supplement your more usual coffee habit. It does cost what an indulgence does, however.

Multi-roaster. Delivery: Monthly. Priced per 10.5-ounce bag. Also available in 3-pound or 5-pound bags.

Bean Box

Bean Box (Subscription)

Bean Box (World Coffee Tour)

Seattle-based Bean Box was a pioneer among multi-roaster coffee subscriptions, and it still has one of the largest selections of roasters to choose from if you pick out your own bags.

But the fun of a coffee subscription is often discovery. Bean Box's Curator's Choice subscription often brings out roasters who lean toward the cocoa side of coffee; I discovered this after tasting the Curator's Choice subscription for six months this year. Trend-hunting roasters often lean funky and fruity these days. But Bean Box seeks out depth, balance, and rich chocolate or toffee notes in its featured bags—even on light roasts meant for drip, such as the single-origin Ethiopia by Seattle's Middle Fork Roasters.

This makes Bean Box an excellent pick for those who favor medium roasts, and the chocolate or brown-sugar flavors that surface well in espresso, cold brew, and milk drinks. In future tests of the service, I'd likely favor medium-roast and espresso subscriptions, or a cold brew subscription for the summer.

Bean Box is also an excellent gift for lovers of literal chocolate, with terrific gift boxes offering chocolate pairings that were beloved by WIRED staffers. Gift subscriptions are also available. Bean Box's prices are low for craft coffee of this caliber, and the bags are big (or at least they're the full 12 ounces). Sometimes you can get premium roasters like Equator for less than the price of a bag straight from the source.

But take note that for most options, you'll be adding $6 for shipping on each delivery unless you commit to an annual subscription. At the annual rate, Bean Box has an excellent intersection of price and selection.

Retailer. Delivery: Once every two to six weeks. Priced per 12-ounce bag.

Equator Coffees

Equator Coffees (Single-Origin)

Equator (Gift Box)

Another favorite bag of coffee I tried last year came from Equator Coffee. It was funky, cool, weird, and roasted feather-light, a single-origin bag from Mae Chedi in Thailand with tasting notes of raspberries and aged rum. But then one of my favorite decaf bags came from Equator, too: a lovely single-origin Ethiopian that was gently reminiscent of a chocolate blueberry muffin.

This 30-year-old Bay Area pioneer, once a maverick best known for roasting the French Laundry's house blend from its founding partners' Marin County garage, is now a powerhouse. Equator offers wonderfully diverse tastes, sourced from farms in 50 countries. The coffee bean subscriptions trend toward wild single-origin coffees, espresso-friendly roasts, fair trade and organic beans, and balanced blends. A rotating supply of interesting decaf is also available as a subscription. These days, Equator is maybe the oldest craft roaster to still consistently taste so fresh. Just pick your style, and let the coffee come.

Roaster. Delivery: One through 8 weeks. Priced per bag, generally $19 to $22 for 12 ounces.

Bean & Bean

Bean & Bean (Roaster's Choice)

Bean & Bean (3 months prepaid)

Bean & Bean sources some of the rarest and most precious coffee beans on the planet, and roasts them to delicate fruition. There are only about 400 certified Q Graders in the United States—basically, the master sommeliers of coffee. Two of them are the mother-daughter team of Rachel and Jiyoon Han at New York's Bean & Bean. Together, they roast some of the world's most exquisite beans, like Geshas from Taiwan and honey-milled Cup of Excellence winners from El Salvador.

You can shop these bags individually. But the more fun option is to let the Hans surprise you with their favorite ridiculously rare light roast of the moment. It's a more expensive subscription than some, and bag size may vary depending on the expense of each rare bean. But you have probably never tried coffee like the bag that will arrive at your stoop.

Roaster. Delivery: Depending on subscription type, anywhere from weekly to monthly. Priced per bag or selection.

Swiss Water

Swiss Water (12 Oz)

Decaf has come a long way, with a few new-school, more natural decaf makers that have emerged as the jitter-free darlings of the premium coffee world. Perhaps the most famous is British Columbia's Swiss Water, the company behind the Swiss Water decaffeination process, which provides decaf to some of the best premium roasters across the United States. But Swiss Water also offers its own subscription service to bring you some of the very best decaf roasts—genuine heavy hitters that remain full-flavored, robust, and delicate without keeping you up at night.

Retailer. Delivery: Weekly, biweekly, monthly, or bimonthly. Priced per bag.

Origin Roasted

Origin Roasted (10 Oz)

No matter where the beans come from, nearly all coffee sold in the United States is roasted in the US. But Origin Roasted is truly globetrotting. Each month they send a 10-ounce bag of specialty beans that are roasted, packed, and then shipped directly from the same part of the world where the coffee was harvested.

Shipping straight from the source within one to three days of roasting means the beans are not merely fresh, but also seasonal. It also means the beans will be a cosmopolitan affair, roasted according to the tastes of exotic locales. A side benefit is that more of the proceeds from sales go directly to the growers and roasters in their home countries.

WIRED reviewer Michael Calore has been drinking Origin Roasted coffee since the service launched five years ago—and anecdotally, fresh bags roasted when the fruit's still fresh … taste fresh. They also retain floral and fruity notes you can't find in supermarket bags. But Origin's beans are also pretty special, and hard to find. Calore's favorite bags (Jalapa Producers from Guatemala, Azahar from Risaralda, Colombia) are actually cheaper through the Origin subscription than if you tried to find them individually.

Roaster. Delivery: Ships on the last Friday of every month. Priced per bag.

Sweet Bloom

Sweet Bloom

When it comes to coffee, the season matters. Different growing regions harvest at different times of the year. And with the Roaster's Choice subscription from Colorado's Sweet Bloom Coffee, you’re always getting very fresh beans. The beans are roasted during each region’s harvest season, or in their “seasonal sweet spot,” to use Sweet Bloom’s terminology.

One of Sweet Bloom's cofounders, Andy Sprenger, made his bones at Ceremony Coffee in Maryland. While working there as a roaster, he won two US Brewers Cup championships, among other awards. He then took that experience—and that nose for flavor—to Sweet Bloom, where he's in charge of the roasting and sourcing.

His sourcing work is deep. Sweet Bloom's single-bag Roaster's Choice subscription ships single-origin coffees from small producers around the world, many of which I'd never encountered until the beans arrived, and some from coffee-growing regions that I had to bust out the map to locate. The flavors are easier to put a finger on: Sweet Bloom tends to favor fruity and floral coffees, and presents them in lighter roasts that let all those provocative flavor notes express themselves at full volume. If you prefer bright, slightly acidic, and very fragrant coffees, this is the sub for you. —Michael Calore

Roaster. Delivery: Every one to four weeks. Priced per 10-ounce bag; 2-pound or 5-pound bags also available.

Cometeer

Cometeer (World Mug Collection)

Cometeer (40-capsule mixed)

Look, I get it. Not everyone has room for a big, beautiful espresso machine and an excellent grinder, or the interest in staring thoughtfully into the middle distance while preparing a meditative pour-over. Or maybe you're just at your office or in a hotel a lot, and yet, you still want terrific coffee that is interesting and full of flavor. Well, here's Cometeer. The first time I tried it, I was, of course, skeptical. But I couldn't believe how aromatic and straight-up distinctive each roast was, despite being flash-frozen.

It goes like this: Cometeer pods contain brew from some of the finest specialty roasters in the world—Black & White, Onyx, Proud Mary, you name it—that's been brewed and condensed with the power of science, then flash-frozen into little single-serve capsules. All you've gotta do is drop them into a cup, then thaw them with 5 ounces of boiling or near-boiling water. And then, blammo—an oddly terrific cup of coffee, miles above powdered instant or pods. It's not quite the same as a fresh cup: The mouthfeel is different; the flavors are rounder, smushier, and less crisp. But on light roasts especially, the aromatics are big, bold, and wild. I truly enjoy it.

They don't come cheap if you order a single box at a time, but subscription prices are reasonable—about $2 a capsule for very fancy beans. They'll keep in the freezer for months, but you'll need to drink them soon if you thaw them: They keep full flavor for one day at room temp or three days in a cooler or hotel fridge. The introductory box these days is a wild and woolly world tour of coffee beans with 32 capsules from 16 coffee-producing countries.

Retailer. Delivery: Variety packs or single-varietal packs arrive once every four weeks.

Sightglass

Sightglass (Blend)

Sightglass (Single Origin)

San Francisco's Sightglass Coffee is headquartered right in the middle of the city's South of Market neighborhood, which is SF's tech hub (and also home to WIRED). Just think of all the Github commits, UX prototypes, and vibe coding chatbot prompts that have been fueled by this roaster's beans. The subscription service is flexible, so you can pick to have the same bag sent every time, or you can have them curate the selection so you get something different. Sightglass ships bags at 12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds, and the two heavier options ship for free in the US.

The Owl's Howl roast is great if you have an espresso machine at home, and the Blend Shuffle option is a good choice if you prefer some variety, or if you just want to try all the blends to see which one you like best, then tweak your subscription to get that one delivered all the time. My personal recommendation is the single-origin Seasonal Variety Subscription. You'll get a bag of beans from different producers every month. The sourcing is all over the map: Colombia, Ethiopia, Guatemala, Kenya, Mexico. I tried one 12-ounce bag per week for two months, and everything was just outstanding, with unique and distinct flavors from each of the producers. —Michael Calore

Roaster. Delivery: Every one to four weeks. Priced $19+ per 12-ounce bag.

Fire Dept. Coffee

Fire Department Coffee (Coffee of the Month)

Fire Department Coffee (Coffee Club)

More than most years, 2026 has been one of wildfires: They started early, and we are on track to experience the biggest El Niño in 150 years. A bag of coffee, or even a year's worth of coffee, is a relatively small gesture, but Fire Department Coffee was created to support injured firefighters and underfunded fire departments all over the country.

The coffee is mostly medium and dark—less trendy than a classic, chocolaty profile, especially in the blends. The basic coffee club subscription is best for those who love espresso, or a strong and roasty French press or moka pot. The premium coffee-of-the-month selections veer more medium and are more suitable for those who make drip coffee or pour-over.

Roaster. Delivery: Monthly or bimonthly. Priced $14 to $19 per 12-ounce bag.

What Kinds of Coffee Subscriptions Are There?

There are two main kinds of coffee subscription providers: roasters and retailers. Both roasters and multi-roaster retailers sell great coffee. This guide includes both.

Roasters are cafés and small-batch producers who buy raw beans from farmers all over the world and roast them to perfection. By buying from a roaster, you're directly supporting the people who make your favorite coffees. The downside is you usually won't have as broad a selection. Roasters usually sell only their own coffee, but that often means special blends and single origins are available from a roaster that you can't get from a retailer. Your local roaster down the street may also have subscription offers, giving you the chance to buy local without leaving your house—and often catch a discount.

Retailers or multi-roaster subscriptions are coffee subscription providers who buy their beans from many different roasters, then ship bags of coffee to you. A multi-roaster retailer will often have a much broader selection of high-quality coffee available (from multiple brands) to ship to your doorstep—often selected and curated carefully by coffee experts. The downside of some subscriptions is that you're not buying directly from a roaster, which means the coffee may not be as fresh. (That's where this guide comes in. We can tell you how fresh they are because we always test each one and note the roast dates on each coffee bag.)

Subscription Beans vs. Locally Roasted Beans

Look: If you live in a big city with great coffee, the best way to try fresh roasts and new beans, and learn about them, is to go to your local roaster. Nearly every midsize city in the United States has at least a couple of excellent purveyors. Look up your local coffee roasters or visit your favorite coffee shop and ask where they get their beans. Buy the beans. Talk to people. It's fun, if you like talking to people.

Heck, this is also true when you're traveling. The best coffee you can find is often the cup you drink when you're on the road, in a new place, tasting something new. Even if you don't live on the road, it's fun to explore different shops when you do travel.

But the wonder of the internet is that you're not limited to only the best of what's local. Subscriptions allow you to take the temperature of the most interesting roasters from all over the country and world, without going anywhere in particular. Heard about that one roaster in Delaware or North Carolina making crazy coffee with co-ferments and natural fermentation? A roaster in Guatemala highlighting beans from their neighbors? Are you new to the world of premium coffee, and you'd like some help from the curators at Trade Coffee or Podium Coffee Club to learn what you like? Let them inform and surprise you.

This is why you might take a subscription. The world is at your door—even the world you've never even visited. I'm also lazy enough to order subscriptions from roasters a 15-minute drive away, but this is between you and your local ecologist.

But also, sometimes it's homesickness for what used to be local. For me, one of the best in this country is a tiny spot in South Jersey called Royal Mile. They used to be my favorite local coffee shop when I lived in Philly and would drive to Jersey to get the coffee. Now they aren't local at all, because I moved. But through the magic of the internet and the US Postal Service, I can still get their truly wild, surprising, mad-scientist single-origin bags anytime I want. What a privilege.

How We Test Coffee Subscriptions

To test these subscriptions, we try a variety of beans from each service, both our own picks and any curated options. We brewed each bag in different ways to see which beans were best suited to which brewing method. Over the subscriptions he tested, Scott Gilbertson covered the spectrum of grinds with espresso, moka pot, French press, pour-over, and Turkish or cowboy coffee. Matthew Korfhage wanders through espresso, AeroPress, drip, cold brew, pour-over, and a wealth of somewhat unclassifiable devices.

It's worth doing the same if you have access to different brewing methods, especially if you opt for a subscription that offers a lot of variety. A roast that makes a great shot of espresso does not necessarily make the best pour-over coffee, and vice versa. Some roasters, like the excellent Equator Coffee, offer one subscription specifically for espresso, one for decaf, and another for light single-origin roasts that lend themselves to drip and pour-over. It can also be rewarding to take notes on your favorites. Some of these services offer a way to do this on the site, which is handy, though a paper notebook works well enough. If you'd like some more pointers on brewing, be sure to read our guide to brewing better coffee at home.

Are Coffee Subscriptions Worth It?

A coffee subscription service often offers discounts on shipping or the base cost of each bag, compared to buying single bags for delivery. But usually, subscriptions will be premium beans, so it won't be as cheap as the less-fresh, often pre-ground coffee from your grocery store.

But if you're the sort who likes to try the best freshly roasted single-origin Ethiopian or Guatemalan beans from roasters all over the country? This is where coffee subscriptions shine. You're also often getting the best specialty bags a roaster has to offer, or a curated selection from a certified Q Grader—meaning you're a lot more likely to find new roasts and origins you wouldn't have come across on your own.

I have no dearth of local roasters that I love to support. Portland, Oregon, where I live, is perhaps the densest home to craft coffee in the country: Heart, Coava, Stumptown, Roseline, Sterling; multiple national coffee publications; and a craft coffee festival. I've been writing about coffee in Portland and elsewhere for more than a decade.

But a coffee subscription gives me access to beans from all over the country and world. It's a mix of ease and adventure, and a chance to be a barista at my own home multi-roaster café. I enjoy that I can get fresh-roasted beans from a coffee farm in Guatemala that roasts their own impossibly fresh beans onsite, alongside world-famous beans from other farmers right down the road—or taking a world tour each month with beans from my favorite globe-hopping roaster, Atlas Coffee Club.

But for others, a coffee subscription is just a way to get a steady drip of their favorite bag from their favorite roaster, guaranteed to arrive every week or every two weeks. Simple convenience is its own form of worth it.

How Does WIRED Select Coffee Subscriptions to Be Reviewed?

There's a lot of good coffee out there, and I am always trying something new—drip, espresso, cold brew. I've been writing about coffee for 15 years on both coasts, and I'm always on the lookout for new and exciting growers, roasters, and beans. I keep abreast of coffee industry publications like Sprudge, haunt subreddits, consult friends and industry contacts, and take tips.

Coffee can be subjective, of course, and everyone has their preferences. I include my personal favorite roasters among this list, rotate in discoveries I think readers might be interested in, and also solicit favorites from other WIRED (and very wired) reviewers with different palates. But when deciding what subscriptions to include in our curated list, I look into what it offers that others don't. I'm often looking for ones that best serve particular types of drinkers—a new service, a new delivery method, a clever way to cater to what you (whoever you may be) really want at your doorstep each week.

Often, a unique or uniquely useful or just kinda cool subscription model or roaster will be the first I'm in line to test. Other times, I get sent a sample bag of beans, and it sends me over the moon. Always feel free to send a note in the comments about a particularly terrific roaster or subscription.

How Have Tariffs Affected Coffee Prices?

Tariffs matter. So do fuel prices. Pretty much all coffee roasted and sold in the United States is imported. If it costs more to bring into the US, it will eventually cost more to buy.

This is one of many factors that affected coffee prices throughout last year, including extreme weather in Brazil and Vietnam, increasing demand, and relatively flat supply. All of these factors, including tariffs, have contributed to coffee prices rising dramatically in 2025. While coffee prices stabilized a bit after court rulings striking down tariffs in February, tariffs are now back in the conversation. Almost immediately, coffee commodity prices seem to have responded in kind by increasing yet again to levels not seen since January.

Subscriptions can absorb high coffee commodity prices in part by selecting which beans get sent. In many cases, subscriptions are able to charge less than the individual bags you see at the supermarket because of guaranteed sales (the same way subscribing to a magazine costs less than buying at the newsstand).

But coffee subscriptions aren't immune to price hikes, even if they're better suited to weathering the vicissitudes of chance and the market. One service decreased the size of its bags from 12 ounces to 10 ounces last year, while others raised prices only on select bags. One way or another, I tend to see price increases on at least one or two coffee subscriptions every time I check. The volatility of US trade relationships is a key factor.

There are so many coffee subscriptions out there, and honestly, a lot of them offer very good coffee—some are even amazing. This list would need to be at least three times as long to capture every one of them. I have way more subscriptions I've loved than I have space to talk about them, so here I've gathered some past picks that we here at WIRED like. Have a favorite we haven't tried? Drop a recommendation in the comments.

Partners Coffee ($20–$23 per bag): Partners Coffee is a Brooklyn-based small-batch roaster that offers subscriptions by blend as well as a single-origin option that swaps out every two weeks. Partners roasts and ships all orders within two days, so it arrives at your door as fresh as possible. The whole bean Manhattan roast and Ghost Town decaf are great for those who like light to medium roasts. Even better, you can manage your subscription via text message.

Gento Coffee ($48 for two bags): Gento is part of a new and welcome trend: growers who roast their own coffee and ship directly from the source. In Guatemala, Gento takes this a step further, roasting beans from other local growers that rank among the most esteemed bean farms in the world. But in this case, the beans might only travel down the road to be roasted. The single-origin subscription is really the play here. Alongside roasts from Gento's own beans from the Prentice family farm, you might find roasts from highly regarded Guatemalan growers like Genaro Juárez and Petrona Perez. If those names don't mean anything to you yet, they will after you try them.

Camber Coffee ($24+ per 12-ounce bag): Bellingham, Washington, roaster Camber Coffee slipped under the radar for me for maybe too long, but amid its 10-year anniversary celebrations, I finally remedied this. Camber makes distinguished, aromatic, balanced single-origin coffees and a truly chocolaty espresso blend called Big Joy that lives up to its name: it's like a fudge brownie in espresso form. Subscriptions net you 10 percent off list price on each bag.

Sunday Coffee Project ($27 per box, $45 for two): Portland's Sunday Coffee Project produces some of the most distinctive, funky, fruity, and interesting coffee I know in this country. This could be a yeast-fermented Thai light roast that tastes a whole lot like Sangria, or an Ethiopian so floral you'll swear you got invited to a spring wedding. Plus, the coffee comes in a little art box, designed to look like a coffee-themed children's cereal complete with games on the back and a little cartoon character on the front: maybe a sheep lifting weights or a snake playing tennis. It's a small roaster, and they've dialed back their offerings from weekly new roasts to monthly. But if you like light and adventurous coffee, a box from Sunday Coffee Project may be your favorite thing you get in the mail that month.

Trücup ($17 per 12-ounce bag): Are you sensitive to the acids in coffee, but you love coffee? Trücup makes unique, low-acid coffee through what it calls a natural steam process, which makes it a great option for caffeine lovers with sensitive stomachs or those who suffer from gastroesophageal reflux disease or heartburn. (Disclaimer: If you've been diagnosed with GERD, talk to your physician before you try any coffee.) Either way, even those with well-fortified stomachs may want to take note. WIRED Reviewer Scott Gilbertson loves this coffee for a more mellow cup in the afternoon or evening.

Grounds and Hounds ($19 per 12-ounce bag): We've recommended this as a top pick in the past, for its mix of feel-good donations to animal shelters and excellent roasts. Grounds and Hounds offers small-batch roasted blends and single-origin beans, with 20 percent of its profits going to benefit animal shelters. The brand has some of Gilbertson's personal favorite coffees, especially the dark roasts. (Try the Snow Day Winter Roast when it's available.) Subscriptions are mostly recurring, individual-bag subscriptions.

Wonderstate Coffee ($19–$21 per 10.5-ounce bag): Wisconsin's Wonderstate, previously named Kickapoo, is quite possibly the nation's first fully solar-powered roaster. Besides being an excellent roaster, it has a long and vocal commitment to paying farmers higher wages. The most recent batch of single origins I tried had a tendency toward light, subtle, mild-mannered, and lightly tannic brews—a cosmopolitan palate that's also Midwestern-polite.

French Truck Coffee ($17–$22 per bag): French Truck Coffee got its start in New Orleans and now has a dozen of its signature yellow storefronts scattered around town. Gilbertson is a fan of the Big River blend, which has a deep, rich, and very robust flavor profile that's especially well-suited to pour-over brewing. In fact, French Truck has some of the most detailed brewing instructions around.

Birds & Beans Coffee ($18+ per bag): Like birds? Clear-cut coffee farms can be hard on them. But Birds & Beans is a coffee roaster devoted to making sure its coffee is grown in Smithsonian-certified, bird-friendly farms with tree cover that helps birds thrive. The dark roasts in particular are delicious and genuinely dark: Scarlet Tanager is a favorite of Gilbertson.

Stone Creek Coffee ($36 for two bags): Milwaukee-based Stone Creek Coffee delivers its fresh, flavorful coffee in big 1-pound bags, with a variety of blends and single-origin options available. The Cream City blend in particular is a delightful medium roast with warmer flavor notes like chocolate and brown sugar, rounded out by fruity flavors—giving the coffee an almost cacao-nib flavor. Add a little milk, and it's almost like drinking hot cocoa. A monthly subscription delivers two bags per shipment.

Grit Coffee ($17+ per bag): From its roastery in Charlottesville, Virginia, Grit Coffee creates excellent blends, including a roasty, chocolaty Side Hustle blend with a subtle high note of acidity to balance it out. But what really differentiates Grit from other roasters is, well, grit: The roaster makes long-term, often 10-year commitments to its coffee farmers.

Lady Falcon ($49 for two bags): Lady Falcon Coffee Club may draw you in with the art nouveau-style bags. But the luscious, velvety coffee within is what will keep you coming back. Each coffee blend is thoughtfully mixed to heighten the flavors present in the contributing coffees, and the flavor notes are spot-on.

Angels’ Cup ($28 per bag, plus shipping): Angels’ Cup is more like a distance-learning coffee school than a box subscription service, and the Black Box subscription is like a blind coffee tasting from afar. You will learn what you actually like and dislike about coffee, along with some education through the app, roaster's notes, and notes from fellow tasters.

Mistobox ($20+ per bag): With more than 500 different coffees from 50-plus roasters, Mistobox makes a good gift subscription, especially if you don't know what kind of coffee to get someone. Somewhere in those 500 choices, your coffee fanatic should find something that will make them happy. One of the most compelling and surprising offerings: Misto lets you choose the most you're willing to pay per shipment, and your offerings will change accordingly. Delivery frequency can also be customized down to the day. But as it appears they're in the process of transferring to a new back end, we'll give them a moment before assessing the new website and ordering system.

The Best Handheld Fans for People Who Are Always Hot

Wired August 06, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

When I was first hired as a commerce editor at WIRED in summer 2024, one of the first media requests I fielded was from a nationally renowned talk show. The ask was for an editor to speak on the popularity of portable and neck fans. High-temperature records were breaking all over the US, and abroad, neck fans were suddenly the “it” accessory at the Paris Olympics, hugging the nape of athletes like Simone Biles. “I can't do this,” I told my manager at the time. “I've never even worn a neck fan! I don't have an opinion!”

How times have changed. Two years later, curiosity has gotten the best of me, and I have tried both neck and handheld fans. I can say with confidence that, once you've gotten used to having a little fan with you everywhere you go, enduring high temperatures without one will henceforth feel unbearable. I now own an entire bin full of neck fans, and half of my office is now overtaken by boxes of portable fans, misting fans, and all manner of inexpensive, portable cooling devices. And now I have an opinion. Many, in fact.

An Amazon search for “portable fan” will yield more than 60,000 results, many of which feature weird names and AI art, dubious battery-life claims, and wildly varying features and build quality. Even if most of these portable fans are just $20, no one wants to waste a Jackson on an item that's going to fall apart after one season or stop misting halfway through a vacation.

I spent all summer (and in some cases, last summer, too) testing the fans I recommend below. Be sure to check back periodically, as I’ll update this guide regularly with new products and observations.

Keep keeping cool with our guides to the Best Fans and Best Window Air Conditioners and Portable ACs.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Diveblues

Amazon

A good portable fan serves a variety of purposes. You can wear this one around your neck, pointed upward, or place it on a desk or table. Amazon sells a lot of fans in this style for $15 to $20, with wild variances in size, quality, and features. This one from Diveblues bested others I've tried by a significant margin. Not only is it cheaper than many options, but its head also is nearly 3 inches across for a wide breeze; it’s got a digital screen to display battery life and power level; it has a carabiner on the bottom to clip it to your bag; and it folds totally flat for easier transport. It’s a little bit loud, at 56 decibels on its highest setting, but most of these fans are noisy. Fortunately, it lacks the common high-pitched jet engine whine that can make your ears ring after a while. Images online show users standing this fan upright on top of the squared-off carabiner, but I didn’t find this position stable enough to be a practical option. There’s also a nearly identical version that does away with the carabiner for a nonskid base, which can stand upright ($19), but it doesn’t have the digital screen, which I found super useful.

Shark

Amazon

Amazon (rose gold)

Shark Ninja

New this year, Shark's entrée into the handheld fan market looks like two stacked cylinders—one the controller, the other a tube that can variably be a regular fan, a refillable misting fan, or a metal cryo-inspired cooling plate you can press to your neck or pulse points. That last capability is a super-unique one that I love, but I didn't like that you have to swap out separate attachments for each function (and carry them around in a bag—which is not included—if you're traveling). The unit itself is a little awkward to hold, and it also does not come with a lanyard or an easy way to carry it, which one might expect at this price point. It might not be practical, but after testing it all summer, I've decided this thing is just plain fun. The misting attachment also creates the finest, most consistent mist of any handheld fan I've tried—no need to worry about getting your shirt soaking wet.

Jisulife

Amazon

Sporting five speeds, this no-nonsense neck fan looks a little bit like headphones. It's the lightest of these types of fans I tested, and the most comfortable if you need to wear it for long periods. I wore it during a daylong hike around New Orleans’ Garden District and Audubon Park, and I frequently wear it while playing pickleball. However, the ends don’t adjust or angle, so if you don’t like where it naturally directs air, there’s nothing you can do about it. It’s also not too loud, at around 40 decibels on low, but this also means it's not super strong. Color options used to be limited to black and white, but new this year is access to more shades like navy, forest green, and pink.

Jisulife

Amazon

This cute two-speed fan has little plastic ears and a printed-on bear mouth. It produces a decent breeze for its size, at 472 feet per minute (measured with my anemometer). It’s quiet and lightweight at 4 ounces, making it easy to slip into a pocket, and the blades immediately stop spinning if they come in contact with an object—a feature that makes the fan safe for kids to use. It's also cheap enough that it's not a big deal when your kid inevitably loses it.

A light on the bottom doubles as a mediocre flashlight, and a USB-C port on the back makes it a portable power bank. However, note that the 2,000-mAh charge capacity isn't the strongest, and it lasts for about one phone charge. If the blue model pictured here isn't your thing, there are seven other color options.

Aecooly

Amazon

Aecooly

If you've ever worried about forgetting to charge your fan or having it run out of battery at an inopportune time, this fan, just slightly squatter than a film tube, is your solution. It plugs into your phone's USB port (or an auxiliary power bank’s!) and runs off its battery for an instant breeze anywhere, any time. It hasn't caused a noticeable power drain on my phone when I’ve tested it, but I haven't used it for more than 20 minutes at a time, for reasons outlined below. It's also great for kids and teens who may want a hand fan but never remember it needs to be charged—my teenager keeps one permanently in his soccer bag to take out and use at halftime and water breaks.

The only downside is that it doesn't fit well into a lot of chunkier phone cases, including my iPhone 15's Casetify case. The Phone Fan comes with a little USB-C extender, which allows it to work with my case, but it's a loose fit and constantly falls out if I'm not holding it at the perfect angle. Those with slim phone cases, however, will not have this issue.

Aecooly Portable Handheld Fan Air Gimbal for $35: I was originally interested in this handheld fan for its fun World Cup–edition designs, which are now on sale. (There are also World Cup versions of the Aecooly’s Cold Air Ultra misting fan, shown below.) It’s a fine fan, but it is quite loud for the amount of airflow it puts out. There are other fans with more features for half the price.

JisuLife Ultra2

Jisulife Handheld Fan Ultra2 for $76: This fan is so strong, it’s almost comical—1,614 feet per minute on my anemometer. (For reference, this is stronger than a typical full-sized tower fan.) It also emits a high-pitched whine not unlike a jet engine (60 decibels on its lowest setting), and its mallet-like shape makes it too bulky to slip into a pocket. However, it does double as a power bank and a flashlight, and it’s got a short carrying lanyard you can attach to make it slightly less unwieldy. The 9,000-mAh battery capacity is also a plus. Jisulife says this can last up to 25 hours, which I have no reason to doubt, as I’ve been using it on and off for most of the year and the battery has yet to run out.

Dyson HushJet Mini Cool for $100: With so many decent portable hand fans on the market for around $20, I'd expect great things from a fan that costs $100. While this one is fine (aside from a resemblance to—I'm sorry to have to say—a worm anus), the wind speed and overall performance were only marginally better than that of the cheaper fans. I do like that it comes with a stand for use on a desk, though, as well as the ribbon lanyard for wearing around your neck, but it's also—despite the name—quite loud at nearly 70 decibels on high.

PlayHot Handheld Turbo Fan

PlayHot Handheld Turbo Fan for $19: WIRED reviewer Kristin Canning loved the versatility of this fan, the contained blades, and the fact it fit into her small crossbody bag. I've used it all summer, and it's a solid fan, but the Diveblues above offers better performance and more features for the same price.

JisuLife Pro 1S Handheld Fan for $75: A handy scroll wheel controls the speed (as opposed to up-and-down buttons) on this lightweight fan, and the magnetic center cap comes off in two phases. The first section reveals an absorbent pad about the size of a pea, for saturating with essential oil, and the second section comes off to reveal a digital screen that shows power level and battery life. However, I was never able to test the full wind speed, as my unit would shut off as soon as it reached its max.

Aeecooly Waist Fan

Aecooly Waist Fan for $30: I liked the 3-in-1 design of this chunky waist fan, which lets you wear it on your belt or waistband inside or outside your shirt, on a strap around your neck, or propped up on a table or desk. It's not super lightweight at nearly three-quarters of a pound (which means you can't wear lighter-weight pants or shorts if you plan to clip it on your waistband). It's also not exactly quiet at 53 decibels, but with five speeds and a top wind speed of 866 feet per minute, it's one of the more powerful waist fans I've tried. There's also a “flashlight” on the side with a strobe option, but it's about the size of a BB, so don't count on it illuminating anything important.

Aecooly Aero Pro

Aecooly Aero Pro Hand Fan for $20: Aecooly's periscope-shaped “powerful turbo air tube” won both a Red Dot and iF Design award last year, and the curved shape is both easy to transport and hold. I also like that there are no rotors or blades to knock into. It doesn’t double as a flashlight or phone charger, but it does come with a digital display, which shows you the battery and speed levels. You’ll also get a short lanyard for carrying. Don’t plan on using this one if you plan to have a conversation, though, as it was one of the worst offenders for having a high-pitched jet-engine whine.

Gaiatop Portable Handheld Fan for $10: WIRED reviewer Kristin Canning found this fan to be a great companion during a late-summer parade, providing airflow without too much noise. Like the Jisulife Handheld Mini above, the Gaiatop’s soft blades stop automatically if they hit anything, and it can stand upright on a table. It's got pointy owl “ears” on top, which is cute, but it doesn't double as a flashlight or power bank like other fans of this style and price point.

Aecooly Cold Air Ultra

Aecooly Cold Air Ultra Personal Cooling System for $80: Behold, another pricey entry with super-high airflow, impressive battery life, and a jet-engine whine. The key difference with this Aecooly is a little sealed compartment at the bottom you can fill with water. Press a button on the front, and it will dispense a wet spray along with the breeze. This is the second model I've had of this fan—the first one stopped misting after about six months. It should also be noted that the misting function makes a quite loud “unnnnhhhh” sound when it's happening, kind of like a miniature pressure washer. The first time I used it, it alarmed me and the person sitting next to me.

How I Tested

I (or another WIRED reviewer) tested each of these fans in real life. The fans came to weddings, festivals, and tournaments; they went on vacations; and they sat on desks to gauge if the noise level was distracting or livable. I tested all available features and attachments, used a decibel meter and anemometer to measure noise and wind speed, practiced holding a conversation while running them, and transported them in a bag to see if they were awkward or easy to carry.

Why Does Charge Capacity Matter?

Charge capacity is the total amount of electricity—and cooling power—that rechargeable battery-powered fans can store and deploy. Measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), or one-thousandth of an ampere-hour (the ability to provide one amp of power for one hour), the higher a fan's charge capacity number, the longer it can go between charges. How this measure translates to run time heavily depends on speed, fan size, and features used. The measure also varies widely between fans.

How I Obtained the Fans

Some fans were samples I obtained from the fan companies with no promise or guarantee of coverage; other fans I purchased and expensed. After testing, I keep the fans on hand for future testing, noting any malfunctions.

The Chinese Philosopher Americans Can’t Stop Fighting About

Wired August 07, 2026

Yiyang Zhuge learned last week that when you go extremely viral, the people you have been following for years suddenly start following you back. Zhuge logged onto X and found that a string of famous professors and scholars were in her list of new followers. A PhD candidate in political philosophy at Boston College, Zhuge had previously only lurked on X to keep up with the latest debates and gossip in academia. The vast majority of her social media activity happens on the Chinese internet, where she goes by the alias Zhong Shu and hosts a popular podcast with hundreds of thousands of loyal listeners.

Late last month, Zhuge, who is in her late twenties, interviewed Christopher Nolan, one of the most influential directors in Hollywood, who was in Beijing promoting The Odyssey. Rather than asking about celebrities or Hollywood, Zhuge posed a series of deeply philosophical questions to Nolan about the Christianization of Greek philosophy and how to portray heroes in films. The first thing she asked: “Are you a bard for a civilization at dusk?”

Nolan was visibly impressed by Zhuge. After the interview was published in China, Geoff Keighley, a video game journalist and the son of Nolan’s longtime friend David Keighley, shared the interview on X, calling it “a great listen.” Keighley’s video has been watched over 18 million times, and when Zhuge later posted the interview on her own X account, it racked up another 6.9 million views.

For the first time, Zhuge had become the main character of the English-speaking internet. She was being praised, mocked, criticized, and defended all at the same time. Many people said it was the best interview Nolan has done for The Odyssey, while the National Review called it a “CCP hostage video.” But everyone ultimately wanted to know the same thing: Who was this young Chinese woman with a bob haircut talking about the decline of civilizations?

While almost no one in the West knows her name, Zhuge is already one of the most prominent young intellectuals in China and has been interviewed by many of the country’s cultural elite. She was featured in Vogue China as an example of a successful woman in her twenties and frequently shares yoga and fitness tips to her 360,000 fans on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu.

When I spoke to Zhuge this week, she framed her success as being born out of personal tragedy. “I was going through an adulterous divorce in which my ex-husband sued me and I accumulated a lot of legal debt,” she says. “I felt discouraged in the English-speaking academia because of certain personal experiences related to that personal tragedy, so I turned my attention back to the Chinese-speaking world to build a career there and pay off my debt.”

When I started digging into Zhuge’s career, I was shocked by her level of productivity. Aside from publishing philosophy translations and writing articles for Chinese media outlets, she has recorded more than 360 episodes of her podcast Monologues of a Committed Observer in just the last three years. That’s an average of one new episode every three days. Most of the time, she just monologues about political science concepts for a half an hour, seemingly unscripted. On XiaoyuzhouFM, the most popular podcast streaming platform in China, she has over 940,000 subscribers.

But despite her prolific posting, Zhuge claims she isn’t interested in being famous. “I have no attachment to fame and no desire to preserve it for its own sake,” she tells me. “What I want is enough freedom and time to build a life centered on thought. That life requires some money, but not very much.”

When Zhuge asked Nolan if he saw himself as “a bard for a civilization at dusk,” she says she didn’t have a particular civilization in mind.

She views the question instead as part of the long philosophical tradition of pondering the demise of value systems. “I was not primarily attempting to issue a verdict on the contemporary United States,” she says, but “people are free to interpret the phrase through current debates about American or Western decline.”

That’s certainly how many people on Western social media interpreted it. On X, YouTube, and Reddit, commenters lamented about how Western interviewers are seemingly unable to ask the same kind of rigorous questions to their subjects. Some wondered why a Chinese woman was the one to ask philosophical questions about Greece, while others asked if Western institutions are still teaching students humanities and the classics.

To be fair, Zhuge was educated in the Western system. She has been studying in the US since high school, lectured at Boston College and Brandeis University, and translated books by Hannah Arendt and Plutarch (an ancient Greek philosopher) into Chinese. She lives in Boston for most of the year. Her academic work draws on Straussianism, an influential school of conservative political philosophy that has shaped the thinking of people like Peter Thiel. Her fame in China, which earned her the opportunity to talk to Nolan in the first place, is mostly tied to the way she can succinctly explain the American political system, though some critics think her own conservative ideological leanings show up often in her work.

“She was trained in American conservatism, so the questions she asked really resonated with the US’s educated public,” says Chenchen Zhang, an associate professor in international relations at Durham University. When the familiar insecurities of American conservatives came out of the mouth of a Chinese woman, the audience instantly believed “this is how China views the Western civilization,” Zhang says.

The internet’s reaction to Zhuge’s interview reminds me of “Chinamaxxing,” the meme that persisted through the first half of 2026 on platforms like Instagram and TikTok. The trend was promoted mostly by left-leaning, Gen-Z Americans trying to numb their anxiety about America’s decline by deliberately endorsing China and Chinese culture. Now, right-leaning Americans are indulging in the same kinds of worries by fawning over Zhuge’s reverence for the classics. They are really two sides of the same coin.

As the American right rushed to claim Zhuge as one of its own, the far left moved to distance itself from her. On X, @zei_squirrel, a prominent but anonymous progressive account with 346,000 followers, called her either “a deranged fanatical neocon Zionist lunatic” or a Chinese state-media psy-op, pointing to the fact that Zhuge follows several conservative figures.

Zhuge says she’s no stranger to people across the political spectrum being mad at her. “In China, I try very hard to remain above the fray of the mob rather than let public controversy determine what I think or discuss.” she says. “The labels may differ across countries, but the vulgar human impulse to sort people into political camps is universal.”

As for the anonymous account’s claim that she is a Zionist, Zhuge posted one rebuttal on X but says she won’t engage further. “An account that searches through someone’s following list for Jewish names is not conducting any meaningful analysis,” she says, “This mentality is one reason American online public life has become so polarized. People no longer examine arguments; they investigate affiliations.”

Still, this brief moment of virality has clearly shaken her. In her most recent podcast episode published on Thursday, Zhuge talked about how this was the first time she truly felt that she became the subject of public discourse. There’s a not-so-subtle hint of rage in her tone, and the audience seemed to notice it too. One commenter noted that she had forgotten to say her signature farewell message at the end. Instead, she ended the podcast episode by playing Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3, which the composer dedicated to heroes. “I would rather listen to how revolution collided with destiny in the ‘Eroica’ Symphony than a bunch of people in my notifications speculating who was my puppeteer pulling the strings,” she said.

This is an edition of Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis’ Made in China newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

The 7 Best TV Shows to Stream This Month

Wired August 07, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The big screen is having a moment. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is breaking box office records, while Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has people dusting off Homer for the first time since high school. But television is keeping pace with a slate of can’t-miss new releases and beloved old favorites that are worth revisiting.

While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Ted Lasso), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.

From prestige dramas to absurd comedies and one truly groundbreaking sci-fi series, these are the TV shows we think are worth making time for this month.

On September 8, 1966, science fiction changed forever with the premiere of the original Star Trek TV series. In the 60 years since, Gene Roddenberry’s ahead-of-its-time tale of the USS Enterprise crew’s journeys into deep space has spawned dozens of films, TV series, and video games, plus hundreds of books and comics—not to mention a number of real-world tech innovations. The legendary series has also shaped pop culture in countless other ways, giving us everything from Vulcan salutes and Klingons to the Prime Directive and the immortal command to “beam me up.”

Whether you’re a lifelong Trekkie or a curious newcomer, there’s never been a better time to see where one of television’s most influential franchises began. Though it ran for just three seasons, Star Trek: The Original Series left an outsized legacy, breaking barriers with one of television’s first interracial kisses, featuring a remarkably diverse cast at the height of the Civil Rights Movement, and inspiring generations of scientists, engineers, and storytellers to imagine a more optimistic future. Sixty years later, its blend of adventure, social commentary, and boundless curiosity remains as compelling as ever. Best of all, Paramount+ is home to nearly every corner of the Star Trek universe, from the beautifully remastered original series to its many spinoffs and feature films. If you’re celebrating the franchise’s 60th anniversary, there’s no better place to boldly go back to where it all began.

Following a decade-long hiatus, Futurama made a triumphant comeback in 2023, complete with gags about The Twilight Zone and “Momazon” drone deliveries. Created by Matt Groening and David X. Cohen, the animated sci-fi comedy is set in the 31st century and follows the employees of the Planet Express delivery company as they stumble through bizarre adventures, alien encounters, and laugh-out-loud takes on everything from AI to corporate greed.

On August 3, the series kicked off its 14th season, which delivers more of the razor-sharp tech satire and surprisingly thoughtful science that have long made it one of television’s smartest comedies.

This summer is a particularly ripe moment for fans of irreverent animated sci-fi, as it also brings President Curtis, a new spinoff set in the Rick and Morty universe. While Futurama looks ahead at the possibilities—and absurdities—of the distant future, President Curtis takes a stranger route, following President Andre Curtis (voiced by Emmy-winning baritone Keith David) and his eccentric staff as they navigate inter-dimensional diplomacy, paranormal investigations, and other bizarre crises. The 10-episode series, which premiered on July 26, airs new episodes each Sunday night on Adult Swim, which then drop on HBO Max on Monday.

DC is taking its Green Lanterns in a decidedly darker direction with Lanterns, a new series that trades traditional superhero spectacle for a cosmic murder mystery. Starring Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, the series follows the two Lanterns as they investigate a mystery that stretches across Earth and beyond.

With Lost cocreator Damon Lindelof, True Detective producer Chris Mundy, and comic book writer Tom King behind the series, Lanterns—which arrives on August 16—brings a noir-inspired edge to one of DC’s most iconic franchises.

In the early morning hours of November 13, 2022, the city of Moscow, Idaho, changed forever when four University of Idaho students were killed in their off-campus home. The investigation that followed captivated the nation, as authorities worked to piece together what happened and identify a suspect in a horrifying quadruple murder that appeared to have no clear motive.

The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare chronicles the investigation through access to victims’ friends and families and police footage, while examining how digital evidence and forensic technology helped investigators unravel one of the most closely watched true crime cases in recent years.

What if the life you’re living isn’t the one you were meant to have? That’s the question at the heart of Dark Matter, the sci-fi thriller based on Blake Crouch’s best-selling novel. Season one followed physicist Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton), who is pulled into an alternate version of his life after being transported to a parallel reality.

Season two, which premieres on August 28, picks up with Dessen and his family attempting to build a quiet existence in a world that finally feels safe … until new threats force them back into the multiverse with the help of a mysterious device known as the Box. As the search for the Box continues, the series dives deeper into questions of identity, choice, and the endless possibilities of the paths we could have taken.

Four years after its debut, The Undeclared War is back with a chillingly timely premise: a cyberattack targeting a nation’s election system. The British thriller returns to the shadowy world of GCHQ (the UK’s intelligence, security, and cyber agency), where analysts battle digital threats that could have devastating real-world consequences.

Set in a post-pandemic 2024, the series follows a team of analysts racing to defend the country’s digital infrastructure as tensions with Russia escalate. With Shaun of the Dead star Simon Pegg starring as operations chief Danny Patrick, the new season, which arrives on August 27, explores how cyberwarfare has transformed the nature of modern espionage.

Zohran Mamdani’s NYC Tech Team Is What DOGE Should Have Been

Wired August 07, 2026

A go-kart track is an odd location to launch a tech initiative in the nation’s biggest city. Yet last month there was New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, zipping around the 900-foot oval at Coney Island’s Luna Park before stepping up to a podium to unveil a program called Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews. Thus the go-kart theme.

PIT will consist of five “game-changing” teams that, Mamdani promised, will “raise the bar for what New Yorkers can expect from City Hall.” Working closely with city agencies, these small groups of engineers and designers will strive to change the hidebound and confusing tenor of current city services by using state-of-art skills to rapidly whip up specialized apps that solve real problems. “We want to transform how New Yorkers interact with the government,” said the mayor. “We want to raise expectations on what government can deliver, because we really can deliver.”

Do those words sound familiar? If you follow government tech, they might. Because Mamdani’s message could have fit quite comfortably in the pitch that Barack Obama’s chief technology officer, Todd Park, delivered in 2014 while recruiting tech talent for what would become the United States Digital Service. The USDS was an idealistic effort to bring top Silicon Valley talent into the executive branch to bypass the logjams caused by outdated and inefficient IT, by building great, user-centric software.

The agency somehow survived the first Trump administration and kept going through the Biden term. But in 2025, Elon Musk and his DOGE wrecking crew infiltrated the agency and pulled the plug on much of the useful stuff. (Now, with the National Design Service, the Trump administration is ostensibly trying to revive some of what it destroyed.)

Mamdani’s PIT crew initiative adopts much of the original USDS ethos, with a timely twist: It embraces Silicon Valley expertise while taking a skeptical, almost adversarial, stance toward Big Tech itself. The combination of mayoral charisma and a chance to make software that doesn’t serve advertisers, the military, or the pocketbooks of centibillionaires makes the Mamdani team an attractive, high-status, mid-career change of pace for some techies. Suddenly, one of the sexiest places in geekdom is the Brooklyn headquarters of New York City’s Office of Technology and Innovation.

Mamdani’s transition team set the stage for an urban, democratic-socialist-adjacent, USDS-style tech squad when it tapped Lisa Gelobter for the city’s chief technology officer job. Gelobter’s résumé includes stints at big companies and startups, but the standout item was her post at the United States Digital Service, where she was embedded in the Department of Education. She led the effort to create a College Scorecard that focused on nuts-and-bolts criteria like costs and graduation rates. To this day, she gets misty when recalling her Washington experience; she even remembers what she was wearing when the USDS team took a group picture with Obama just before he left office.

“I’m really excited about trying to recapture that essence, that energy here,” she says. Her budget for the program is $5.24 million, with an additional $2 million grant from the Rockefeller Foundation, which will fund one of the crews.

Gelobter says she brings an engineering mindset to New York City government. “I know how to build software,” she says. “I know how to run a technology organization from a technology perspective.” It’s also a cultural thing for her. “I’m wearing jeans to work—not because I don’t look great in a suit, but it’s a statement, right?” she says. (The same norm-breaking happened in the USDS, which had to overcome objections from bureaucrats who didn’t want to meet with anyone wearing a hoodie.) Naturally, the two people Gelobter hired to run the PIT crew program are also USDS veterans, Luke Farrell and Maya Israni.

The projects Gelobter and her team choose to tackle will set a tone for the way the government works under a mayor whose future depends on how well he manages his city. “Without technology, policy is just words written on a piece of paper,” says Gelobter. Seen that way, the PIT crews are essentially Mamdani’s symbolic stand-ins in his fight against self-interested consultants and inefficient contractors. They will make their case by actually building things, in frantic 12-week sprints.

On its face, the first project of the PIT crew seems nonintuitive. The mission is to implement a pet mayoral project: click-to-cancel. On July 10, Mamdani announced this regulation, which penalizes companies that make it difficult to cancel subscriptions or ongoing payments. The rule takes effect on October 1, which is the exact date that the PIT crew plans to launch software that empowers citizens to blow the whistle on services that force people to go through hoops to end the relationship. (Mamdami might be the first customer; on Coney Island he admitted, “I am currently subscribed to something I don’t even know my login for, but they have my credit card information, and I don’t know how to cancel it.”)

The city hasn’t yet announced what the other four PIT crews will work on. My guess is that they will concentrate on more nuts-and-boltsy city services, and at least one will address the housing problem—but it’s telling that this first choice provides a way for ordinary people to stand up to bullying corporations. “It will show that we can directly affect people’s lives. It’s supposed to save, like, $160 million for New Yorkers,” says Gelobter. The project, she confirms, was a “mayoral priority.”

It’s perfect Mamdani branding. Even though much of Hizzoner’s personal tech surge is based on the USDS playbook, the conditions in 2026 are considerably different than they were in 2014. Back then, most people saw Silicon Valley as an enviable font of innovation, gumption, and high standards. The Obama-ites wanted to reflect Silicon Valley’s glory. These days, Big Tech is seen as an oppressive force, especially by progressive politicians and young people. So the choice sends a message that Mamdani’s version of a geek squad can not only make services accessible, but could also check the impulses of oligarchs.

That message seems to be resonating among techies who want to do something other than develop AI that might decimate the labor force. Farrell says that in the first week after the city posted PIT crew job opportunities, over 3,000 people applied for the roughly 35 available slots, and résumés are still pouring in. A shocking number have come from people who currently hold high-salaried jobs in big tech companies. (The city jobs pay considerably less, with no equity.)

“We've heard from a lot of folks recently who are disillusioned with the private tech industry and maybe went into tech because they wanted to apply tech for good,” says Israni. If those people make it to PIT crews, they can indeed apply their skills for good. Or, at the least, for Mamdani.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
